“it’s really happening,” jeredino says. “afters at mister gray’s… we’re going to go e-tarded on his ass. he’s going to legally change his name to ‘mr. grEy’ once we’ve had our way with him…”

V - afters at mister gray’s

VI - 25% homeless

it’s 4 am and it’s time for jeredino and me to take our twenty-two-minute uber back to garfield so i open up the app in the parking lot of the lbj library and check the prices and oh fuck! the ubers are $80 now, fuck that, i say to jeredino, so we walk ten minutes away from the library and check again and the ubers are now a much more reasonable $33 so i request one and wait and wait and wait and i get a sinking feeling as i realize no one wants to pick us up, so we walk another ten minutes to a more urban part of the city and i call another uber and wait for another ten minutes but nothing comes, so i ask jeredino to try on his phone and the penny-pinching bastard hesitates for a bit but eventually he does it, but the app now is trying to charge 90 bucks because now it’s “surge pricing” because they received two requests from different phones on the same corner, wow what a wondrous algorithm, and i’m getting a little nervous because my phone is at 15% battery and jeredino’s is at 20%, so we are just one or two bad moves away from being actually stranded homelessly on the streets of austin so we better pick our next move wisely, and i try to request ubers two more times but no one wants to drive 19 fucking minutes out of downtown austin, satan’s asshole, the worst city in the known universe, so i look at google maps and it’s somehow 110 minutes by public transit back to garfield, even though 90% of the journey is just on two highways, i don’t even know how this is mathematically possible, the non-euclidean nature of austin’s public transit system has eluded greater minds than mine, and i start maybe-screaming on the street i hate this city i hate it and every fuckhead who lives in it and this psyop convention filled with losers and schizos fuck it fuck it! and jeredino looks at me for a moment like i’ve lost my mind, and i think, whoops that wasn’t funny at all, that was unsettling and sort of annoying, so i collect myself and turn to jeredino and say, it’s 4:15 am and my mind isn’t working well, and i’m actually afraid i will stop making decisions that make sense, so we need to check into a hotel tonight, and we’ll get back to garfield in the morning, to which jeredino replies, cool yeah we can go to embassy suites for free basically because my mom has a lot of hilton honors points, to which i say, god bless you mamadino i’ll take it, but also i have a meeting tomorrow at 11 am which is when people normally have to check out of hotels and i need to take this meeting or i’m completely fucked, and jeredino replies, don’t worry my mom is a hilton honors diamond member which means that you can request a noon checkout, and i say, this is fucking lit brother let’s do it, so jeredino then gets on google and finds a nice embassy suites hotel in north austin and double-checks that there are beds available, and i order an uber to it, but to my surprise a waymo comes instead, which is just about the coziest thing in the world at 4:25 am, and in the waymo (which is nice and air conditioned precisely to our liking) jeredino and i have a leisurely chat, and jane texts me on discord, i’m at the dennys wya, and i’m like yippee! jane is at denny’s let’s videochat her, so i call her on discord and see her beautiful face and i go, jane you goof jeredino and i already left the denny’s and we’re going to a hotel in north austin pull up let’s party afters in embassy suites, and to my horror she rotates the camera and she’s sitting in a booth with avi and cook and preet, and i can’t believe that these goofuses have been sitting at that denny’s for over two and a half hours, but anyways jeredino cuts in to do a hail mary and goes, hey jaaaaane could you drive us to our friend’s place in garfield?, and jane says, i just want to respect that i’m very tired and need to drive thirty minutes west of austin to go home and you guys want to go thirty minutes east of austin so you’re just asking me to drive an extra hour, and then i say to jane, haha jane we were just kidding don’t worry we’re going to a hotel, and avi overhears this and says, hey guys i got two extra beds in my motel room you two can stay the night, and i think FUCK NO am i ever going to spend the night with this clown, satan will not trick me again, so i lie and say, no it’s okay avi we already booked our room, and hang up and jeredino is scream-laughing, and when we get out at the embassy suites we are greeted by a nice nigerian hotel manager and jeredino strolls up and says one unit with two beds please, and the manager says sorry gentlemen we’re all booked up since it is holiday, labor day, and jeredino says, no no we saw that there are vacancies online, and to our horror we realize the mistake we made is that pretty much no one on earth is up at 4:40 am trying to book a room for that same night, so google showed us vacancies for the day after, so i feel like crying right there in the lobby, but the kindly manager lets us stay for a bit to charge our phones at this bizarre faux-granite lobby table, and i say to jeredino, please you have to get the next one right and you have to do it alone, i cannot think anymore, and so he looks on his phone and sees that there is an americas best value inn nearby with vacancies and it’s super close as the crow flies, but it’s a fifteen-minute walk through and around a highway, because of course it is, it’s austin, the anus mundi, so i say to jeredino that sounds great but please call them up and confirm with your own voice that they actually have a bed, so he does and they do, and we get up and walk in darkness to the americas best value inn and in the distance a bottle breaks, and a shirtless black guy rides his bike right up next to us for a couple seconds before pedaling off, and i think i am currently about 25% homeless and i know that if we fail one more time there’s a fair chance i will actually crash out, smoke some fent, and become 100% homeless for real, and at 5:01 am we arrive at the motel, which is so beautiful, an antiseptic white, and it’s run by a patel, a patel with a motel, who greets us and jeredino says, hello i just talked to you about a room, and he says yes welcome you can book a room but i have to say if you book right now you will have to be out of your room by 11 am and you will only get six hours of sleep, but if you wait until 5:30 am to book the cycle will roll over and you will get in effect a whole day for free, and i say that sounds fucking awesome i can take my meeting in peace here then and after that we can fuck off and go back to sleep, and so jeredino says yeah that sounds great, so we sit in the lobby for twenty-nine minutes looking at X and at some lobby magazines, fantasizing about sleeping, and at long last 5:30 am arrives, and mr. patel with a big smile on his face gives us the keys to the room, and we jog merrily in and slip into our beds and snooze our woes away, and i have the sweetest sleep i’ve ever had, and when i wake up i shower and take my meeting, and then noah and jacqueline pick us up and we get a devilish breakfast of eggs and chocolate chip waffles at waffle house and then we all head back to garfield, back to home, far away from mary the psycho who wants to stab me, and from preet and avi and mr. gray and discourse vanguard and hbd jesus and the two row wampum treaty and all the other people and concepts i never want to encounter again, but also away from jane, who i still want to take to johnson city, texas, but i know that will never happen now, and i’m worried again about my mom who is suffering and feeling alone, and i’m worried about myself who is suffering and feeling alone, and fear for the future and the end of the human race, and in this mood i come home and see that jacqueline last night, perhaps due to being disappointed by her night at the velvet industrial, rearranged the magnetic letters on the refrigerator to read “fuck E” and this frankly really hurts my feelings.

VII - everybody wants a piece of you

the johnson city dream is dead. jacqueline refuses to go, and there’s no way i’m risking leaving the safe orbit of noah and his car. jeredino, also a bit shell-shocked from last night, goes “maybe we just stay in and bookgoon…”

nevertheless, we manage to muster up the courage for one last outing: the four of us go to the cidercade, an unlimited-play arcade chain that sells fifty different flavors of cider. i ask jeredino if i can invite jane, and he says, “yeah, of course she can come, but—and i cannot emphasize this enough—she must come alone…” i send jane the addy and instantly she replies, “okay wait lowk this looks lit.”

on the road to austin, jane sends me the usual:

the signs are clear.

before jane arrives, i stand around and gawp as jeredino has his way with the pump it up cab. he’s a serious rhythm gamer—a top-800 pumper on the global leaderboard. jeredino insists that his obsession with pump it up has ruined his penis. (“it over-strengthens the pelvic floor. all that jostling is bad for… down there. but it’s worth it, really… if i play pump, i stop getting hard, and consequently stop being attracted to women; however, once i get off the pump, i just become a fat fucking chud, and then it doesn’t even matter how horny i am…”) i have not met a single person outside of jeredino who buys his penis-pump theory, but it does make the experience of watching him play pump far more gratifying to me, for i know that, at any rate, he believes that he’s actively atomizing his own manhood. that’s kino.

by the time jane arrives (“what the fuck is up—where the cider at? tcg girls in control. and the ‘c’ stands for cider!”), jacqueline is annoyed and bored and wants to go home. i watch jane pump it up with jeredino, and then we yap for about ten minutes.

“so how was last night with maye? did you spend the night with her or something?” i ask jane.

“nooooo, no. it was one of those crazy dynamics: maye, mr. gray, and me,” jane says.

“what do you mean?”

“you know when, like, two parents are scolding a child? that’s what it was like. mr. gray and i the parents, and maye our child,” jane says.

mr. gray gave maye a one-hour talking-to after we all left. as it turns out, mr. gray and maye aren’t even sleeping together. they used to date briefly but it didn’t work out, and now mr. gray is just letting maye live on his couch until she gets her life together. he does it simply because he “believes in her.” she just has a tendency to fuck his life up, and to self-sabotage in ways big and small.

“basically,” jane continues, “mr. gray’s like, ‘maye, it’s time for you to grow up,’ and i’m like ‘fuckkkk that’s so true, she does need to grow up.’ but that means that i need to grow up, too. i need to grow up so i can help maye grow up. i can’t just be going to her place every weekend and, like, bumping fucking coke with her. that’s not going to help her grow up at all…”

and right in the middle of this supremely important and revelatory conversation, jacqueline announces that it’s time to go: she’s going to leave us behind if we don’t follow her promptly. i tell jane, “we need to go. sorry about johnson city by the way. next time.”

“oh, sad,” jane says with a pout.

“thanks for inviting me to your event,” i say hornily. i give her the tightest hug i can within the bounds of politeness, and then run off to follow jacqueline who has already started the car.

on the way back to garfield, i once again think that god must be laughing at me. i decide to send jane a text.

vishal: he wanna hang with a tranny…

jane: nooooo i wanted to hang out too

on my flight back to los angeles, i mull over all the goofuses i’ve just met and speculate on what their lives reveal about the strange logic of the clout economy. my whole weekend was about hunting down statusful people and inspecting them up close, but once i came sufficiently near i invariably found that each and every one was a fool or a fuck-up. status is always somewhere else.

jane, vanguard, maye, mr. gray… people line up to take from them. everybody wants a piece of jane because of her incomparable beauty—but she’s an innocent with a fragmentary mind, and thus cannot make gainful use of all the inbound attention. everybody wants a piece of vanguard because he throws cash at them—but no one in the end bothered to come to his big event. everybody wants a piece of maye because she has 100,000 twitter followers—but she’s just living on someone else’s couch. everybody wants a piece of mr. gray because he’s the king—but king of what, exactly?

everybody wants a piece of you, but you’re a fucking loser.

essays.title: Be More Ambitious
essays.html:
Life

I am one of the laziest people I know. I don’t really want much in life. I would be so much happier just rotting on the couch and watching TV all day. Okay, I am joking about that (I think). I am lazy, and I don’t really wake up wanting anything, but looking back I have almost always been up to some shenanigans. Again, not because I want anything in particular or because I want to execute and achieve my grand vision, but because doing something is better than doing nothing. A lot of my projects are like “Wouldn’t that be cool?” “Wait, is that even possible?” “Why not?”

Maybe being more ambitious means breaking the cyclic nature of life and stepping out of your comfort zone. Trying something new. Trying something different. Trying something you were always scared of doing because you didn’t want to fail at something. What you define as ambition is completely up to you. You don’t have to shoot for the moon; you just need to do something that you didn’t before, or didn’t think was possible before. I remember this advice in chess: when a piece is moved, you should look at the lines that were not possible before. Perhaps, this applies to life too.

I used to have a whole backlog of silly ideas that I couldn’t even attempt before. Now, I can spin up an agent on my computer from my phone by asking Siri to text this iMessage agent completely hands-free while driving, and have initial results ready before I even reach my destination. How cool and cyberpunk is that? Just like Jevons’ paradox though, I didn’t end up completing my entire backlog. I ended up adding even more crazy projects to it that I couldn’t just one-shot prompt my way out of. I ended up intensifying the kind of problems I tackled. If you are able to do everything, and aren’t failing, it means you are not pushing yourself enough and haven’t found your limits yet. When was the last time you actually failed at something? Pick something you’re sure you can’t do, and try it.

If you don’t keep on trying new things, it becomes harder to try new things. The inertia of the comfort zone is enough to lock you in. If I go to a new restaurant, I will keep trying new things until I find something I like. And, once I like something, I will almost always get the same thing. So, the only way for me to try new things then becomes changing the restaurant. Thankfully, I am okay with trying new places. Otherwise, I would never be able to find new things!

If you want to be really pedantic about this, there is the Gittins index,Introduced by John C. Gittins in 1979, the Gittins index gives the optimal strategy for the multi-armed bandit explore-versus-exploit problem: it assigns each option a dynamic score combining its expected reward with an uncertainty bonus for how little you have tried it, so you keep exploring unfamiliar dishes until every untried option’s score drops below your favourite. which tells you the absolute decision theory maths way of doing this.

Now, instead of trying to rely on your willpower to try something new, you need to put yourself somewhere where your default option isn’t on the menu.

We can try to rationalise that the fear of failure is kind of silly using some crude logic. If you are not familiar with Pascal’s wager, it basically says that it is better to believe God exists than it is to not:

God exists God doesn’t exist
You believe Infinite gain (heaven) Finite loss (not much lost)
You don’t believe Infinite loss (hell) Finite gain (nothing changes)

Pascal’s wager is famously a bit of a cheat, but it is a useful cheat. So, applying the same logic to trying new things:

It works out It doesn’t work out
You try You get the thing You learn what didn’t work / you find your limits
You don’t try Impossible Guaranteed loss + atrophy (next time gets harder)

Which means, not trying something new when you aren’t going to lose something if you fail is irrational! Yes, I filled the table to get the answer I wanted here, but if you are going to rationalise something, rationalise towards trying.

Nobody wants to admit that they are picking the bottom row, hence why you might be thinking, “If only I had X, then I’d be able to do Y.” But, have you actually pushed what you already have to its limits? Have you actually reached the failure set yet? Or are you trying to push off things because it is easier to not try?

Anytime you catch yourself waiting on X before starting Y, attempt Y without X until you actually hit the failure set and can definitely prove that X is what broke it.

If the frontier labs are to be believed, “programming is solved.” Even if that is true, it doesn’t mean every problem under the sun has been solved. It means that if you pose the problem, you can get a solution. Ambition used to be constrained by what you could do. Nowadays it is constrained by what you can think to attempt.

Personally, I don’t think we can brute-force every possible question-answer pair in the universe just yet, at least not until we understand the limits of our “search space.” So, what matters? What matters is asking questions you want answered. Your wants and needs in life made you ask that question. Just because you don’t want to achieve a grand plan doesn’t mean your petty annoyances cannot help you form a worthwhile question.

You should also ask yourself, “What is it that you are providing that is not being covered by the model’s weights already?” If 10 different people prompt “innovative ideas in cybersecurity”, there is a good chance that they are going to get the same or similar ideas. Try asking LLMs to tell you a joke. How many of them are going to eventually say the joke, “Why don’t scientists trust atoms? They make up everything”?

You should ask yourself whether ten strangers without your weird life/hobbies could have asked the same question. If yes, you are going to get the atom joke. You should be pulling from your own uber-specific annoyances and curiosities instead.

Life is full of contradictions, though! What if your question-answer pair was too simple in hindsight? Like anyone could have asked for it and gotten to it. Well, my dear reader, this is a question as old as modern art (if not older). “It is just a shade of blue; I could have done that.” I was recently at the Guggenheim, and although the day was very memorable for a very different reason, one of the art pieces, as you might be aware, was the famous banana. I am not saying I like modern art, but I kind of agree with the age-old adage:

“Anyone could do that.” “Yes, but they didn’t.”

Simply, ask for things that you are curious about.

Frank Calegari had a couple of really cool quotes on his guest post on Terence Tao’s blog:

Choosing worthwhile problems may end up mattering more than producing proofs.

The difference in reaction between the optimists and the pessimists is that, for the pessimists, the game is over. For the optimists, the game has just changed.

I am in the camp of hope-core. I would rather foolishly be optimistic about everything than be realistic. The fact that you are reading this piece probably means you have enough curiosity and/or will to live that you want to try and change things. You don’t have to radically change anything in your life to take the smallest step towards being more ambitious. Because isn’t it already being more ambitious by trying to do something new while still maintaining the status quo? You don’t have to quit your job or blow up 99% of your comfortable life: keep the status quo intact and bolt one weird experiment on the remaining per cent.

You don’t need to want more out of the life you already have. You just need to be curious enough to not let that stop you from finding out what else is possible. So, (if and only if you want <or not>) why don’t you turn those knobs up to eleven, and be more ambitious?
essays.excerpt: Ambition for people who don’t really want much

essays.title: You Can See Everything: Notes
essays.html:
Essay #1 for Just Write!

I went to see You Can See Everything last night with some blogger friends.

Disclaimer: I have not read much about Theranos. My only context on it is this movie-documentary. Hence I’ve classified this blogpost “Speculative; might contain errors”. I’m posting this primarily because I think it’s good to put up a beacon so likemindeds can find each other, and because I’d like to participate in Just Write :). LLMs will reduce search costs. I would stop reading here unless you have a scholarly / particular interest in Theranos, You Can See Everything, and 22yo Silicon Valley women’s reactions to it.

Contents:

#1: Concerned about the prison system

#2: Bikeshedding — the wrong questions asked

#3: How sympathetic are we to the investors?

#1: Concerned about the Prison System

I remember reading once that prison has four social functions — rehabilitation, retribution, incapacitation, and deterrent.

I saw Liz Holmes say “Oh, there’s milk in the fridge for Ivy” and ~saw red. I think it’s really bad to separate a breastfeeding mother from her baby. I think, insofar as Holmes needed to go into a high-security facility like that (and we can discuss this), ideally the baby should have been allowed to live with her.

Rehabilitation — there are clearly better ways. Retribution — this is barbaric. Incapacitation — there are presumably better ways. Deterrent — I’m not sure deterring people from embarking on ambitious public ventures is ideal.

And the life in prison, and it being deliberately unpleasant. The two-minute phone calls. The children at the center of all this. I’m fairly sure children suffer and are worse off when they have a parent in prison, particularly a parent who is capable of providing consistent love and affection.

Besides, I wouldn’t do this, but I wouldn’t be surprised if some viewers called Child Protective Services after viewing Billy’s erratic behavior on-screen. I’m unconvinced he’s a positive primary caregiver for their children.

I have a ‘hot take’ that an instinctual/reactive aversion to surveillance subjects us to greater horrors.1 I think it’s possible to incapacitate Holmes without sending her to prison. You can surveil her; you can forbid her from engaging in most business/employment; you can limit her movement; you can subject every visitor / new location to an approval process (& give her only limited requests, to reduce paperwork) — you can place her under sophisticated house arrest. Presumably her parents/family can fund much of this — I know, I know there are concerns about equality (and being ‘equal before the eyes of the law’), but ultimately this leaves more funds for inmates who do ‘choose’ ‘prison’ over a such arrangement.

I was also struck by the justice system’s facelessness. Who actually wants her in there? From a preference utilitarian perspective, who is waking up and having their preferences fulfilled by her being jailed, (over merely incapacitated / rehabilitated through more humane means)? & can their ~spiteful preference outweigh other preferences?

I can sense potential social opprobrium as I express skepticism that it’s good to jail non-violent criminals. I feel nervous about it; I know there might be backlash. I feel the way my words probably warp social perception, as well — if I write “white-collar criminals”, it looks like I’m excusing ‘Silicon-Valley-sympathetic’ SBF/LH-likes; if I extend this more broadly to “non-violent criminals”, it starts to pattern-match more to an overall ~leftist-adj critique of the prison system and the financial waste and the suffering involved.

The justice system & prison feels barbaric, inhumane, backwards. This was my first and main takeaway. I will do my best to put it out of my mind, and do my best not to commit any crime. I don’t have capacity to work on criminal justice reform.

From 2013 to 2021, Open Philanthropy donated $200M to criminal justice reform. I’m glad someone did. I feel blessed that I can even get away without thinking about prison too much, when the children / families of incarcerated parents can’t.

#2: Bikeshedding — the wrong questions asked

Nathan Fielder mentions in an early scene:

A part of me maybe is a little insecure that you look at me as someone who is uneducated on science and scientific things so I can’t question you in a way that another person who is would.

He’s right to be insecure. It makes the movie worse.

I’m also confused why he regards himself as both ‘non-technical’ and incapable of educating himself — though I admit 2023 was pre-modern-LLM. LH had only <2 years of college education.

The questions I’m most interested in are:

  • Was LH trying her hardest to deliver a fully-functional machine?

    • Were such ambitions realistic, or was she being grossly reckless / irresponsible / negligent / blinkered in pursuing them?

  • Given more time, would the Theranos team have succeeded?

The team was disbanded in 2018. Now, in 2026, we still don’t have the technology they promised. Were they the team best-equipped to deliver it? Could they have delivered it by now, had they forged on?

This is what really matters to me. Because we still have children and adults getting diagnosed too late, suffering and hurting and dying prematurely, due to the cost and complication of running diagnostic panels.

#3: How sympathetic are we to the investors?

I was not super sympathetic to the investors. I felt it was their responsibility to perform full due diligence.

Margot pointed out that not being able to take somebody’s word on faith / on its face raises transaction costs. Right now, it’s fairly easy for investors to send money to ambitious new deeptech ventures, because they can trust founders are speaking true, with the force of the law to back it up.

To be honest, I found myself surprised that this is the current status quo. I had always presumed, if I were considering investing in some founder, that it’s my responsibility to do due diligence and satisfy myself that their technology works and they are speaking true / of good character. I also wouldn’t really want to prosecute someone younger than me — I don’t know why I’m old-fashioned(?) like this, but I really just believe older people have responsibilities to me and I have responsibilities to younger people.

Margot pointed out that LH’s deceit could’ve led to misallocation of funds — investors funded in Theranos when they wouldn’t’ve, had they known the real state of the technology. This meant other, honest biotech companies went without funding. And now biotech companies have a bad name — investors have been ‘burnt’, and will be slower to invest in future.

We’d need to measure effect size to be sure. But Margot’s comments are the most compelling I’ve found as to why the Theranos’ team’s conduct was such a big deal as we’re treating it. Of course, Nathan didn’t get into ramifications on other biotech companies / the biotech industry at all. 😒

My intuition is that it’s my fellow citizens’ liberty to choose how candid to be, and it’s my liberty to choose whether to enter business with them.

I’m shocked that my fellow citizens can be prosecuted for lying to me. In my mind, I’d just be the fool for not having checked the tech worked in full & run background checks/references, and that’s roughly the end of the story.

On Bullshit (Frankfurt, 1988)

essays.title: San Francisco plans expansion of No-Turn-On-Red program

author.name: Barak Gila
author.bio:
growth @votewithsway | yimby, urbanist, techie, aspiring journalist, chef, film/art fan. blogger http://barak.substack.com @berkeley_eecs 🇺🇸🌉
substack bio: Barak writes about urbanism, life in San Francisco, local politics, and whatever else comes to his mind. He also publishes voter guides that dozens of people use to vote!

essays.html:
San Francisco’s transit agency has posted a notice of an upcoming hearing, online at 10a on 11/13, for an expansion of the city’s No-Turn-on-Red (NTOR) program into the Marina, Van Ness/Franklin/Gough, and the upper Mission.

Per agency policy, additional details will be posted tomorrow, 10 days before the hearing. The poster promises a decision within a week of the hearing, 11/20. Public comment is accepted at the online meeting or via email. The posting recommends “visiting the site below” for further details, but their given link redirects elsewhere and I was unable to find any additional details online.

As context, a 2021 pilot program implementing No-Turn-On-Red (NTOR) in the Tenderloin showed substantial compliance. In 2023, safety advocate Luke Bornheimer advocated for citywide NTOR, starting a petition which reached 9,000 signatures. The following month, Dean Preston authored Resolution 481-23 to support citywide NTOR and it passed the Board of Supervisors (SF’s city council, called that because we’re a combined city-county) unanimously 11-0 on 10/3/23. Mayor Breed did not sign the resolution.

Mayor Breed instead directed SFMTA to propose a more limited change. They approved a downtown expansion of 200 signals in March 2024. That program appears to have cost $2.2M, $2M of which was federally funded, a cost of around $10,000 per intersection.

In August 2024, SFMTA staff proposed NTOR at ~2/3 of San Francisco’s 1,300 signals, those with “high pedestrian activity.” That proposal appears to have been abandoned.

Instead, they applied for and received in February 2025 a $4M federal grant, again 90% of the project cost, to add NTOR signage in a few neighborhoods. The current Phase 3 proposal appears to be a somewhat more limited version of that 2024 report.

In June 2026, SFMTA updated the project timeline for Phase 2, extending it from Aug 2025 to Sep 2027. They also released a progress map. There’s still no timeline for Phase 3 — the expansion to be discussed at next week’s meeting.

essays.title: Math and Me

author.name: Manuel del Río
author.bio:
文士. Also, biological machine learning ('teacher'). Curious and passionate about math, truth, literature(s), art, physics, history, languages, people.
I'll be writing on any of the above topics. I think the first essay will be about Mathematical Platonism.

essays.html:
There is sand on the shore, but the sea will not yield.

There are blots on the paper, and its blood is ink.

There are symbols in the book, but their meaning is null.

There is sand in the chips, and it shows us its work.

There is sea on the shore, but the sand will not yield.

Picture a child, playing on the beach.

He’s six years old. Not in the water – he can’t swim, in fact, and won’t learn until three years hence. For that matter, he’ll never learn how to ride a bike, or much enjoy participating in group sports and activities. He isn’t with friends, either. His labour seems devoted to building a sandcastle, but with one specific, utopian hope in mind: that if he works hard enough, he’ll be able to make one capable of stopping the rising tide and remaining an island of sandy walls against the sea.

You might guess he is of the introspective type: the type who prefers spending his free time devouring books, absorbed in deep reading. You would be right.

Fast forward nine years.

Picture a teen, turning a sheet into a map of the past.

The child is now a teenager. While he has changed in many ways, in others, he remains mostly the same. He once had a deep religious faith, which he’s just lost, and is unconsciously making space for the Next Big Thing that will colonize his brain. As no one else in his family is the book-loving type, he has had to pull himself up by his own bootstraps intellectually, developing his interests in a haphazard way. These have converged to make him a history nerd who now spends the summers not on the beach, but in the local library. One of the things he does there, besides reading, is carefully drawing up a timeline of the Islamic presence in Spain on a large sheet of poster board.

He does quite well at school, but is thoroughly uninterested in some subjects. Grammar is one of them. Math is another. If he makes the effort, he can get good grades in math, but he sees no purpose in it and feels no curiosity about it. He appreciates that it is instrumental in, say, pursuing a career in science, but at that time, useful was one of the dirtiest possible words in his lexicon, as a result of having absorbed the classical Greek disdain for manual labour and the elevation of intellectual pursuits above practical ones. For him, useful rhymes with dull, boring, rote, and physically and/or intellectually painful, and he puts it in the same bucket as the family enterprises he has to help out with in his free time (a small funeral business and a furniture shop), which he is determined to escape through a university education.

Fast forward fourteen years.

Picture a man, poring over a book that he can’t understand.

The teen is now a young man. He succeeded in going to university, the first in his family to do so, and somewhat abusing his parents’ indulgence and financial help, has collected a bunch of Humanities degrees. In his defence, it has to be said that degrees in Spain cost more in time and opportunity than in money.

While he has enjoyed his studies considerably, he’s starting to worry about his job prospects and has acquired enough common sense to know that heeding his mentor’s siren call to give a career in academia a shot would be too risky a gamble. Besides, he’s starting to experience a certain frustration with the academic subjects he has engaged in: while he’s comfortable writing long articles when required and has a blueprint for his doctoral dissertation, he’s starting to feel that both academic history and literary criticism are rhetorical exercises rather than truth-seeking ones. In both there doesn’t seem to be a real mechanism for adjudicating what counts as true or correct. One can start with whatever premises suit one’s fancy and bend all the evidence (to the extent it exists) towards them. While this is easy and satisfying when you do it in support of your beliefs, you also have to watch those holding the exact opposite beliefs do the same thing, with the same apparent validity. Even worse: many in the field (the young man included) have a tendency to treat academic work and study as a sort of surrogate (and rather ineffective) politics.

On the math side, while our young man is glad to have left the sciences behind and frowns when he has to endure economic metrics creeping into some subjects, he does feel that a well-rounded education must include more than basic mathematical literacy, and he tries, unsuccessfully, to acquire it. Back in the late nineties and early noughties, during his university years, online learning resources were still very rudimentary, so he tried two books that fell into his hands: Mathematics, Its Contents, Methods, and Meaning, edited by Aleksandrov, Kolmogorov and Lavrentiev, was the first one, and it was a complete disaster: it was far too advanced for his abilities, and all he retained from it was a very nice picture of different numerical systems in different cultures. He made more progress with a cheap book on Basic Modern Mathematics and Geometry, but while he managed to recover much of what he had already learned at school, the book offered little in the way of effective guidance and scaffolding, and he was too rusty in mathematics to make much headway. He kept getting stuck along the way and never even reached the calculus section. The Book of Nature may be written in mathematical language, but it’s not that easy of a book to read.

Fast forward six years.

Picture a teacher teaching himself.

To his non-trivial surprise, the man has become a teacher of English for adults, and actually enjoys his job. That was an interesting lesson for him to learn: there are more things, Horatio, that you might a priori consider dull and uninteresting but that, once you’re in the thick of them, can become intellectually satisfying. While preparing a lesson plan about education, online learning and new technologies, he discovers something called Khan Academy, which is meant to help students learn their subjects better. He toys with it for a bit, and soon becomes hooked. In the next few months, he’ll achieve what the books couldn’t help him achieve, i.e., cover all the basics of a pre-university math education, including calculus. Here are his words from the time, scribbled in a blog and now translated into English:

“This is something I’ve been discussing with my students; and in my own case, besides the usual promise to lose a little weight this year, I’ve set myself a somewhat more innovative goal, one that I’ve actually been quietly working towards for several months now: to refresh my knowledge of mathematics and physics, becoming able once again to perform the calculations I used to do in high school, and perhaps even go a little further.

I now have the interest, the freedom from pressure, and the maturity that I lacked back then. And since I have what some of my colleagues regard as an exaggerated respect and reverence for the ‘hard’ sciences, it’s only fitting that I should become better acquainted with them. Deep down, I’m also taking to heart C. P. Snow’s admonitions, which I’ve read recently.”

The teacher is somewhat proud of himself, and with this positive reinforcement, starts thinking that he might be able to go somewhat further. In the meantime, some of his old preconceptions have been eroded by further reading and the passage of time. He no longer holds the same rather closed-minded beliefs about who he really is and what the set of things he likes has to be, so he’s becoming open to some refashioning of his sense of self, not with a bang, but with a whimper. Or in the mathematical language he’s started to use and assimilate, discovering that he’s a continuous, but not constant, function of time. Over the following year or so, he’ll read a lot of popular math books, some textbooks, and even try out some undergraduate mathematics courses at a couple of online universities.

Fast forward ten years.

Picture me, playing on a beach. But the beach is different, and so is the sea.

I feel like I can move to the first person now, as I’m pretty sure that, while writing these words, I am me in a way in which my past selves, the ghosts of my departed quantities, aren’t. I started studying math as a side project, as part of an effort to round out my education and, perhaps, as an indirect intelligence test of sorts, pushing my limits to see what I could achieve. In the latter respect, I’d say it has failed somewhat: math is a harsh mistress, I am likely dumber than I imagined, and I progress at a snail’s pace during the few and insufficient hours I can allot to it between work, duties, and lighter learning and entertainment.

But I’ve come to love it in a way that would flabbergast most of my previous selves. I started with the picture of my younger self stubbornly building sandcastles against the sea. In a way, math serves the same function today: with all its limitations, carefully mapped out by Gödel and others, math gives us Truth and Certainty and Beauty to the degree that any human discipline can. And I find it a noble enough purpose to devote a lot of my future time to sifting the sand, strengthening the walls, and striving to maintain this little bulwark against the Sea of Entropy, Ignorance and Uncertainty that will one day engulf us all. But that day is not today. And, being somewhat naively optimistic, perhaps it never will.

essays.title: Why today’s physics PhD students are so lucky to have Claude Code
essays.html:
I wish Claude Code had been available when I was a PhD student.

Today Claude Code found and fixed a bug in code I wrote during my PhD in thirty minutes. During the tail end of my PhD I had searched in vain to find that bug for over three months (more on that below).

A large portion of my PhD research was spent sitting in front of a computer for 8-10 hours a day writing code, usually in Fortran.

Today that same code could be written at least 10 times faster by AI and with better style and documentation.

If I had Claude Code when I was a PhD student I guesstimate that I would have been two or even three times as productive, all else being equal.

The initial goal of my PhD research was to achieve greater understanding of liquid water and why it has such a high dielectric constant. We were also interested in what happens at the molecular level when water absorbs microwaves and infrared radiation. Water has been studied for hundreds of years and its properties are well known. However, there have been open questions about how some of those properties arise, owing to the complexity of hydrogen bonding. For instance there has been debate about whether there are low density and high density clusters of water molecules in liquid water.

Writing code to simulate water and analyze the simulations was a means towards achieving greater understanding of the physics of water.

Many computer scientists I have met have a deep intellectual interest in programming language design, software engineering best practices, and the optimization of algorithms. Those topics never interested me much, nor were they within the core intellectual interests of many of the physicists around me.

We didn’t obsess about optimizing our algorithms except in some cases where it was necessary. We coded things in whatever language would get us what we wanted the easiest. In some cases that was Matlab, in other cases Mathematica. In many cases it was Fortran, a language which computer scientists hate but is sometimes faster than C++ and is much easier to learn. (I wrote about why physicists use Fortran in 2015).

We coded things in a procedural manner since it made the code very easy to write and understand. We didn’t spend time thinking much about “best practices” for writing code and making it maintainable. We just wrote code in whatever way made sense to us at the time to get the desired functionality as easily as possible.

Later during my PhD I researched new ways to simulate nuclear quantum effects in a more computationally efficient manner. One of the things that interested me and others was why light causes water molecules to split into hydrogen and oxygen at the surface of catalysts like platinum (photocatalytic water splitting). We were excited about discovering new ways that hydrogen could be produced from sunlight.

Other researchers I worked with were using quantum simulations to understand how lithium ions are stored in materials, or to understand why D2O ice has slightly different properties than H2O ice.

In short, we were primarily intellectually interested in the physics, not the computer science. We were physicists after all!

Of course, this lack of interest in CS best practices among myself and other physicists had a big downside. It was very hard for physicists to build off each other’s code because it wasn’t written with understandability, maintainability, and extensibility in mind.

The fields of quantum simulation and computational materials science were plagued by lack of data standards. The situation is better today with the rise of Python and owing to the work of data standard initiatives, but much of the same situation exists.

Physics PhD students write the minimal code necessary to solve their problem and are not well-incentivized to do much more. Claude Code on the other hand writes code that follows style guidelines perfectly and is well documented.

In 2015 I developed a new method for incorporating nuclear quantum effects into the simulation of water. Unfortunately, in August that year the simulations started to yield an unexpected peak in the calculated absorption spectra of liquid water.

I spent three months trying to figure out the origin of that peak. I had originally planned to graduate in December 2015, but my advisor wanted me to fix the issue with the peak before I graduated. My PhD defense had to be put on hold (which I was mostly OK with since I didn’t have a job lined up anyway).

My advisor and I were both convinced there was a bug in the code.

I remember going home for Christmas that year and being very stressed out and irritable the entire time because I couldn’t solve the issue. I was really in over my head. Instead of enjoying Christmas with my family I was SSHing into a compute cluster from my laptop, running simulations to try to nail down the precise circumstances in which the issue occurred.

In the end, I never figured out where that extra peak came from. My advisor allowed me to finish my PhD but she didn’t want to publish a paper I had written that contained spectra with the spurious peak.

It was not until after I had left graduate school that I convinced my advisor to allow me to publish the paper. Part of what convinced her is that I had noticed a similar artifact in other published work. Additionally, at the location where the peak exists there’s supposed to be a small peak anyway (for the OH-stretch/bend combination mode) and that gave us a bit of cover in case anyone asked about it.

Out of curiosity, I recently gave the above spectra figure and the old codebase from my PhD to Claude Fable 5.1 and asked it to investigate the issue.

A half hour later, Claude had thoroughly analyzed the code, found the bug, fixed the bug, and had run a short simulation to prove it was fixed.1 As a side note, the code runs absurdly fast on my modern desktop compared to my desktop eleven years ago.

I read Claude’s full explanation of the bug. It’s been almost eleven years now since I worked on that codebase, but Claude’s explanation rings true. The issue has to do with how boundary conditions are handled, which I remember I had some trouble with. I think it was also due to me having a poor understanding of the SIESTA codebase. It is hard for humans to understand complex codebases others have written, but trivial for today’s AI.

I had Claude Fable update the code on Github even though nobody is using it and the code was obsoleted by a better codebase a year or two after it was published.

If the paper were highly cited I would ask the journal to publish an erratum, but this is my least cited physics work, having only one citation. Besides, the method we describe is sound, it just had a bug in implementation. I highly doubt anyone cares where the extra peak comes from.

During my PhD I spent countless hours trying to get other codes to compile and installing all the libraries they needed. In our lab we used to joke that half our PhD was spent getting codes to compile. This was all before Docker became popular (although Docker has its own headaches).

It was drudge work that consisted of copying compiler errors into Google and randomly trying different solutions people had posted online until the code compiled. We had no idea what we were doing, we were just copypasting stuff from online until the compile finished. Today Claude Code can install and compile codes easily.

The first four months of my time as a Staff Scientist at NIH were spent porting a very complex and highly disorganized C++ code from Windows into Linux. I don’t know how long that work would take with Claude Code, but probably less than a few days, and possibly only a few hours with Claude Code ultracode turned on.

As a PhD student I also spent many hours creating figures in Mathematica and with a program called Grace. I would spend hours carefully tweaking how the figures appeared, since I was very particular about the aesthetics of graphs and I thought having nice graphs would lead to my work being read and cited more. I enjoyed that work, but neither Mathematica or Grace made it particularly easy. It was extremely time consuming.

Nowadays creating figures is absurdly easy with Claude Code. However, the default AI aesthetics is not great, so human aesthetic discernment is still important.

Theoretical physicists have to chart paths through complex mathematical territories. Sometimes these are territories that are completely new (string theory for instance led to many new mathematical vistas). Other theoretical physicists find themselves working at the intersections of mathematical fields where there are few human experts.

The way physicists approach math is very different than the way mathematicians do. As with code, physicists often look at math methods as tools.

If you look at a random theoretical physics paper from arXiv you’ll very rarely see it containing definitions, lemmas, and theorems (although occasionally they might). The way physicists do math is much looser. The way physicists write about math is different — it’s more of a narrative format.

Theoretical physicists often end up using techniques that give the right answer even though they haven’t come up with a rigorous proof that those techniques are always going to work. The work of rigorously proving out methods often falls on mathematicians to complete, sometimes years or decades later.

Recently OpenAI announced that AI had solved half of one of the millennium problems in mathematics. The solution puts Yang-Mills theory, which undergirds the Standard Model of physics, on a more rigorous footing by deriving it from a set of axioms and proving that “the theory actually exists”. One of my friends from graduate school recently wrote about this.

In a recent YouTube video, theoretical physicist Gabriele Carcassi describes how in the past he would have to beg mathematicians to get interested in the math problems he was facing. Sometimes he would wait days, weeks, or months to get a reply from a mathematician. Often the reply would be “sorry, that’s not in my area of expertise”.

Now every theoretical physicist has access to AI that has an understanding of math that is on par with the best math professors. Unlike human mathematicians, the AI is always available, doesn’t get tired, and has expertise across all fields of math. The AI is happy to spend hours explaining complex mathematical topics or helping make math more rigorous. And all that expertise is available for only $25-$30 a month.

In a recent arXiv preprint even Ed Witten acknowledged getting help from Claude Opus 5.5.

The preprint describes some of the ways Claude contributed:

(for the record, I have precisely zero understanding of what he’s talking about here!)

I believe in the next few years theoretical physicists working with AI will be able to break new ground on many longstanding unsolved problems in theoretical physics.

What I found most enjoyable during my PhD research was achieving a clear and precise understanding of complex physical phenomena. Writing was how I achieved that. Writing was central to my research process and the intellectual development I experienced during my PhD.

If I had outsourced a lot of my writing to AI I don’t think I would have grown much intellectually. I probably would have gotten papers published, but my brain would not have developed and the papers would not have been as good. I am worried about physicists and other scientists today outsourcing too much of their writing to AI, because they are outsourcing important thinking as well in the process. The prospect of too much AI use stunting intellectual development is real.

I often found papers going back decades that had explored the origin of the dielectric properties of water. Those papers used different terminology and modeling approaches, and fitting them altogether was a big puzzle.

At other times I had to reconcile the physics theory I was understanding from the literature with the outputs from my simulations. I found solving such puzzles intrinsically fun and rewarding.

Writing was how I solved such problems - I used the page as an external memory for organizing information. Writing was how I synthesized large amounts of technical information from disparate sources into something I felt I could understand in my own tiny brain. While tackling such synthesis problems I developed important skills I still use today. (Those skills make me a better AI user, for instance.)

Like all good writers I chose the words and terminology I used carefully to maximize clarity and for my own sanity so when I returned to my writing I could refresh my memory easily.

I wrote in LaTeX, and a lot of what I wrote made its way into my thesis and papers. My thesis is on the longer side (317 pages) because writing was so central to my research process. I noticed that others did not write as much as I did. Instead, they collected tons of notes and raw data and then wrote everything up later.

I sometimes think that having a lower IQ than other physicists meant that I had to spend more time distilling and organizing things into clear writing. Counter-intuitively, cognitive constraints can force the creation of clearer explanations.

I like to think that one of the reasons why my physics papers are still cited today is due to the clarity of their exposition.

Of course, it is true that AI is also good at synthesizing and distilling large amounts of technical information into efficient, clear, logical prose. However, I still think doing it manually like I did during my PhD will lead to a better result. That may not be true for long, however.

Even as AI advances, I still recommend PhD researchers undertake the work of synthesis and distillation themselves and not rely too much on AI to do everything. The skills I obtained by doing such synthesis and distillation manually have proven useful for me in many ways.

Additionally, doing the synthesis work manually allowed me to be able to answer questions from peers that were couched in different terminology. AI would have given me one way of explaining things. Doing the work manually exposed me to multiple ways, which allowed me to better communicate with scientists that were working with different approximations, models, and terminologies.

Two out of four of the physics papers I wrote during my PhD had their genesis in “a crazy idea” that I have a hard time imagining today’s AI would come up with. My first paper had its genesis in a crazy idea from my advisor that the physics of relaxor ferroelectrics may be relevant to understanding the dielectric properties of water. The idea ended up having a grain of truth and led us in fruitful directions.

If you ask an AI for promising research directions, it will give you a bunch of things that are the logical next steps to build slightly off existing work. It’s not good at coming up with the sort of “crazy ideas” that humans sometimes do (I have tried to prompt this, but haven’t figured out a way — if you have tips please comment below).

In short, I think humans still have an edge when it comes to creativity and “taste” for finding good directions to work in.

I also enjoyed the physical experience of going to a library and finding hard copies of obscure books and journal articles that were relevant to my research and reading them. Looking at dusty manuscripts from the 1950s I think gave me a bit of an edge in my research because it sometimes led me to make creative happenstance connections that otherwise would not have been made.

I highly doubt an AI asked to do a literature search for ideas and connections would go down the sort of random rabbit holes I explored which sometimes yielded interesting things.

Of course, the field I was working in was especially good for mining forgotten insights from old literature. Water is really important and there has been an absurd amount of experimental and theoretical research published on the properties of water over the last ~150 years.

I’m also not sure how important the specific connections I found from random explorations of old literature actually were. Usually what was surfaced was just underappreciated ties into other bodies of work that were old and outmoded. I like to think that surfacing those connections was useful to other researchers, though.

Terence Tao has recently been talking about how human cognitive constraints mean that we are forced to distill complex mathematical proofs into “insights”. As you may have noticed, AI loves to get into gory details. It has no compunction about spewing out dozens of pages of complex derivations.

Of course, AI can distill things if asked, but according to Tao it doesn’t distill or explain math in a way that is easy for humans to understand. It seems to lack a good theory of mind for how human mathematicians with their puny brains understand things.

Just as AI is making a lot of progress in math on its own, as we look further down the road, it’s clear that at some point a lot of progress in theoretical physics will largely come from AI working in isolation.

As we move to more and more scientific advances being made by AI, what should be the role of humans? Should humans still study math and physics even if AI can solve all problems? These are philosophical questions beyond the scope of this present essay.

However, in the near term I think humans will still be better than AI when it comes to distilling what the AIs are finding in ways that are understandable and insightful for other humans.

1

Here’s Claude’s explanation of the bug in simple terms: “The setup. In the monomer PIMD scheme the forces on a water molecule are split into two parts. The forces inside each molecule, the two O–H stretches and the bend, come from the Partridge–Schwenke monomer surface and are applied to every bead of the ring polymer. The forces between molecules come from SIESTA and are applied once, at the centroid. For this to work, the force SIESTA hands back must contain only the between-molecule part. Your modified SIESTA did this by evaluating a fit to the DFT monomer surface for each molecule and subtracting it from the DFT force, so what came back was DFT minus fit. Adding Partridge–Schwenke on the beads then counts the intramolecular force exactly once. That is the intended scheme, and most of the time it is what ran.

The weak point. The subtraction has a safety check. Before SIESTA subtracts the fit for a molecule it evaluates the fit energy, and if that energy is above 2.5 eV it assumes the fit is being used outside its range and skips the correction for that molecule. When the correction is skipped, SIESTA returns plain DFT for that molecule. Plain DFT already contains an intramolecular force roughly equal to the fit. Adding Partridge–Schwenke on the beads on top of it now counts the intramolecular force twice. A spring that is twice as stiff vibrates √2 times faster, so the 1611 cm⁻¹ bend moves to about 2290 and the 3922 cm⁻¹ stretch to about 5550.

What tripped the safety check. PIMD-F90 wrapped atoms back into the periodic box one atom at a time. Whenever an oxygen had been wrapped and one of its hydrogens had not, the two atoms sat on opposite faces of the box. SIESTA evaluates the fit on the raw coordinates without applying the minimum image, so it saw an O–H distance of nearly a box length, a huge fit energy, and switched the correction off for that molecule. Molecules diffuse, so this is not a fixed set of molecules. At any instant about one molecule in five was straddling the edge, and over time every molecule spent about a fifth of its time in that state…. The single-molecule runs show the same pattern for the same reason. A lone molecule drifts with its thermal velocity, several ångströms per picosecond, and crosses the box edge constantly…”
