essays.title: Trust your eyes over your brain in AI progress.

author.name: Rahul Swaminathan
author.bio: I want to write more as a way to organize random thoughts I have better. I'll try not to stick to any one theme, but it's hard not to think a lot about AI nowadays.

essays.html:
I remember the first time I saw a tweet about GPT-3 generating some code around 6 years ago:

and it blew my mind. There were hunderds of so called “no-code” tools promising to bring development to non-developers, and a lot of skeletons because most of them had failed. Finally, no-code tools may actually be viable! My immediate next thought was this would be a massive boon for existing developers, and I should probably start playing around with it.

When the “aider” CLI tool launched in late 2023, I couldn’t sleep for a couple of nights with my excitement playing around with it. It was a huge jump from the autocomplete / copilot style suggestions that we were used to that had alreadymade me a much better developer (or so I thought). People had spent thousands of hours fine-tuning their editors with dotfiles for languge-specific hotkeys to make them more productive engineers (including myself), and this was a generalized version of that that just worked, and it worked surprisingly well over the last year or so.

But complete agentic code-editing was a huge step up. Just describe what you wanted, and it edited the files right on your existing hard-drive, and you just refreshed the browser and saw it change. For another year, the tooling kept getting better, and so did the models, and I was moving from tool to tool every few weeks with glee. I don’t think I was too early as an adopter, but just using popular tools / models that the online hivemind seemed to converge on. But still, it felt powerful. It seemed obvious to me, and a bunch of people I asked anecdotally that AI tools were obviously improving our productivity. It seemed like a pretty basic thesis that even the copilot style autocomplete was a decent boost to my productivity as a software engineer.

Then this METR study came out a full 2 years later in July 2025 -- “Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity“, and its headline finding was that I was lying to myself. Here’s a snippet from the original announcement‘s tweet thread

The results surprised us: Developers thought they were 20% faster with AI tools, but they were actually 19% slower when they had access to AI than when they didn’t.

The study itself seemed well conducted, and there were no obvious flaws in it. And yet, it went against everything I could feel in my bones. But science is science I guess, and I needed to update. This was a full 16 months ago, and my tools had updated quite a bit at that point. Maybe they didn’t use the right harness or they didn’t pick the right developers, but it was hard to argue with the study as it was presented. So it felt right to update away. They have since published an update in early 2026. But I think I would have been better served by just ignoring this and moving on, when my gut said it was obviously not true.

The next visceral feeling like this was this article which I discovered through Hacker News:
Where’s the Shovelware? Why AI Coding Claims Don’t Add Up by Mike Judge. Judge felt a very similar reaction to me and updated

I was an early adopter of AI coding and a fan until maybe two months ago, when I read the METR study and suddenly got serious doubts.[...] This was unsettling. It was impossible not to question if I too were an unreliable narrator of my own experience. Was I hoodwinked by the screens of code flying by and had no way of quantifying whether all that reading and reviewing of code actually took more time in the first place than just doing the thing myself?

He goes on to make an even stronger claim:

It turns out, though, and I’ve collected a lot of data on this, it doesn’t just not work for me, it doesn’t work for anyone, and I’m going to prove that.

And prove it, he does. You should read the original blog post, but I’ve reproduced a couple of charts there that struck me the most.

By Sept 2025, it was clear to me that there were a bunch of vibecoded apps that I regularly interacted with at least weekly. Of course AI meant there were a lot more apps, websites, repos etc than there would be otherwise. Seemed like an undeniable fact of life. But the charts here were undeniable too. And actual data. What’s happening? How are my instincts so far from reality? I wasn’t sure, but again, I updated as a wise bayesian should.

I don’t think anyone would seriously be writing that blog post today 9 months later. I haven’t checked what the actual data says either, but I assume it has updated. But at the time, it was a very well received article, and was insanely hard for me to argue against.

Everywhere I look around me, I can find countless examples of the data not matching my experience, or what feels like obviously true, but I can’t in good faith tell them why they’re incorrect. Since early this year, all my software engineer friends have had harder times finding jobs. The ones that have stable-ish careers are scared that theirs can be gone at any moment. This wasn’t the feeling 12 months ago, where most of them couldn’t see AI actually replacing what they were doing yet. But according to data, there’s nothing to worry about. Software engineering job postings are up 15% from last year. Believer’s chant “Jevon’s Paradox” like it’s a magical incantation that means we have nothing to worry about and show endless charts about jobs and postings:

Maybe it’s true. Just say it enough times and it comes true - just like all good prophecies. But I find myself trapped. I can’t argue with charts. Like a good scientist, let’s throw away what feels intuitive and trust the data. But this time, I feel my future self 6 months from now watching engineers getting fired en-masse telling me: “You idiot, maybe you shouldn’t have changed your mind”.

If your principles keep leading you astray, what good are your principles?

Geoffrey Hinton’s famous quote that AI would outperform radiologists has been used in dozens of articles to say why he’s wrong. In fact, in a recent response to Jensen Huang on live TV, he seems to have even convinced himself that he was wrong. Have people tried giving raw MRI data to an AI? I have, and as far as I can tell, it outperformed the report I got from an actual human radiologist. His actual statement from Nov. 2016 was that we should probably stop training radiologists. But, this in hindsight seems obviously true! It takes approximately 10-13 years after high school to become a radiologist. A bright young student starting on this career path in 2016 when he first said would potentially be starting his career today. I would not be expecting a long successful career in looking at an image and outputting a textual analysis if I started on that today. 1(#fndencc3z9zlu)

In July 2024, Deepmind published that it’s model had won silver in the IMO. The mood amongst mathematicians was “it’s cool, but not yet a peer”. Most seemed cautious. In November 2024, there was a new benchmark called FrontierMath by EpochAI. In a quote by famous mathematician Terrence Tao, he says:

Tao anticipated that the benchmark would “resist AIs for several years at least,” noting that the problems require substantial domain expertise and that we currently lack sufficient relevant training data.

Of course, it fell pretty shortly after that, and even a harder tier added later didn’t take much longer. Unless you’ve been living under a rock, you’ve heard of AI solving Millenium Prize class problems and mathematicians updating pretty hard but only after that happened. And mathematicians have been in my opinion one of the least skeptical of all the major fields of AI progress. The conversation has now shifted to AI will never come up with new concepts in maths. Or AI will never be the one to create the new interesting problems, only to solve them.

It feels like re-experiencing early Covid every few months. All I keep hearing is “Covid has only caused 10 deaths so far, so you’re wrong”.

Something obvious to me is already happening, and everyone is writing 10,000 word articles with proof - data, charts, expert citations telling me I’m an idiot. Someone slaps me out of my dreams by showing me the facts on the ground don’t justify my beliefs. So I change my mind.

A few months later, everyone just forgets they were wrong and moves on like nothing happened. reality slaps me once again in the face telling me I was an idiot for changing my mind in the first place. How do I stop getting slapped in the face so much?

The obvious counter-argument is “if you’re so correct, then why aren’t you so rich?”. Just like some people probably made a lot of money during the Covid pandemic by correctly timing the market crash. This is the standard argument from economists, and I think it has some merit.

For example, Atlassian (whose claim to fame is JIRA, software to create tickets to help organize a bunch of developers to create something my frontier AI can one-shot in a few minutes) stock is still trading at basically where it was in 2023. But still this is crazy high valuation at a 38B market cap / enterprise value. I have no idea how this company is supposed to make $38B in profits over its lifetime given the state of the world today and even if AI capabilities hits a brick wall tomorrow. Even as an option value for some successful pivot it executes, it obviously too high. Okay, so I buy some puts and maybe turn my $100k to $400k by next year (AI calculated expected values, could be wrong).

Sounds great, but that’s not exactly Elon Musk rich. And spending my days analyzing prediction markets and stock markets for hours isn’t something that intrinsically motivates me anyway.

People with truer beliefs in general should end up richer. But it doesn’t seem like as much of a gotcha argument that invalidates everything else.

No one bats an eye if you tell them GDP will go up 3% next year and 30% in the next 10 years. Everyone will happily extrapolate that to eternity. And that’s a pretty recent phenomenon! Like only since the Industrial Revolution 99.9% into humanity’s lifetimes did that start happening. But tell them AI progress may continue and everyone is suddenly filling news papers and blog posts about why that’s absolutely stupid. “Of course AI doing AI R&D is crazy”. We’d need to see a bunch of that already happening and GPT-6 fully creating GPT-7 for 10 iterations before we end up believing that is plausible.

I think when it comes to AI progress, there’s enough data to show that you should just trust your own eyes instead of well written essays and blog posts. And yes, the irony is intended.

  1. ^

    Yes, I’m aware that a radiologist doesn’t only do this one thing, and this will be used as an obvious reason why the job is safe. Just like a developer doesn’t just write code, and apparently does hundreds of other things like having important meetings for which he can never be truly replaced.

essays.title: On Spontaneity
essays.html:
An excerpt from my journal in January

The week’s all-encompassing focus is getting a research paper out, but I’ve been practicing defending my free time so that my 15-16hr work days are manageable for the next week or so. Today, I want to do some illustration.

I leave in the evening to go to the art room, Arav tagging along, to try something new. Robert, the guy who goes to the art room more than me, texts me Sarah’s not in, I am stressed but hopeful-- she said she’d be around today. We walk on Merton Street, my favourite street, with a crisp crescent moon just visible in a spot through the clouds, golden light from the sodium lamps cutting through the blue of twilight, ah how I love Oxford.

We’re at the art room. Sarah, my art teacher and dear friend, is not there yet... until she pops out from her office, wearing her usual maroon apron from Wernog Wood, the art retreats she runs in Wales. Reunited after the winter holidays, we hug and jump and talk about it all: of grief, family, babies, food, love. I pick up a bottle of drawing ink from the shelf -- I sketch with ink and nib fairly often -- and was picking from the communal art studio dip pens when Sarah says they’re no good. She looks to her collection for a pen for me, with no luck. I shrug it off, I’m used to working with the cheap pens, and start pouring ink into a repurposed jam jar...

A few moments later she comes with a large grey feather, and scissors, and with force, slices off the end at an angle, into a nib! I didn’t realise they literally just cut a feather to make a quill... but that makes sense.

We make some test marks on the page. The quill has a mind of its own: it stores ink in an organic way, it comes out in an organic way. The quill naturally turns in my hand as I draw with it, producing fluid, changing lines. The mark-making potential is amazing. You can press it very hard without worrying. Sometimes a lot of ink comes out all at once, and you don’t expect it. I ask what bird this quill is from, Sarah tells me it’s a goose! I’m enjoying listening to Sarah meet my friend Arav, for the first time, for they are very different people but they were quickly able to find that they are in fact quite similar. I meet Frank, Sarah’s partner! I had only ever seen him depicted in Sarah’s sketchbook, and, god, he looked just like her drawings. They brought two friends, a couple that own a farm, to visit the art room before a Burns Night dinner. They see my drawings and think of all the many kinds of trees... and they ask us, how did so many trees come to be? It’s a good question, I realised I take evolution and mutation for granted. Sarah is explaining the nature of randomness, or rather the randomness of nature, Robert diving into the dense details of cell division, the couple are not keeping up with either explanation, but they are left in awe of the intricacies of academic theories.

On the other hand, my drawings are no good. I’m frustrated with the quill... its mind of its own... the paper getting scratched by my heavy-handed strokes. I’m trying to copy a very detailed image of a forest... and it’s just not working. I get frustrated and switch back to my fine metal nib. That piece also frustrated me: after using the quill the dip pen seemed to hold the movement of my hand back, requiring a lot of force to produce fluid lines. I discarded both drawings, unfinished.

On top, the quill drawing. on the bottom, the nib drawing:

I’m home now. I’m desperate to learn how to use this strange quill. This first sketch was for learning: the paper was too small, and too thin, but as I gave into the sensation and the randomness, the quill no longer scratched, and instead glided on the page. I remembered Sarah had told me I could use the feather as a brush: I tried that out. It started to feel like play, and I enjoyed the contrast in this piece... though it was definitely unfinished and scrappy.

On my next attempt, the marks come out how I want. I am slightly directing the image towards a general composition like the last one, but I’m not trying for detail or fine lines. I’m surrendering myself to what the quill does. We stop fighting and we can now dance.

When I left the art studio that day, I nearly left the quill behind, frustrated at its stochastic nature. Oh how grateful I am that I didn’t. It’s late, time to get to bed, but I want to make more and more quill drawings. I prefer drawing the same thing again and again until chance gives me a good drawing, instead of spending a long time drawing one: it is these loose sketches that happen in a burst of flow that I like most. It would be wonderful to sketch from life with this pen, figures on the street, the English countryside, maybe a goose, or the lines on the face of someone I love.

It’s so interesting to come back to this journal entry after reading Impro by Keith Johnstone, in which the middle chapter is about spontaneity, and I feel like it puts into words many feelings that I have on the subject. Johnstone writes about how spontaneity is key to improvisation (sounds obvious), and through strange exercises like word disassociation or one word story, he is able to cultivate spontaneity in his students. They end up saying things that come straight from their deep consciousness, rather than constructed by their rational mind. Johnstone also writes of how a lot of spontaneity is squashed out in the education system-- school encourages us to follow rules and ignore our weird internal thoughts and be agreeable.

I see now how classic exercises like 10 second life drawings were how I was made to cultivate spontaneity. Pure repetition also helps: if you draw frequently, at some point you will run out of ideas and end up drawing whatever comes to mind spontaneously. Drawing in ink scares most non-artists (and many artists). There’s no undo, it is an exercise in trust and letting it happen, in natural movements. Otherwise your drawing will look tight, your regret (or whatever you are feeling) shows in your lines. There’s a clear analogy to one word story -- each line is like a word blurted out, and you must follow the picture/story that your subconscious wants to put out into the world.

In the excerpt above, I’m clearly deep in my time at Oxford. Now I have left to San Francisco, and I look ahead at the rest of my life, and think about how to do good work in this life somehow. Does spontaneity have a place in this? It seems really hard, in many ways work as it is right now is optimizing, trying, forcing, designing, planning. There is inherently a goal to create some outcome. This seems in contrast with spontaneity, in which we must be okay with any outcome. But we also think about being authentic, entering flow states, equanimity through painful situations, communicating what we want, moving people. So how can we dance between forcing something we want and cultivating spontaneity?

This turns out to be a very old problem. Early Chinese philosophers held up wu-wei, effortless action, as the ideal. Edward Slingerland writes of the paradox of wu-wei: how do you try not to try? And he claims that this tension drove the trajectory of Chinese thought. The Daoists said culture and striving were the problem, and to return to naturalness; the Confucians said to practice, through ritual and repetition, until the effort wears away and what’s left looks natural. Maybe my experience of drawing is Confucian. Zhuangzi tells of Cook Ding, a butcher whose knife stays sharp for nineteen years because he no longer hacks at the ox; he finds the spaces between the joints and lets the blade move through them. Did he stop trying, or did he keep trying until he stopped hacking?1

I think the drawing session reaches towards this too. That night I was not okay with any outcome; I wanted a good drawing badly enough to stay up late for it. But I was trying to get the quill to draw a perfect forest, and the drawings came out forced. When I stopped asking for something and felt where the pen wanted to go, it worked. Instead, the forcing went into everything around the drawing: leaving my desk mid-deadline, not abandoning the feather, drawing the same thing again and again. Our lives are full of ideal compositions: the question we’re supposed to ask, the work that sounds right. Spontaneity, as I’ve come to understand it, is seeing what is actually there, instead of what we want to compose.

This essay feels incomplete, probably because I haven’t figured all of this out, and maybe I never will. But these last few months have felt like progress!

1

Zhuangzi was Daoist, so he probably intended for Cook Ding to be perceived as someone who just stopped trying to cut hard. But if you read this excerpt he does have progression: “When I first began cutting up oxen, all I could see was the ox itself.” -- suggesting practice. Also I’ve greatly simplified both schools of thought in this paragraph, and recommend reading more.

essays.title: The Singularity as a 24/7 2Fort Instant Respawn Server
essays.html:
Continual advancements in the domain of automating everything (AI) have moved the question of playing god from idle speculation to a serious policy debate. Many people find this prospect terrifying. So terrifying that we should abandon this whole enterprise even if we can be reasonably certain a good outcome will be achieved (for some definition of good).

Bourgeois Blues

After Work, We'll Have Each Other compares the social situation when all work is automated to 18th-century aristocrats. When labor is automated, it'll be "a world where our connections to other humans are what give us structure, identity, and meaning". Since aristocrats "did not work for pay" and "did not see work as a source of meaning", they are "as close to a purely relational world as anything [Collier] can think of".

In Collier's account the 18th-century aristocrats were profoundly boring. Their memoirs are interesting to read only "in large part because of the contrast between the keenness of [their] observations and the inanity of their content". Their "conversation consisted overwhelmingly of political gossip" and they are "ruthlessly pragmatic in the pursuit of power". Since their relationships are all that matters to their social standing, any action they take is somehow in service of preserving or expanding their relationships.

The Solve Everything Button

Suppose then we give "two cheers for the American work ethic" and accept work as a primary source of meaning. What happens when a new way to do the same work faster is developed? Market pressures tend to render the old way unprofitable and obsolete rather quickly. Many people still create things in ways that are not economically efficient, but these are, by definition, hobbies, not work. Suppose then we could cheaply make a button that instantly did a specific job. The existence of this button, then, would convert that job into a hobby.

An AI that could do every job would similarly convert every job into a hobby. Suddenly all the meaning through work would be gone. This is why people who find meaning through work are so scared about AI. Yet consider the decision to not develop AI: is this not already deciding to not take the most efficient path to accomplishing an outcome? If you're preventing a new technology on the grounds it's more efficient, you already believe your current activities have value beyond their mere economic value.

A Walk Down 2Fort

People already do plenty of things with little plausible economic value. Consider, for example, the video game Team Fortress 2 (TF2). Released in 2007 after nine years in development, it was a pioneer of Western live service games and continues to have a large active playerbase to this day. Similar to many more modern titles, players queue into matches where they use class-specific weapons to help their team achieve a gamemode-specific objective. Unlike newer titles, these outcomes do not feed into any sort of visible skill rank.1 Matches exist essentially in isolation; they are not building up to anything.

One map, 2Fort, is rather infamous. The official wiki run by the game developers notes that "due to the map's design with long, narrow corridors, it's easy for a team to become entrenched and for stalemates to occur". Since the map runs the "Capture the Flag" gamemode, there is no in-game timer and matches can last seemingly forever. Many players treat this as a sort of feature, queuing for games of 2Fort with no intention of playing to achieve the provided objective. Instead, they blow each other up, form conga lines, and throw sandviches at each other with no purpose other than to have fun. Community-run servers have been created specifically for this purpose and often feature modifications such as removing the objective entirely and removing the delay before respawning after death.

Perhaps it could be explained that these people don't find value in what they are doing or it is somehow instrumental to economic efficiency. Maybe Sam Bankman-Fried provided a similar explanation to himself for why he spent his time hardstuck Bronze in League of Legends. This reframing is far too hasty: leisure does not stop being enjoyable without it being towards something else. Of course not everyone will enjoy the same things, but rollercoasters, sports, walking outside, swimming, etc. are not fun simply in virtue of furthering employment.

The Spectre of Marx

In Karl Marx's transformation to the preeminent avatar of the left, the multiplicity of his thought has been flattened into a caricature. Marx the critic of the industrial revolution, Marx the condemner of the bourgeoisie, Marx the socialist/communist, Marx the revolutionary advocate, but almost never the Marx who pondered if capitalism had gone far enough. This sounds preposterous, but this line of thought has been a quiet-yet-persistent undercurrent of Marxian theory--one waiting for its moment to come.

One of Marx's great insights was that people's social relations are in large part determined by their economic circumstances. His 1859 Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy provides an account of historical epochs based on this insight. One epoch transitions to another when the "existing relations of production" that once served to develop the productive forces "turn into their fetters", restricting their further development. Capitalism, like feudalism before it, would become a fetter, giving way to communism. In this account, communism is not less productive than capitalism, but more. With this, Marx's declaration "we say to the workers and the petty bourgeois: it is better to suffer in modern bourgeois society, which by its industry creates the material means for the foundation of a new society that will liberate you all, than to revert to a bygone form of society which, on the pretext of saving your classes, thrusts the entire nation back into medieval barbarism"2 makes perfect sense.

What then does this new communist society look like? With the radical productivity under communism, the economy would no longer be a significant determinant of social relations. Instead, communism would allow for the "free development of human energy". In the unpublished Saint Max3, Marx and Friedrich Engels consider painting:

The exclusive concentration of artistic talent in particular individuals, and its suppression in the broad mass which is bound up with this, is a consequence of division of labour. Even if in certain social conditions, everyone were an excellent painter, that would by no means exclude the possibility of each of them being also an original painter, so that here too the difference between “human” and “unique” [in the egoist sense employed by Max Stirner] labour amounts to sheer nonsense. In any case, with a communist organisation of society, there disappears the subordination of the artist to local and national narrowness, which arises entirely from division of labour, and also the subordination of the individual to some definite art, making him exclusively a painter, sculptor, etc.; the very name amply expresses the narrowness of his professional development and his dependence on division of labour. In a communist society there are no painters but only people who engage in painting among other activities.

They are not painters because "painter" is an economic category. People are free to engage in activities as they wish, but these activities do not define them. Instead, their limits are defined by "the boundary created by matter itself", as G. A. Cohen puts it.

Solve Metaphysics Make No Mistakes

"Philosophy with a deadline", warns Nick Bostrom; "anyone trying to work out what they think about accelerationism better do so quickly", rejoices Nick Land; "think fast, chucklenuts", says Scout TF2. Let's then quickly sketch out the problem: (1) AI that economically obsoletes humans will be capable of enacting a very large amount of change in the world. (2) That capacity will be used towards some goal. (3) It is therefore important to get this goal correct.

(1) and (2) are basic preconditions of the deadline, so it is (3) that merits attention. To illustrate (3), in Superintelligence Bostrom considers a superintelligent AI tasked with hedonism. Such an AI would want to tile the universe with "hedonium", which is "matter organized in a configuration that is optimal for the generation of pleasurable experience". If it was wrong about what produces pleasure, it might then be doing its best to convert the universe into something essentially worthless, and if hedonism is wrong, it's practically guaranteed.

This problem structure repeats across other goals we could explore: the AI optimizes the goal and then we get buyer's remorse. If we can't be confident we have the perfect goal, we should therefore delay until we do. Yet it's unclear what this would even entail. Are we supposed to just keep sciencing and philosophizing until words like "consciousness", "qualia", "soul", "good", and "evil" can be empirically measured? Has the long history of philosophy given us any indication this would work?

Natural Intelligence Doomsday

AI is not the only deadline we face: the earth continues to get hotter, the nukes are all ready to blow everything up at a moment's notice, and a pandemic could wipe everyone out. The natural world is fraught with peril. So far we've been able to avoid the worst of it. Will human intelligence be enough to face all future challenges?

The question with AI is not if it will achieve the maximally good outcome, but if it can achieve a better outcome than without it. So long as the outcome with AI is better than without it, anything else is just a bonus. Preventing the development of AI is not a neutral act. It could perhaps sometimes be justified to delay it to work towards circumstances for an even better outcome, but we should not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

The Curious Task of Left Accelerationism

Supposing then that giving AI a good goal is akin to aiming for the broad side of a barn, the path forward still remains murky. All current AI systems are developed under a capitalist mode of production. With AI becoming an increasingly important part of the global economy, it is difficult to take beliefs in machines of loving grace, gentle singularities, or five-year plans at face value. The suspicions that advances in AI will simply perpetuate capitalism, perhaps in a more dystopian form, are difficult to shake.

Yet searches for other revolutionary paths have turned up empty: using capitalism to defeat itself remains the most plausible line of flight. The problem remains difficult, but it is difficult in human terms. A pause in AI could be ruinous because it lets AI developers think hard about who they cut out or because it prevents AI entirely. Accelerating AI too carelessly could risk missing the barn entirely. Nationalization could prevent AI companies from running away from the rest of us, but it could also be the demise of AI.

The task of left accelerationism is then both obvious and elusive. Obvious in that there is a clear target to aim for, but elusive as the path has not yet been forged. Yet if we are to believe in any sort of indomitable human spirit, surely it is in solving a political problem once rather than solving increasingly difficult challenges forever.

  1. ^ There's technically a hidden Glicko system, although it does little to achieve balanced games.
  2. ^ Montesquieu LVI, Neue Rheinische Zeitung
  3. ^ MECW and others present Saint Max as part of a book Marx and Engels supposedly wrote called The German Ideology. Saint Max was intended for standalone publication and The German Ideology, as it is standardly presented, does not exist. See Farewell to The German Ideology for more information.

essays.title: Fresh and Strange Ideas
essays.html:
The future demands fresh and strange ideas. —Peter Thiel, “A Time for Truth and Reconciliation”

I’ve agreed to be an editor at The Elephant. I’m interested in commissioning pieces related to AI, politics, and history (specifics listed below), and data-driven pieces on any topic. You can pitch me on Twitter @panickssery.

As a kid I was concerned that life might be a bit boring. I figured that a lifespan from roughly 1870 to 1960 was the most interesting in terms of extreme change.

  • Bertrand Russell (1872–1970) lost both parents (to diphtheria and bronchitis) by age four and in 1876 went to live with his grandfather, the last Whig prime minister, who as a young man had met Napoleon at Elba. At age 94 in 1966 he met Paul McCartney, whom he persuaded to oppose the Vietnam War.

  • Churchill (1874–1965) rode in Britain’s last great cavalry charge (Omdurman 1898) and later in life ordered Britain’s first hydrogen-bomb program.

  • W.E.B. Du Bois (1868–1963) was born three years after the Civil War and died the day before the March on Washington.

Some other people whose lives seem to stretch over a vast historical period include Laura Ingalls Wilder (1867–1957), Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959), W. Somerset Maugham (1874–1965), and Picasso (1881–1973). Outside the West there were even more extreme cases:

  • “Syngman Rhee (1875-1965) [was] one of the last people in Korea to pass the old Confucian civil service examinations and later became the President of South Korea, playing a pivotal role in the early Cold War … He was born in a preindustrial world where the old Confucian social order still held sway and nobody around him had ever seen a train and died in a world of jet planes and manned space travel.” @avrilbradley23

  • “A curious Surmic born [c. 1885] would have seen the forging of the Ethiopian Empire, the end of the witch-chiefs, Christian missionaries, the Italian conquest, literacy, new crops, and maybe the moon landing.” @Peter_Nimitz

In 1931, Churchill wrote in “Fifty Years Hence” that just as Tennyson’s predictions in his 1842 poem “Locksley Hall” of air forces and transnational governance had arrived, he forecasted

  • video calls: “Wireless telephones and television, following naturally upon their present path of development, would enable their owner to connect up with any room similarly installed, and hear and take part in the conversation as well as if he put his head in through the window.”

  • lab-grown meat: “We shall escape the absurdity of growing a whole chicken in order to eat the breast or wing.”

  • fusion power: “If the hydrogen atoms in a pound of water could be prevailed upon to combine together and form helium, they would suffice to drive a thousand horsepower engine for a whole year.”

  • artificial wombs: “They will not be made, but grown under glass.”

But in 1981, these mostly hadn’t materialized. Instead, by the 2010s it seemed that “our surroundings are strangely old,” that in the 1970s there had begun a Great Stagnation and that fertility rates would condemn us to population decline, de-industrialization, and gerontocracy as the Earth increasingly resembles a nursing home.

Now that has all changed. While international travel actually slowed down with the Concorde’s decommissioning in 2003, the FAA is moving towards eliminating the overland supersonic ban and Boom’s XB-1 broke the sound barrier last year. We’re experiencing rapid advances in space tech, automobiles, biomedicine, and most of all in AI. Who today doesn’t expect the development of lab-grown meat, fusion power, and artificial wombs, unless trends are arrested by even stranger outcomes like AI takeover or extinction? So I’m interested in commissioning pieces on how to measure and influence institutional trends especially as they relate to explosive growth.

Growth.

  1. Equality. A century ago, about 10% of Americans died before age 5, including John D. Rockefeller’s daughter and grandson. Based on the individual variance in actual quality-adjusted consumption and in health measures like lifespan, is America the most equal society in history?

  2. Leisure. The “unemployment rate” counts those looking for work relative to the labor force. But with a more literal “employment rate”—the percent of annual life-hours spent working—are we in an age of unprecedented leisure, given our longer educational and retirement periods?

  3. Red tape. Would today’s institutions have thwarted the Industrial Revolution with red tape, regulatory capture, and risk aversion in the face of popular opposition? What changes can we make that would put us in a good position to capitalize on the next such episode?

Politics.

  1. War. While not the world’s only hygiene, war (and interstate competition generally, and domestic uprising) can select for good governance. How does governance look when states are free of these insecurities—for example, if AGI falls into the hands of authoritarian governments like those in Britain or China?

  2. Democracy. In 1981, Argentine president Viola said “We believe we are already within a democratic system. Some factors are still missing, like the expression of the people’s will.” The term democracy is often used as a synonym for “legitimacy” rather than governance that is more responsive to the mass public.

  3. America. Over the past 150 years, America has been the best governed of the world’s large countries (say, the top 10% by population). Why? What are the key aspects of geography, culture, or governance?

AGI.

  1. The “human touch.” What preferences for human service have survived past technological advances? How accurate were past predictions in the cases of automatic switchboards, elevator operators, self-checkout, and robotaxis?

  2. Successionism. In a YouGov poll from July, 8% of Americans think some AIs are conscious and another 37% say they probably will be eventually; 54% said they wouldn’t give AIs rights even if they were conscious, but is that position sustainable among the public? Can technical decisions by frontier labs influence the policy outcomes here?

  3. Effective altruists. How did a few thousand effective altruists gain such wealth and influence? What are historical analogues of a small, ideological, elite-oriented movement like the Jesuits, Fabian Society, or Quakers?

  4. Taxation. The labor share of income has been roughly constant despite technological changes (one of the six Kaldor facts), but if that changes, how might we change taxation in a way that doesn’t throttle output?

  5. Data centers. In this week’s midterm elections, voters passed 43 out of 44 restrictive measures on data centers. Where will data centers ultimately be built, and how?

Demographics.

  1. Boomers. How do we measure boomer influence—such as with the composition over time of important positions like congressmen and university presidents—and how do we forecast the handover of power as they retire?

  2. India. Over 1.1 billion Indians could emigrate to Europe and North America until they became the majority in both continents and India would still the world’s third most populous country. A few changes of fate could have seen a simultaneous American president and British prime minister of Indian ancestry. What are the medium- and long-term implications?

  3. China. As de Gaulle apocryphally said, “China is a big country, inhabited by many Chinese.” China also has one of the lowest percentages of foreign-born residents of any country, even as historically closed countries like Japan increasingly accept immigrant workers. What will this look like in the future? And what are the implications of China’s extreme AI optimism if American policy turns against AI?

  4. Fertility. What were the causes of the Roman fertility collapse and the government response? What is Japan like now that it has gone from a poster child of fertility decline to actually having a higher TFR than its neighbors?

  5. Gender. How and why have young women moved radically toward the left in many Western countries? What is the longer historical trend and narrative for gender polarization in politics?

essays.title: Towers of Agency
essays.html:
There is basically one reason to build a tower, and that’s access: There is something that is available higher up that is not available on the ground. Most commonly, that thing is either “empty space” or “information transmission”. A skyscraper can access more space than a shorter building, and so it fits more real estate in a smaller footprint. A watchtower can access strategic information from the land below; a church steeple is tall enough for the sound of the bells to travel far through the air. Many of the tallest structures in the world maximize line-of-sight for radio transmissions.

Imagine a stone or brick tower of your favorite type - one whose purpose is to access something high up. Or, if you prefer a specific suggestion, imagine the brick steeple of Old North Church in Boston, which held the signaling lanterns for Paul Revere.

Consider some unremarkable block in the tower: On either side of this block are other blocks. Sitting on top of this block are more blocks. Below, holding our block’s weight: more blocks.

One can ask, about the block we’ve chosen, the question “how?”: How is it that this block is at this spot? And the answer to that question is, locally, that it is held up by other blocks immediately below. Those blocks depend on others below them, and so indirectly our block is here by the grace of the whole set of blocks transitively beneath it.

One can ask, about the block we’ve chosen, the question “why?”: For what purpose is this block at this spot? And the answer to that question is, locally, that it is holding up other blocks immediately above. Those blocks are holding up others above them, and so indirectly our block is here in order to help hold up the whole set of blocks transitively above it.

“How are you going to put a stone there in that empty space?” asks Alice. “By first putting stones in the empty space beneath it.” replies Bob. “Why are you laying that brick?” asks Alice. “I want to rest this other brick on top of it.” replies Bob. For Bob, the bricks lower down in the tower are more “instrumental”; the bricks higher in the tower are more “terminal”.

This is sort of what plans are like - or at least, some “well-behaved” parts are structured like this. “How are you going to get a job as an engineer?” asks Alice. “I’m going to apply with an impressive resume and all the required certifications.” replies Bob. “Why are you going to get a job as an engineer?” asks Alice. “I’ll have a good steady income, and respectability in the community.” replies Bob. Bob sounds like he has a plan. Plans are kind of tower-y, and so are strategies and even agents themselves.

But as you follow the trail of blocks down to the bottom of a tower, you eventually meet the ground upon which the tower rests. And as you follow the trail of blocks up to the top of a tower, you eventually meet empty space above.

Plans are stranger. As you follow the trail of goals “down” a plan toward the more-instrumental, it’s not clear where the “ground” is, or if there even is a ground. “How are you going to actuate your finger to apply the force to press the key to write the sixtieth character of this essay for your engineering class for your engineering degree for your engineering job?”

And as you follow the goals “up” a plan toward the more-terminal, it’s not clear where the “sky” is, or if there even is a sky. “Why do you like to eat ice cream? Why do you want to start a family? Why do you want good things to happen to you?”

We see, and embody, lots of examples of “locally well-behaved” agents. Sometimes we literally place blocks one on top of the other to build towers. Some of us have written software, typically by assembling a hierarchy of procedures that the computer executes to accomplish a task. We execute simple or complex strategies to win at games and do our jobs.

But as we ask “why?”, moving upward from the well-behaved regions of human behavior - the tower wall segments we can see through the clouds - the answers stop sounding like “because I want X”. Instead we have to start giving answers that depart from the frame of seeking more-terminal values: “because that’s the kind of person I am”, or “because my neurons fire in such-and-such a pattern”. Answers to “why” questions that mysteriously sound more like answers to “how” questions.

In principle a person could be a single coherent tower with a single apex, the tip of a spire that’s the fruit of all the stonework below. Many explicit models of agency, like those used by economists and computer scientists, fit well into a tower structure. The top of the steeple becomes a utility function, or a reward function, or a goal. Lower blocks might be preferences, or subgoals, or resources, or actions.

But the top of a real human tower appears to dissolve into something not-so-hierarchical and not-so-neat. Somehow my body is inhabited at times by a relatively coherent writer of software, and at other times by a relatively coherent writer of English sentences, but whatever is selecting between the software-writer and sentence-writer modes does not look like a simple and coherent mode-chooser. My pizza-seeking mode does not seem to neatly descend from a food-optimization goal. When I was a child and my mother would call me for dinner while I was in the middle of a book, I’d sometimes be quite frustrated at the interruption, even if I was very hungry. From within a flow state, even a life-saving interruption could carry a twinge of that pain of interruption.

These tower-like hierarchical models of agency do not seem to explain human behavior very well, or at least when they describe behavior well they don’t do so very simply. Whatever we humans are, we seem to “grow” or “host” pockets of tower-like agency, rather than fully embodying it.

You can discuss this post on LessWrong.

essays.title: The China case for US pacing drills
essays.html:
US labs should practice pacing the frontier. Beyond general trust-building arguments, US pacing drills could also make reciprocal pacing from China more likely:

  1. US pacing drills can serve as confidence-building measures. US-China coordination needs trust, which is built through reps over time. By sending appropriately costly signals of restraint — e.g., verifiable pacing drills — US labs can help start a virtuous “spiral of cooperation” with China, improving the chances of reciprocal pacing.

  2. More directly, Chinese sources have already asked for verifiable evidence of US pacing!

As evidence, I analyze five Chinese commentaries on pacing, from policy researchers and a state media outlet. These sources are strongly skeptical that US companies would actually pause, and cite concerns about lack of verified evidence. Caveating my small sample size, I read these as moderate demand signals for US labs to build confidence.

My advice to US labs is as follows:

  1. Listen to China’s demand signals. They’re out there!

  2. Make appropriate costly signals in response. As a lab, you can choose how much cost to take on in your pacing drill. In weighing costs, consider designing drills with international pacing actors in mind: what evidence would China find credible, and how can this evidence be demonstrated?

Five Chinese sources on pacing

The following sources are taken from Chinese policy experts and Chinese state media commentary. They were published between June and October 2026, in response to Anthropic’s RSI article and the post-Coxon pacing preference cascade. I expect the commentary sample is a relevant chunk of the Chinese AI policy landscape, but not intended to be thorough or representative of official views! Any CN → EN translation errors are mine.

A summary:

  • There is strong skepticism about US lab pacing credibility: Somesources are more US-hawkish than others, but the common questions are: will US labs actually accept constraints? do they genuinely want to pace? Chinese sources suspect that there are commercial and geopolitical motives: pacing is a pre-IPO play for Anthropic, it is a tool of regulatory capture, it is intended to undermine China’s technological progress.

  • Useful preparation can begin before a political agreement: Xiao Qian calls for clarifying what a slowdown would involve and creating conditions for future action.

  • Who defines and verifies pacing matters: The most US-hawkish views from below (Li Yuhua, Yuyuan Tantian) worry that verification could preserve American advantage. In addition to credibility of evidence, the terms and design of verification drills are important as well.

Would China agree to slow AI development? That’s the wrong question.

By Xiao Qian, published in the South China Morning Post on October 6, 2026.

Policy relevance: Xiao Qian is deputy director of Tsinghua’s Center for International Security and Strategy (CISS) and vice dean of its Institute for AI International Governance. She has taken part in unofficial US-China talks on AI security.

CISS is relevant in the China AI policy landscape: it does policy consulting, and its founding chair, Fu Ying, is a former vice foreign minister. In Matt Sheehan’s model of how Chinese AI policy gets made, CISS is in the “world of ideas”: the layer of think-tank, academic, and media debate that does not represent official positions, but supplies important “intellectual grist for the bureaucratic mill.”

Selected quotes:

  • “What exactly would constitute a slowdown? Would limits apply to training runs, compute, model capabilities or deployment? How could compliance be verified? Who would have both the technical capacity and the political legitimacy to conduct such verification? Until these questions are answered, it is not realistic to expect a definite answer from any government to the larger question of whether it would agree to slow down.”

  • “Rather than waiting for a definite answer from China, perhaps we should think about what can be done to create an environment in which governments are more ready to take action when the question becomes more urgent.”

如何看待Dario Amodei关于AI减速倡议的讨论？ (How should we view the debate over Dario Amodei’s AI slowdown proposal?)

By 东不压桥研究院, republished by 安全内参 on September 14, 2026.

Policy relevance: The 东不压桥研究院 account is run by Zhang Peng, a nonresident senior fellow at the Center for China and Globalization, a Beijing-based nongovernmental think tank. He calls for jointly agreed cooperation rules and a US commitment not to tighten technology restrictions further.

Selected quotes:

  • “China will assess AI risks based on verifiable facts, objective risk assessments, and national and public interests, and must never blindly follow others’ lead.”
    “中国对AI风险的判断，会依据可检验的事实、客观的风险评估，以及国家和公众利益来做出，绝不能盲目跟风、随他人起舞。”

  • “Since this is cooperation, both sides should be allowed to raise questions, discuss evidence, and jointly determine the rules.”
    ”既然是合作，就应该允许双方提出问题、讨论证据，共同确定规则。”

Anthropic得了美国病 (Anthropic has caught the American disease)

By Yuyuan Tantian (玉渊谭天), published August 30, 2026 (republished by CCTV on August 31).

Policy relevance: Yuyuan Tantian is a commentary column created by China Media Group, the state broadcaster that operates CCTV.

Selected quotes:

  • “Only once the US has shown that safety rules apply just as effectively to its own model companies can substantive discussions between China and the US begin.”
    “只有当美国先证明安全规则对本国的模型公司同样有效后，中美之间才可能进入实质性的讨论。”

Anthropic为什么大力呼吁暂停前沿模型研发？ (Why is Anthropic calling so strongly for a pause in frontier model development?)

By Yao Xu, Xin Yanyan, Zhang Ao, Huang Kaiyue, and Wang Yibo, published by Fudan University on June 16, 2026.

Policy relevance: This piece comes from the research team at Fudan’s Center for Global AI Innovative Governance, another academic think tank. The lead author, Yao Xu, is the center’s secretary-general and previously worked on secondment at China’s National Data Administration. The authors question whether a pause can work when companies could announce restraint publicly while continuing privately.

Selected quotes:

  • “For a pause proposal to work, each institution must be confident that the others have actually halted research and development.”
    “暂停倡议若要成立，前提是每家机构都能确信其他机构真正停止了研发”

  • “Companies could easily announce a slowdown publicly while continuing to develop new versions in private.”
    “企业完全可以在公开层面宣布放缓，私下持续推进迭代。”

美国AI减速论暗战背后，又为中国设下“鸿门宴” (Behind the U.S. fight over slowing AI, another trap is being laid for China)

By Li Yuhua, published in Guancha on September 17, 2026.

Policy relevance: Guancha is an influential private outlet; Li, the author is affiliated with Fudan’s School of International Relations and Public Affairs. Li questions who sets the terms of pacing and verification, and worries that verification could preserve American advantage.

Selected quotes:

  • “If a joint slowdown is to be genuinely binding, the question of how to verify it must be answered.”
    “共同减速如果要真正具有约束力，就必须回答怎样验证的问题。”

  • “By what standards would the parties slow down, and what system would verify it?”
    “按照什么标准减、由什么体系来验证”

Why trust China’s asks?

A natural Western reaction might be: “Of course China wants US labs to practice pacing — it gives China a chance to catch up in the AI race! They don’t actually genuinely want to reciprocate.”

And very reasonably so! There is much skepticism from all sides, given that none of the AGI actors have yet established (trustworthily) that they want to slow down. In particular, these Chinese sources do not establish that China would reciprocate.

I hold that skepticism can coexist with a willingness to take incremental steps, with bounded costs, in the “trust, but verify” direction. US labs have a strong opportunity here.

What would good US pacing drills actually look like?

For general notes, see existing writing:

  • Sophie Kim, How to Pace the Frontier

  • Jason Hausenloy, Burn a day, then offer to pause

  • Nikola Jurkovic, We urgently need to practice before we can pause

In response to specific Chinese concerns, US labs could consider the following arrangements (ordered roughly by increasing cost):

  • Work with credible 3rd-party US auditors to run drills;

  • Release thorough evidence that can be analyzed by Chinese counterparts (evaluators, labs, etc). One option is to use verification tech;

  • Run preregistration exercises: before the drill, seek input from Chinese counterparts about what evidence they would accept as credible. Update and communicate appropriately afterwards;

  • Consult or jointly develop terms and verification arrangements of drills with Chinese counterparts.

essays.title: Most people nod at AI risk and move on
essays.html:
I’m concerned that AI may cause catastrophic harm in the near future. I’ve failed to get the people around me interested, and I don’t understand why.

I first encountered AI risk in 2016, reading Bostrom’s Superintelligence. I mulled over the ideas for five years, and in 2021, I left my job in IT to try to help the transition to powerful AI, whenever it came, go well. Then ChatGPT arrived, and what had felt theoretical and far away started to feel real and enormous, at least to me. Scott Aaronson captured a feeling common among people working in AI: that the rest of our lives will mostly revolve around it. Outside the AI bubble1, the technology was treated as a toy or a tool, and the risk barely registered.

I spent most of my time from 2021 to 2025 writing articles for aisafety.info, a site explaining AI risk to a lay audience. I’m proud of what we wrote, but it never gained traction, and we stopped adding content at the end of 2025. Visitors were few, and most left within a minute and never came back.

Clearly we were doing something wrong. We tried redesigning the interface, paying for feedback, and interviewing friends. When asked whether the scenarios we were describing seemed too far-fetched or sci-fi, people agreed they sounded a bit crazy, but reported the content was well argued, well sourced and engaging enough. They even came away more concerned than before. But try as we might, readers kept bouncing off.

We also tried widening the funnel: Rob Miles2 promoted the site in some of his videos. A typical video with roughly 100k views brought a few hundred people to the site, who read for a minute and never returned. These were people already interested in AI safety who had gone out of their way to read more. That they bounced too suggests either something else was wrong with the site, or written content just can’t compete with video. Written outlets like 80,000 Hours have done fine, so I suspect the former.

I’d write this off as poor product-market fit, but I get the same reaction in person. I tell friends and family about AI risk, they nod, say “huh, that sounds concerning”, and then never ask about it again. After some (forced) conversation, many of them could explain the arguments for risk reasonably well, and most have no objections on hand. The problem doesn’t seem to be understanding as much as interest.3

Why does this happen? I don’t know. These are smart people, so I want to explore what they bring to the question that I don’t. I’m setting aside people who have objections, good or bad. This piece is about caring, not believing.

Doomsayers are usually wrong

This has been a reasonable heuristic for most of history, and it’s still my default if I see somebody on the street with a sign proclaiming “the end is nigh”. But the people warning about AI risk are not standing on street corners. They include the people building frontier AI and some of the world’s most cited scientists. More personally, my friends know me as (somewhat) well-adjusted, with opinions that usually track reality, and I doubt they see me as a crank. So I don’t think this hypothesis holds much water.

A finite pool of attention or worry

Maybe people have “apocalypse fatigue”: they feel like the economy is terrible, the environment is dying and fascism is on the rise, so they just don’t want another source of “we are all f*cked” in their lives. I’ve seen friends disengage from environmental discussions because they simply can’t take any more bad news.

Research suggests that there may be a finite pool of attention, but finds limited evidence for a finite pool of worry. This matches the polling: high concern, low salience. In one recent poll, 27% of voters said AI would likely cause human extinction, but only 6% listed it as one of their two top issues.

I’m of course not immune to this. Take nuclear weapons: I know there are enough warheads to blow up most of the world’s major cities, and I’ve read the alarming list of close calls, but I rarely think about it. Still, if I had a friend who worked on preventing nuclear war, I would pester them with questions until they started avoiding me at parties. My friends have exactly that friend for AI risk, one who would happily talk their ears off, and they mostly don’t take me up on it.

There’s nothing I can do about it

When a threat feels real but there’s nothing you can do about it, you tend to manage the feeling instead of the threat, usually by ignoring it. What would my friends actually do with “AI might kill us all”? There’s no equivalent of recycling or buying an electric car, and few people vote on it. Changing the subject is the easy move, and I take the hint and stop bringing it up.

Climate communicators have been dealing with this for decades, and the standard fix is pairing the threat with things people can do. We did that on aisafety.info, with plenty of calls to action such as calling your representative,4 but people still bounced. So the problem isn’t the lack of an ask. It may be that the asks on offer don’t feel like they’d make a difference.

Yoshua Bengio describes how shifting his work towards the problem eased his anxiety about it, but I can’t expect the people around me to change careers to relieve a background worry. If calling your representative feels pointless and a career change feels too big, it can seem like there’s nothing in between. There is: aisafety.info has a whole page of in-between options.5 They just don’t seem to register.

No one has been hurt yet

The hypothesis I find most convincing is that AI risk lacks salience because it hasn’t hurt anyone yet. If Robert Oppenheimer had gone around in 1944 warning about the dangers of the atom bomb, people would have dismissed him (and then he would have lost his security clearance). After Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the same warning would have been heard very differently.

The mild bump in public interest after the Hugging Face incident suggests there’s something to this. Jacob Coxon’s resignation got far more mainstream coverage than earlier ones, and I suspect the Hugging Face incident was the tinder.6 A family member who usually avoided the subject asked me my P(doom)7 a couple of weeks later. But apart from him, the people around me mostly shrugged and moved on again, which fits: nobody was actually hurt.

AI risk has no clear villains

Maybe people don’t care because AI risk is mostly not politicized. The AI safety community has done a good job of keeping it that way. That’s probably good for public epistemics, but it may have cost us public engagement. Most dinner-table topics have a clear political angle, with good guys and bad guys, and a nuanced topic like AI risk doesn’t fit that pattern.8

Compare that with data centers. In affected communities, there is a large new building (salience) that sometimes raises electricity costs (someone gets hurt).9 There are clear villains (the companies building them, sometimes through shady secret agreements), and the US administration has picked a side, which makes the issue easy to politicize. For what it’s worth, I think data centers are broadly fine, and it still feels strange that they get more attention than catastrophic AI risk, even given all of the above.

Different priors

Each of these hypotheses is a guess at how people who bounce off AI risk see the world differently from me. If around a quarter of people think AI is likely to cause human extinction, why do so few of them want to talk about it? The concerned and the unconcerned look at the same evidence and come away with very different pictures of the future, and very different reactions to it. That suggests we start from substantially different priors. This blog is an attempt to find out where that split happens.

1

No, not the financial one.

2

Rob was instrumental in founding the project as well.

3

Part of this may just be that people rarely ask about each other’s jobs. Since I work in AI safety, asking about my job and asking about this worry are the same thing.

4

ControlAI has an international version.

5

There is also the sister site aisafety.com, which focuses on action rather than information.

6

Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor see it differently: they argue the hack got little attention because AI isn’t a salient topic, hacks are routine news, and no ordinary people were harmed, and they credit Coxon’s resignation itself with the breakthrough. I agree with their last reason, which is this section’s hypothesis, but I find it hard to explain why Coxon landed when earlier resignations didn’t, unless the hack had primed people.

7

He didn’t use the term P(doom). I recall him asking point blank, “Just how likely are we to be f*cked by AI?”

8

You can find villains if you want (the AI companies racing ahead, Marc Andreessen, China), but they are not especially compelling to a wide audience.

9

There are also fears about water use, but I’m quite confident these are mostly fake.
