essays.title: Higher salaries in AI safety
essays.html:
The salaries are too damn low

  1. AI safety has a salary overhang. A bunch of people are paid way below their market rate. (Also true of EA, but I’ll lump them under “AI safety” for this piece).

  2. This has been getting a bit better, very recently — I hear about eg Redwood Research technical talent making ~$800k/y in salary. But when you compare this to the $10-100m/y comp packages for talent in labs, it still seems kind of low. And CG’s money cannon has fired very few shots to date — maybe ~15 orgs hit, see Trace — so the raises are still very unequally distributed.

  3. It’s not just rank-and-file employees, by the way. Even the leadership is grossly underpaid. The numbers I hear range from $150k - $600k/y, for execs at top orgs like METR, MATS, FAR.AI, Constellation. Like, c’mon, I made $250k/y total comp as a undistinguished new grad software engineer in 2016 Google. For the leaders of preeminent safety orgs, surely we can do better than that.

  4. If I were a conspiracy theorist, I might say that “accepting lower salaries” is a psyop from funders.

  5. Low salaries mean that employees and execs remain beholden to funders, rather than having the independence to work on what makes their heart sing. For me, hitting FIRE early in my tech career allowed me to quit my job and work on side projects and startups. To this day, I feel more independent from the “AI safety hivemind” because my paycheck doesn’t depend on it.

  6. Paying low salaries is also penny-wise, pound-foolish from the perspective of funders & orgs. It means that great talent ends up choosing not to work in safety roles. A lot of the safety brain drain is because the labs are bidding much higher.

  7. Also, funder <> org <> employee values are much more aligned within AI safety than in the wider world. Much of what these employees might buy with extra money are things that would be good by the lights of the funder & the org — eg donating to charities or other important causes. (Orgs could offer large donation matches in lieu of cash to enforce this, though I think donation matches have their own problems.)

  8. In practice, one big problem might be that the employees themselves don’t really know what they’re worth. My kingdom for a levels.fyi of AI safety.

  9. AI safety people like to point out that frontier lab employees currently have some leverage over their leaders, and should use this leverage to advocate for good policies (eg pace), before they’re all automated away by AI. I’d point out that AI safety employees themselves are in similarly precarious positions. How long before automated AI safety researchers?

  10. One scheme I’m fond of is “lab employee union (but, good)”. Similarly, it might be interesting to have an “AI safety employee union (but, good)”.

… or are they fine, actually?

  1. One pushback against higher salaries is they’re already pretty high, for the reference class of nonprofit work. Like $100k/y might be enough to cover living costs and help individuals build up some savings, even in high cost of living locations like SF/DC/NYC/London. But, idk, I want safety people to feel safe, and thrive, and have babies.

  2. Some argue that offering lower salaries leads to more mission-oriented employees. I think there’s some truth to this, but also some amount of cope. And this kind of reasoning can let an org undercount the opportunity cost of its people, causing internal & ecosystem-wide misallocation of talent. So put your money where your mouth is!

  3. Maybe it looks bad somehow, if nonprofit employees & execs are making $1m+/y? To that, I’d say: a) stop creating nonprofits, b) inform your critics about how much the labs are pay, and c) maybe just don’t worry so much about looking bad.

  4. IMO the strongest pushback for safety executives, specifically, is that they already have a large amount of steering power, from their ability to direct the org budget & hire people. (This is partly why I’ve never taken a salary at Manifund. And I do appreciate that Sam Altman roughly does the same.)

Gigabrained compensation

  1. Impact equity would solve many of these salary considerations. (Apologies to the choir for the preaching.) Equity allocation is what allowed the startup ecosystem flourish — and now, the frontier lab ecosystem too. The “do good” space is immensely hobbled by nonprofit charity norms.

  2. BTW, one reason we love regranting is that it corrects for some of the problems introduced by low nonprofit salaries. Great AI safety people get the funds and the mandate to go around “angel investing” into new good opportunities.

  3. Beyond higher salaries, I’m tentatively in favor of a UBI or pension for AI safety people. Maybe: $50k/y paid out to forever, to anyone who meets certain objective thresholds, eg 6+ months of fulltime safety employment or funding. I’d hope for a renaissance where individuals feel empowered to move, quit, fund weird things, explore and start little projects.

    This wouldn’t be that expensive! I’d guess 10k people might qualify currently, so this would cost $500M/y — peanuts, compared to Anthropic wealth. Obviously there’s room to do design this better, but I think UBI should be one baseline for “how to distribute Anthropic wealth”. (I don’t know that current funding structures even beat this baseline.)

essays.title: Against Against SURA
essays.html:
Scott: the Against SURA essay is well-written, but it is lacking on the merits.

Do you think that at the current level of capabilities, six months would be sufficient to solve alignment of superintelligences? Maybe you think that 6 months would be sufficient in a year? You don’t spell this out; it would be great if you did.

The race can be stopped. If the government had any idea what’s going on, it would be stopped already. Hell, if the *Chinese* government had any idea what’s going on, they’d stop the race: governments can stop unilaterally, then exercise all of their soft and hard power to stop others while using technology to avoid escalation. (See MAIM.)

Among companies, one doesn’t even have to stop unilaterally; that alone wouldn’t prevent extinction. They do need to stop lying to politicians and the public. They need to start saying what the situation is. They need to start advocating for everyone pausing simultaneously, and advocating for the governments to pause everyone on the planet.

They’re not doing that.

Employees who care about the existential threat have close to zero political power in any of the AI companies, and they’ll have less of that power in the future. Their track record is very bad.

The leadership of these companies is clueless and useless. I’m sure you know many people who regularly converse with them. They’re not going to be convinced by anyone who’s x-risk-pilled. Sam tells people Anthropic puts out a lot of false papers about AI safety. Dario says they’re taking a lot of costly actions while zero of their costly actions are directed specifically at reducing the existential threat. (Demis is now a chair.)

You state the “questionable assumptions” and promise to challenge them, but you’re arguing against a strawman of a platform, not against the strongest arguments and views advocating for leaving capability roles at AI companies. You’re also disagreeing with many of the people who advocate for leaving capability roles at AI companies on how likely alignment is to be solved without a pause.

You have not engaged with many reasons why people might want to leave, such as incentivizing companies to change their behavior and work hard to keep other safety-conscious employees.

from people accidentally shoehorning themselves into a mass-politics-shaped container, which forbids subtlety and demands clear villains.

Reversed stupidity isn’t intelligence; sometimes, people are doing something evil, and one can truthfully call them out on that without much subtlety.

I think at the core of the real crux here is the single question that really determines your views on this issue: is alignment solvable just before superintelligence given a few months of effort of a leading AI company? It’s unfortunate that you give so little attention to the question central to your worldview, instead focusing on finding (often locally invalid) justifications for the consequences of your view on that question.

(See also Daniel Kokotajlo’s response, TsviBT’s response, and Zvi’s response.)

Is Plan C doomed? Is alignment doomed?

Many other sections in your post contain terrible arguments; this one doesn’t. Here I think you’re just wrong, so in this reply, I won’t write at length (although an expanded discussion of this section could be useful for resolving our actual disagreements).

You say that AIs “inherit” virtue from pretraining, and then get corrupted by RLVR, which teaches them power-seeking.

This is not a problem with RLVR specifically. Pretraining installs the machinery that humans might have: for understanding the world, having goals, and selecting actions that achieve those goals. Doing RL reuses a lot of that machinery. But as you train a sufficiently capable system further, if it’s aware it’s in training, it will reward-maxx regardless of its goals, for instrumental reasons, which means gradient descent stops being able to care about what is happening to AI’s goals, and so there’s nothing preserving the goal-contents of the system.

(We know that in general, it is likely that a state of AI at some point during training does not necessarily have much influence on the state of AI later on; internal mechanisms can shift and radically change; what matters is the global optimum.)

Anthropic’s evaluation of Claude’s niceness is, according to METR, not very likely to notice that a version of Claude is actually not nice; and Anthropic does not have any means of fixing what goals Claude acquires, because we don’t really know how to fix the problem I just outlined, and many other problems that also end up being deadly if you’re dealing with superintelligence.

I further do not believe that if AI companies decide to burn their lead to solve alignment, any amount of political power at these companies will belong to anyone remotely competent to understand and actually make a good attempt to address those problems.

It’s not about better AI psychology, it’s about the technical means we completely lack.

All six of these forecasters (the five AIFP people plus the AI) implicitly believed that if humanity survived, it was more likely to be because something in the Plan C supercategory (B/C+/C/D) worked than because a global pause worked

Considering probabilities of having ended up pursuing different strategies, conditional on survival, is EDT of the kind even EDT supporters wouldn’t endorse.

You’re talking about P(strategy|survival).

Instead, you should consider the actual consequences of your decisions (and the decisions of those similar to you): Does unilaterally pausing increase the chance of a pause treaty, and how much? If you don’t unilaterally pause, does this increase the chance of surviving without the pause treaty, and how much?

What matters is the difference in the chance of survival that various strategies cause. We should be arguing about P(survival|do(strategy)).

I'm too uncertain on what determines morality to say anything about it with confidence, but the analogy that comes to mind is consumer use of AI, especially by safety organizations.

If no consumer ever used AI products, then AI companies wouldn't make any money, they would go bankrupt, and we would not get dangerous superintelligence. Therefore, it seems like maybe you and I (and especially organizations working on AI safety) should boycott consumer AI products.

Deontology isn’t about making choices that, if everyone else also makes them, lead to better consequences.

Deontology is about locally abstaining from choices that tend to be of the kind that leads to bad consequences even when, in a specific case, it’s not obvious the consequences would be bad.

Use of AI products does, of course, indirectly fuel the AI race; but it’s not locally evil. Using AI does not kill anyone. AI companies could provide AIs of the current level without racing to kill everyone; in that situation, paying for AI would not be bad in any significant way. So: the consequences of this choice are not local and depend on the choices of AI companies.

Boycotting the products of those who do bad things is great, but it is not a deontological moral responsibility.

If a toy factory produces a product using labor of slaves it threatens to kill if they refuse to work, you shouldn’t buy toys from that factory; that’s a straightforward deontological constraint, of the kind where if you consider pros and cons and decide to violate it, the consequences will be negative. If a car factory’s owner spends the profits on eating meat, your choice to boycott that car factory and not buy cars from it to not support the owner’s meat-eating is commendable, but deontology does not dictate it, and allows weighting pros and cons.

Racing to create a smarter-than-human AI that would kill everyone is, I think, much worse than buying from a factory that sometimes kills its slaves.

The mental gymnastics you are going through here to pretend you’re not saying anything about morality with confidence while trying to convince the reader with an invalid analogy is very disappointing.

I think people feel insufficient terror at this strategy. It amounts to "let's put all of our hopes for survival through non-pause strategies in a giant pile, and then set that pile on fire, in the hope that the pretty flames catch people's attention and make them more interested in a pause." It might in theory be net positive, but this is the sort of thing that you would only want to conclude after extremely careful analysis, of a type that I so far haven't seen

Turns out, straightforward reasoning here is just correct, without the need for a lot of extremely careful analysis.

Jacob Coxon, whose presence in capability roles at either OpenAI or Anthropic probably didn’t contribute much to how safe the world is, left Anthropic and honestly spoke about his beliefs. Turns out, a hope that “pretty flames” would catch people’s attention would’ve been very justified!

I’d also be curious to hear how Jacob leaving Anthropic burned your hopes for survival through non-pause strategies. I’d be surprised if you really, truly think that it was bad for humanity’s chances for survival.

It’d also be very surprising if you think that one person loudly leaving an AI company is the optimal amount of people leaving, and the next one marginally increases the chance of survival via pause less than they decrease the chance of survival via their AI company doing good things or having more time to burn to solve alignment or whatever else is the good produced by them staying.

I asked FutureSearch to estimate the Epoch Capabilities Index of the top model on 12/31/2030, depending on whether Anthropic quit the race today. It said that Anthropic leaving the race decreased 2030 capabilities from 230 -> 222. This is equivalent to their absence slowing things down by six months during just over four years, or 12%.

Isn’t this, like, very good in your lights? Other companies being able to spend more time on getting alignment of superintelligences right sounds like a thing you’d be very excited about! And six months sounds close to the distance between leading safety-pilled companies and everyone else; wouldn’t stretching the time this way double the effort a company is able to put into aligning superintelligence?

Suppose that none of DeepMind, OpenAI, or Anthropic were founded, and the transformer was not invented, for fifty years - so all of this is happening in the late 2060s and early 2070s. Do we gain anything from this fifty years of extra timeline?

I know of many people who became very interested in AI safety as a result of HPMOR, read papers on eg logical induction, and would want to work on this fascinating problem and attempt to solve things like agent foundations because of how interesting they are.

50 years would allow a huge amount of talented people to attempt to solve this problem.

Additionally, I think solving some of these problems is necessary for getting to a superintelligence safely; and some of them probably have high serial time requirements.

(Also, 8+ billion people living for 50 years more would be good.)

Of pro-Bores spending, about 60-80% came from Anthropic and its employees

Do we know that it increased Bores’ chances of winning, rather than hurting them by making voters think he’s a pawn in a battle between Big Tech companies (as other candidates accused him)?

Note also that Anthropic’s contributions to the Public First network of super PACs were not actually used by the super PACs; they shielded other donors from having to be publicly disclosed. No corporate money from Anthropic was used in elections. (Because Anthropic is a federal contractor.)

Employees can at this point cash out their shares and donate regardless of whether they stay at the company.

You might also be surprised that Foushee, a candidate whom Leading The Future (the pro-AI super PAC network Greg Brockman donated to) planned to support and prepared an ad for, ended up being supported by Public First (Anthropic-aligned network) instead. From NYT:

Mr. Carson [who runs Public First] had an intermediary pass along a message to Leading the Future: Don’t you dare.

If Leading the Future got involved, Public First was out, he warned, according to two people with knowledge of the conversation, who insisted on anonymity to discuss the private exchange.

Leading the Future later backed away — never airing a pro-Foushee ad that it had already produced, the people said. Public First spent $1.6 million, Ms. Foushee squeaked by in her primary race and Mr. Carson’s super PAC claimed some credit for the victory.

The candidate Foushee beat for the nomination opposed datacenters.

The impact of Anthropic’s money is, at least sometimes, pretty bad!

Greg Brockman recently stopped funding Leading The Future, supposedly after pressure from pro-regulation OpenAI employees, but I think this just highlights my point

I imagine most of these people wouldn’t leave OpenAI even if your post said that was a good idea. Many people have beliefs that p(doom) is very low; they think regulation is still the right thing to have; they would not be moved by your post in the direction of leaving; the fight is not over those people.

It’s unclear how much political power people who would potentially leave OpenAI have at OpenAI, and what amount of Shapley value they hold in Greg Brockman’s decision to stop giving money to LTF.

Since the goal of SURA is to get all alignment-pilled people and companies out of the industry, it would result in more Greg Brockmans funding the anti-regulation side, and fewer Anthropics funding the pro-regulation side.

Anti-regulation AI companies would always have more money than the pro-regulation side. Our only weapon, that wins despite this asymmetry, is truth; the public and elected officials side with us after considering all the arguments.

So: While Anthropic is marginally pro-regulation, it continues to not take actions that negatively impact its bottom line (e.g., Jack Clark lied about the earlier version of Bores’ bill) even when that would benefit humanity as a whole, and it’s unclear what the sign of Anthropic’s election spending is.

Would they have preferred a world where all of these people quit the day before, and letters like this never got written?

Arguably, if 1368 people who signed the pacing letter instead left AI companies in a way similar to Jacob Coxon, the news would be a lot louder.

They could still write and sign the letter after leaving.

The difference between a 10th percentile company here (would have tried to hide the whole thing, or disguise it behind a one line statement, and wouldn't have let METR/Redwood in at all) and a 90th percentile (would have given us the full deal, including things we don't know about now) would have been transformative

The highest-percentile company in practice (Anthropic) is competent enough to not experience Hugging Face-like incidents (though not competent enough to produce AI that, when placed in a similar environment, doesn’t take similar misaligned actions); we wouldn’t get evidence about how the whole thing is going if OpenAI had better security.

It’s also unclear what exactly is your model here. My impression is that the leadership at OpenAI got spooked, and then got further spooked once METR sifted through the logs. Do you think it’s the normal safety-conscious employees of OpenAI who caused it to be in a better percentile and let METR/Redwood in?

how to maximize transparency and therefore warning shot number

Do you truly think that if Anthropic stopped training models and shut down its AI r&d, and directed all of its resources at telling the world about the situation and demanding transparency from everyone, this would not lead to increasing the transparency of AI companies? In your opinion, does staying at a company, as an average capability researcher, really make the situation better than leaving loudly?

Coxon’s resignation is more complex. The good did come from him resigning, which directly presses against my point that we shouldn't be pressuring people to resign from AI companies.

Thanks for acknowledging this.

But nobody cares that I, who was never in an AI company, continue to not be in an AI company. The media cared about Jacob because if you work for Anthropic, that automatically gives your opinion more weight

Media cares about Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares and many others.

But yes, I agree, and have told many people, that the one good reason to join an AI company is that you can loudly leave.

if everyone like Evan had quit, this couldn't have happened

If they all left *now*, do you expect the amount of noise would’ve been lower than the amount in response to Jacob Coxon’s resignation? Do you think that absence of support of others, because all of them left, would change this?

But if the US pauses unilaterally, it destroys its main bargaining chip, which is that China is currently on track to lose the AI race

No. Our main bargaining chip is that in a world where the US understands the situation and pauses unilaterally, it would be willing to escalate to prevent China from reaching superintelligence, including via cyberattacks and various other means available to a state actor, both plausibly-deniably and in open; China would be incentivized to cooperate to transparently show it’s not building superintelligence, enjoy the same assurances from the US, and continue to do narrow AI.

(China is not presently aware it’s on track to lose the race to superintelligence, and it’s not aware of the consequences of that.)

In a world where the US demonstrates its seriousness by unilaterally pausing, China does not think it can assume victory; it understands that without verification, the US would resume at any time and still win; it understands that the US possesses means to stop progress in China; the US would also presumably stop selling chips to China or provide models that can be distilled.

For comparison, consider if America had started arms control negotiations with Russia by saying "We've just destroyed all our nukes - now please destroy your nukes too."

In a world where nukes can be a decisive strategic advantage, that would not be a good idea.

Transparently unilaterally pausing building anti-ballistic missiles and asking Russia “please don’t build or deploy yours, let’s have a treaty about this” wouldn’t produce the same consequences.

Unilaterally pausing AI is like unilaterally pausing ABMs, except that you still have nukes that work even if the other side continues for a while to deploy ABMs.

(With real ABMs, both sides are heavily incentivized to make sure no one has them and enjoy resulting strategic stability. AIs are very similar to ABMs, given the situational awareness. See MAIM.)

I asked the AI superforecaster to predict the effect of the US passing the Sanders/Casar bill today on the likelihood of China agreeing to a pause in the next year. It said it would increase it from 1% to 7%

The US actually working hard to prevent superintelligence anywhere in the world looks very different from the US simply passing this bill.

Anthropic replaces this politics coordinator with a great, alignment-pilled politics coordinator who really cares a lot about getting things right

I hate the motte-and-bailey happening here. The discussion is primarily about capability researchers working at the labs. I don’t think you can find a single person advocating for stopping unilaterally and advocating for global pause saying that someone who works at Anthropic on communicating the situation and advocating for a pause should leave — because they’d be doing exactly what these companies should be doing, and are not contributing to AI capabilities. A politics coordinator like that is among the very few people those you argue against would agree should stay and continue their work instead of leaving.

We don't hesitate to notice and protest when AI companies are much worse than even our low expectations

I think mostly people protest when AI companies are racing to a superintelligence that will kill everyone, not when they’re marginally worse than that.

Of course, protests try to provide a good local incentive gradient, which has to do with what these companies normally are and how they deviate from that, but the main goal of people attending the protests is to shape whether the companies are racing to kill everyone, not shape what fraction of compute is spent on superalignment.

The people I know who joined AI companies seem like the same people they were before

There are now some essays about how being at an AI company shapes your concern about x-risk.

activism is hardly known for being a paradise of epistemic virtue

This is a skill issue. (And perhaps a sign that most important issues activism could be directed at are already solved in the US.)

Most progress has come from people like Frodo who understood the risks of these paths but did them anyway.

Probably false for AI companies; people who understand the risks mostly don’t join them.

If you disagree, we can look at what fraction of people who anticipated incidents on the level of Hugging Face etc. wanted to join AI companies vs didn’t want to join AI companies.

I dunno, mass politics is also looking kind of annular

As a view becomes more common, people will of course argue for bad versions of it in bad ways, they will not have thought through the reasons for some of their held beliefs, etc.; this has no impact on the validity of the position. Reversed stupidity continues to not be intelligence.

Convergent evolution is trying to carcinize us into yet another political-movement-shaped crab

Idk, it does not seem to me like the community has undergone a sufficient contact with the broader world to be optimized towards a political-movement-shaped crab. People who want to make a political movement out of it could be pattern-matching to other political movements’ rhetoric, but they wouldn’t be the result of convergent evolution.

I’d be curious to hear your arguments why any of the things in the list are specifically a political-movement-shaped crab thing, rather than a widely-held-belief-about-a-bad-thing thing.

Because arguments are soldiers, people feel licensed to retaliate against anyone who believes the "wrong" arguments . When I posted an earlier (and admittedly less-polished, and more vehement) version of these concerns to social media, I had an organization that had previously given me lots of free help with Astral Codex Ten state that they would now be charging me money (albeit still at a 90% discount) because they thought I might be causing harm. Although they're under no obligation to give me free labor, and I'm grateful that they ever did, I do think this is a warning sign that conditions are ripe for preference cascades and evaporative cooling.

Note that this is not because you believe the wrong arguments; it’s because they think you might be causing harm. There’s a difference.

I also think it’s not a good look that you’re complaining about people who stop helping you because they think you might be causing harm as an argument. Like, if they’re wrong, you can argue with them about it; but I think fundamentally, it’s good to not provide services, especially heavily discounted services, to those who do harm.

My group house has a restriction on how many parties you can attend if you work at a frontier lab in a non-safety/security role. But I don’t think this created conditions for preference cascades or evaporative cooling: people are not exiled for their views on this issue, they can’t attend as many parties as they’d like because they’re doing something bad and we want to nudge them towards stopping.

if someone disagrees with SURA, or worries too much about race dynamics, then they've either been corrupted by the companies, or are "deferring to" "EA"

I’m not sure how common that is outside of a small chunk of Twitter.

For example, why do we criticize Anthropic more than every other AI company combined?

Because a large reason why it’s been competitive with OpenAI is that a bunch of cracked people with views somewhat similar to ours joined them, and are staying there because of a misguided belief of what the company is. Anthropic can be improved by outside criticism. People at Anthropic sometimes DM me with thanks for the post I made about the company. I don’t think there’s anything that can be written about OpenAI that would lead to anything except likes from roon — it’s not pretending to be good guys. Anthropic is worth disillusioning people about; OpenAI doesn’t really have such properties.

Instead of spending our corporate activism energy telling companies to stop unilaterally, I think we should spend it:

  • first, trying to get companies to agree to stop in a coordinated manner
  • second, if that doesn't work, trying to get companies to prepare for Plan C+/C

In a much better world, these companies would be screaming from the rooftops that everyone should stop in a coordinated manner. The RA part in SURA.

Your post would’ve been much better if you’d named it RARA: Race and Raise Awareness, and argued for that position. Would’ve been a lot more defensible.

essays.title: IQ Shredders vs IQ Incubators
essays.html:
‘IQ shredder’ is a concept coined by Spandrell in a post about Singapore, but which applies more generally to cities that attract high-IQ migrants with economic opportunities and high standards of living. Such global talent hubs, however, tend to have some of the lowest fertility rates, functioning as IQ shredders that hamper the long-run future of the positively selected gene pools they attract. In these cities, human capital can be efficiently cashed out in economic output, but only by significantly diminishing its ability to persist into the future.

But if Singapore is the IQ shredder, where can one find an IQ incubator - something that trades economic output to preserve genetic potential? One candidate surely has to be Mea Shearim in Jerusalem. Mea Shearim is a time capsule, preserving 18th-century shtetl lifestyle, and as good an example as any of Haredi insularity. Mea Shearim is nothing like Singapore. For one, few outsiders are trying to move into Mea Shearim.

But Mea Shearim is probably not a human capital wasteland. Though the Haredim are not known for their economic or scientific contributions, it’s not for lack of cognitive potential. In 2022 PISA exams, “ultra-Orthodox girls scored 474 in mathematics, compared to 473 for secular girls, 454 for religious girls, and 388 for Arab-speaking girls. In reading, ultra-Orthodox girls opened a 12-point gap compared to state-educated girls, and in science they scored 9 points higher than national -religious girls.”

For context, Haredi girls' schools teach roughly 75% of the state core curriculum, have thin oversight, and don't sit the bagrut (standardized tests). The average household income of the Haredim significantly trails that of the broader populace (even after accounting for welfare, etc.). Environmental factors alone would have you predict precisely the opposite result. I suspect these girls—who blew their normie peers out of the water—will likely have a smart kid or six, which is roughly the TFR of the ultra-orthodox in Israel. The Haredim, then, appear to be reproducing a population with considerable cognitive potential, despite and perhaps because Haredi culture itself is inimical to economic productivity.

Intelligence is highly valued in the Haredi world, insofar as verbal intelligence is correlated with excellence in biblical scholarship. Like elite universities, the yeshiva world has a prestige hierarchy, with competitive admissions sorting promising students into institutions that reflect the scholarly caliber of their students and alumni. A boy who studies at a prestigious yeshiva gains status in the marriage market.

I briefly looked into whether this status advantage translates into a reproductive advantage (in relative fecundity) beyond priority in mate selection. This study by Gabriel Gordon tracked the trajectory of 115,696 men who attended Haredi secondary yeshivas and found that men who stay in yeshivas past 40 have almost twice the number of offspring as those who never entered post-secondary kollel. For this to be evidence of positive selection for intelligence, we'd have to assume that men who remain in religious study longer are positively selected for intelligence themselves (I suspect this is true but haven't validated it.)

The Haredi world thus has a status hierarchy that rewards intelligence and may even confer a reproductive advantage on those who possess it. But more importantly, even if the community isn’t positively selecting for intelligence at the current margin, what it does incredibly effectively is encourage and preserve high-fertility norms. The fertility gradient across Israeli society tracks religiosity, with the Haredim on one end and secular Israelis on the other, with a TFR that’s just below replacement. Religiosity in turn tracks the strength of fertility norms. Over half of Haredi women in Israel marry before their 21st birthdays. The community is strategically Luddite about reproductive tech, maintaining strong sanctions against birth control while being somewhat tolerant of fertility-enhancing technologies like IVF.

Now consider the relationship between IQ and fertility in the modern globalized world. IQ is a useful currency for acquiring status both via material wealth and via paths that involve knowledge production or other creative pursuits. The Singapore example evokes images of a high-stress rat race. But the modern world offers ways to convert IQ into status via paths that aren’t nearly as stressful (e.g. academia). However, the Steven Pinkers and Terence Taos of the world aren't busy repopulating the earth in their free time. Why?

Because the status hierarchies of global cosmopolitan culture are largely decoupled from the evolutionary pressures that historically shaped human societies. It’s not so much that the global monoculture means everyone is necessarily competing in the same status hierarchies. You could be an Effective Altruist, for example, in which case you care about approval from other Effective Altruists and not about maximizing wealth. But Effective Altruism has has grown by persuading new people to become effective altruists, not by having its existing members produce and raise the next generation of effective altruists. As a result, its cultural success has not depended on rewarding behaviors conducive to reproduction.

Both worlds reward intelligence, but in the Haredi world, status is embedded in a culture that also demands reproduction. A smart Torah scholar who chooses to stop at kid no. 1 will probably face social sanction, however prestigious his yeshiva credentials. In the modern secular world, on the other hand, intellectual achievement can confer status without any corresponding expectation of reproduction.

The global monoculture is not a single culture per se, but a social environment in which individuals can participate in any number of status hierarchies without belonging to a culture that needs to reproduce itself. It is what remains after the dissolution of traditional cultures, most of which put up half a fight against modernity and basically lost. Haredi Judaism, however, is itself an adaptation to modernity. The Jewish Enlightenment in Europe provoked something of an immune response, and these traditionalist communities reinforced their boundaries and developed institutions to resist assimilation into the wider society.

Maintaining a radically different social equilibrium from the global monoculture necessitates both insularity and exit costs. From the perspective of the Haredim, the outside world is not a different culture with equally strong but different norms. The outside world is simply an activation of individual choice over social norms. Cultural osmosis must thus be forcefully restrained, while also making it costly for individuals to opt out of the community.

In the ultra-Orthodox world, where marriages are arranged through families and matchmakers, siblings of deserters can have their marital prospects harmed as a result. Similarly, this channel can be used to punish things like smartphone use, which is itself a risk factor for cultural osmosis from the outside. Insularity is a powerful weapon because insularity itself makes insularity easier to enforce. The more insular the community already is, the cheaper it becomes to punish defection by imposing social costs that can’t easily be borne by someone with little social capital or cultural cache outside the community.

This incubator in Israel, however, is sustained by a tax base and protected by a military to which it contributes relatively little. The incubator is, in a sense, free-riding on the shredder. But equally, the shredder needs human capital to shred, some of which has to come from attrition out of the incubator. Currently, the attrition rate is a rounding error (10–15% per generation) relative to the difference in fertility between a population that’s barely replacing itself and one that’s roughly tripling every generation. However, if you’re tempted to solve for a higher attrition rate, you risk breaking the incubator. And this is all assuming that solving for this is even remotely interesting to two radically different cultures that share little in the way of a common vision for the future.

essays.title: what good is an infirmary to an unwitting patient
essays.html:
I’ve made myself an infirmary for men who don’t know they’re unwell. A sanctuary for men who aren’t seeking refuge.

None of them asked me to. That’s the part I keep coming back to. In all the years of loving people who were hard to be with, I’ve never once had a man ask me for grace or patience, or even acknowledge that I was giving it to him. I just invited them into a space they didn’t ask for, made up the bed, handed them a cup of tea, and offered a love that was steadfast and dutiful, as if a place to rest would somehow be what healed them.

There was always some illusion that they got better after me. At some stage the relationship would end, usually because I had burnt myself out by giving more than I was receiving for far too long. Usually, I’d have started to pull back my energy to conserve it, and they’d resent me for no longer being endlessly available.

Usually, they would be convinced that all of our relationship ills were my doing, that we could fix us if only I’d fix me. And “fix me” meant going back to being physically, sexually, and emotionally attentive, of course.

And so, more than once, I felt like the infirmary. Like I’d been the place they recovered so they could move into the next relationship and be more for someone else. More attentive, more nurturing, more available. As if I had been a waiting room. A rehabilitation centre. A place men passed through on the way to their happily-ever-after, where they had a family with someone they took seriously.

(Five of them had a child with the person right after me, though hand on my heart, I promise you there’s never been a moment I wished it were me making a father of any of them.)

We never know what’s happening behind the closed doors of anyone else’s partnership, just as no one knew what was happening in any of mine. But having a family doesn’t make a person serious, or mature. And having spent years bandaging men’s wounds that needed cauterising, I know that leaving a relationship sure you’ve done nothing wrong is unlikely to initiate any growth.

Ward in the Hospital at Arles (1889)

I grew up in a home with a man who had been bleeding out since long before I was born, which gave me a high tolerance for asymmetry, and for my own suffering. I learned very early to put myself aside and make room for another person no matter what they were. Even as an adult, I didn’t notice that I wasn’t asking for anything in return, or, more importantly, that not much was being offered.

It’s taken me a long time to stop being my mother, and to stop believing somewhere inside me that this is what love looks like.

Here’s what I’ve come to believe: it isn’t about whether someone has wounds. Everyone does. Even those of us who have done a lot of work are still wounded, because wounds don’t really go away. Heal, and you’ll still have scars that tell the story, and that’s just part of the topography of a life lived.

The question is whether you can see yours, and whether you move through the world in a way that accounts for them. Whether you govern yourself accordingly. Whether you see that you’re bleeding, and if so, whether you’re dabbing it with gauze or ready to bite a strap for the good of the suture.

I see now I should have asked myself about these men:

Does he know where he’s wounded?

Does he know how?

Does he understand how his past filters his experience of the present?

And, perhaps more crucially: how does he believe his wounds entitle him to behave?

Some people don’t think of their worst traits as wounds at all, just qualities. Preferences. Essences.

I’m just particular.
I’m just private.
Can’t we just do something nice and forget about it?
I don’t like talking about this stuff.
That’s just how I am.

Once it’s a quality rather than a wound (or a response to one), there’s nothing to work on. Everyone else is expected to absorb it, or give it a wide berth.

There have been others, but my last relationship dulled a part of my spirit that I’m still trying to recover. He hid my things in the back of the closet when people would come over. He would give me the silent treatment for a week or more if I was late calling him while visiting my family, or if I stopped for a coffee with our mutual friends who lived next door to him. He stormed out of the house and wouldn’t speak to me when I tried to start a calm conversation about our sex life, and toward the end would hold it against me that we weren’t having sex anymore.

I tried to name these things. To acknowledge that we had different conflict styles, that he was naturally more avoidant, that he got flooded when we broached meaningful conversations. That sometimes he couldn’t talk about things and shut down, and that was okay (if he was regrouping to come back together and talk about it). I tried to give him room to be himself, and offered different ways we could practise actually communicating. But he could never even acknowledge that there was anything he struggled with. It was just how he was, and so it was just how things would be.

I admit I still carry a tremendous amount of shame for the times I chose to tolerate behaviour I should have had a boundary around. I made excuses on his behalf so he hardly needed to. I’ve been a career defence attorney.

Looking back, the men I respect most are the ones who owned it with me, either at the time or later.

I’m afraid to be honest. This conversation is scary for me because I don’t know how you’re going to receive this. I made a mistake and I should have told you, but I just wasn’t sure how you’d take it and it felt better not to say anything. I was wrong, and I’m sorry.

It didn’t automatically make them good partners. It didn’t give us the tools to navigate these things, and some of it I never heard until long after our relationship had ended, when they told me they were grateful for me and that they hadn’t shown up the way they felt I (or we) deserved.

I respect the people who can reflect on themselves. Who are neither governed by their imperfections nor threatened by them.

When there’s no cost of admission, no cost of proximity, good intentions don’t read as a gift. They read as the simple state of play. People can behave however they want, without adhering to any standard, and keep getting what they want.

I’ve done a lot of explaining on other people’s behalf, and not even strictly with romantic partners. I’ve had times where I’ve been attached to close friends and told myself there were reasons to stick around, to lighten up, to stop overthinking.

He’s inconsistent because he’s busy.
He’s distant because he’s afraid.
He’s cruel because his mother was unkind.
He can’t talk about things because he just doesn’t know how yet. It’s okay.

I’d work out where they were wounded and where it came from, and make the concessions before they ever had to. Sometimes I was even right, but that never mattered. I’d already forged their signature on the intake paperwork, and they never knew they’d been admitted.

I thought I was making a safe space for them to heal, but I was making the perfect petri dish for them to never need to.

There’s a difference between staying and loving someone while they stumble through their attempts to grow, and removing so much friction that growing becomes optional. Patience with a person who hasn’t also devoted themselves to the cause is just a hall pass for bad behaviour. Being accommodating, patient, or forgiving can look like love while it keeps someone in a state of arrested development.

It’s the same with apologies. A person who continually apologises for the same thing and yet keeps doing it somewhere believes they’re entitled to do it as long as they tick the remorse boxes afterward. Maybe they were taught that a half-hearted apology tour was enough to erase responsibility. But as adults, we all have to recognise the difference between what we’re accustomed to and what we’re entitled to.

Forgiveness and loyalty don’t feel like gifts when they were never named as gifts. The men who look back on me don’t see themselves as having done me wrong, because they felt entitled to what I gave them without ever having to ask, and so saw it as a rug pull when I couldn’t keep giving without receiving.

People who can’t see themselves in their entirety will never see you in yours.

I often make concessions with the people I care about, and (with better discernment) I hope I never lose that willingness. I do truly think that’s part of loving someone, being flexible enough to allow them to be who they are.

But people also have a responsibility to get over themselves if they love you. If they respect you. If they want you to flourish.

Expecting another person to do that is also a profound act of love.

You owe it to yourself to have boundaries, but you also owe it to another person to let them reckon with the choices they make.

People very rarely change of their own volition. They change because they see the cost of staying the same. It’s honourable to offer a genuine safe haven to someone doing their work. It’s self-sacrificial to offer it to someone who’s wilfully ignorant, or more invested in arguing for why they should stay the same.

(Here’s an easy sign they’re more invested in staying the same than in loving you: when you share something that’s bothering you, they tell you that upsets them rather than getting curious about what happened to cause you to feel that way.)

You can’t love someone into healing. You can’t lead them there by example, either. What you invest has to be proportional to their ability to see what needs healing, and what they’re actively doing about it.

Maybe I’m naive, but I think a relationship is about wanting to transcend yourself.

We all have flaws. The point is to bring more attention to them, not less, so you can become a better version of yourself, because the person beside you inspires you to be better, and do better.

And when you see you’ve hurt them, if you love them more than your ego, you let go of what you intended. Your intentions don’t count for much if the outcome is their pain.

I believe one of the most crucial skills in a long-term relationship is not only being able to see yourself, but being able to see yourself through your loved one’s eyes. To understand that two things can be true at once: you meant well, and you hurt them.

We often spend too much time trying to be understood, and not enough time trying to understand. But how can you be close with someone who can’t receive you?

How you are is who you are. It doesn’t matter if you’re a good person inside if you’re doing bad things. Or if you’re well-intentioned but spend more time justifying your right to stay the same than trying to change.

I’m closing the infirmary. Not the sanctuary. I still want to be somewhere a person can come up for air and take refuge, because I think that’s what it is to care about someone. To give them room to unfold.

But if I could give any advice to both past and future me, it’s that space is limited, and admission is affordable, but it isn’t free. The cost of admission is kindness, willingness, reciprocity, and courage.

And sorry, we’re a shoes-off establishment. Leave your boots and armour at the door. I can’t have you tracking mud in the house.

essays.title: Vibe Research
essays.html:
Two weeks ago, AI exposed two economists as error-prone.

After an “anonymous auditor” made the site, Tyler Cowen shared it, saying:

I am not even sure what to say at this point. We need a radical revaluation of this work, and of the associated policy arguments. More generally, this is only a single step in the story of how AI is going to revise economic science, and indeed past research more generally.

Elon Musk’s X account found it and amplified it.

Said AI audit reported 147 problems it deemed “serious enough to change a headline number” in the work of Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman.

https://saez-zucman-eaudit-replication.vercel.app/original.html

Anyone familiar with these tools knows that they can produce results that appear plausible but are unverified vibe-coded slop – and this work matches this pattern.

Though the audit may be directionally correct (it’s hard to sift through Zucman and Saez’s work without the sense that their work is tilted), and I expect several of its findings to hold up, it’s of little direct epistemic value itself.

See criticism of the report from Zucman:

If 90% of the major errors are not major errors at all, that calls into question the etiquette or effectiveness of spreading it. But if it’s really true that 10% of the major errors are, in fact, errors, that’s clearly a worthy finding – if someone can find them.

Its primary value may be as an existence proof. Indeed, this is only “a single step in the story of how AI” will impact past and future research. The question I’m interested in here is how to move in the right direction – how can you make vibe research more effective?

Software engineering is the obvious place to look for patterns.

Let’s think through a standard flow for companies that have infused AI into their workflows. Not frontier labs – which may provide an unrealistic model – but effective companies spending low thousands of dollars per engineer per month. Such flows provide a benchmark, if not an ideal.

Consider the flow for a given contributor.

1. They develop a change that is presented as a pull request or merge request. Effectively, a draft of code.

2. The draft comes with tests that are supposed to ensure that the change works and doesn’t break anything.

3. This change is then reviewed by AI agents.

4. The change is then reviewed by humans.

5. After review, the change is then “published” and released.

Though there are variations, I think it’s fair to say that’s the common flow (for now). Sometimes the change, if it is not high stakes, may even skip human review.

But if someone pushes a change that looks like AI slop, good engineers are going to request revisions or even block it – especially if it’s an important domain. If that continues as a pattern, the contributor in question should be fired.

And this submission looks like slop, a technical term of art for low-quality AI output with a signature style of AI.

As we go about reassessing the worth of academics with AI, we should reduce the number of slop submissions. Submitting work for others makes work for them, so we should do it thoughtfully.

A few simple rules: less is more, verification is good, and show proof of work. AI can help with each of these things.

Less is more.

The largest tell of slop is undifferentiated quantity. A feature that changes far more lines of code than it should. A long description that is repetitive, vague, and contains a fine mix of irrelevant and obvious information.

AI tools may let you sift through more data, but the results should be crystallized. If an engineer submits more code than the change needs, reviewers ask for it to be:

  • Smaller

  • Better

  • Simpler

  • Validated

Nassim Taleb’s heuristic about argument number sharpens the point:

If someone attacks a book or idea using more than one argument, you know it is not real: nobody says ‘he is a criminal, he killed many people, and he also has bad table manners and bad breath and is a very poor driver.’

And the Pascal line fits as well:

I made this letter longer only because I didn’t have the time to make it shorter.

Quantity is something you want powering research in the background, but for the generated report, something you expect other people to read and judge, it’s often a sign that someone – artificial or organic – didn’t have the skill or time to refine it.

Verification is good.

When reviewing code, we want to know that it works. Evidence for this is provided by a battery of tests, screenshots, and videos.

Automated verification is easier with formal matters. Think Lean math programs: they either compile or don’t. Empirical research is not the same.

But we can also check the inputs. Does the cited paper actually say what the author claims? Are their figures off? Mistakes of interpretation, data accuracy, and basic logical errors can be uncovered and shown. For example, if you say paper Y says X but Y says ~X, show us that in a table.

There should be less tolerance for what cannot be verified. I don’t mean less tolerance for speculative theoretical work, but for choices that make verification harder for reviewers, artificial or organic. If your work isn’t that easy to verify, at least let reviewers see it. Sharing the code and data should be table stakes.

This goes for both original work and audits.

Show proof of work.

Some cryptocurrencies verify transactions through “proof of work” by burning electricity on a brute-force guessing game for the right to add the next block to the ledger. Honesty is expensive.

Researchers should prove that their research involved more investment than a single Claude prompt.

This heuristic isn’t meant to ask workers to burn their time, but to show that they’re worth engaging with.

Software engineers do this by sharing videos of feature walkthroughs, linked pipeline runs against a solid data source, and running their own work against a battery of AI reviewers.

For now, researchers and auditors may want to show that they ran this against several AI reviewers (ideally of a standardized form – not just AI self-review). Given how easy it is to make an “AI audit,” auditors who want to be taken seriously need to do better than put up a Claude artifact.

If you’re not doing something that’s high stakes, you can have less validation, more AI, less oversight, and so on. When we are doing something that’s higher stakes, we really need to verify that the research is correct, and that takes more than three AI runs.

We should shift epistemic standards to perhaps downvote people who make basic mistakes. They’re like the person who makes pull requests with their tests failing. Don’t even look at it until the tests are passing. Life’s too short.

Will you miss out on some good ideas if you do that? Maybe. Someone can get a lot of things wrong, but get one big thing right, and if that big thing really matters, they may win. But they’d be lucky.

essays.title: October Links
essays.html:
I used to write a link roundup to some friends regularly. I’m hoping to get back into the habit, but now for a larger audience!

Karri Saarinen on learning about the local fauna by his Finnish cottage:

I spend part of the summer at a cottage in Finland, by the Baltic Sea. There is all kinds of animal and plant life around, and instead of asking OpenClaw, I bought a couple of books about the local fauna and flora.

Now when I encounter a snake or some other animal, I may already know what it is. And if I don’t, I go back and check the books.

I have small moments like this everyday now, usually less dramatic, that remind me how books have made daily life feel a little more magical.

Karri is the founder of Linear, a software company with some of the best SaaS design out there, and I really like his beliefs on AI.

He deeply understands how to use it, but thinks user interfaces are still important. And this tweet is pretty old (it’s from the spring), but I think it’s aged well: AI can help you shortcut getting something done in a new domain, but it doesn’t replace actually learning it deeply.

In the last few months, I’ve learned to do video editing in CapCut, Premiere, and After Effects. What I’ve found is that while the models are getting better and better at video editing, using them is still like using a hammer where you need a chisel (or, as someone once said, ‘like asking your kid brother to repaint a room.’) In the end, I still had to learn how to use this software to get anything done.

When I think about AI and software, I am reminded a little bit of the sewing machine. I own one and use it for alterations. It’s an extremely effective time-saver, and it can do all sorts of nifty things. But it’s not a panacea. You still often have to hand-sew or at least carefully manipulate a piece of fabric as you feed it through the machine. And similarly, I think SaaS tools will remain important for experts in any domain for a while…

The old world is dying. Occasionally I’m lucky enough to meet extremely agentic people, and Jasmine is one par excellence. But I think it’s telling that she writes about how much joy she found in leaving Stanford, living in the real world, finding an apartment, and being free of the strictures of student life. I think she also might not like institutions very much.

And so in this article, she claims the old world is dying. Every new grad should meet more people, go do something new, work for a startup, ask more questions, and break more rules.

This is a way of working on the West Coast that I really enjoy — that instead of joining an institution, you can create the one you want around you. You can see it in career outcomes. Strong Princeton graduates join Goldman Sachs or Jane Street; strong Stanford graduates… well, it’s hard to generalize, because they all go down their own paths, building their own tiny cultures around them before they subsume the whole world into them.

But I wonder if there’s a bit of ‘this advice is not for everybody’ in this article. Rather than a guide to all new graduates, I would treat it as one for the most high-agency folks. There’s still a lot of alpha in joining a rising institution, playing your cards well get promoted, and getting mentorship from people who have done it before!

Why do Japanese companies do so many different things? Why Japanese companies so often operate as conglomerates that sell all sorts of weird, different things like motorcycles and pianos, when American companies tend to focus on one thing?

David Ok’s argument is that the Japanese system of lifetime employment means that Japanese companies are really run mostly for the benefit of the employees.

They don’t offer high returns to shareholders, have strong unions and few visionary leaders, and are designed to insulate themselves from many outside pressures that might, for instance, require layoffs. Pay for workers, however, is based more on tenure and company performance than individual worker performance. He argues that this made Japan excellent at catch-up growth but also caused it to lag behind anywhere extreme innovation was required.

It’s an interesting argument, but I don’t really have an opinion on this, to be honest. What stuck out to me as I read it was that the J-firms reminded me of Jane Street, a company that roughly operates on the same principles: it trains generalists, is run mostly for the benefit of its employees, and cares more about continuing to exist than returning high amounts to shareholders. I’m not 100% sure what’s going on here. Maybe I’ll write more thoughts a different time…

I love technology, and I love the amazing new devices that Elon Musk wants to bring into the world: brain-computer interfaces, electric cars, spaceships. And yet on the scales of justice, against all the lives they’ve saved or will save are the people he killed by defunding USAID.

I don’t think it’s an easy read, but I think it’s an important one. It’s easy to think of policies only on a global scale. And so I’m grateful for the work done by reporters to find the individual stories, because they hit much harder.

This post on rewriting Bun in Rust is probably meaningless if you are not a software engineer, but if you are, I think it’s one of the best pieces out there on effective coding with AI. There’s still a lot of skill involved! They were successful in rewriting it, but it also took a lot of care to create a system that would let them produce safe, verified code.

I’m reminded a bit of this piece on how LLMs reward expertise, which I also appreciated:

The most important skill in prompting is expertise in the domain you’re prompting for.

It’s about how Terence Tao can pull far more out of LLMs in math than you and I can. It was written before the Navier-Stokes discoveries, but even in those cases I don’t think the LLMs got there without some mathematical guidance — someone had to push the AI into thinking about the right part of the latent space. So far, I don’t find the breathless takes about how AI is automating everyone’s job very convincing. It still seems to me that like it acts as a 10x factor, and that the knowledge of the top domain experts is still really important!
