essays.title: Software Development as Theory Building
essays.html:
Coding agents’ time horizons have been doubling about every 4 months. If the current rate of progress continues, one engineer will be able to build a PostgreSQL-scale system (1.4M LoC) in a 2 week sprint by 2027, and the cost of that build would have fallen from ~$37M of human labor baseline today to low-digit millions in token cost plus human review time in a year…

I continue to believe that much of a firm’s value comes from its “world model”. Software firms tend to be particularly good at generating precise world-models. Put another way— the value in a software org is in its technical world-model, scaled through its codebase across its team and its customers. Consider Peter Naur, in Programming as Theory Building:

Programming […] should be regarded as an activity by which the programmers form or achieve a certain kind of insight, a theory, of the matters at hand.

As software generation scales: comprehension debt & code-to-comprehension ratios star to determine the activities of the next software firm.

For coding tasks, 80% time-horizon has scaled from ~6 mins last year to ~2-4 hours today. As this trend continues, we can expect the following:

Human time vs. Agent time

1. Time horizon: length of a software task, in skilled-human time, that an agent can complete. 2. 80%-time horizon: length of a task an agent finishes successfully 80% of the time.

As a thought experiment, it is worth imagining what kind of ‘software’ these horizons correspond to.

Unprecedented Software

This rising tide brings with it a new datum for ambition & opportunity, with expectations for product surface area and outcomes increasing with every model release. To gauge the outer limits of ambition a new SW firm can tread over the next few years, consider the crude estimations below on resources need to build increasingly complex software.

One-owner threshold: the system size one senior engineer can build in a two week sprint. 

System size by one-owner threshold = p80_model_horizon (H) x typical_lines_per_human-task-hour (75) x chunks_one_human_can_integrate (40)

Production cost

Human baseline

PostgreSQL (1.4M lines) is ~190 engineer-years, costing about $37M (@ $200k per engineer year) today, not accounting for overhead + assuming 7,500 new lines from an avg. human engineer year.

Token cost

PostgreSQL = $7.6M at today’s token prices. 

Cost = 190 engr-yrs (380k hrs) × 2 re-tries x $10/token hour.

Human review time

Assume each code chunk takes 2 hours of review to reasonably integrate. Anecdotally a human owner can maintain context for up to a fortnight, therefore 40 is the number of concurrent work items a tech lead can hold a coherent “theory” of (in Naur’s sense). This is also in the range of what one maintainer handles on a busy open-source project.

Until horizons lengthen considerably, and one-owner threshold is met, multiple owners are needed and coordination overhead dominates the costs of review.

Human review cost scaling 

Total review time:= A (num_chunks × 2 h review per chunk) × B review time scaled by chunk size (chunk lines ÷ 1,500)^αlpha(=0.5) × C review time scaled by system size (system lines ÷ 100k)^k(=0.2) × D review time scaled by coordination pairs (1 + 0.02 × pairs)

  • B. Chunk-size

    Larger chunks take more time to review, where alpha = 0.5

    := (lines of code / chunk_size)^alpha hours.

  • C. System-size

    Review time increases as the underlying system grows: checking a change in a 1.4M-line system is slower than the same change in a 100k-line one.

    [Claude; Classic effort models like COCOMO imply k between 0.05 and 0.2. For our PostgreSQL build assume k = 0.2]

  • D. Coordination time

    Add 2% overhead per coordination pair, where n owners imply n(n-1)/2 pairs between them.

  • 40 h → 3000-line chunks → (1.4M/300 = 467 chunks)→ (467 chunks / 40) → 12 owners.

  • At 467 h → 35,000-line chunks → 40 chunks → 1 owner.

Software Factory

Continuous regeneration & re-imagination of scope with each model release, along with the increased OpEx to productize software suggest a new type of business: the software factory.

As ambitious builds become tractable, well-capitalized firms will take on larger bets, shifting the bar for what customers expect, fundamentally changing the competitive field of software. For scaled software surfaces, it is reasonable to expect a high security bill and increased expectations to build and verify complex systems at a fast cadence. (Although prosumer or indie software segments may not see such an escalation of costs). This makes it challenging for a small talent-dense team to stumble into greatness without considerable resources as scarcity shifts from technical org to token allocation questions & high quality supervision processes.

Returns to Specialization

A good spec and conformance suite for a 10M line-of-code build is rather costly. Where business logic and domain judgement can be captured, advantages accrue to specialized vendors who can amortize the bill. Specialized firms will treat the spec and test development as a one time flat cost, and spread the token OpEx for each build across a customer base that has committed to regeneration contracts.

Subscription → Regeneration contracts

Under regeneration contracts, the spec must evolve: the vendor’s job is to anticipate and adapt to the changing world; with new releases expected at major capability jumps. Finally, someone has to sign off on what correctness means for a given domain, and be held liable when there’s an error— accountability also accrues to dedicated vendors.

Coda

I am not sure what supervision of a hundred-thousand line code diff would look like. We have started to experience what superhuman capabilities on tap feel like. Already, in those moments, it is hard to check a model’s work. E.g. when asked a simple scenario, model jumps quickly to abstractions and nested calculations, making it hard to comprehend without a visual explanation. At the very least, we get a dazzling illusion of intelligence. All these operations in a sequence would be very cognitively taxing for a human to follow and to verify. Despite these leaps, today models fail to follow instructions, and remain sub-par at system architecture.

Yet demand for software was never really demand for lines of code. It was demand for reliable systems that a community of humans understood well enough to guarantee uptime for. Useful software is bounded by the number of domains that can be theorized in this way, and by people/firms who can steward the theory building process in an ever-changing world. Even as code-generation costs decline, I am not sure we’ll ever be in true software over-supply!

essays.title: Bits, Atoms, and the Lonliness crisis
essays.html:
“A few years ago I investigated how medieval Europeans built cathedrals. It was just incredible to me that anyone completed anything over multiple generations- how did anyone possibly stick with anything that long?

My conclusion after a fairly brief investigation:

  1. they mostly didn’t. Many more cathedrals were attempted than finished.

  2. a major contributor to the finished ones was a lack of competing options. Yes, people were poor, but given resources and a desire to spend them on something in the class of a cathedral, the local cathedral was really the only option.

I’m reminded of this every time I think about modern socialization. There were lots of reasons people participated in bowling leagues and rotary club, but one of them was that there wasn’t a lot else to do. You could lock in without worrying about the opportunity cost..”

  • Elizabeth, Lesswrong

A lot of people on twitter like to muse about the loneliness crisis. You will probably die alone. A surgeon general wrote about it. Join or die, etc.

I do believe that a big part of this is the entertainment tech ecosystem, specifically that we have significantly improved short time horizon free entertainment compared to hangouts. At this time I’m not trying to make a principled argument, more a quick outline of my view.

I did a quick brainstorm with claude to come up with a list of significant changes in culuture/tech for solo entertainment and another one for hanging out with others/shared entertainment.

First, the solo version. Note this is a log scale.

Here is the shared version.

A few patterns stand out.

Not all changes and innovations for shared hang outs are positive (in terms of utility over short time spans, which is what impacts a lot of human behavior). Suburbs, agricultural revolution, and 9-5 jobs are potentially negative changes. For solo hangouts, basically all innovation is positive. This is a fundamental asymmetry. You could say this was just caused because of my biased choice of data, but I think it’s capturing a real idea. When you do stuff alone, basically you just need a room to yourself and so societal changes don’t really matter. This isn’t entirely true, but overall ~every change in solo entertainment is opt-outable, as in if someone makes a shitty video game, you can just not play, whereas many of the things that effect shared hangouts you cannot opt out of.

Second, the really important hang-out tech was invented earlier, while the majority of the major innovations in hanging out alone have come since the invention of the computer.

The last thing, which is sort of a subpoint of the previous paragraph, is that the solo innovations are much more profound changes than the shared hangout changes. Many of the shared hangouts are barely different than what we were doing as hunter-gatherers (or for the bigger changes like car culture, maybe seem negative?), and many are actually just trying to make it easier to get back to the hunter-gatherer baseline. For instance, cars + group chats + weekends allow us to go on a hike with our friends, which we could have done in 50,000 BCE with no technology. Sports and game nights are definitely better than what they had before but probably not so different.

OTOH we are getting pretty close to the infinite jest experience machine on the solo side. Tiktok and Reels are already able to zombify a significant portion of the population and just feel like a very different thing that staring at a rock. In the next few years, It looks like we will also be getting

  • Hyperrealistic AI shortform reels

  • Hyperrealistic AI voice

  • Better than expert short form video editing

  • Better than expert video games

And then the final boss

  • Her quality companion

I don’t know if these are actually a huge gain in utility per time period over the dopamine waterfall that we have already created but it will certainly do something.

I think most of this comes down to the fact that you can make solo entertainment better with just bits, but to make shared hangouts better you need atoms and trust. Bits are basically free and also have almost instant iteration loops. This is a big part of the story unfolding on the AI capabilities vs diffusion debate as well.

The equivalently profound hangout tech doesn’t seem economically or physically feasible. You would basically need teleportation, perfect weather, aligned schedules, better trust mechanisms and much more.

I worked on an event app 2 years ago - the most tarpitty app in existence which never works - and when I was working on it I would have dreamed of getting a meta aggregator for every community event in a city that is highly filtered to deliver you the best thing happening around you. I thought for sure if I could deliver that it would make a big difference. Now you can make this in a few days, either by building a repository of parsers, or more simply, just use a few $$ of exa credits. I did this for Philly, and hooked it up to muse to ping me for events that were cool, and it turns out this barely matters. I maybe went out 1 more time every 2-3 weeks.

Partiful, luma, etc. have barely moved the needle. How much easier is running a community and events with luma? The hardest part of running a community is showing up with a positive attitude and excitement.

What really matters is a good space to hang and a few friends you like to text you to come over.

To flesh this out visually, I asked Claude to try to assign some “utility” difference in the innovation compared to baseline for solo and shared hangouts. Shared hangouts are split between how good the hangout is (dark blue) and how easy it is to hang out (light blue). The notion is that it might actually be a bit harder to hang out than when we were all hunter gatherers, but the hangouts are a bit better. Meanwhile the quality of solo entertainment is way better than it used to be, and looks like it will get a lot better in the next few years. The y axis is supposed to mean how much utility will I get in the next ~5 minutes, since that is a good proxy for what we will choose.

Here is the linear since 1800 version.

Now If we think about how much more utility these tech will give us over a ~ year long timescale, things look a lot different, it’s unclear the entertainment tech is actually better over long timescales than in person. However this doesn’t really effect what we (I) choose to do.

Don’t take the data too seriously, but it reflects my general intuition. The short is that we are seeing a fast climb in the utility/$ or utility/Time of solo entertainment relative to shared hangouts starting about 80 years ago. This seems likely to continue for the foreseeable future until we acquire more jurisdiction over atoms, although even then it might just be the case that the matrix is significantly better than hanging with friends (at least for the next few minutes). In the meantime, solving the housing crisis and having more flexible schedules would help a bit.

essays.title: Fluid org boundaries with AI
essays.html:
posts

Cosmos & Inherent asks: How can AI address a specific coordination problem that has historically dogged human organizations? What would adopting this solution mean for the organization’s structure and the day-to-day experience of individuals within the organizatio**n?

AI may radically change our conception of “who is in an org”.

Historically, there is a sharp delineation between an org’s staff (on the “inside”), versus its users (on the “outside”). The relationship of a fulltime employee of an org is radically different than that of one of its customers. This is especially true for consumer tech startups & companies: think Google, Meta, Reddit, X, now perhaps OpenAI and Anthropic.

With AI however, the bar for an external user to be able to contribute, drops drastically. At the same time, employing and compensating this user will be much easier, as AI obliterates transaction costs. Overall, I expect org boundaries to become much more porous: more part-time workers, more volunteers, more collectives and communes.

Stepping back: why is it the case that orgs have a relative few fulltime employees? What makes it hard for a single org to stretch to encompass more humans? I’ll go through four major historical drivers, and how AI might change each.

First, it’s hard to hire and onboard. Hiring requires a lot of trust. An org wants to know that a person is a good fit, worth paying for. The job market is famously a market for lemons. Orgs try to vet candidates, but resumes are low-signal; interviews cost precious staff time, and also select for people good at interviewing. Ideally you would see the person doing the job — in a work test or work trial.

AI can change this by making search and matching problems much more efficient. And this is not just “pair up existing resumes & job listings”. AI can form a much more detailed model of a human based on all their public outputs, and a role’s requirements based on all of its outputs. Or: have your Claude apply for jobs, have their Claude interview your Claude to see if the fit is good.

Second, larger teams incur higher communication costs. The number of pairwise relationships grows quadratically with team size; Dunbar famously pointed to a cap of ~150 people per stable community. Startup literature preaches the gospel of small nimble teams.

Prosaic technology (Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, Zoom) is already enabling much larger & profitable orgs. AI can improve on this in several ways: connecting data sources smoothly (eg MCP); making it easier to spin up custom software to serve internal use cases, and (speculatively) by simulating other humans, letting one speak with a colleague’s digital twin.

Third, on-the-job learning historically leads to specialization. As an employee continues in an org, they build up skills and tacit knowledge that are hard to replace, sometimes unique to their particular role. You’ll notice that great orgs work hard at staff retention. However, this kind of specialization is a double-edge sword for the employee. While it helps with job security, it also means that tenured employees accrue all kinds of responsibilities which hold back new work.

As more work is intermediated via LLM, LLM systems can hopefully take on more of specialization, first via in-context learning, then building up memory to reinforce particular skillsets. Humans today are still better at generalizing from few-shot examples, so their comparative advantage may remain as generalists, attacking new domains.

Fourth: humans are just really expensive! Paying for staff compensation is a major check on the growth of orgs. Successful orgs today draw an economic boundary around a few extremely great people, and pay them handsomely in cash and equity.

But in the long run AIs will drive down the cost of human upkeep. Surplus and abundance driven by rapid technical growth means that human consumption needs can be met much more easily. When people no longer rely on a paycheck to cover needs, they can spend their time with orgs which help fulfill their higher values.

Given all this, how might orgs operate in the future?

Maybe: membership & employment norms would change. You might work 5 “jobs” each at 1-10h/week. You might switch between orgs the way you hop between different social media sites today, polyamorously, without jealousy.

Maybe: you might switch between jobs much faster. If transaction costs are low, if you can onboard and offboard faster, your median tenure at a job might change from 2 years to 2 months (or, 2 weeks), as you impart the essential wisdom and craft that make you “you” — then parachute off to the next opportunity.

Maybe: we might end up with vast, nation-level superorgs, like the hives of Terra Ignota, entities glued together with AI support and radically different governance. Imagine X, except if the money was universal, people drew significant paychecks from their posts and work, and there’s taxation, election representation rather than just top-down Elon-controlled. (What is a network state in the era of transformative AI?)

Why am I excited for these more porous orgs? We’ve seen how solid org boundaries can lead to an “us vs them” mentality. Enshittification or shortform videos or gambling addictions or doomy content sucking out unendorsed hours from its prey. And, at the extreme end, xrisk: frontier lab employees endangering the rest of humanity.

If instead such an org could wholly integrate its leaders, staff and users, it might be unstoppable. I admire OpenAI’s commitment to offering free intelligence to the world; Anthropic’s commitment to spending its gains for the public benefit. Imagine if these orgs were not just serving, but also governed by all of humanity, by virtue of having all of humanity on the inside!

Thanks to Lydia N for reviewing an early outline.

essays.title: SF Solidarity Club looks forward in packed meeting

author.name: Barak Gila
author.bio:
growth @votewithsway | yimby, urbanist, techie, aspiring journalist, chef, film/art fan. blogger http://barak.substack.com @berkeley_eecs 🇺🇸🌉
substack bio: Barak writes about urbanism, life in San Francisco, local politics, and whatever else comes to his mind. He also publishes voter guides that dozens of people use to vote!

essays.html:
INNER SUNSET, SAN FRANCISCO — “You can really see this is going to be here to stay,” opened Saikat Chakrabarti, addressing more than 100 attendees this Sunday afternoon, inviting those who may not yet be members of San Francisco Solidarity Club to join “if you don’t necessarily have a political home, or even if you do.” He thanked the club’s officers for helping make it a success, and then jumped into a panel discussion with sitting Supervisors Chyanne Chen, Bilal Mahmood, and Myrna Melgar.

The club event was held at Chakrabarti’s former campaign headquarters, which served as Chakrabarti’s Solidarity PAC office after the primary and will now be shuttered. The space was buzzing with grassroots energy. There were tables for DSA’s San Francisco chapter, sign-up information for dozens of local groups organized by topic area, campaigns for a National Popular Vote and for removing Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries from leadership, and even for California’s Office of Emergency Services, Planning & Preparedness. Some of it was organized by club officers, and some by club members and committees.

Beyond Solidarity Club members, several local politicos came to the event. Former Supervisor Joel Engardio, Supervisor candidate Darshini Patel, City College Board-elect Elijah Ball, and several former campaign and supervisor staffers were present. The crowd skewed youthful: Chen pointed out that the room was full of young people, at which point Mahmood joked that he was the only bald person in the room. Even after the 80-minute-long panel, folks stayed for several more minutes, taking a group photo, mingling, and organizing.

Per the event title, “What’s Next,” the discussion was forward-looking. The supervisors detailed their wish list for Congressman-elect Scott Wiener — bringing federal money to San Francisco, regulating AI, growing the Supreme Court, and banning Congressional stock trading (this earned applause) — but didn’t rehash the race. The club’s endorsement for Congress, Connie Chan, didn’t come up in the discussion.

Chakrabarti’s questions were substantive and the supervisors, particularly Melgar and Mahmood, gave detailed, wonky answers. Relatively niche measures like Prop 38 (the $8B immunology bond, which funneled $4B into its funder’s tiny nonprofit) were discussed. Mahmood argued that the fact that San Francisco’s electorate rejected the proposition showed that it was highly informed. He said similar education work is needed across the state going forward.

After Supervisor Melgar called the results “a clear urbanist majority of victories,” Chakrabarti asked her to expand on the “traditional progressive and moderate coalitions” being in flux. She described the moderate coalition as unstable, “made up of folks who are pro-cop, law-and-order, plus the urbanist YIMBY pro-housing folks.” She pointed to the issue of the recall of Joel Engardio over the Great Highway as evidence that those parts of the coalition can be at odds. On August 27, 2025, the SF DCCC, which is mostly controlled by the moderate coalition (as described by Melgar above), deadlocked on whether to oppose the recall and took no position. She described the other coalition as defining what’s progressive “in a more traditional, conservation, baby-boomer-generation kind of way.” She said what worked in the ’70s doesn’t work anymore to address climate change or housing affordability, making this coalition unstable as well.

By contrast, Mahmood rejected the notion of a progressive-moderate divide, at least on the Board of Supervisors. He mocked an SF Chronicle analysis characterizing Jackie Fielder as the least “pro-tenant” and most “pro-development” on an axis that pits those against each other, drawing a huge laugh with the quip “The way people try to think in binaries doesn’t work, and you’d think people would know that in San Francisco.” He said that on this Board, more than past boards, votes break down on an issue-by-issue basis, and supervisors have the ability to compartmentalize and collaborate on areas of agreement.

Melgar and Mahmood also dug into what types of political action are effective in winning elections. Mahmood used Prop 40 as a detailed example, noting that because SEIU-UHW didn’t first get buy-in from other unions, those other unions either recommended No on 40 or else didn’t spend money and energy to pass it. He said that measures that voters saw as consensus, like Prop C and Prop J, passed with huge margins, while those that seemed more controversial did worse. He also emphasized the importance of affirmative messaging, saying that Prop 40 focused too much on opposition to billionaires rather than what it would create, and that conversely Prop 38 had a more positive campaign, and no organized opposition. Melgar rejected “beautifully articulated ideologies” moving the needle; she instead emphasized organizing, saying that the only way she’s seen change happen is community organizing, with food, “aunties taking care of the children,” etc. She said we have to do the hard work of organizing, and that there’s no shortcut. Chakrabarti synthesized that discussion, offering that organizing is not sufficient, because with the wrong messaging, you’d lose anyway.

Mayor Lurie was criticized repeatedly throughout the panel by all three supervisors. Melgar opposed his measures D, E, and F, which tightened the rules for placing measures on the ballot and tightened executive control over city departments and over procurement. The club had endorsed No on those measures as well. Melgar pointed out that the officials in past corruption cases, Mohammed Nuru, Harlan Kelly, and Tom Hui, were “mayor’s-branch people” (although none served under Mayor Lurie).

Mahmood said that now that the mayor’s charter reforms have passed, “there are no more excuses… the onus is on the mayor to deliver.” Melgar agreed, saying that the next case of corruption “will clearly be on him.”

Mahmood called out the mayor for taking credit for work the supervisors had already done, and likewise Melgar pointed out that the west-side zoning overlay (which she characterized as a win) had been in the works for three years when the mayor took credit for it. Chen said that while the mayor may generate headlines like $100M investments in parks from his philanthropic friends (she scooped today’s news), he should instead be delivering more housing. She also said his homelessness policy is merely displacing people into other neighborhoods.

On the other hand, Melgar did acknowledge the mayor’s popularity, saying “people do credit him with the economic success of the city and the perceived safety improvements in the city” and that the Board should “address the quality-of-life issues that people are worried about every day, because it is really important.” Mahmood said Lurie is a “good person” who could be doing anything else if he wanted to, and that both he and the board are “trying to genuinely solve problems.”

essays.title: Don't Just Do Something, Stand There (DJDSST)
essays.html:
I’m playing with some new practices for how I move through the world.

Frustrated with the experience of spending most of my time simply reacting to the state of my things around me (usually my computer) I’m exploring how to do something more volitional.

The first step is to do nothing.

Only by not doing anything, can I trust that I’ve actually let go of any intentions I was implicitly carrying already without having chosen them. Intending to do something momentarily counts as doing something.

I do nothing—

—perhaps sitting on a chair or couch, or at a table, or on the train
—perhaps standing
—perhaps looking at my computer, but with the computer closed or off, beholding it as an object or a tool, in its state prior to being a portal
—perhaps, even, with a paper or digital journal in front of me, that might receive some of my thoughts.

I do nothing, and I notice what inclinations arise.

In a messy room, I might notice some inclinations to tidy things.

Depending on my mood, I might choose to tidy one or two or three of these things. Tidying is risky business, a satisfying slippery slope of avoidant distraction from difficult, daunting darings. It presents itself as practice, here. Taking a thing, putting it in place, and then resuming rest—returning to actually… doing… nothing. Letting lie the inclinations to clean the next and next thing. Even while tidying thing one, tidying only that thing, and not letting additional out-of-place objects hop onto me like a bus.

Often better not to risk it. Let me not fool myself into thinking that great art can only be made in a clean room.

So I do nothing, and notice what inclinations arise.

Sometimes inclinations arise with a clear concept of the whole of what I would do, and why.

Sometimes they arise as more like a hazy hunch of an unhandled situation that haunts my ease, with a fickle first step in the foreground and a paltry poverty of plan for what follows. This way lies madness. Making moves while missing a mandate means meandering into a mess. But! Briefly bracketing my idle inclination, scoping my sketch of a scheme, saying “I’ll check if Charlie has confirmed re the concert, and if he hasn’t I’ll close my phone”... that can work. That’s a whole plan, with an ending.

Sometimes I merely sit, relaxed but not motionless, and let my mind unwind, and there arise puzzles I’ve pondered for years, questions whose quest overlays have all but faded to dust, but which greet me with delight now that I’m attending to them again. I may muse for moments, or many minutes. From there I might be moved to write a word on a whiteboard, begin a blog post, or to text a reflection to a friend.

And then I do nothing again.

Sometimes I fail: I launch myself into an intention without clarity of what it really is (or even the meta-level clarity that I’m there to explore ‘til I bore).

Sometimes I fail: I set out to send one message, and get pulled into another chat, and I open a link, and now oh god where was I—

Whatever happens, the most important thing, as with any meditation, is to begin again. And this is a meditation. I told a meditation teacher about a preliminary version of this practice I found in 2022, and she was all excited about my doing nothing and “dying into the moment” until I said that then from there I would get up and go pee (while aiming to continue dying into the moment). And indeed, if you get up and go, you probably won’t go to the void today. The void is a great place to go, but there are other lovely places as well.

A friend joined me recently when I hosted an afternoon of this at a retreat, and she was like “this is hard!” …I felt seen.

Gentle vague gamification

Early on in playing with this practice, I decided to gamify it a bit. I printed out sheet of paper that had six 10×10 grids. I wrote “Don’t Just Do Something, Stand There” on the top. (I often just shorten this to “DJDSST”)

I sat there and did nothing for a good moment. I put a dot in the first square. When I completed the first thing I set out to do, I put a checkbox in the second square. Well, except that I got distracted partway before refocusing and finishing… so… a little loop-de-loop then a checkbox, in the second square. Okay nice, the second thing I set out to do, I just did it and nothing else: CHECKMATE ADHDtheists. Then I just sat there for a few minutes… great. Another dot.

There’s no right way to do this, whatsoever.

Sometimes I do three things that are all sort of one thing and I put three checkmarks in one box. Sometimes I get interrupted, then finish, and I put a line and a checkmark in. Sometimes it’s a giant squiggly mess because, well, that’s what happened. In retrospect, I won’t know what any of the dots or lines or checkmarks referred to. There’s no prize at the end (though there could be!) But there are numerous advantages to having this concrete representation:

Having there be an external marker helps motivate me to go through the “do nothing” ➔ “do something” ➔ “do nothing” cycle repeatedly. Number go up. Exciting!

Having to go back to the piece of paper to check it off makes it much more vivid that… Suppose I go to the kitchen to get a drink. I get the drink. Then I think “great I did that, now I’m gonna do the next thing which is emptying the dishwasher.” To do so would be failing to properly do the “do nothing” step. And sure, I could pause in the kitchen with my glass of milk and do nothing, and then emerge “now it’s time for the dishwasher”. But it’s easier to be honest when there’s no “while I’m there” convenience factor and when I have to go somewhere else to truly mark that I have reset. Likewise with picking up / putting down my phone, or opening/closing my computer.

Speaking of which, having it be on a piece of paper keeps me from getting distracted by my phone or computer. Plus, an analog checkbox can be filled with anything you want—no fixed ontology. It helps keep there from being any right way to do this. I make up the syntax slightly differently every day, depending on what serves me and feels best.

Inspiration / related ideas

Do one thing at a time
Do it slowly, and completely
Between things, pause
Sometimes make the thing you are doing nothing

— Romeo Stevens on twitter (I don’t always insist on “slowly”!)

People need almost as much unstructured reverie time as they do “meditation time,” at least long-run, in order to “go all the way.”

— Mark Lippmann, Meditation from Cold Start to Complete Mastery: a Manual of Global Wayfinding Meditation, mirrored for a better reading experience by me here

There’s never a million things you need to do. It’s either 1 or 0.

— this t-shirt I wore til it faded

Find that you go to your computer to do one thing, and get overwhelmed by a dozen other things you left open? Try my new tool SlateWiper, which closes it all out (after archiving it for reference, in case you discern later something is worth going to get). You can even set it up to push a button from your phone! Note that “push the wipe button on slatewiper” is one whole act, after which a DJDSSTer would again do nothing. Doing something on your computer afterwards is a second act.

Also if you like the overall vibe of this, you might enjoy intend.do, my to-do list app that involves throwing out your list every day.

Instructions, phrased some other way

I was at an intentional community retreat recently, and I posted to our groupchat:

Invitation!

I’m going to be spending [daughter]’s nap (now til ~3:30-4) doing a practice I call Don’t Just Do Something, Stand There (DJDSST).

Basically you do nothing, release all intention, rest fully. Then eventually some intention arises—best to start small like “pee” or “send that one text” and then you do that, and once it’s done, return to doing nothing. Aim to not get distracted by some other intention on the way, and notice if you do (or if you did). Play with what feels/works best for how to handle interruptions. Enjoy the satisfaction and relief of doing exactly one thing, or zero things.

My HQ for this is the Octagon room. I would welcome company; this is a relatively solitary activity, but I think it could be joyous to share the kind of space it creates.

I have little sheets of paper with grids on them which I find to be a helpful scaffold for the intentionality. I prepared a few extra :)

My friend Blake didn’t join at the time, but he tried out following the instructions later, and said it was helpful.

Blake Borgeson’s version

He texted me:

I’ve been doing DJDSST for a while most days since LARC, really finding it helps me get out of my manic doing stretches that go on too long, and helps me feel more okay at the end of a day

I asked him what he actually does, since he hadn’t joined me and so as far as I know he only had the above “invitation” which I hadn’t intended to be sufficient although obviously one can just try following it.

Often at the end of the day, I realize I’ve done too many things in a row, and I feel spent and stretched, and not in a way that feels like the good kind of pain. Like a piling up of tension on top of tension on top of tension, each unresolved in my emotional being. Scheduling breaks sometimes can help. This different approach is: after each thing I do, I let myself do nothing and come back to okayness. Sometimes that is quick. Sometimes it takes time. When I feel moved to do something from a place in me that I like and trust, I do that.

That’s kinda long. Trying again.

Once I’m oriented to my day, know what clearly matters to me that day, and have a stretch of time that supports it, I:

Do nothing. Rest. See what impulses and intuitions come up to do different things. When one comes up I trust, where I feel a yes that sits in my okayness, I do that. Repeat.

Shorter

Coming back to rest and okayness, after each thing, and doing things only from that place. For a while.

essays.title: what is Nvidia worth without Jensen?
essays.html:
the interesting financial question about Jensen Huang is what Nvidia would be worth if he left. we have a stock market, an options market, analysts with spreadsheets, and an enormous amount of commentary. getting a separately traded market answer to that specific question is still surprisingly difficult. i think that says something about what our markets are missing.

Nvidia’s board has announced an independent investigation following reports that Jensen was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort. its statement says it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, and that it retains confidence in his leadership. an investigation is not a finding. departure is a hypothetical here, not an announced outcome. the financial question is worth asking without pretending otherwise.

start with two investors. one thinks Jensen is almost certain to stay, but that his departure would be disastrous. the other thinks departure is plausible, but that Nvidia would do fine without him. both can arrive at the same valuation. they agree about the stock price while disagreeing about the thing everyone is discussing. watching the stock cannot tell you which investor you are trading against.

this is because a share bundles possible futures together. leadership, demand, margins, competition, export policy, interest rates: all of it goes into one price. that is appropriate for an asset you own across those futures. it becomes a problem when you want to extract a particular belief from the bundle. a price can aggregate information without revealing how the information fits together.

the conditional market version is straightforward to describe. what is Nvidia’s stock worth at the end of September 2027, conditional on Jensen leaving the CEO role by June 30? alongside it, ask the same question conditional on him remaining. someone who understands Nvidia’s organizational durability could trade the departure scenario without first needing a strong view about whether the board will actually replace him.

suppose those markets imply $140 if he leaves and $180 if he stays. these are invented numbers, not price targets. the useful thing is that they separate two disagreements: how likely departure is, and what the business looks like in that world. a market asking only whether Jensen leaves gives you the first. the stock bundles both together with everything else investors care about.

this makes “Jensen is irreplaceable” a more demanding claim. irreplaceable over what horizon? does the stock lose 5 percent on announcement, or does Nvidia permanently lose its ability to make good bets? Nvidia without Jensen would still have engineers, software, products, and customer relationships. a large departure discount needs an account of what those assets lose without him. perhaps it is coordination, customer confidence, or judgment about which projects deserve another year.

the opposing view deserves a market too. perhaps investors give the most visible person too much credit for an institution’s capabilities. perhaps a successor would preserve the important things. it is easy to say either version in a research note. i want the person convinced that Nvidia survives its founder to be able to trade that view directly against someone convinced that it does not.

“just buy puts” is a reasonable response, but an ordinary put pays according to the stock price regardless of what caused the decline. you are buying protection against weaker demand, a market selloff, and other things alongside leadership risk. that may be exactly the protection you want. it is still different from exposure conditioned on a particular event. conditional instruments add specificity; they do not make options obsolete.

there is a portfolio reason to care. an investor might be comfortable with Nvidia’s commercial prospects but unwilling to carry a particular leadership scenario. today, reducing that concern often means reducing the whole position. a conditional hedge could let them retain more of the exposure they actually want. it would also make research more useful: expertise about succession could earn a return without requiring equal expertise about the next earnings report. that is a modest claim compared with automating corporate governance, but it is a much more immediate use case for real investors.

the construction matters. a claim paying Nvidia’s future price if Jensen leaves, and zero otherwise, does not by itself quote the conditional valuation. its price also reflects the likelihood of departure. you need appropriate paired claims or conditional settlement rules to separate those quantities. even then, collateral, risk premia, and liquidity affect prices. calling something a conditional market does not make every displayed number a pure forecast.

there is a more important limitation. the difference between the two branches is not automatically Jensen’s causal contribution. a planned succession after reassuring news is different from an abrupt exit following damaging findings. traders in the departure branch will price the circumstances they expect to accompany departure. the condition selects a whole set of worlds, including the other things likely to be going wrong in them.

this is the causal-correlational gap i have written about before. observing that Jensen leaves is different from intervening to remove him while holding everything else fixed. a shareholder may care about the entire departure scenario, so the conditional forecast is useful anyway. a board asking whether it should replace him faces a different problem. it cannot read the spread between branches as the value created by keeping him.

resolution is also less boring than it looks. does becoming executive chairman count as leaving? does temporary leave count? what if resignation is announced before the deadline but takes effect afterward? measuring the first close after departure asks a different question from measuring the stock three months later. these details determine which belief the instrument expresses. they need answers before trading starts, when nobody knows which wording will benefit them.

and only one branch happens. if Jensen stays, we never observe the stock price in the alternative world where he left. settlement rules can specify what happens to inactive claims; they cannot manufacture the missing counterfactual. this puts limits on how confidently we can evaluate the forecasts afterward. conditional markets organize uncertainty. they do not remove the inconvenient parts of it.

liquidity is the other constraint. a precise question with three disengaged traders is not much of an information product. splitting markets by event, deadline, and successor can fragment participation faster than it adds useful detail. market makers need a reason to quote, informed traders need a reason to participate, and everyone needs confidence in resolution. the mechanism has to work with actual capital, not just look elegant in a diagram.

despite all that, this seems worth building. analysts already construct these scenarios privately. investors already distinguish the probability of a shock from its consequences. the missing step is giving those judgments counterparties and public prices. the question is familiar; the tradeable instrument is what needs work.

Nvidia makes the point concrete. someone can be bullish on the company and worried about Jensen leaving. someone else can think he will leave and still be bullish. ordinary shares compress those positions into the same conversation. conditional markets would let us see where the disagreement actually sits. “Jensen is irreplaceable” would remain an opinion, but we could finally ask what price its believers are willing to pay.
