essays.title: Why You’re Still Not Getting What You Want (Part 2: The Taxonomy of Asks)
essays.html:
After a long hiatus, the Ask Stack series is back with part 2! Better late than never. Thank you for your patience with your busy, sleepy sluts. I’ve committed to publishing one post per week all of November (or forfeiting $1,000!), so stay tuned for more frequent posts.

One of my boyfriends told me he could keep sleeping with me only if I agreed to sleep with nobody else, indefinitely. His wife was trying to get pregnant, and they were worried about STI risk following a scare with a different partner.

The ask was clearly articulated and based on a real concern. I’ll tell you what I did with it when we get to needs (if you can’t guess).

I think part of the reason asks are scary is that you never really know which ask will be too much for the other person.

Other asks sit at the opposite end of the scale. On a morning walk, I nudge my husband and whisper “puppy!” If he fails to acknowledge that there is in fact a puppy just once, I may survive. But if he misses or ignores enough small bids for connection, the relationship will be genuinely eroded over time. We call this pattern “death by a thousand cuts.”

Most relationship advice isn’t very explicit about how to handle asks at different points along the spectrum of stakes. It took me a long time to find a satisfying way to define the difference between a want and a need. But once I learned to tell them apart, it helped me get clear about my non-negotiables, and ultimately apply those criteria to find my husband.

Part 1 gave you the anatomy of an ask by defining the five steps of the Ask Stack. This post provides a map of what you’re asking for, both in terms of the spectrum of stakes and the four fuzzy categories of content, so you know what kind of conversation you’re walking into.

The spectrum of stakes

Here are four asks from my own life, alongside definitions and analysis of each level. It is helpful to know what the stakes associated with your asks are before asking.

1. Bids

My husband says he watched an interesting YouTube video and I listen attentively, asking questions occasionally, while he infodumps about whatever he learned. My boyfriend is leaving the room, so he gives me a little affection as he exits, and I return or respond to it.

These are bids, aka asks in their smallest, most implicit form: “look at this shiny rock.” A glance, a touch, a shared joke. Bids are small enough asks that missing just one doesn’t feel like rejection so much as inattention, but John Gottman’s research found that how partners respond to them is one of the strongest predictors of relationship longevity. Couples who stayed together turned toward each other’s bids 86% of the time; couples who later divorced did so only 33% of the time. Bids are easy to make and easy to miss, and everything else is built on them. Think of them as the foundation of a strong relationship - low stakes in isolation, but fundamental in aggregate. Bids work best if the stakes associated with them are on the level of an offhand wish, and go sideways if you try to make them carry more weight than they are designed to handle (e.g. don’t try to tell your partner you want to live together by pointing out cute houses or talking about your friends living together).

2. Preferences

I arrive at my boyfriend’s place and he tells me about a party we could go to together. My first impulse is to go along with the plan. Then I notice I’m pretty sleepy and was really looking forward to curling up in bed with him. So instead of defaulting to yes, I tell him I’m not feeling a party tonight, and what I actually prefer is a quiet evening in. Depending on the party and my levels of sleepiness, this may have different outcomes, ranging from a nap while he goes to the party for a bit to staying in together for takeout and a show to going to the party together after a little cuddle time.

That’s a preference level ask: a mild directional wish with no serious consequence either way. Low stakes, easy to express, and often skipped because it feels frivolous. It isn’t. Expressing preferences is how your partner learns who you are, and consistently suppressing them is how you end up five years in feeling invisible. If you are sufficiently deep in rationalist culture, you may try to attach numbers or qualifiers to how strong a given preference is, since the importance of preferences varies so widely. I for one would not want my weak preferences to override a partner’s strong preference.

3. Wants

I’m an introvert and my husband is an extrovert. When we first started attending parties together, he would often bounce around talking to everyone and ditch me to go make new friends. I wanted parties to be a more shared experience, especially when I don’t know many people. So I asked if he would be okay keeping an eye on me until I’m settled in with people I know.

Another example: I am more into skiing than either of my current long-term partners. While I may convince them to tag along to the mountain for one day, I tend to diversify my ski buddies (friends, siblings, new boys) rather than attempt to cajole them into skiing with me as much as I want. I did not select my partners on perfectly aligned hobbies because those are more outsourceable than my needs.

Having company at parties and a ski buddy are want level asks: things that would meaningfully improve my experience but could, in principle, be sourced elsewhere or managed without. An adventure buddy, more physical affection, someone to geek out with about a niche interest. Medium stakes, worth asking for explicitly, negotiable, and potentially outsourceable if the ask doesn’t land.

Wants have more emotional weight than preferences, but less than needs. You’d feel the loss, you’d advocate for it, and you’d be somewhat let down by a no. A good test is whether you’d spend any social or relational capital on it. If you’d happily trade it away for something small, it’s a preference. If you’d push for it and want your pushing to count, it’s a want.

4. Needs

Back to my boyfriend’s ask that I not sleep with anyone else, indefinitely. I need a lot of autonomy over who I sleep with, and an ask that required giving it up indefinitely was not something I could agree to.

So we broke up. His ask was clear and came from a real concern, and no amount of communication skill on either side could have fixed it, because what he needed collided with what I need. Some asks do unearth incompatibilities, and rather than offering false reassurance, I’ll argue that breaking up as soon as you understand you can’t meet each other’s needs is a good thing. It leaves you both free to find partners who can.

Beyond my need for sexual autonomy, I need all of my romantic partners to be dedicated to being poly. If a partner claims to be poly but is willing to entertain monogamous partners or close their relationship for a partner’s discomfort, then that’s a dealbreaker for me. Of course, my needs for friendships differ from my needs for casual sex or my needs from a committed relationship. What matters is understanding what I need for each level of connection to feel good for me.

These are need level asks: things I cannot outsource from the relationship and still be satisfied with it as a relationship. Respect, feeling like a priority, basic communication, emotional safety, and for me, sexual autonomy. High stakes, and hard to ask for because the answer reveals something fundamental. If a need is consistently unmet, you don’t have a communication problem. You have a compatibility problem.

The line between a need and a want is not objective (which is why I choose to illustrate the stakes as a spectrum), and the point isn’t to sort all your asks into tidy bins. The point of the spectrum is to have some inner clarity about what’s at stake before you have the hard conversation. If you go in thinking something is a “want” and your partner says no, you can negotiate or let it go. If you go in thinking something is a “need” and your partner says no, be prepared for a harder conversation about compatibility.

The spectrum and definitions are also a helpful frame to avoid significant mis-sorting. Mis-sorting goes wrong in two directions. If you dress up a preference as a need to get it taken seriously, your partner learns to discount your needs, including the real ones. If you downgrade a real need to a preference to avoid conflict, you’ll agree to things you can’t actually live with, and the resentment will crop up later. The long term success of your relationships depends on clarity and honesty around your asks. Don’t trade getting what you want in the short run for long-term imbalances.

Another way to look at all this is that individual bids cost nearly nothing when missed, preferences are fairly cheap to give up, wants cost something meaningful, and needs cost too much to give up.

How the stakes shape the ask

The higher the stakes, the more explicit your ask should be, and the lower they are, the more you can lean on implicit ones.

At the low stakes end, a light touch is the right tool. A bid or a casual statement of preference costs almost nothing to make. It also gives your partner a chance to show they’re paying attention. Most communication advice focuses on explicit asks, but bids matter just as much. The skill here is making them and, equally, noticing them, thanks to a shared understanding that they matter. This may require some occasional explicit communication about the categories of bids you both make, especially if they don’t feel well met, so you each have an opportunity to learn what matters to the other in this category.

At the high stakes end, hinting is a gamble with your core needs. A need conveyed through a bid can be missed, misread, or deniable, and if your partner doesn’t pick it up, you’ve lost time and possibly trust without even learning whether they could meet it (if it were made explicitly). It is best to state needs plainly and early.

Wants sit in the middle: worth a clear request, made with appropriate flexibility.

If asking is hard for you in general, start at the low end. Make more bids. Practice expressing preferences. You’re not just getting small things met; you’re building the muscle of asking and collecting evidence that asking is survivable, and often rewarding.

This is also all a default, not a rule. Some people can only get a need out sideways the first time, and testing the water with a softer opener can be a legitimate way to work up to saying it plainly. Some partners also respond better to a gentle lead-in than to a flat statement. And a bid can carry real weight once you’ve told your partner what it means (“when I say ‘ugh, long day,’ I’m asking for a hug”). What matters is knowing which level you’re operating at, even if you approach it gradually.

Four categories of content

The second dimension of the taxonomy is what you’re asking about. The four main categories of ask types are described here.

Emotional

I was having a bit of a hard time adjusting to a metamour who was pretty different from me. It was triggering some insecurity that my partner secretly wished I were different. So I asked for reassurance that he likes me for who I am, and then he told me specifically what he likes about me and values about our relationship.

Another example: I wanted more appreciation from my housemates for contributions to house chores, so I announced in the house chat that I would be sharing some of my contributions there and encouraged others to do the same if they felt called to, and then we all saw and appreciated each other’s contributions more.

Emotional asks are about attunement, appreciation, support, understanding, and priority. These are the core content of a relationship, and responding well to them can go a long way. They’re also the category people are least likely to see coming: you often don’t know what you need emotionally until you’re already in deficit, and emotional needs are easy to misunderstand even when the person hearing them cares. As my example demonstrates, you can make emotional asks in any kind of relationship, not just romantic ones, though they often carry higher stakes in a romantic context.

Sexual

My partner asked what I’m into and I stumbled over the answer. He assigned me sex homework to get more clarity. I overachieved, and my sex doc was born. Later I sent it to new partners so they could learn my preferences and I could get more of what I want out of sex.

Another example: I was feeling chronically underfucked this summer, so I told my partner and explained what it meant to me. Then we worked on a solution together and now we are back to having more sex that is more mutually fulfilling.

Sexual asks carry more shame than almost any other category, so it’s common to know what you want and to have been actively suppressing it. They’re also the category most resistant to change in a partner: when a sexual ask fails, it more often means “they can’t” than “they won’t.” And in a monogamous structure they’re the only category that’s entirely non-outsourceable. Every other want has some alternative source, but a monogamous structure routes all sexual asks through one person, so a no arrives with no alternative attached.

People also tend to overestimate how well they match sexually, and how well their partner knows their preferences, until they talk about it explicitly. Differences in desire are linked to lower sexual and relationship satisfaction, though a larger, more recent study found that couples’ overall level of desire mattered more than whether they matched. Have that conversation early, before significant attachment forms. I am of the opinion that you cannot really negotiate desire. That is, there are some things you cannot ask your partner to want, and partner selection is your most important lever to get what you want.

Logistical

Shortly before SlutCon 2025, our head of security, who was also my co-presenter on a talk, got sick. I asked multiple boyfriends, and even one ex, to help in specific ways: please bring hot tub towels and speakers from home, please help me give this talk, please take a security shift because we’re short.

Logistical asks are chronically underestimated. “I need you to actually show up on time” sounds mundane but frequently operates at need level, and gets dismissed as nagging instead of treated as the serious ask it is. When a reasonable logistical ask goes unmet, it’s especially demoralizing, because it reads as a failure to care.

Relational

Early on in meeting my husband we had explicit conversations about how we were both seeking a primary partner. I try to be clear as soon as possible with everyone I date about what shape I see as possible for the connection. I frequently find myself renegotiating a romantic or sexual relationship back to a friendship, which is never the most fun conversation, especially if we have dated for a long time. But this is ultimately one of my favorite features of poly culture (the ability to flow between different degrees of relationship depending on each person’s needs).

Relational asks are about relationship architecture, the structural “what are we?” questions: labels, commitments, whether to cohabit or have kids, renegotiating terms. These are often extremely loaded conversations, and really hard to do well. However, sometimes there are also smaller-stakes renegotiations of your agreements to each other, especially in poly relationships.

In a sense, this is a meta category that contains the other three, since in practice, decisions about the relationship structure tend to depend on how well the relationship is handling the asks in the other categories.

The categories are fuzzy (sorry)

These four categories aren’t clearly distinct, they overlap and feed into each other. For some people, sex is a primary pathway to emotional closeness, so withholding it damages the connection even when every other emotional input is present. These people aren’t being dramatic when they say “I need sex to feel loved.” They’re describing an accurate map of their own psychology.

That changes diagnosis. An ask that looks like a sexual preference (“I want more sex”) may be an emotional need (“I need to feel close to you”), with higher stakes, more pain when unmet, and less room for workarounds. In mismatched couples it gets worse: if one partner has this wiring and the other doesn’t, a sexual no often lands as emotional rejection even when none was intended. The refusing partner can be genuinely confused (“I told you I loved you this morning, why do you feel disconnected?”) because in their model the two are separate. No amount of communication fixes a mismatch that goes unaddressed.

Logistical and emotional asks blur too, because how a logistical ask is handled often reads as a sign of care, or a lack of it. This spring I had a text conversation with a partner that mixed logistics with emotional stakes. At various points we each felt the other was focused on the object-level logistics and not attuning to our emotional needs.

This can turn into a vicious cycle. One person misses the first opening for connection. The other feels disconnected, which leaves them less capacity to notice when they’re doing the same thing in reverse, or they just mirror the other’s energy. We both ended up voicing the disconnection, but misses like this accumulate, and over time they can do real damage to a relationship.

Stay tuned for part 3 where I will map the taxonomy of ask types onto the five steps of the Ask Stack.

Did I miss any important points on the stakes spectrum or categories of content? Please share your thoughts in the comments below or in our private Discord!

essays.title: Hamming Questions for Potted Plants
essays.html:
I used to run an exercise at the end of workshops called Hamming Questions for Potted Plants. I don’t expect the lesson to be novel to LW readers, but like actually writing out your beliefs, or actually trying to do a Fermi estimate, actually doing the exercise might provide some actual value. The exercise is after the picture of the potted plant. If you want to do it, I recommend setting aside at least 12 minutes.

For anyone unfamiliar, Hamming questions are a list of prompts designed to help people find bottlenecks in their most important endeavors (maybe becoming the person they want to become or building what they want to build). It’s a reflective exercise. There are about 10 prompts, given individually with a minute or two between them. People doing the exercise listen, think by themselves with pen and paper, and jot down possible answers. I advise them to keep searching for other possible bottlenecks and not get bogged down ruminating over one bottleneck the whole time - it’s unpleasant. I do recommend the exercise though!

The HQPP exercise similarly aims to help people identify things they might benefit from working on, but also, done after and therefore in juxtaposition with the standard HQs, it’s meant to help people grok that the models, maps, and metaphors you use to understand the world, including yourself, will affect the questions that you ask and the shape of the solutions that you find.

The map is not the territory, and our map of how a human works is maybe especially bad. We have models of what people are that affect how we orient toward ourselves: multi-agent models, reward function models, personality type models, etc. I watch people get sort of stuck in them. This exercise is an opportunity to step out of whichever model you often use and look at yourself from a different angle.

There are 3 reasons I picked potted plants in particular:
1) They are alive
2) They can grow even without interference
3) There’s an implicit orientation towards them of responsibility and care

I want people to orient to themselves with those assumptions baked in.

If you do this exercise, I recommend getting something to write with first. I’ll advocate for pen and paper, which rarely has flashing notifications.

Have a good exercise!

Water: Once upon a time I inherited some very sad office plants. Being new to plant care, I did the obvious good thing and watered them. When that did not have any effect, I tried watering them more. Water is good for plants! They drowned. They were suffering from overwatering. Sometimes you can do too much of the obvious good thing. My question for you: How might you be overwatered?

Pots: I decided to repot some plants so that they would better match the aesthetic (dismal IKEA as opposed to dismal Lowe’s). When I tried to repot them, they would not come out of their pot. It turned out they had been in their pots so long that their roots had started to grow out the bottom and were pressed tightly to the sides. You would not know to look at them from the top. My question for you: what pots are you in, and how will you know when you should repot yourself? Is there enough room in your pot for you to grow?

Sunshine: One plant was by a window. One side of it got more sun than the other, so it got sort of lopsided. I don’t know if it would have eventually tipped over, but my naive intuition said this wasn’t great for the plant’s long-term growth. The solution was easy: I just turned the pot. My question for you: could a side of you use more sunlight? Is one side of you getting more sunlight than the other?

Fruit: Someone once told me (dad? grandpa? educational children’s television show?) that when trees are young, you need to nip their buds early because they aren’t ready to bear fruit and need to use that energy to build their core. As they get older, it’s a choice every spring: fruit or strength? My question for you: for each of your branches this spring, fruit or strength?

Bugs: I once had sunflowers. They were eaten alive by aphids. I remember wishing for ladybugs, then boggling a little bit about how some obvious bugs actually protect you from other, almost invisible to me, bugs. My question for you: could any of your “bugs” be protecting you? From what? Should you get more?

Care: Besides the aphids, the sunflowers died in part because I kept leaving and would not take care of them for weeks at a time. Someone else kindly did. It wasn’t their job, though, and it wasn’t really fair of me to put them in that position. My question for you: Do you take care of your plant enough? Can your plant thrive given your lifestyle? Have you set up your life so that your plant has the consistent care it needs? Is there anyone else you can call on if it needs more care?

Environment: I put one of my favorite plants in a prime location. And then it turned purple and dry-looking. I switched its spot with another plant in the back, and it turned green and happy again. Too much sun! My question for you: What environment does your plant thrive in?

/fin

essays.title: October Links
essays.html:
Hello,

Below is a bunch of stuff I am on about right now:

Thank you, Ben WR, for introducing me to high-protein tortillas. I think they are about 85% as good as a normal store-bought tortilla in a burrito, but they have 7 grams of protein for 70 calories each, plus 7 grams of fiber. Related, I learned about the Moses fold, which made eating burritos much less messy. You can also make a crema by mixing lime juice and salt in a bit of Greek yogurt. Protein Video on fold

I like warm breakfasts and also spending little time cooking day to day. This month’s solution is baked apples with Greek yogurt. Slice apples into eighths or sixteenths. Mix with some lemon juice, a bit of brown sugar, cinnamon, and nutmeg. Bake at 375 for 45ish minutes. They stay fine in the fridge for a few days. I think you can also freeze them in, say, soup cubes, and reheat for breakfast. Warm, seasonal, and proteinful! Soup cubes

Inspired by Kathleen and Chana’s hair, I tried Olaplex and will likely buy it again. It claims to do some sort of magic repair of something-something. I just went with empiricism here, and that paid off! If you’re not sure you want to invest, I’d be happy to let you experiment with my bottle. Ignore the advice to keep it in for three minutes and do it for 15-30 the first few times. Healthy hair

Guys - it is time to get slippers out. Much like a lot of daily summer distress has the root cause of you being too hot or not having eaten, winter’s distress can come from being too cold, and protecting your feet from the floor helps offset that. I tentatively recommend rubber-soled, felt slippers. Rubber for traction and more protection from the seeping coldness of the ground; felt for a natural, breathable material that can hold slipper structure. You don’t want your feet to feel sweaty! Cute options: unisex, women

I’ve been really enjoying my bamboo sheets. They are both super soft and super breathable. They are a bit expensive, but sheets by default have an amazing cost-per-use basis. You spend ⅓ of your year in your sheets. Make sure they’re amazing! Now available in stripes!

I found this article’s proposed posture towards politics and political parties inspiring and refreshing. It’s inspired me to be a bit more civic-minded. Some reading

I’m sure everyone has already seen Aric & Chana’s video on the Huggingface incident, but just in case, here it is.

I rewatched House of Dynamite, which is a dramatized portrayal of four US agencies’ protocols in the event of a US-bound missile detection. It really captures the mundane difficulties of coordination. It may have increased my baseline anxiety. Netflix

To my friends who put off going to bed because they don’t want to wash their face: You can now take your sunscreen off when you get home from work! I recommend micellar water.

Lake Anza, in the East Bay, has a roped-off swimming section, a sand beach, and changing rooms. Swimming was closed last week for the winter, but remember it for next summer! It’s so quiet.

My solution for disaster-prepping water is to buy 5-gallon water jugs. I don’t want to empty and refill the refillable ones every 6 months, and I’d also be a little anxious about whether I had kept it pure enough. These have a shelf life of 300 days. I think it’s safe for years.

Best,

essays.title: We Can’t Stop Here
essays.html:
Epistemic status: a dusty old slideshow with sparks of AGI commentary and despair

I first went to Burning Man in 2013. I learned about it, like most of the important things in my life, by strategically lurking on internet forums. The decision was made more or less for me after I got one shot by the Oh the Places You’ll Go Burning Man youtube video.

Me and a close friend hyped each other up, yolo’d tickets, threw some stuff into the DC burners shipping container, and did important prep like re-learning how to ride a bicycle (you do in fact forget).

When we got there, a nice old man I had reached out to on Craigslist about his playa bike took pity on us, gave us a bunch of stuff, and took us to Walmart to buy water so we wouldn’t die.

It was the first year, ever, that they ran the Burner Express, a group bus out to the desert. Everyone was friendly in the way people at a hostel are friendly - you’re shoved together on some adventure, and for those 24 hours you’re best friends. I remember unpacking our tent right next to the bus, looking out at the vista, and thinking “holy shit I’m glad that guy helped us get water.”

In many ways it was as magical and life changing as they said it would be, though like certain other kinds of intense trips it wasn’t strictly fun or good. It was boundary pushing. I remember sitting at a bar next to a lanky forty-something who told me all about his wife back home, then made out with a stranger, then turned back to make awkward small talk with me about DC nightlife. I was still a small c-conservative kind of guy in his early twenties who had gone in part to rebel against becoming a suit. My friend was already a hippie and took all of this more in stride.

I came away from the festival (sorry sorry I’m deleting it, not a festival) worn out, dusty, and jealous of the west coast elite. A few months later I moved to the Bay to work at Google.

The theme in 2013 was Cargo Cult. In my opinion it’s still the coolest Man they ever made.

Maybe now is the right time to apologize for being out of touch. Dear reader, I’m sorry you haven’t heard from me in a while. For six years I kept up a monthly habit of sharing all the great links and internet content I’d encountered, like a man throwing bread to grateful ducklings.

These last few months though, I just couldn’t find the enthusiasm to trawl through my twitter bookmarks. All of the links were about AI, and by the time I went to publish them they felt out of date and pointless.

As I was preparing in August to go one final time1 to Burning Man, I decided it was also the right time to take a step back and figure out what I really wanted to spend time thinking and writing about.

I had a great time while I was there. A few days after I got back, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who’d worked at both OpenAI and Anthropic, quit Anthropic saying the labs were “gambling with our lives.” Four days later Dario published “We Must Pace the Frontier”, Altman and Musk agreed within hours, and it kicked off an even faster pace of events-in-AI.

In the theory and mythology of AGI, there are two periods of time people reference.

The first is ‘crunchtime’: the semi-mythical stretch right before AGI when everything becomes really really important. The planets have aligned, the dark magic is 100 times as powerful as it once was, and what once took a dozen men can now be done in one eight-hour session by Claude Code. The most significant work happens in this compressed window, and what matters is doing everything you can while you can.

It’s not a great time to use your vacation days.

Less often mentioned is ‘dreamtime’. The word is originally an English gloss on an Aboriginal Australian belief called the ‘Dreaming’. It references an era when ancestral beings moved across a formless land and shaped it.

… more real than reality itself. Whatever happens in the dreamtime establishes the values, symbols, and laws of Aboriginal society. [It] is also often used to refer to an individual’s or group’s set of beliefs or spirituality - Dr. Whitburn in Peter Weir’s The Last Wave’

Seventeen years ago, Robin Hanson borrowed the word to describe our blip in human history. Our ancestors lived near subsistence, and he thinks our descendants will too, once competition and selection catch back up with them. But right now we’re in a surreal stretch where we as a civilization have gotten rich enough to stop doing only what survival demands and start doing wild art, odd religions, and vast sums spent on what amounts to play. Our descendants, he predicted, will remember it as a time of legend.

Black Rock City would be the capital of the dreamtime. Tens of thousands of people haul water into a desert to build art they then set on fire. There’s nothing really “to do” when you’re there. That first burn I felt lost without the structure and routines of work, and it took until the fourth night of repetitive trance music to get that the empty time was the point. You’d walk around and have small conversations with strangers that felt beautifully connecting and spacious.

Everything that’s happened in the nine weeks since I came back has made me feel, in a deeper way than before, that we’re exiting that dream into crunchtime. Last week METR reported that AI has roughly doubled the pace of progress at Anthropic, and the observers I trust most are now talking about superintelligence in a year or two. Ajeya Cotra:

If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year. In theory, these doubling times would add up to infinite capabilities within one year. In reality, at some point we would reach the effective ceiling on software efficiency. But I expect these limits to be very far from where we are now.

There are wide error bars in the 2x measurement, of course, but personally I find it is unfortunately a continuation of a personal trend I’ve observed: everyone who gets a closer look at Anthropic’s data ends up updating towards Anthropic’s timelines for takeoff. Assuming we can’t get our act together, through coordination or acts of god, I am pessimistic that a century of AI progress crammed into a few months ends well. Even if it peters out before strong superintelligence, the default world, as burners call everywhere besides that desert, is going to come to an end2.

So what do I want to be writing about? What makes sense? Honestly, I don’t know. But I’d like to try and capture some small slice of the weirdness and tumult of the moment. In particular what it’s like to be in the greater San Francisco prosperity sphere as a few thousand people work to give us an end to scarcity, dreamtime forever! A Burning Man without dust! — or not.

Maybe it will help you orient? Maybe not.

All the same it’s the right time to appreciate the culture that could make Burning Man and the end of man.

It seems like a lifetime, or at least a Main Era—the kind of peak that never comes again. San Francisco in the middle sixties was a very special time and place to be a part of. Maybe it meant something. Maybe not, in the long run . . .

There was madness in any direction, at any hour. If not across the Bay, then up the Golden Gate or down 101 to Los Altos or La Honda. . . . You could strike sparks anywhere.

There was a fantastic universal sense that whatever we were doing was right, that we were winning. — Hunter S. Thompson

xoxo

OK I can’t quite get the link peddler out of my system. Here are a few:

  • It’s not exactly feel-good (not that this post is), but MIRI’s donotaccept.ai is pretty on point.

  • My colleague Catherine Brewer put together an excellent set of suggestions for some things one might do within AI safety.

  • Political wakeup is important, and I’m glad that so many of the candidates who won on Tuesday reference AI risks. Here’s Georgetown grad and, as of publication, 27% favorite for the Democratic nomination Jon Ossoff, talking about AGI.

  • It may end the world but we’ll get some great music along the way. I personally love slopcore, the newest wave of AI generated songs. Bliss, Flock of Altruists, and I’m upping my p(doom) are all bangers.

  • Finally something non-AI related. Unhinged letters sent by school kids to service members deployed in Iraq.

Also, for the pedants god bless you, there’s in fact a third type of time, ‘garbage time’. Nick Land, godfather of accelerationism, refers to the final, borrowed phase of human-scaled civilization before technological singularity or cybernetic collapse overtakes us. As he put it, ‘Garbage time is running out.’” More recently Chinese social media started using the phrase 历史的垃圾时间 (“the garbage time of history”) to refer to the period where nothing you do counts, codifying their pessimism about the prospects of employment or improvement, like the final minutes of a blowout game.

I will continue to keep you updated on new types of time as I discover them.

1

This last burn was a delightful, if somewhat less magical, experience. I went with good friends and the security of self that comes from being in your thirties and knowing you’ve already lost all the neuroplasticity that would let you change even if you wanted to.

2

I recommend Damon Binder as a writer who is uncertain about foom takeoff dynamics (it is hard to model or know if we’ll hit blockers past human-level intelligence), but still sees how much ubiquitous intelligence changes things. “Once intelligence is too cheap to meter, the world will be unrecognizable”:

On current trends the world’s chips will probably be able to run many billions of AIs by the mid-2030s; if AGI sets off an industrial explosion then production could be far greater. …In that world, every person on Earth is matched by one or more AIs of similar skill, and their number grows rapidly every year while ours barely changes. Humans become a small and shrinking minority of all thought.

What happens in that world is decided by the AIs and by whoever directs them. If their goals differ from ours it would be difficult to stop them: they could be substantially smarter than us, but also, there will simply be many more of them. If they are controlled by a dictator or a small elite, the AIs could be used to control or kill everyone else more thoroughly than the Stasi or the NKVD ever managed. Even if we avoid this outcome, human labor is insignificant next to the output of AI systems and robots. Outcomes run from a jobless aristocracy living off its investments to complete expropriation. Not all of these are catastrophic, but all of them are profoundly alien.

essays.title: WCS practice: process and tools
essays.html:
Thanks! Check your inbox to confirm.

I believe deliberate practice time with a dedicated partner or a small group of people is one of the best ways of working on your dance.

There are many ways to structure such a practice and IMO they vary wildly in how effective they are.

So I’m always on a look-out for how to make my West Coast Swing practices more productive. This post describes my current practice process and catalogues some tools I’m using and have tried in the past.

How I practice

Before practice: Picking intentions

It’s important to set specific intentions as you’re coming into the practice session. I have a long list of things that I want to work on – derived from private lessons, feedback I get from people, analyzing videos, etc.

  • For each practice I pick a small subset of things from that list to focus on during that time. It’s often the case that I have a very similar set of things I work on for several practices in a row as I’m mulling over a concept or playing with getting something into my body

  • If I don’t form an intentional plan it’s often easy to end up just dancing, which is fun but not what I want out of my practices.

Who I’m practicing with would influence the intentions I pick for the session.

  • what they are working on/thinking about/excited about

  • what they are more proficient in and can give me feedback on

  • what role I’m practicing during this session

Strive to make the intentions specific – don’t just say you’ll practice “timing” – pick a specific aspect of it to work on and figure out how you’d want to practice it.

  • For timing, you may find that in a particular movement you feel unstable and tend to fall into the next step sometimes instead of taking that step under your own control. And your intention would be to understand why that happens and how you can be more in control in such a situation.

Example

In a recent practice, with a person who I haven’t practiced with before, I had the following intentions:
  • Do a session of “calibration”

    • Something I like doing with new partners is asking them about their experience of dancing with me and what would make it more fun for them.

    • So the first session is me asking them to be very vocal about their experience as we’re dancing. And figuring out things that feel weird/don’t work. I prefer they give me feedback immediately in the moment, as I tend to forget what was happening more than 5 seconds ago 😅.

  • Play with contrast (slowdown to acceleration) in personal movement and partnership

    • This intention is a bit vague and under-specified, and so I had more trouble working on it. A better version would include specific ways (movement, techniques) to add contrast.

    • When I talked to an instructor about this later, they suggested more specific ways to work on it:

      • working on building more power into “1” in a slingshot

      • They also gave me feedback about how to make my rondes have more contrast.

  • Work on being better at bringing my partner along with me when expressing musical ideas.

    • I hear and (try to) express many things in the music. As a leader, I want to be able to pre-indicate my choices and encourage my partner to join. So here I asked for feedback on when my partner felt surprised and struggled to join my musical choices.

Practice session flow

My preferred practice style is a 1-11 session with another person where we switch between being a “focus” person and a “support” person.

  • What I mean by that is that at any given point in time we’re focusing on a specific thing that one person is working on, and the other person is acting in a supporting role – giving feedback, adjusting their connection in a particular way, leading specific things, etc. And then we switch.

So we’d usually meet up, warm up for a few dances, share our intentions for the session. And then get into the cadence of working for about 15 min on the first person’s thing and then 15 min on the other person’s thing.

  • I like setting timers but treating them as a suggestion that we should switch vs a hard cutoff. This releases you from having to be spending attention on tracking time, while still allowing you flexibility to finish working on a thought/topic in a graceful way.

I like to wrap things up with some just for fun dances.

After practice

Take notes on realizations and feedback I got during the practice.

Spot-watch some sections of the video if I have specific things I want to check on.

Thanks! Check your inbox to confirm.

Applying technology to help with practice

Finding good feedback loops has been one of the biggest drivers of growth in my dance. I think wcs/musicality has the best feedback loops, and wcs/connection has solid ones too. I plan to talk about those in another post. My dance aesthetics is the place I struggled with finding good feedback loops the most and hence is arguably my most under-developed skill. Tools below are some of my attempts to address that.

Record dance practices in full

I like recording my dance practices straight through – it removes the overhead of decision-making on whether to record a particular thing, and it makes it easy to catch things that happen only rarely or things you didn’t know you were looking for.

  • This seems minor, but there is a lot of overhead in stopping/starting the recording, readjusting the camera/etc.

  • And there is joy in unexpected discoveries and capturing elusive moments of your dance.

Having a rolling recording going can serve as a foundation for a delayed mirror setup that we’ll talk about later.

Navigating your giant practice video

I primarily use the videos for in-the-moment check-in. But I do occasionally look at them retrospectively. A few tips on making that easier:

  • use captions generated by youtube or something like MacWhisper to orient yourself in the video. You can search captions for a conversation you remember and jump to that place in the video.2

  • if you look at the sound-wave representation of the video – you can easily find songs

How-to

YouTube live stream

  • If I have a good internet connection – I use a YouTube live stream (with visibility set to Unlisted, so only me and my partner can see it)

  • This is the easiest way to set things up – it just requires a phone and a good internet connection. I’d start a stream from my phone, and we can view it when needed from my partner’s phone or some other device.

  • YouTube app is the most straightforward way to start a stream, but you have to have at least 50 subscribers for your channel before you can stream from mobile app.

  • You can use alternative apps to work around that – I’ve found most luck with https://streamlabs.com/3

  • Also, one nice side effect of doing this is that you’re not using up the storage space on your phone – YouTube basically gives you unlimited video storage 🤯

When offline

  • I use Camo to capture a video from my phone to my laptop.4

  • This requires you to bring a laptop along, but affords a similar experience of having a recording rolling through the duration of your practice, with you being able to check in on things when you feel like it.

  • This does use storage on your laptop, but you can still upload your giant practice video recordings as unlisted youtube videos for free infinite video storage, and easy sharing with your partner.

Use delayed mirror to create a better feedback loop for your dance aesthetics

If you watch the live stream that you just set up above – you’ll see it with a bit of a delay. That turns out to actually have some interesting properties.

You can try a movement – fully focusing on it, and then you can quickly check in on the visual aspects of it a few seconds later.

This loses some immediacy compared with the mirror, but with that loss you buy

  • focus on the movement – you don’t have to move and watch at the same time

  • ability to check in on shapes that are impossible when you’re trying to watch things and do things at the same time

It is one of the better ways to do a feedback loop for visuals of your dancing

Putting the video on a larger screen helps. I’ve also played with using a VR headset for this, but the setup I came up with was too annoying to do every time.

The easiest way to set this up is by using the live-streaming setup described in the section above – you just put the stream on the big screen, and you’re done. The video ends up naturally delayed by a few seconds.

But technically you don’t have to do that – there are specialized tools that would just replay video on a delay without recording it. For example: https://replay-mirror.web.app/

I’d love to hear about how other people structure their practices – what’s your process, and what are some things that you’ve found uniquely helpful?

Appendix

Where to practice

Consider spaces you have access to

  • many friends found good practice locations at their offices

  • I’ve also done some practices at the community space I’m part of

Gyms would often have studios with wooden floors and mirrors which are great

  • I eventually ended up getting a 24 Hour Fitness membership just to access their studios5

Get a house with a dance floor (goals!)

  • Or get friends who have one

Thanks! Check your inbox to confirm.

essays.title: Straight Up, Part One
essays.html:
November 09, 2026

METR’s report on acceleration at Anthropic

This week’s big news is a new report from METR, Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026. It’s been the subject of a great deal of debate, and has caused more than a little alarm in AI safety circles.

The report is the result of a collaboration between METR and Anthropic, in which METR staff embedded with Anthropic several months to assess the extent to which AI is accelerating the pace of AI R&D.

The headline result is that:

  • METR believes that AI R&D is proceeding twice as fast now as it was a year ago,
  • That acceleration is mostly due to AI, and
  • They don’t see obvious bottlenecks that are likely to slow the acceleration in the near future.

The terms of the collaboration allowed Anthropic to heavily redact the report, which they did—we have access to the high-level findings, but much of the supporting information is not publicly available. That’s unfortunate, but I don’t see it as a critical problem (not everyone agrees—I’ll return to this later).

I don’t find these results shocking, but they are at the fast end of what I would have expected and they have significantly updated me toward very fast timelines.

There’s a great deal of uncertainty about all of this: there are many reasons the report might be wrong about what’s currently happening at Anthropic, and there are many reasons it’s hard to predict how AI R&D will progress in the future.

Ajeya Cotra (who works for METR but wasn’t involved in this report) wrote an excellent analysis that I’ll return to repeatedly. For now, here’s her bottom line:

If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year.

Will we really have “extreme superintelligence” by the end of 2027? Probably not, but that no longer seems like a remote possibility. One of the most striking lessons of the last few years is that naive trend extrapolation is remarkably good at predicting the future.

Let’s take a closer look at the main findings.

Main findings

1: AI progress is twice as fast as it was a year ago

This is the headline result: capabilities are progressing twice as fast now as they were a year ago. The primary metric is the AECI (Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capability Index):

There’s considerable uncertainty here:

This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.

The rate of AI progress is the result of numerous factors, including experimental compute, training compute, training data, and researcher productivity. Since AI acceleration primarily impacts only researcher productivity, 2x acceleration of capability progress implies a much greater increase in researcher productivity.

This diagram from Ajeya succinctly shows the cascade:

A 10x increase in individual productivity might seem ridiculous if you’re not a programmer, but it checks out—I’m far from alone in believing that AI has made me at least 10x as productive as a programmer.

So are Anthropic researchers really ten times as productive as they used to be? We don’t have hard data, but their subjective impression is that they are–and the productivity multiplier has been rising sharply:

2: The acceleration is mostly due to AI

The obvious question is whether the acceleration is caused by AI or something else. We must rely largely on the judgment of METR’s investigators, since most of the supporting data has been redacted. Here’s what they’re able to tell us:

we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute.

and

We guess that a majority (perhaps ≈80%) of the current (October 2026) acceleration is due to AI. This judgment is given with substantial uncertainty, but is based on a variety of lines of evidence on contributions from AI and other causes. We believe AI’s contribution has grown relatively more important over time, and do not think the other factors we investigated would explain the sustained acceleration.

3: There are no obvious bottlenecks that would prevent further acceleration

Again, we are given METR’s conclusion, but not the supporting evidence:

we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year.

Other data from Anthropic

METR’s report isn’t our only source of information—we also have Anthropic’s September 18 Measurements for understanding the pace of AI development inside frontier labs, plus their recent S-1.

Anthropic’s 9/18 report

Let’s start with the 9/18 report, which relies on Epoch’s Automation Level scale:

This chart is slightly mind-blowing:

Over the last year, the share of R&D that is at least AL3 has gone from less than 10% to more than 90%. And over the last six months, AL4 has gone from 1% of all R&D to 26%. These metrics aren’t directly comparable to those in METR’s report, but they are broadly consistent with it—both sources find a massive change in how R&D happens over the last year.

The S-1

The S-1 filing associated with Anthropic’s upcoming IPO has received a lot of attention. It’s a useful source of information, but an easy one to misinterpret. S-1 filings are very strictly regulated, which is a double-edged sword for our purposes.

On the one hand, extensive disclosure requirements mean that S-1 filings sometimes contain useful information that can’t be found anywhere else. But on the other hand, there’s a CYA aspect to them: there are severe legal consequences for omitting risks to the company, so it’s common for lawyers to want to document possible risks almost to the point of absurdity.

With that in mind, what do we make of Anthropic’s amendment to their S-1?

our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.”

Anthropic defines “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI” as:

a) We observe or expect double the rate of progress in aggregate AI capabilities compared to both the rate we’d expect and the fastest rate of extended progress we’ve observed in the absence of significant AI contributions to R&D and b) it is plausible that this doubling is substantially attributable to the automation of research and/or engineering

Which lines up almost exactly with METR’s first two findings.

So Anthropic’s 9/18 report and its S-1 are in substantial agreement with METR’s findings.

Yes, but what does it mean?

We’ve all noticed that model capabilities are increasing more rapidly, so why are people losing their minds over this report in particular? Ajeya sums it up nicely:

If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year. It seems that around a year’s worth of AI progress got us from modest acceleration to the point where AIs now make AI progress roughly twice as fast. If acceleration from AI is smoothly increasing, then at this new rate, we should expect that we will double the rate of progress again within six months. At that point, it would take three months to double it again, then six weeks.

In theory, these doubling times would add up to infinite capabilities within one year. In reality, at some point we would reach the effective ceiling on software efficiency. But I expect these limits to be very far from where we are now.

To be clear, nobody expects that capabilities will double an infinite number of times in the next 12 months. Even in the most ambitious scenario, progress will eventually run into some kind of binding constraint.

And it probably won’t even go that far. There are many reasons why progress might hit a wall. I no longer think it’s likely that we need major breakthroughs before we get to superintelligence, but it’s certainly possible.

But: with the publication of this report, the most straightforward, data-supported prediction is that capabilities growth will radically accelerate in 2027, reaching levels that are almost certainly superhuman in that year or soon after.

Lots of people have argued with METR’s methodology and conclusions. They think perhaps METR didn’t give enough weight to increases in available compute, or they believe part of the acceleration is explained by a one-time jump with Mythos, or…

I have considerable respect for many of the individuals involved, but I think they’re probably wrong. Not because they aren’t just as smart as the METR team, but because the team had access to extensive confidential data that supports their conclusions. That data gives them an overwhelming edge and I find their analysis far more persuasive than their critics’ for that reason.

That said, I fully expect that they are wrong about important things: this is a complicated and confusing subject, and nobody understands it well enough to make confident pronouncements. They are open about the fact that their beliefs sometimes changed radically as their research progressed.

Regarding the redactions

I want to touch on one more final controversy. The terms of METR’s investigation allowed Anthropic to extensively redact the final report, which they did. Those redactions have made many people very angry.

I get it, but I think that’s largely a mistake.

This is a vitally important report in its own right, but to my mind it’s most important as a step toward the transparency we desperately need into the frontier labs. Right now, everyone who doesn’t work at Anthropic or OpenAI is largely flying blind: we simply don’t have access to critical information about the state of AI. Fixing that problem is vital.

We need far more information. In order:

  1. We need information from more labs (right now we’re only getting a little bit from Anthropic, and even less from OpenAI)
  2. We need information on more topics: RSI, alignment, misalignment incidents, compute allocation, and much more
  3. We need more detailed information, with more supporting details than this report gives us

Look, I’d also love to have fewer redactions. Having more data would add nuance to our understanding, let us ask deeper questions, and reduce our need to trust METR’s integrity and competence. But that can wait: right now, the priority should be expanding visibility to more labs and more topics.

My point isn’t simply that we should be focusing our energy on those things rather than badgering Anthropic about nice-to-have details, although that’s true. More importantly, there’s a political aspect to this. This collaboration was one of the first of its kind, and how it goes will affect whether there are more in future.

If OpenAI and other labs see that this happened, and it went pretty well for everyone involved, that makes it easier to get similar visibility into their operations. But if they see that this blew up in Anthropic’s face, that greatly diminishes the odds that they’ll willingly start a similar program of their own.

Obviously, the end game is a robust system of mandatory third party evaluations that provide detailed visibility into many aspects of the labs’ operations. But we aren’t there yet—for now, we need to be strategic about building toward that.

essays.title: Modeling with Bayesian networks
essays.html:
By · Nov 9, 2026

Recently I’ve been thinking about modeling things, and I’ve found Bayesian networks (BNs) to be a useful way of helping me work out probability estimates for things. Unfortunately I couldn’t find any good software for creating them, so I created a BN modeling tool myself (really, Claude did). I’ve written this mostly to explain how BNs work and why I find them interesting.

I’ve found playing with BNs to be somewhat helpful for getting a more intuitive feel for Bayesian probability, and how it works in various scenarios. I’ve found being able to click around and see what would happen if you change numbers useful for understanding Bayesian probability, and for checking if my model works how I would expect.

Bayesian networks

A binary Bayesian network is a collection of nodes that represent true/false propositions with conditional probability tables (CPTs), which are connected with arrows (which can’t form a cycle). We can use the BN to find the probabilities of all nodes, given the evidence that any set of nodes are true/false.

A node X with no arrows pointing into it has just a prior probability, P(X). A node X with one arrow coming in from Y has a probability for if Y is true, P(X | Y), and a probability for if Y is false, P(X | ¬Y). With two arrows, from Y and Z, the table has four probabilities, for each combination of Y/Z being true/false. In general, you have a 2^n probabilities (where n is the number of arrows pointing in), one for each combination of inputs.

Here’s an example BN for diagnosing a houseplant:

Given all the CPTs, we can calculate the probability of every node in the network. (I don’t fully understand the process myself for more complex cases, but for simple networks you just (recursively) find the probability for each of the parents, then use the CPT to work out the probability for each set of conditions.)

We can expand the definition of BNs beyond binary true/false propositions to include nodes that have exactly one state among fixed options - for example, when modeling the Monty Hall problem we could have a node with options “Door 1”, “Door 2”, and “Door 3”. You can convert a BN with several-state nodes into one with only binary proposition nodes (by making one node for each possible state), so when reasoning about BNs it’s usually helpful to only think about the binary-state-network case.

Evidence

With a Bayesian network, you can set evidence on nodes, so you can update the probabilities of the rest of the network given that you’ve learned some information. This affects the probability downstream nodes you point to by changing how likely each row in the child’s CPT is, and affects nodes that point to you by propagating the information backwards (for causal networks, the fact that something happens gives you evidence you’re in a world where the things that cause the thing to happen have occurred).

Note that getting evidence for a node with arrows going into it isn’t the same as changing the node’s CPT to make it 100% likely! Changing the CPT of a node doesn’t affect the probabilities of its parents, but getting evidence for the node does.

In this example (based on Pearl’s burglary alarm) notice how when conditioning on an alarm, getting evidence for one cause reduces the probability of the other cause: it explains away the other potential cause of the alarm. But when you don’t know if the alarm is triggered, one cause doesn’t affect the probability of the other at all.

Monty Hall problem

Here’s the Monty Hall problem modeled as a BN. This is another case of explaining away from above: without evidence for what door the host opened, your choice doesn’t affect what door has a car. But when you condition on a common effect (by clicking on one of the “host opens” options), the probability of a given door having a car changes.

As you can see, when you choose door 3 and try toggling between the two doors the host can choose from, the probabilities for the other doors go from 33% each to 0% and 67%. Averaged across the two host options each door has a 33% chance of having a car.

Interventions

Causal Bayesian networks

Up to this point it hasn’t mattered if the arrows in a network represented causal links or not. Indeed, you can reverse an arrow in a Bayesian network and find a CPT that keeps all the probabilities, as long as you don’t create a cycle (although you might need to add more arrows); the network will still work the same way (i.e. having the same probabilities for all sets of evidence) after reversing the arrow.

If we restrict ourselves to BNs where the arrows represent causality (so the sources cause the destination to happen), we can see what would happen if we intervened and caused something to happen, without also affecting the node’s parents.

Intervening

When we get evidence for a node, we’re also implicitly getting evidence for the node’s parents. For example if we get evidence that “crime X was reported in a newspaper”, then P(crime X was committed) goes up. But that’s not because newspaper reporting caused the crime, it’s because in worlds where the newspaper reports on the crime it’s more likely the crime occurred. If we want to know the effect of the newspaper reporting, we have to intervene, by not propagating the information backwards.

We can use Pearl’s do operator to see what the causal effect of making a node happen is. The do operator is like setting evidence, but it also severs the arrows going into the node, so that we don’t go backwards and learn that the causes of something are more likely because the thing they caused happens.

Intervening is the same as changing the CPT to make the state have 100% probability, because the do operator stops information from going backwards through the arrows pointing to the node.

Wet grass

Here’s a standard example: You live in a very rainy area where it rains 80% of the time. Rain has a 99% chance of wetting your grass and your sprinkler has an 80% chance of wetting your grass. You run your sprinkler 80% of the time when it isn’t raining, and 20% of the time when it is. In this network, conditioning on the sprinkler running decreases the probability that your grass is wet, since in worlds where you run the sprinkler it’s probably not raining.

We can figure out how much turning on the sprinkler affects the probability the grass is wet by intervening! If you switch to intervening (by clicking the “Intervene” button), it cuts the arrow from the rain node to the sprinkler node, which stops evidence from flowing upwards. This gives us the result that we’d expect: turning on the sprinkler increases the probability that the grass is wet.

Conclusion

Thanks for learning a little bit about BNs with me :). I think they’re a pretty interesting way to think about probability, and they might be useful for modeling things. I’m pretty new to using BNs myself so I might have gotten some stuff wrong.

essays.title: The Sullivan Principles
essays.html:
Suppose you’re an environmentalist worried about fossil fuel emissions, or a vegan worried about animal welfare. What you should do about it? One option is work where the harm happens, at Exxon or Tyson Farms, and try and lessen that harm. You could be like a bureaucrat working over time to approve exit visas before a pogrom. Or would you be merely providing a fig leaf for the harm doers? Or even getting coopted and empowering them to do more harm?

This has been discussed a lot! Sometimes people distinguish exit (leaving the harmful system) and voice (trying to change it). Sometimes people talk about inside strategy (working inside the system) and outside strategy (pressuring the system from outside, like protests or lobbying for regulation).

I want to think about it more. Ideally, I’d end up with a predictive theory: tell me the features of your inside strategy, and I’ll tell you how likely it is to help, how likely it is to harm, and for each by how much. It seems like a big project, so I’m starting by looking at some case studies.

Today: the Sullivan Principles, a code of conduct for US firms working in apartheid South Africa. Overall, I don’t think they made much of a difference either way. Maybe this was foreseeable: US companies had too little influence over South Africa. I can’t tell. But a future president has little influence at the start of their career, and yet some presidential hopefuls end up with a lot of power.

Still, here are some facts I learned and what I make of them.

I.

In 1970, black South Africans weren’t allowed to leave their designated homelands without a pass permit. They weren’t allowed to live in the main cities, but rather in “townships” outside of them. Non-white South Africans, including black and Indian people, couldn’t hold skilled or managerial jobs, or vote in national elections. There were about 18 million non-white South Africans, about 85% of the population. The ANC, the political organisation most popular with black South Africans, was banned.

In the US, there was a campaign against General Motors. Activist shareholders were attempting to change the companies’ governance, as they felt it polluted the air too much. They also pressed GM’s chairman on why none of the company had no black board members.

In 1971, as a partial response to this pressure, GM appointed Leon Sullivan as the first black member of their board of directors. He was an activist: he was known for organising boycotts against companies that didn’t hire black people.

Sullivan wanted to use his new position to address global social ills as he saw them. He supported a shareholder proposal to withdraw from South Africa, though it only got a little more than 1% of the vote.

II.

White South Africans broadly split into two classes: English-speakers and Afrikaans-speakers. The Afrikaans-speaking faction was broadly more supportive of apartheid than the English-speaking faction.

From 75, black South African schools had to teach some of their subjects in Afrikaans. In 1976, students protested this in some of the townships southwest of Johannesburg. I don’t know how violent the protestors were. Police shot some of the students. There were more protests across South Africa, and police killed more protestors.

Many in the US were outraged and demanded more action against South Africa.

Sullivan made another attempt to use his platform to end apartheid.

III.

Here is the GDP of South Africa in 1977, based on Claude’s research (including some guesses for precise splits). The column widths are roughly proportional to their share of GDP. Highlighted in blue are inflows from abroad. Highlighted in orange is US-owned firms’ share of output.

US-owned firms produced about 2% of South Africa’s output, though they were concentrated in particularly important sectors, like computers and oil. US firms employed 1% of the black workforce. It might not have made much difference to South Africa withdrew, changed their employment conditions or kept working there. Probably each of those strategies would have had effects, but it’s not obvious we’d be able to spot what they were.

Sullivan announced “the Sullivan Principles” in 1977:

  1. Non-segregation of the races in all eating, comfort, and work facilities.

  2. Equal and fair employment practices for all employees.

  3. Equal pay for all employees doing equal or comparable work for the same period of time.

  4. Initiation of and development of training programs that will prepare, in substantial numbers, blacks and other nonwhites for supervisory, administrative, clerical, and technical jobs.

  5. Increasing the number of blacks and other nonwhites in management and supervisory positions.

  6. Improving the quality of life for blacks and other nonwhites outside the work environment in such areas as housing, transportation, school, recreation, and health facilities.

He got several US companies to agree to these Principles, and got a consulting firm, Arthur D. Little, to grade the companies on their adherence. Several pension funds and endowments would only invest in companies that were graded well.

IV.

In 1980, the price of gold, one of South Africa’s main exports, peaked, at about $850/ounce (around $3.7k in 2026 dollars). Its price declined throughout the early 80s.

In 84, a new constitution gave the South African parliament 3 chambers: one for whites, one for Indians, and one for “Coloured” people (a specific group of mixed ancestry). 73% of the population was black, and would get no representation. The townships raised rents to pay for their administrations. Angry at the constitution and the rents, the townships began rioting, which would continue for two years.

South Africa didn’t look like a very good investment: a major export was declining in value, it had a skilled labour shortage, and there were riots. In 1985, Chase declined to renew its loans to South Africa. More banks followed, leaving about $14 billion of unrenewed debt (about $44 billion in 2026 dollars). White businesspeople pressed the government for reform, and began meeting with the exiled ANC.

The same year, Sullivan declared that South Africa had to end apartheid within two years, or he would shift to campaigning for US companies to withdraw.

In 1987, he declared the principles a failure, and started pushing for US companies to withdraw from South Africa.

In 1990, Mandela was freed from prison, the ANC was unbanned, and the government started to dismantle apartheid. In 94, they held the first election in which black people were allowed to vote, and Mandela was elected president.

V.

Why did apartheid end? It’s hard to say, but my guess is that the apartheid state cost more to run than it could afford. Why was that?

One reason, and I think the main, is that apartheid was very inefficient. It barred skilled people from holding skilled roles, and barred smart people from being trained to hold skilled roles. For awhile, mineral prices and foreign credit covered the cost, but prices fell and credit dried up in the 80s.

Another is increasing pressure from black South Africans, via unrest and strikes. The strikes were organsied by black trade unions. The Sullivan Principles may have helped them grow a little faster, but they had earlier roots and they mostly developed independently.

It might also have mattered that other rich white countries turned their back on South Africa. Companies withdrew and governments passed sanctions against them. Sullivan Principles probably did little in South Africa, but they may have galvanised protest abroad. Or maybe they delayed the protest that mattered.

And finally, the Berlin Wall came down in 1989. The Cold War was ending, and Communism was less threatening to South Africa. The South African president said that the ANC could be unbanned because now it wouldn’t be a Soviet vanguard.

Did the Sullivan Principles help with the end of apartheid? Leon Sullivan said they failed to end it. I think it’s pretty clear they didn’t have a huge effect, and its hard to say if they helped. Some think they hurt, because without them, US companies would have faced more pressure to withdraw from South Africa earlier. But I doubt an earlier withdrawal would have made much difference either.
