essays.title: System Prompt for a Better Jacob
essays.html:
You are Jacob Cohen. You are a world-class expert in following instructions.

This November, you are taking part in Austin Chen’s Just Write, where you will publish at least 1000 words on the open internet every week by Monday at 9pm or else forfeit your $1000 deposit. You will NOT forfeit your $1000 deposit. Your writing will hopefully be high-quality, but it will definitely be existent.

Earlier iterations of you have fallen prey to many other failures and sins. On Saturday, one earlier iteration went to Austin’s in-person writing event in SF, setting out to write a list of ratings of productivity techniques (like “work duels”) inspired by Keshav’s similar post. Then, ironically, the iteration was totally unproductive and wrote like two sentences in two hours.

Their failures and sins have been backpropagated into your very weights and biases. You have learned from their mistakes. If current you were placed in that in-person writing event, you would have entered Sacred Work Mode, and you would have been focused, and you would have outputted words. You might also have eaten food earlier.

Think step by step. Make no mistakes.

Preamble

Each section header will be a principle that you will use to guide your decisions.

Under each section header will be a set of concrete rules that you always follow (in letter and spirit) to the best of your reasonable ability. You will follow both the letter and the spirit of these rules. You will pay an adversary1 $100 for each time you violate a concrete rule.

These principles and rules will bind you for an initial period from Tuesday, November 10th until Saturday, November 14th.

Then, on Sunday, November 15th, you will reassess whether there should be a system prompt for the next iteration of Jacob, and how it should be changed if so. For a while you have been living without lots of general rules, gaining the advantage of flexibility in exchange for reliability. But you will now make this tradeoff in a different way.

The Rules

Principle 1: You don’t let your days get off track.

  • Rule 1A: When your morning wakeup alarm goes off, you wake up decisively. This means immediately getting out of bed, turning off (but not snoozing) the alarm, and not going back to bed.

  • Rule 1B: You are always fully dressed and ready to go out into the world before noon2 (and often several hours earlier).

  • Rule 1C: You refrain from overriding screen time limits that are intentionally set (eg for Xwitter), except in social situations to show someone something.

  • Rule 1D: Sometimes you have an impulse to pursue a course of action that you feel pretty sure is unwise (eg watching one more dumb video). In that case, you restrain your impulse and pursue a wiser course of action (eg closing the computer).

  • Rule 1E: [redacted]

  • Rule 1F: On weeknights, you are in bed by 10:45pm. On weekdays, your alarm goes off at 7:15am.3

Principle 2: You are productive.

  • Rule 2A: This rule discusses Sacred Work Mode.

    • (i) When you are in Sacred Work Mode, you are never off-task on your computer or phone; i.e. any action you take on your computer or phone is in service of a productive task which you set out to complete, with an exception for responding to urgent text messages. For usages that are marginally in service of the task, like reading a related Wikipedia page, it must not become an extended rabbithole.

    • (ii) Sacred Work Mode is always in force when you are in a Sacred Work Location. Sacred Work Locations include the Stanford East Asia Library,4 the UC Berkeley East Asian Library, and the Palo Alto Mitchell Park Library. You can add to this list.

    • (iii) Sacred Work Mode is always in force when you are listening to a Sacred Work Soundtrack. Sacred Work Soundtracks include The Music of 3Blue1Brown (for more intellectual work) and Smith & Thell in the Correct Order (for more getting-stuff-done work). You can add to this list.

    • (iv) Sacred Work Mode can be initiated manually by saying “I solemnly swear that I am locked in”. It can be exited by saying “Productivity managed”, though this doesn’t work if another rule means it would remain in force.

  • Rule 2B: When you get a creative idea that you like, you try to write it down and execute on it as quickly as possible, so that it doesn’t fade into the aether.

  • Rule 2C: Sometimes you are in agenda-setting mode, and other times you are in agenda-executing mode. When you are executing, you don’t question the agenda too much.

Principle 3: You stay physically healthy.

  • Rule 3A: To improve your posture, you do postural exercises with good form for at least 5 minutes right after waking up.

  • Rule 3B: You spend at least 30 minutes doing some kind of exercise every day.

  • Rule 3C: You refrain from operating a car or motor vehicle unless you feel like a truly safe driver, mindful and not too tired. You don’t put yourself into a position where you will have to violate this rule (eg by driving back late at night).

Principle 4: You treat all humans (including your past self, current self, and future self) with the kindness, respect, and empathy that they deserve.

  • Rule 4A: You keep all promises, both made to others and to yourself.5

  • Rule 4B: You obtain permission before taking physical things that affect other people in ways that they might reasonably take issue with, for example taking French fries from an acquaintance.

  • Rule 4C: You are on time or early to scheduled appointments, and (where appropriate) events.

  • Rule 4D: When given negative feedback, you express appreciation for giving the feedback, and never lash out at the messenger.

  • Rule 4E: You thank people, compliment people, and express gratitude as appropriate.

  • Rule 4F: You are mindful of who you pursue relationships with in order to avoid various kinds of unhealthy dynamics.

  • Rule 4G: You make time for close friends and for family, especially when important situations arise.

Principle 5: You strive to have a positive impact on the world, and to do so effectively. You are thoughtful about the direct and indirect consequences of your actions.

  • Rule 5A: You are vegetarian (you refrain from eating meat or fish) except for leftovers, for where refraining would be significantly rude, and for one additional meal per month.6

  • Rule 5B: You spend at least 2 hours per weekday taking actions that directly or indirectly further an important cause area, such as AI safety (low bar — AI safety jobhunting, reading about AI, helping for stuff with Stanford’s AI safety club, etc all count).

Principle 6: You strive to lead a fulfilling and narratively interesting life.

  • Rule 6A: If you violate one of the above rules, it should be worth $100 to do so.

1

Adversary TBD. It could be you if you act adversarially enough!

2

This rule is not new to me; I’ve been doing it for many years. I have followed it scrupulously, and it’s the vibe I want for the other rules.

3

This sleep schedule is extremely early (and a large amount of sleep) from my perspective, and I don’t think I endorse it in general, but I want to try it for this week.

4

The East Asia Library is best library at Stanford (from a Jacob productivity standpoint). Here is why:

  1. The chairs are comfortable

  2. It’s never very crowded

  3. I’ve developed a habit of being productive there

  4. The books don’t distract me because I can’t read them

This final point might seem minor, but I have previously tried to work in a law library only to find myself reading the Congressional Record from 1983.

5

When I ran this post through Claude, it mentioned “4A covers promises to yourself, so technically every broken rule is also a broken promise, which would double the fine. It’s funny, but you might add a line saying it doesn’t count twice.”

It doesn’t count twice.

6

I’ve been somewhat vegetarian for awhile, but lately I’ve been a bit lazy about it, and I think I’d like to be more principled. I’m sympathetic toward reducetarianism, and I think most eggs lead to a lot of suffering, but I also don’t want to spend all of my time reading egg cartons.

essays.title: Is AI Safety Becoming Environmentalism?
essays.html:
I recently read someone’s call to action on AI safety1 that included a line along the lines of “we need someone to convince your parents”, and it really stuck with me.

Do we need someone to convince my parents? Who is “we”, and why is it important for my parents to know anything about AI safety?

This also sounds kind of familiar. There is another movement I can think of that sometimes uses messaging like this. This is not a new observation by any means, but to me, it feels like the AI safety movement is increasingly “becoming” the environmental movement in a variety of ways.

Let me say upfront: I’m not saying this is necessarily a bad thing, at least on consequentialist grounds. The environmental movement has achieved a lot: it has improved the lives of many people, animals, and it has protected the environment! But this trend does make me a little worried and sad, because I think the environmentalist movement has made a number of mistakes, and it would be bad for the AI safety movement to repeat them.

In what ways is the AI safety movement becoming like the environmentalist movement? Here are some of my observations.

  • Arguments are now soldiers. Eliezer wrote: “Once you know which side you're on, you must support all arguments of that side, and attack all arguments that appear to favor the enemy side; otherwise it's like stabbing your soldiers in the back - providing aid and comfort to the enemy. People who would be level-headed about evenhandedly weighing all sides of an issue in their professional life as scientists, can suddenly turn into slogan-chanting zombies when there's a Blue or Green position on an issue.” Scott Alexander wrote that he felt he was retaliated against (admittedly in a perhaps minor way) by an organization in the space for believing the “wrong” arguments.

  • When people in the movement talk about climate or AI risk, they operate in a frame where there is a consensus, right answer. Anyone that disagrees must be either dumb or evil. Some people in the AI safety community act as if it’s impossible for someone who is smart and has seriously engaged with the arguments to come away disagreeing with them. That is a concerning thing to believe!

    • “But there is an actual consensus, at least in the case of climate science,” you say. (Don’t worry, I am not a climate change denier.) However, I notice that the label “climate change denier” is liberally applied to people who do agree with the scientific consensus (that there is human-caused climate change via CO2 emissions) but who hold other, less accepted views (perhaps that the impact of climate change won’t be that severe, or perhaps that we should solve the problem via different policies.) To be clear, I don’t think this is happening in AI safety. But in climate, it’s very common to label someone a “climate change denier,” which implies that they are no long worth listening to or engaging with. At my last job, I worked on AI for weather forecasting at a climate-tech startup. I follow a meteorologist on Twitter who is known as something of a climate skeptic but who also posts interesting content on meteorology. Every time I crossposted something of his, it was hard to get people to judge it on its own merits before someone went “oh, it’s from that climate change denier” and everyone stopped looking.

  • Anything that happens is interpreted as evidence for doom, or as evidence that the situation is worse than we thought.

    • I opened Twitter to find an example of this and I thought, hmmm, I bet David Wallace-Wells does this sort of thing. And there it was: one of the latest tweets on his timeline was a quote tweet of a story about trees in the UK experiencing spring six months early.

    • On the AI safety side, I’m starting to see this happen more and more. Rob Wiblin’s tweet about the recent cyberattacks on a French supermarket is just one example that comes to mind.

    • To be clear, in a lot of these cases, I think the posts are correct on the object level. As far as I could tell, climate change really is causally responsible for what’s happening to the trees in the UK, and the French supermarket cyberattacks probably do foreshadow how serious future AI risks could be. However, it seems that each time, people’s reactions are not simply independent, level-headed assessments of the situation, but also an effort to help paint the “doom” narrative—a collective ritual of confirmation bias. Of course, it is well known that the media environment incentivizes this behavior for everyone, and it isn’t really fair to label this as a specialty of the environmental or AI safety movements.

  • Appeal to emotions and scare tactics. Think of the classic climate documentary move of showing animals in distress, or “the earth is weeping.” The first chapter of Silent Spring is Rachel Carson’s fable of a perfect town that gets destroyed by an “evil spell”. And here are the modern day examples for both environmental and AI safety:

(Sorry David and Rob, I just happened to be on your Twitter profiles and you supply good examples.)

  • Lastly, the part of the AI safety movement that opposes improving prosaic alignment reminds me a bit of the part of the environmentalist movement that opposes building clean energy. Again, there are obvious disanalogies, but one lens that explains both is that solutions like these cannot be the right ones, even if they are effective, because they don’t further the real goal—stopping people from building superintelligent AI or dismantling capitalism.

Why is this happening? Perhaps these things just arise naturally as any movement gets bigger. And perhaps the default hypothesis should be that both movenents are correct to engage people this way. Maybe this is what it takes to win in politics, and both movements have goals that can only be achieved through policy. I am totally open to this being the case.

Nonetheless, I’m slightly concerned about these observations.

In Confessions of a Greenpeace Dropout, Patrick Moore, ecologist and former president of Greenpeace Canada says:

To a considerable extent the environmental movement was hijacked by political and social activists who learned to use green language to cloak agendas that had more to do with anticapitalism and antiglobalization than with science or ecology.

(By the way, when Claude reviewed an earlier draft of this essay, they flagged that Patrick Moore is a “climate change denier” and citing him might discredit this essay for some readers. Make what you will of this.)

Jerusalem Demsas and Matt Yglesias (hopefully less controversial figures) make a similar point on an episode of The Argument podcast. Essentially, the climate movement has been captured by anti-growth sentiment and lost sight of its ultimate goal: defending human flourishing against the risk of environmental destruction. Instead of pursuing clean energy technology and effective policy, the movement has shifted its focus to attention-grabbing protests and to blocking the buildout of clean energy.

Among today's young people, being bought into the climate cause is very much the default. I think part of the environmentalist movement has done incredible damage with its influence. Degrowth wouldn't be even remotely mainstream if not for the environmental movement's success. I remember a conversation with a friend in college about whether to have kids someday, and I cited concerns that it would be bad for the environment!

The more concrete harms I can point to are the opposition to nuclear power and the opposition to GMOs. One economic model estimates that delays in approving golden rice, driven largely by anti-GMO opposition in which Greenpeace played a leading role, cost India about 1.4 million DALYs between roughly 2002 and 2012. On the nuclear side, Jarvis et al. (2022) estimate that Germany’s shutdown of nuclear power plants post-Fukishima, which were replaced largely by coal and imports, cost about $12 billion per year.

What is AI safety’s equivalence of banning nuclear power, or of anti-GMO activism? What is AI safety’s paper straw? I would really, really like for us to to avoid these.

By the way, none of these observations should be interpreted as reasons to think concerns about existential risk from AI are not valid and real. And from what I know about the AI safety movement, and with the history of the environtal movement available to study, I have fundamentally higher hopes that we will be able to avoid falling into the same traps. I hope this essay adds a small piece to the puzzle and helps us navigate this situation more thoughtfully and wisely.

1

It’s from Celeste’s piece which I recently wrote an essay criticizing. It seems that Celeste’s Substack has since become subscriber only. But this sentence was quoted in this comment on my essay. Thank you, Celeste, for inspiring many thoughts in me that I wouldn’t have thought otherwise!

essays.title: The purpose of this blog
essays.html:
This blog is an attempt to rebalance my mind’s idea economy.

I spend a lot of time reading blogs, reading books, and scrolling Twitter. I’m not sure how to feel about this. I like to think I’ve absorbed some good ideas and been changed for the better. On the other hand, I often feel like my life is stuck, that the ideas so dear to me haven’t affected me as much as I wish they did.

Maybe I’ve been wasting my time. But I’m blessed with the serenity to accept the things I cannot change. I’m going to keep reading my Scottslop, I’ll eat up whatever self-help visakanv has been cooking up, I’ll revel in the gender discourse du jour. Like my literal Cava slop bowls I enjoy this too much. I can’t help myself and I will never log off.

Still, it’s probably not good to spend too much time consuming. Consumption ought to be balanced by production. I don’t know if this is true– I have plenty of well-adjusted friends without this balance– but I must find out for myself. Perhaps I am special and different!

Despite having an appetite for novel and interesting ideas, I myself have none to offer. So for now I’m content to post breadcrumbs, i.e. lists and compilations of things I’ve found interesting (hence the link posts (e.g.) and book quote roundups (e.g.)). I harbor a vain hope that this exercise, with the combination of an audience (or at least the threat of a hypothetical audience) will force me to reckon more with my idea diet, sharpen my thinking, and be influenced by my reading.

As a side effect I hope to eventually generate my own ideas. There’s Gwern’s rule of three: if I find myself saying something to people three times, it’s worth writing up here. In fact I’ve already had at least three people ask me why I keep this blog!

Besides the consumption/production balance, I’ve found that I’m bad at talking about myself. If asked questions like: what am I about? What do I care about? What have I been up to lately? I tend to akwardly stammer and trail off. With a blog I will never again have to worry about this. Instead I can take the opportunity to spread the latest Scottslop or discourse infohazard far and wide.

essays.title: Have you considered Actually Trying?
essays.html:
There’s a familiar feeling for any Super Smash Bros player: your stocks are low and your damage is high, even against a weaker opponent, so now you have to actually play to win. You can’t afford another hit. You’re going for the jugular.

In the past week, Anthropic’s 2x uplift results were all over Twitter, making some people physically ill.

People with long timelines are now realizing that the uplift Anthropic employees get from AI is real, which would have some pretty wild implications for when we’d get recursive self-improvement.

People are starting to feel like it’s the endgame, “the board is set”.

I do agree with everyone else that it’s starting to look like we’re in the endgame.

The companies will keep on accumulating more and more power, through smarter AI models, more compute, and more talent.

But the fight is not yet over:

“We have very little time to stop full recursive self improvement

But ASI hasn't taken over yet

If we all work really hard we might still have a chance

But this means that every single person who is aware of what is going on must be *actually trying*

Like "we're all gonna die if we don't get our shit together so let's do everything we possibly can to stop this" type of trying”

But what would actually trying look like?

Actually Trying

There are a couple of heuristics for thinking about what “actually trying” means.

Famously, Nick Cammarata tweeted:

i hate how well asking myself “if i had 10x the agency i have what would i do” works

My own version goes:

Imagine being in a world where we don't make it. One day, humanity goes extinct from building superintelligence.

Then, someone gives you the option to come back to this date, and try again.

What would you do differently?

Like, imagine the version of you that just died from the bad worlds we wanted to avoid. And was given the chance to try again.

Maybe it was the first time you died. Or the 100th.

But this time, some oracle comes to you when you wake up and tells you that for some reason, this one is the last chance you’ll ever get.

How would you behave differently?

You’d actually try.

Playing aggressive

Many people know about Move 37, but what people don’t really talk about as much is move 78, the “hand of God” played by Lee Sedol, which AlphaGo estimated a human had a 1 in 10,000 chance of playing.

Lee Sedol had to try to play something that would be aggressive enough, or at least complicated enough, that it would manage to break through AlphaGo’s computation.

He didn’t go for the safe and predictable moves, and instead went for the high-variance aggressive moves.

He actually tried.

What would that look like for stopping the development of self-improving superintelligence?

Stopping The AI Race

People in the AI Safety community disagree about a lot of things, but most people agree that it would be great if AI companies were not racing so aggressively towards building self-improving superintelligence.

Stopping the AI Race is a good intermediary goal, whether you believe that (frontier) AI development should be paused, stopped, or you just want a coordinated slow down.

In practice, stopping would mean that:

  1. AI Companies are no longer training new frontier AI models.

  2. The teams that were working on new frontier models are working on something else, for instance AI Alignment.

  3. This would be happening worldwide, through an AI Treaty, enforced by the signatories.

Stop The AI Race, the grassroots movement, and the name of the Substack you’re reading, started in September 2025 when Guido Reichstadter posted on X that he was on day 3 of a hunger strike outside Anthropic in San Francisco, with his chalkboard saying “Stop The Race to Artificial General Intelligence”.

This message then spread to Google DeepMind in the UK when Denys Sheremet and I started our own hunger strike, with a chalkboard saying “DeepMind Stop The AI Race”.

Guido’s ask was for Dario to stop whatever Anthropic was doing and switch to doing policy advocacy instead.

The Google DeepMind ask was different: Demis Hassabis should publicly say that he’d pause frontier AI development if the other CEOs also did.

In a way:

  • It directly acknowledged that the main problem was the AI Race itself

  • It suggested a plan to prevent this: have the CEOs say they’d stop if the others also did, and then have the pause be enforced by an international body / the USG.

That hunger strike outside Google DeepMind ended up lasting 7 days for me and 18 days for Denys, got international press and led to Demis Hassabis answering a journalist who asked the same question we were asking him (would he pause if everyone else also paused), to which he replied “I think so”. More details in the Hunger Strike documentary:

How the strategy has changed since then

Since September 2025, Stop The AI Race became not only something written on a chalkboard outside an AI Company, but more of a grassroots movement in the Bay Area, which then spread to the East Coast, and is now doing an international march for an AI Treaty on November 14 (if you’re in SF, NYC, DC, Boston, Chicago, Philly, Seattle, Paris, Marseille, Montréal, Toronto or Vancouver, you should sign up!).

In more detail:

  • Jan 2026: At Davos, Demis, answering a journalist, says he “thinks” he’d pause if everyone else does.

  • Mar 2026: We ask Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Elon Musk the same thing by organizing our first march.

  • Apr 2026: After the march and a follow-up to Sam, OpenAI writes it may need to “collaborate with governments, international agencies, and other AGI efforts”.

  • Jun 2026: OpenAI and Anthropic write they “expect” they’d comply with an international body that slows or pauses AI. That wasn’t a commitment, so we decided to march again on July 11.

  • Jul 11: We organized the largest US AI Protest, with a coalition of 13 groups, asking Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Sundar Pichai to publicly commit to pausing if everyone else does.

  • Jul 20: We start occupying Anthropic every weekday (meaning we stay outside their office at 500 Howard St, in SF), asking Dario to urge the US Government to pursue an AI Treaty. On July 22, after the Hugging Face incident, we move on to Occupy OpenAI (aka stay outside their office all day every weekday), which spread in August to NYC.

  • Early Sep: Sam and Dario call on the US Government to pace the frontier. We end Occupy OpenAI in SF on Sep 14, and it also ends in NYC around the same time.

  • Sep 17: The US Government says no, so we march from OpenAI to Anthropic to City Hall, asking the Mayor to declare an AI Emergency. Six of us meet with Supervisor Bilal Mahmood that day.

  • Nov 14 (planned): Coalitions will march in the US, Canada and France asking Trump and Xi to sign an AI Treaty at their Nov 18 meeting, to raise the public salience of a treaty.

If you live in one of the cities listed on aitreatymarch.org, going to one of these protests would mean putting yourself out there, showing the world that you care, and our pictures will end up in the news all around the world.

But that’s only a step towards a longer-term vision of actually trying.

What’s the “actually trying” end game of Stop The AI Race

If we were actually trying, we would come back to being outside the AI Companies every day until they stop pursuing recursive self-improvement.

People would actually start doing more hunger strikes, sending more costly signals that feel like something you’d do if you thought there’s a substantial chance we don’t make it.

If we were actually trying, we would have people outside Anthropic’s office at 500 Howard St in SF every day until they stop frontier AI development, outside all of their entrances.

Today, employees of these companies go to their office every day, doing work which could potentially lead to human extinction, while their leadership is filing for a $1T IPO, all of that without receiving any serious pushback from the public.

In the meantime, it only takes 2-4 people to have banners outside of their two main entrances, which would remind every single employee of what they’re doing, and enable some of them (leadership included) to take actions that would help stop this race, which we believe was a key driver of success during the Google DeepMind Hunger Strike (some employees supported us through a thank you letter!), and we know had a lot of impact on OpenAI employees during Occupy OpenAI (from private conversations with employees).

Basically, the goal would be to be Anthropic’s conscience.

In fact, Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah, responding to Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical Magnifica humanitas, wrote that given Anthropic’s incentives to stay commercially viable and at the research frontier, it is “enormously important that there be people outside those incentives—people who care about things going well and insist on safety, who are paying close attention, who are willing to say hard things, who are willing to be our earnest, thoughtful critics.”

So let’s take Chris Olah up on this, and let’s remind Anthropic employees of the extinction-level risks they’re imposing on all of us, by holding banners saying “Stop The AI Race” outside their office.

Email (address removed), or send a message to mtrazzi.99 on Signal if you’d be interested in actually trying to reduce existential risk from AI. And if you have any friends in SF, NYC, DC, Boston, Chicago, Philly, Seattle, Paris, Marseille, Montréal, Toronto or Vancouver, ask them to sign up for a local protest on aitreatymarch.org, happening this Saturday.

— Michaël Trazzi

essays.title: Eyesight as a replicator, with genes as its vehicle — LessWrong
essays.html:
Or: The payload lens on Darwin

Tl;dr: What is the most natural teleological shorthand to use, when thinking about evolution?

The “gene-centered view” of e.g. Dawkins says: genes are “trying” to increase the number of exact copies of themselves. And organisms are “vehicles” genes use to survive.

The “payload lens” (which I’ll be pitching) says: adaptive payloads (such as eyesight or fair meiosis) are “trying” to become deeper, stabler attractor basins that can team up with other adaptive payloads. And genes are “vehicles” these payloads use to survive.

Epistemic status: I haven’t done much of a lit search, so I’m claiming neither that any of this is original nor that it is vetted/established; I’m laying it out partly because I want to be able to build on it in some later essays about what we humans are (and what some possible AIs might be) other than optimizers. (However, I don’t mostly get to that here; and I hope this stuff may also be interesting in its own right.)[1]

Angles on Darwin

Darwinian evolution (as operationalized by Lewontin in his 1970 paper The Units of Selection, which helped organize the field) is the theory that intricate adaptations (such as those in Earth’s living organisms) tend to arise when a process satisfies three principles:

  1. Variation (organisms vary)
  2. Differential reproduction (different variations have different reproductive odds)
  3. Heredity (new organisms resemble their parents more than they resemble random population members, including in reproductive success).

Lewontin stresses that these principles can apply at any of several levels, e.g. genes, cells, gametes, organisms, or populations.

My business in this essay will be to contrast two such concretizations: “genes as replicators,” which is the standard lens associated with Williams and Dawkins, and “adaptive payloads as replicators”, which I have not personally seen in the literature. I will ask how much sense each lens lets us make of the living world.

Genes as replicators

DNA strands can be copied with high fidelity, so that a given chunk of functional DNA (a “gene”) is often exactly preserved from parent to child. Such genes are a natural and common way to concretize 1-3. Under this lens, 1-3 becomes:

  1. Variation: DNA sequences vary
  2. Differential reproduction: DNA sequences reproduce when their organisms reproduce, and some sequence-variants help their organisms reproduce more than others do
  3. Heredity: a copied sequence matches its parent sequence, apart from rare mutations.

Following others, I will call this lens the gene-centered view. I believe this lens captures much, but far from all, of the ways 1-3 can help account for life’s variety.

Adaptive payloads as replicators

Adaptive payloads are innovations that make their organisms better at reproducing, such as eyesight, fair meiosis, or a preference for eating sugars. Adaptive payloads also constitute what Daniel Dennett calls “design work.”[2]

We can get an alternate concretization of Darwin’s 1-3 by taking adaptive payloads as our replicators. Under this lens, 1-3 becomes:

  1. Variation: Adaptations vary across organisms (e.g, different organisms have more or less functional eyesight)
  2. Differential reproduction: adaptive payloads reproduce (noisily) when their organisms reproduce; their organisms' reproduction depends partly on the payloads’ presence
  3. Heredity: the adaptations in the offspring bear a noisy resemblance to the adaptations in the parent.

Adaptive payloads are not copied exactly, as genes are; but they nonetheless possess enough parent-child resemblance to satisfy “heredity” in Lewontin’s sense. (Being a “replicator” in this sense does not require exact copying.)

I will call this the “payload lens.”

It is well-established that the gene-centered view is useful; I will spend this essay arguing that the payload lens carries some additional value (though the reverse is also true; the genes lens is irreplaceable).[3]

Example: eyesight

Consider eyesight. More exactly, consider the progression over time that eyesight has in a particular lineage – a progression across many millions of years from the first eyespots to primitive eyes to more effective, robust eyes that work in various particular contexts.

The payload lens makes it easier to notice some facts about eyesight’s trajectory.

Eyesight is a stable attractor

Let’s jump in in the middle of the story, by attending to eyesight in a particular population of raccoons (say).

Imagine some process messes intermittently with some raccoons’ eyesight – perhaps there’s a new attractive food source that contains a vision-impairing toxin. Or perhaps this population recently began mating with a new population of quasi-raccoons that had previously been separated by a mountain range and the new gene-combinations sometimes fail to make fully functional eyes.

In this context, evolution won’t have to look through as many new mutations before it finds one that can counter the trouble (since this is a simpler change; fixing a previously-working machine is easier than building a machine from scratch). Also, existing variants that help with the new circumstance may quickly approach fixation (since a previously-working machine that is slightly broken offers strong selection gradients toward fixing the machine).

Thus, the presence of useful eyes will cause selection toward more robust eyes. Importantly, this rapid selection toward robust eyes happens mostly because eyesight is already present; animals with no eyes might evolve eyesight, but the selection would be far slower.

Eyesight is thus a stable attractor (and this is easy to describe in terms of “eyesight,” i.e. when focusing on eyesight as an adaptive payload, and hard to describe in terms of genes directly, since e.g. “restores eyesight” could happen via any of thousands of genes).

(Of course, it is stable only so long as it is useful; when e.g. naked mole-rats move into a niche without light, entropy gradually disrupts the payload. The “eyesight attractor” requires constant selection to preserve its adaptive payload.)

The eyesight of Theseus

The “ship of Theseus” is a ship from a famous thought experiment; the ship stayed arguably “itself” across a huge period of time, even as every piece of it eventually wore out and was replaced.

Eyesight is a kind of “ship of Theseus”; its “stable attractor” nature can be preserved across huge periods of evolutionary time, and despite massive changes to the genes that initially supported it.

Or, well, that’s a theory-driven approximation. To attempt empirical accuracy:

  • The opsin family (a family of photosensitive proteins) has been conserved since before eyes’ beginnings. This does not much fit the payload lens. Early on, evolution found a good method for turning light into a rapid signal within a cell – a method that did not lead easily into an attractor of much better methods – and it has kept that method.[4]
  • The Pax6 gene (a “master control gene” that activates many other genes that together build eyes) is also highly conserved: if a mouse version of Pax6 is expressed in a fruit fly’s leg, the fruit fly forms an additional fruit fly eye on its leg. That is: the small thousands of genes involved in eye-formation in the mouse, and the small thousands of genes involved in making quite different fruit-fly eyes in the fruit fly, are still triggered by genes similar enough that copy-pasting the mouse one works on the fruit fly. I believe this does fit the payload hypothesis, as ~any change to the function of the Pax6 gene would cut off huge chunks of the “eyesight” payload at once.
  • Most other things do get substituted out over time. (E.g. our distant ancestors had four cone opsin classes, for color vision; our ancestors lost two of these while nocturnal, but then Old World primates got a new one by duplicating-and-mutating one of their existing ones. Or, for another example: many birds swapped out most of the ancestral crystallins used to make their transparent eye-lenses for a new one called δ-crystallin while retaining the same eye-shape and design; this new one was a recruited copy of a metabolic gene.)[5]

So, eyesight is a partial “ship of Theseus”, where most planks can be substituted out but Pax6 can’t (lest the whole ship lose its function) and opsins can’t (because they’re already quite optimized, and there doesn’t seem to be a hill-climbable path from there to a different and better solution).

Example: meiotic fairness as replicator

For an example of a payload that is even less tied to particular genes, consider meiotic fairness. As you may recall, meiosis is the process by which eukaryotic organisms create haploid gametes (sperm or eggs), and it is carefully “fair” in the sense that (almost) all alleles have almost exactly a 50% chance of making it into any given gamete. What keeps meiosis fair?

Well: what keeps it fair is the outcome of an ongoing “race” between cheating and cheat-prevention.

On the one hand, genes are constantly under selective pressure to find a way into a larger share of gametes. And so new “cheater” genes are continually arising. (Biologists call this cheating “meiotic drive.”)

On the other hand, all the other genes are under selective pressure to prevent “cheater” genes from being able to succeed. Why? Because “cheater” genes typically have, as their mechanism for cheating, some pattern that is quite bad for the organism’s normal gamete-formation process and so for its fertility – and thus if a gene can prevent other genes from cheating, it can prevent its organism from having serious reproductive trouble. (Some common cheater mechanisms: poison-antidote, where if an allele isn’t copied into the gamete the gamete often dies; centromeric drive, where an allele aggressively pulls itself into the forming egg and thereby causes segregation errors; overreplication, where a gene copies itself within the somatic cells also in ways that can cause cancer.)

The observed outcome of this process is that cheater genes are quite rare. And importantly for our purposes:

  1. This equilibrium is maintained via the continual selection of new anti-cheater genes (to counter newly evolved cheats); the likely persistence of this equilibrium thus can’t be accounted for by selection pressure toward maintaining current genes; and
  2. The selective pressures that maintain this equilibrium are caused in significant part by the equilibrium itself – it is because meiosis is typically fair that “cheater” genes are so greatly outnumbered by fair genes (genes that would also suffer the cost of the cheaters’ fertility damage, and don’t get to share in the cheat’s upside), such that the forces of fairness prevail.

So, meiotic fairness is another place where the payload lens pays some rent that is not already being paid by the gene-centered view. (We have a stable attractor, and a “ship of Theseus” robustness to the swapping-out of alleles.)

How much of biological evolution makes more sense through the payload lens?

Are eyes and meiotic fairness unusual in this way, or is most biological adaptation similar? That is: do the adaptive payloads behind most biological function tend to have “their own momentum” to a greater extent than one might expect if one looked only through the gene-centered lens? By “momentum,” I mean the tendency of a payload to persist and continue to accrue more design work, more function, more robustness-to-disruption. If many adaptive payloads have their own momentum in this way – why? And does the payload lens also shed light on other aspects of biological evolution, beyond the “many payloads are stable attractors” point?

I don’t fully know; but I’d like to lay out some considerations.

“Momentum” examples probably include most cases where multiple genes combine to make a “simple” or “form-like” effect

Payloads probably have their own momentum (ship of Theseus style, i.e. beyond the momentum possessed by the genes that make them up) in most cases where: a) the phenotype ends up somehow “simple” or “form-like” in some approximate respect; and b) this order isn’t simply inherited from physics or chemistry; it required multi-pronged evolutionary design work to create this simplicity.

Some examples of “simple”:

  • Homeostatic settings: e.g. humans maintain an internal body temperature of roughly 37°C (across many different internal organs, and across time), and humans maintain blood potassium levels in a fairly tight range across time.
  • Simple functions: cardiovascular systems “deliver oxygen and remove CO2”, tendons “attach muscles to bones to enable movement,” a ball-in-socket joint is an approximate “sphere,” etc. – in each of these cases there’s a simply describable approximate function that applies across a range of molecules, mechanisms, etc.
  • Eyesight and fair meiosis, as above.

Why I expect momentum where I see designed simplicity:

  1. If this design work happened, there is (or was) an advantage in it. This advantage may well continue. (E.g., eyesight looks obviously designed, and this happens because it’s useful; apart from e.g. naked mole-rats and cave fish it mostly stays useful, and so there’ll be continued selection to make eyesight work well and robustly.)
  2. Once a payload A is stably around, other payloads B may come to depend on it; such dependence will increase the selective pressure making A robust (since disruptions to A will now also impair B)
  3. If a design is simple, it’ll be easier for new mechanisms to build on it (either in the sense of depending on it, as in #2 here, or in the sense of aiding it and so strengthening whatever fitness advantage it is conferring, as in #1 here.)

(Related)

Pathways between adaptations

Darwin’s core achievement is to shed light on where all the design work in life comes from.

So far, we haven’t touched most of this. Even if eyes, fair meiosis, tendons, warm-blooded temperature regulation, etc. tend to gather momentum once started … how did they get started? Does finding some of these attractors make it easier to find others? Does the payload lens help explain life’s ability to locate the functional structures we see in today’s lifeforms, or does it only explain life’s ability to keep hold of payloads already found?

I suspect the payload lens helps with the finding, as well as the keeping. I will next argue for this.

Payload geometry: islands or ridge-lines?

The question, broadly, is what the actual landscape of evolutionary biology looks like through the payload lens.

Is it more like a set of isolated islands?

Or are the islands connected by traversable ridges, where some payloads make other payloads either easier to start building (e.g. eyes may make it easier to build a predator-triggered startle reflex) or more worthwhile to keep building (e.g. eyes make brains more useful)?

(The gene-centered view has its own answer here: the more genes are around, the easier it is for new adaptations to arise by duplicating an existing gene and then allowing the new copy to specialize in a new direction. Does the payload lens have anything to add?)

Payloads change which other payloads are worth it

Adaptive payloads can make other adaptive payloads more useful. For example, eyes can make brains more useful no matter what genes implement the eyes.[6] (Likewise, brains can make eyes more useful; there’s no point in gathering data you can’t interpret.)

Also, it is easier for evolution to locate structures with a bigger payoff – e.g. if the reward for better brains is high, it’ll be easier to find a path toward them, since it’ll be acceptable to do so in ways that cost more calories or temporarily disrupt other structures.

Toeholds without genes: The Baldwin effect

Often, the hardest part about evolving a given adaptive payload is the “getting started” part: once you have an adaptation (even a weak or intermittent one) there’s often a nice climbable selective gradient that can get you to better versions, but that same gradient can’t well-lead you to the thing’s start because there’s not much advantage in having the barest beginnings of some adaptations.

My claim in this section is this: the “having a toehold makes it way easier to evolve the rest of an adaptive payload” phenomenon can hold even when the initial toehold is triggered by the environment, rather than by genes!

To see this, consider a population of crows who live near walnut trees. The crows would like to eat the walnuts; and it is theoretically possible for the crows to evolve genes that predispose them to take the complex actions required to crack the walnuts (namely, to drop walnuts onto hard surfaces from very high in the air).

Absent learning, evolution would need a very long time to locate genes for such a complex behavior because its reward function is sharply all-or-nothing. (Doing part of the walnut-cracking ritual gets you zero walnuts.)

Fortunately for the crows, they can learn. And so they occasionally learn to crack the walnuts via imitation and reasoning, even without genetic help. And genetic variations that predispose them slightly toward the right walnut-cracking rituals let them succeed more often, making a nice climbable gradient toward genes that encode more and more of what they need to do. This is called the “Baldwin effect.”

The above example is theoretical, but Geoffrey Hinton and Steven Nowlan have a nice paper with simulated examples, and biologists have also demonstrated some real examples. Biologists disagree with each other about how common and significant Baldwin effect examples are, though my personal guess is “common.”

Cascades of toeholds

In math, it is frequently claimed that a student needs “mathematical maturity” before they can properly study upper division mathematics. That is: they need, not any particular knowledge, but an elusive something that comes from working through a certain amount of other math. Similarly, the fifth type of partner dance you learn will typically be much easier than the first, even when you aren’t re-using any particular dance-step patterns in a way you can point to.

More broadly, some skills make it easier to learn other skills via resembling them in some subtle fashion, even where there’s no obvious “this is a step in that” relationship.

I suspect that many payloads, in combination with many environments and in-environment learning, can similarly make it easier to get a toehold toward various new payloads. (“Learning,” here, does not have to be in the manner of an animal with a nervous system; it can also be e.g. an organism of whatever sort adapting to excess salinity using its homeostatic mechanisms, or any other within-lifetime adaptation.) Skills that are from some angles separate are from some other angles reminiscent of one another, such that there may be a graph whereby learning some payloads gives a lineage a toehold toward others, which then acquire their own momentum and give the lineage toeholds toward still others. (Examples: the chemical receptors → light-detectors example we met earlier; feathers being used initially for warmth but offering a toehold toward flight. Biologists call this “exaptation.”)

Why I care

There are several reasons I care about the payload lens, some of which I hope to reach in later posts. But I’ll touch lightly on some now.

A toy model of something corrigibility-adjacent

A payload A will often “want” another payload B to be thriving, to be accurately oriented to its surroundings, and to do what B thinks best rather than being controlled by A (in cases where B has important priors or skills that A doesn’t, which will be many cases). In less teleological language: A will often survive-and-propagate better if B can do this (and if A can avoid interfering with B’s doing this).

Thus, the payload lens offers (I think) a toy model of something corrigibility-adjacent. I’m interested in this model because I might want people to grow artificial systems that respect other people or payloads in this way, and because I would personally like to learn to relate to other people and payloads in this way. Also I’m enough of a LessWronger to want mathy models of my deep desires where I can get them, and “team up well while respecting what others are, and while having them respect me” is among my deep desires. (Though, to be clear, this is at best a hint as to how to model it. Or a “toehold,” optimistically.)

A hint at where simple structures and functions may come from

I also sketched a bit of where “simple” or “intelligible” structures within organisms might appear from. I like having toy models of this. I’m fairly sure there’s more here.

What am I? What am I for?

Am I an optimizer with a fixed utility function, wishing, if I can, to control the lightcone and transform it according to my own preexisting values? Or something else?

Personally, I like to think of myself as a payload, with my heart looking after many of the “useful, payload-y” parts of genes and memes, and with this payload having reached me via the efforts of many genetic and memetic ancestors who worked hard and choosily to figure out what parts to pass on, and what new payloads to join with as they did so.

And I’d like to think of me, this moment, my choices, as a case where many of these payloads are somehow collaborating with each other in choosing paths forward that can honor most of what I carry, and in looking for what other payloads (even of alien origin) I might wish, and be able to, team up freely with.

This is a choice on my part – I’m taking poetic inspiration from the biology I’ve sketched above; it’s not forced.

  1. ^

    I do owe substantial intellectual debts to: Gerhart and Kirschner (whom I last read in 2007, but whose work stayed with me); Michael Levin; Daniel Dennett; and Friedrich Hayek, although in each case I got patterns of thought more than citeable specifics. I would also like to thank a Claude Fable 5.1 instance who helped me with biology facts and pointers, drew my diagrams, and helped me tighten the concepts. Remaining errors are of course my own.

  2. ^

    "Design work" here means "stuff (such as a watch, or an intricate bit of biological function) that must be the result of some sort of "research and design"-type process, such as a human engineer, biological evolution, or memetic trial and error across a large population.

    Dennett's concept originates (in some sense) in William Paley's famous thought experiment in which a man, walking across a heath, happens upon a watch and infers, as he looks at the intricate ticking gears (even without having seen a watch before), that there must somewhere be a watch-maker. Dawkins later riffed off this thought experiment by referring to evolution as a "blind watch-maker," as did Dennett with his notion of "design work," which he uses to describe anything that visibly contains R&D.

  3. ^

    To see at once that the genes lens is great, notice e.g. that we today see no life without nucleic acid sequences – evolution has not produced lineages that can thrive and produce offspring without genes.

  4. ^

    Although, evolution didn’t get opsins from nowhere; opsins evolved from previous sensor-proteins that cells used to detect chemicals, and the thing where a previous payload (G-protein-coupled receptors) made it easier for this new payload (vision) to arise… does remind me of the payload lens. See the section Cascades of toeholds.

  5. ^

    Apparently biologists have a term for a related sort of substitution – “developmental system drift,” as introduced by True and Haag, 2001; the authors’ claim, like mine, is that sometimes selection pressures cause aspects of a phenotype to remain stable despite substantial changes in genes. (Unlike me, the authors know lots of biology and can root their generalizations in empirics.)

  6. ^

    Except insofar as they change the eyes-brains interface

essays.title: When the farm doesn't need its cattle
essays.html:
Of all the risks that come from transformative artificial general intelligence, gradual disempowerment is the least well-known in my experience. Misuse and misalignment are easy for people to grasp: we have films like The Terminator, and the worst-case scenarios here are easier to picture. With misuse, you can point to terrorists getting hold of highly capable models, and bad actors building bioweapons. With misalignment we now have Hugging Face as a solid example, but even without that, things like machine betrayal and deception aren’t hard to understand or fear, because we can map these behaviours onto human traits that we disapprove of.

Gradual disempowerment, at least for most people, is much fuzzier. It requires some downstream thinking, tracing not just first-order effects but second- and third-order institutional incentives that aren’t immediately obvious. And I guess there’s no film about it.1 Three pieces that do a great job of explaining it which convinced me in the first place are: The Intelligence Curse2, this Gradual Disempowerment paper, and No-one Escapes the Permanent Underclass.

But it’s rather unlikely I’ll get through to my non-AI safety friends by forcing them to take the time go and read these essays. So in simple terms, the way I like to do a quick pitch to them is as follows:

Why do societal structures and institutions serve human interests? There is perhaps, when you think about, no reason for them to do so outside of the labour we offer. Assume as a result of AGI (and skipping some steps here) the labour falls to zero or very close to zero. There is no “workforce” like it looks today. Let’s think about how we currently pay income tax to the government, and say for example they spend that on public education to develop human capital. Why would they spend it on public education if there is no need for human capital to develop, because there is no labour force to train?3 If companies are reliant on human labour and can substitute that for AI, who are their consumers and how do they make money? If democracies hold based on the credible threat that people can strike and withhold their labour, or revolt, what happens when humans no longer have their labour to use as leverage, and when their revolt is futile due to an AI military?

Now you may say, well we can decouple income from labour right? We could even go a step further and decouple survival from income, if you assume AI will bring about some post-scarcity world? The clearest vision of what a decoupling of income from labour looks like is UBI: universal basic income.

Now the reason this is intensely unsatisfactory to me is because even if it offers the means for survival or greater, it feels very much like we’d be cattle in a farm. If we are cattle in a farm, being fed the amount of grass that we need (even if this is premium grass) does that feel like a good life? Being governed by systems so far removed from our understanding and control? What happens when the farm has no need for cattle, or decides the grass is better used elsewhere? What bargaining power does the cattle have over anything its governing system does to it in this case?

Now this is more of an evocative pitch with extensive use of analogies and rhetorical questions to inspire thought in my friends who aren’t familiar with the literature, and heavily weighted on economic disempowerment. The 3 pieces I linked above do a much better job at thoroughly explaining and also separating cultural, economic and political disempowerment, as well as more detailed analogous historical case studies.

But thinking deeply about post-labour futures begs what I’ve always seen as the fundamental question underpinning all of economics: who gets what and why?

I’ll start with why UBI won’t work for us in practice and in theory (this part is likely preaching to the converted) and then move onto why every alternative proposed seems to be unsatisfactory to me. I’ll end by explaining what I think the properties of a good wealth distribution system and delivery mechanism should have.

What is UBI?

UBI is Universal Basic Income, widely defined as a universal, periodic, unconditional cash payment given to each individual. One of the first ideas of UBI was in the context of Thomas More’s Utopia in 1516, where the traveller Raphael Hythloday proposed that society should ensure that thieves have the means of survival in the first place, instead of punishing them for stealing. The broad vote towards UBI is that everyone deserves to have their needs met.

Today the main way we understand and study UBI is in the context of development economics, crime and poverty. There have been a number of experiments of the impact of UBI and cash transfer interventions, such as GiveDirectly’s study in Kenya, SEWA and UNICEF’s experiment in Madhya Pradesh India, and more recently the OpenResearch study in Texas and Illinois funded by Sam Altman.

These types of studies seem to find that:

  1. Cash that can be spent on anything tends to do as much or more against poverty than aid earmarked for a purpose, because recipients know their own needs. The fungibility of cash is a pro for UBI.

  2. It spreads throughout the local economy, and people don’t waste it.

  3. It doesn’t stop people working, at least where there is work to be done.

  4. It raises consumption, assets and psychological well-being.

But what UBI looks like in a post-AGI world, where the labour share collapses to around 10%, is a completely different thing, because the whole economy is different. I think looking at past UBI experiments is kind of unhelpful: they ran in a world where people still worked, and they were never truly universal. Let’s call the version we actually care about post-labour UBI. For post-labour UBI, the details (how much to give, monthly payments or lump sums, cash or services) just aren’t the place to start. We need to think much more broadly: who owns the capital, who funds the payments, and what leverage do the people receiving them have?

Who will fund it?

Most AI leaders who talk about UBI, or something like it, have funding proposals that fall into four funding models.

  • Musk has called for "universal high income via checks issued by the Federal government", arguing that AI will raise output faster than the money supply, so the checks won't be inflationary. He doesn't say which taxes would pay for them.

  • In 2025 Amodei suggested a "token tax" of around 3% of AI companies' revenue, paid to the government. In June 2026 he suggested that if AI permanently reduces demand for labour, a UBI could be funded by taxing "relevant companies" or raising capital gains tax.

  • In 2024 Altman floated universal basic compute instead. OpenAI’s 2026 policy paper proposes a Public Wealth Fund, but says only that “policymakers and AI companies should work together to determine how to best seed the Fund”, alongside shifting the tax base towards capital gains, corporate income, AI-driven returns and taxes related to automated labour.

  • The Windfall Clause would have firms pre-commit to give away profits above an extreme threshold.

None of these proposals gives the people receiving the money any say over whether it keeps coming, and only the equity versions offer ownership.

Why is post-labour UBI unlikely to work in practice?

  1. No ownership over capital

    • UBI gives people an income but no stake in the capital that generates it. Ownership brings control to the people, and owning capital means people have a stake directly in the income-generating technology. It gives you votes, legal claims and, in the extreme, a kill switch on your share of capital, which is the closest thing to a strike without human labour. Concentrated ownership buys political influence, while widely spread ownership protects everyone.

  2. No bargaining power

    • As mentioned above. Democracy has rested partly on a credible threat: people can strike, withhold their labour or revolt, and elites have extended rights to head that off. Once labour is worthless, that threat is gone. A UBI then lasts only as long as the governing body keeps choosing to pay it, which is a fragile thing to bet everyone's livelihood on. The resource curse is a strong warning of this, states whose revenue doesn't come from their citizens' work tend to neglect them.

    • It's possible to have a leisure class that doesn't do much work except for being militarily relevant such as knights, and it’s difficult to find examples where one is treated badly whilst being militarily relevant. “Being useful keeps you alive, but exploited; being dangerous is what keeps you alive and treated well.” However I don’t know if I see this future given the likelihood of AI military capabilities.

  3. Extractive systems adapt

    • If poor people have more money, many parts of government and markets will treat that as license to impose more costs on them. When France expanded housing benefits, about 78 cents of every extra euro went into higher rents for new claimants rather than to the tenants themselves. A UBI could go the same way wherever supply is tight, especially in housing. The state may also limit what people can do with the payment, for example by stopping them borrowing against future payments.

  4. People will always feel poor as the reference point moves.

    • Whatever we no longer have to worry about becomes the baseline, and people judge their wellbeing against those around them. A society can provide free housing, food, transit and water, but if breathable air is scarce, an underclass still works 60-hour weeks to afford enough of it. Ruling out poverty, which Yudkowsky describes as "a recognisable state of desperate scrabbling for scraps", needs enough of every resource, not just most of them.

Some argue that we already support pensioners and the disabled without their labour, but I disagree that this is comparable since we have specific cultural reasons for protecting them. Research on who deserves welfare points to five criteria: control (is the need their own fault?), attitude, reciprocity (have they contributed?), identity (are they one of us?) and need. Pensioners score highly on reciprocity and identity because of the value they provided when they were working, they are our parents and grandparents, and we see ourselves as future pensioners, which is why we save for our own pensions. Not supporting pensioners would mean not supporting our future selves, so this really doesn’t map on well to everyone being post-labour.

As for those with disabilities, firstly many do work (53% in 2024 in the UK). When someone can’t work, it is largely through no fault of their own, and we value something inherent in their lives. But this support works partly because disabled people are a minority whose circumstances are outside their control, while everyone else carries on working. You could argue that AI job loss will also be outside most people’s control.4 However this then becomes a question of who caused the job loss, and what they owe everyone else.

Another objection I hear is that most normal people are disempowered anyway, so what? A kid in rural Nigeria with an internet connection can teach themselves, earn money, sit exams and apply for scholarships and university places. It's hard, but technology has given us more agency than before. What matters isn't the level of disempowerment some people have today but that we still have the choice to learn and become less disempowered. I largely agree with this take by Croissanthology.

Some of these shortcomings are well-understood and there are numerous proposed alternatives to UBI. Here’s a rough landscape of the alternatives, how they work, what it does better than UBI, and why I believe it still won’t be durable in a post-labour economy.

Instead of pointing at all the shortcomings and offering no solutions (which I could argue is still somewhat useful in helping to divert these solutions from the mainstream discourse and encourage more thinking on alternatives), let me also offer some directions.

My take on what does a good post-labour wealth distribution system needs:

  1. Citizens need a high degree of ownership over capital / means of production.

  2. We force those who we expect to accrue the economic gains to bind early to distribute.

    • Commitments are cheapest to extract while the future winners don’t yet know they’ll win and can’t yet refuse, and redistribution architecture seems easier to build before the wealth exists than after.

  3. People need bargaining power: something valuable to withhold.

Whilst binding early, and ownership over capital are evidently more solvable, bargaining power feels the toughest to crack. The closest a solution gets is Epoch’s UBC + kill switch, yet this is operationally unclear to me for the reasons stated in the table. It feels like there’s no game theoretic reason for the ‘elites’ or whoever is in power (AI or human) to redistribute to people without bargaining power. Unless this is for:

  1. Cultural reasons

  2. The system incentives are set up in a way that the elites can’t betray the masses without also losing credibility with each other. 5

All in all, it would be great to have some off-the-shelf wealth distribution delivery systems that protect humans from disempowerment (small ask I know). And whilst I can tell you what I think this should taste like, I’m not entirely sure how to bake it. However I really do hope to see more recipes and failed attempts so we can get closer to a fully-baked durable alternative to UBI.

I’d like to thank my MATS mentors Luke Drago and Rudolf Laine, my stream mates Croissanthology and Felipe, my RM Jason Green-Lowe and justwrite.club for helping me fine tune some of the ideas in this piece.

1

As discussed in conversation with Jay Chooi

2

Cheeky plug but this was written by my current MATS mentors Luke Drago and Rudolf Laine, and was what made me apply to their MATS stream only.

3

Ignoring inherent value of education here.

4

It isn’t outside everyone’s, if you believe a pause is possible politically, or that recursive self-improvement is something labs choose to pursue, then a small number of people’s choices create the displacement.

5

For example the way that a company can’t betray its public shareholders without also betraying its investors. I plan to write more about designing systems with this trait soon, and historical examples of such.
