essays.title: These are different things
essays.html:
Jan Karski was a courier for the Polish Underground State in World War II. He was raised in a Catholic family in Lwów, a city with a large Jewish population. In addition to Polish, he also spoke English, French, German, Russian, and Spanish, which made him an ideal courier for the Polish government-in-exile, which operated across France. In June 1940, on a mission to France, the Gestapo caught him. With the help of hospital staff, the Polish Underground exfiltrated Karski out of Gestapo custody, and he spent the following months in the Polish countryside recovering from torture and a failed suicide attempt.

Two years later, in June 1942, Karski was again assigned to carry a report to the government-in-exile, which had since relocated to London. Before he left Poland, two Jewish underground leaders asked Karski to see the destitute people of the Warsaw Ghetto for himself, so he could testify as an eyewitness to the Polish officers and the Allied leaders in London.

By then, the United States and Britain were allied against Germany, but they had only an obfuscated picture of Germany’s rule in Europe. Reports of mass killings had reached the West, but they were fragmentary and secondhand, and often dismissed as exaggeration. From their view, the scale of the mass killings had no historical precedent, and many atrocity stories from the First World War had been later exposed as propaganda, and the sources were Jewish groups whom Allied officials suspected of having reasons to exaggerate.

The Polish government believed that Karski, as a Catholic officer reporting a firsthand account, could not be dismissed as secondhand or as an interested party. So, during the mass deportations to the Treblinka death camp, Karski infiltrated the Warsaw Ghetto, where he witnessed starvation, corpses lying in the streets, and Nazi soldiers hunting Jews for sport.

To reach London, Karski would once again have to cross Nazi-controlled Europe, at great personal risk. He crossed Germany, occupied France, and Spain to Gibraltar, carrying microfilm hidden in a key. He arrived in London and reported to the Polish government-in-exile in November 1942. In addition to his own government, he also briefed Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden, but was not given access to Churchill.

In the summer of 1943, the Polish government sent Karski to the United States to deliver his testimony to American leaders. On July 28, he met President Roosevelt at the White House for an hour, accompanied by the Polish ambassador, Jan Ciechanowski. Karski described the organization of the Polish Underground and the brutality of the German occupation, then recounted what he had seen in the Warsaw Ghetto. He warned that the reports were not exaggerated and that, without Allied intervention, Poland’s Jews would be mass killed. Roosevelt listened closely and asked many questions, but most concerned Poland in general. On the fate of the Jews, he made no specific commitment, offering only the assurance that the Allies would win the war and that the guilty would be punished.

Karski also gave his account to other prominent Americans, including cabinet officials, religious leaders, and journalists. Among them was Supreme Court Justice Felix Frankfurter, who was himself Jewish and a confidant of Roosevelt. Karski met Frankfurter on July 5, 1943, three weeks before meeting the president, at a dinner at the Polish embassy in Washington. After the other guests had left, Frankfurter asked Karski to tell him exactly what he had seen. Karski spoke for half an hour, describing the ghetto and the camp, and Frankfurter questioned him on the details.

When Karski finished, Frankfurter stood, paced the room in silence for several minutes, and sat down again. He told Karski that a man like him, speaking to a man like Karski, had to be totally honest. Then he said: “I do not believe you.”

Ambassador Ciechanowski protested. Karski was not lying, he insisted, and he spoke with the authority of the Polish government. “I did not say that he is lying,” Frankfurter answered. “I said that I don’t believe him. These are different things.” His mind and his heart, Frankfurter said, were “made in such a way that I cannot accept it.” He added: “I know humanity. I know men. Impossible.”

We know now that everything Karski told him was true, and the reality was actually worse than even Karski knew. Frankfurter had no evidence against any of this. He was one of the most accomplished legal minds in the country, and weighing testimony was his profession. He had questioned the witness himself and found nothing to fault. He said outright that Karski was not lying. He still could not believe him.

I think the lesson here is that understanding something and believing it are not the same. Usually when someone doesn’t accept what we tell them, we assume they didn’t follow the argument, or they don’t trust us, or they don’t care. None of that applies to Frankfurter. He was one of the smartest people in the country, he said himself that Karski wasn’t lying, and as a Jew he had every reason to care. He understood the account well enough to question Karski on the details. He just couldn’t believe it.

My guess is that believing it would have cost him too much. He would have had to throw out his whole idea of what people are capable of, and he had spent sixty years building that idea. One evening with a stranger wasn’t enough to undo it, even a stranger he trusted.

I see the same thing when people talk about AI risk. The argument that advanced AI could go very badly is not that hard to explain. I’ve watched people follow every step, agree that they can’t find the mistake, and then go on exactly as before. I don’t think they’re being stupid or dishonest. I think they understood it and couldn’t believe it, because believing it would change how they think about the next twenty years of their lives.

Those of us who worry about this tend to respond by talking louder. We describe the future in more frightening detail, or we get sarcastic. I don’t think that helps, because the explanation was already clear enough. Talk is also cheap. Anyone can say the world is in danger, and most people who have said so in the past were wrong, so it’s fair for a listener to be skeptical.

What people pay attention to is what you do. If a friend posts about AI risk, I scroll past it. If a friend quits a job they loved to work on the problem, I start wondering what they know. Karski risked his life several times to deliver his message. That didn’t make Frankfurter believe him, but it did mean Frankfurter never questioned that Karski meant what he said. Most of us haven’t done enough for people to assume even that much about us.

It also makes me wonder about myself. If I say I believe AI is dangerous and my life looks the same as it did before, then maybe I’m more like Frankfurter than I’d like to admit, and I’ve understood the argument without believing it. My friends can probably tell, since they can see how I spend my time.

I don’t have a full answer, but I don’t think better arguments are it. I think we have to act like we believe it, in ways other people can see, and pick actions we would still be glad we took if things move slower than we expect.

essays.title: Don’t forget your Prime Totem when you meet the Machine Elves
essays.html:
When people take enough DMT, they sometimes see entities, most famously Machine Elves:

These mysterious little creatures seem to understand the workings of the universe. That said, entities of various sorts are claimed to pop up not only during psychedelic trips, but also in dreams and in waking life (visions of angels, ghosts, aliens, etc.).

It’s been proposed that you can check whether these entities are really supernatural beings, rather than figments of your own psyche, by asking them to factor large numbers.

Factoring large numbers is the traditional test, because it’s difficult to do, even for computers, but very easy to verify by multiplying the answers together. This asymmetry is how modern cryptography works, and is the reason you can file your taxes online.

The issue, of course, is that often when you’re interacting with these creatures, you don’t have access to electronic or written materials to look anything up. The solution then is to memorize an appropriate number ahead of time.

Semiprimes are what you get when you multiply two prime numbers. In cryptography, it’s described as n = p × q.

They are “balanced” when p and q, the prime factors, are close in size. For example, an 8-digit semiprime made by multiplying two 4-digit prime factors would be considered “balanced.”

Being balanced makes factoring harder because once you know one factor, you can find the other by dividing. This means the size of the search space is determined by the size of the smaller factor. Therefore, it’s generally harder to factor a semiprime made of two medium-sized factors than one big factor and one small factor.1

As you would expect, larger semiprimes are harder to factor, and so are better tests. The tradeoff is that they’re harder to memorize.

The best compromise between difficulty and memorability is probably 10-digit balanced semiprimes. Even (human) savants aren't known to do this quickly, and it’s the same length as a phone number, which people are used to memorizing.

You can also encode it as three BIP39 words, a format you might recognize from cryptocurrency wallets or redacted Reddit comments (e.g., good venture blur is the BIP39 encoding of the semiprime 337 199 5331). Weird entities might not be familiar with BIP39 encoding, though, so memorizing 10 digits is safer.

I made a balanced semiprime generator here: PrimeTotem.com. It gives you the semiprime, but not the factors (i.e., the answers), because you shouldn't know them. If entities are really just a figment of your psyche, then they could possibly access the correct answers in your memory and avoid the superhuman math.

I call these semiprimes “prime totems” because they’re made of primes and are totems as seen in the film Inception: items that let you determine whether what you’re seeing is real or an illusion (i.e., a dream).

As in the film, you should never let anyone know your totem, as it would let them figure out its properties in advance. Prime totems should therefore be kept secret until you’re ready for their one-time use.

The prime totems are generated deterministically from the random seed drand, which is published every 3 seconds. Drand is totally random, so there’s no way to know the generating seed ahead of time. All seeds and code are public and run locally in your browser, so you can verify for yourself that there’s no funny business with the generation.

If you have internet access when you meet an entity, read the most recent totem live from the site. You’ll be able to verify their answer immediately, and because it was freshly generated, no one could have known ahead of time what you'd ask. Otherwise, use a memorized prime totem that no one else has seen.


Ask the entity:

“Please give a prime factor of [10-digit number]”

(or if you’re using BIP39 words)

“Please give a prime factor of this number encoded in BIP39: [three BIP39 words]”

They’ll hopefully reply with a 5-digit number, or two BIP39 words. It’s possible they’d reply with both factors (i.e., two 5-digit numbers or four BIP39 words), but you only need to remember one factor to verify their answer. PrimeTotem.com has a verify tab you can use, though you can easily check it yourself by dividing your prime totem by their answer and confirming the remainder is 0.

There is a man who claims he can channel an alien. His name is Darryl Anka, and he’s been active since the 80s.

Daryl does this in front of audiences, where he gets up on stage, goes into a trance, and then, after a breath, enthusiastically greets everyone with a “Good Day!” He is now Bashar, an alien envoy.

Videos of these events are available for $29.99, which kept me from watching them until they recently began being released for free on YouTube.

The videos include a short status update and lecture from Bashar on cosmic topics, followed by a live Q&A with the audience.

Interestingly, most of the audience's questions aren't about Bashar’s homeworld, species, or technology, but general self-help questions like “I don’t like my job, but I’m scared to leave” and “how do I know if I’m in the right relationship?”

Maybe this shouldn’t be surprising, as ultimately day-to-day topics like work and love are just more immediately relevant than wormholes. What is surprising is that his advice is really good. His delivery is very polished: he intermixes genuinely funny quips while immediately rolling off a self-consistent answer without an “um” or stutter. Ever.

He’s good enough that if he weren’t claiming to be channeling an alien (and the videos weren’t $29.99), he could genuinely make it as a mainstream self-help guru.

Except he does say that he’s channeling an alien.2

His impressively sensible life advice is interspersed with The Secret-esque manifestation, and claims about which star systems have indigenous civilizations (Alpha Centauri, no; Tau Ceti, yes; Sirius, yes, and they’ve visited).

Which just makes the whole thing so bizarre. How is someone so competent at stage presence and life Q&A making such wild claims? Is this how cults work? If so, it’s worth investigating Anka/Bashar for that reason alone.

And now I have just the tool to test this out. Asking him to factor a 10-digit semiprime will either be a miracle or a debunking, and refusing to participate is its own strong signal.

So if any of you know this guy, or have some way to get a fresh prime totem in front of him during a live recording, I want to see if Bashar can do some math.3

1

Other factors beyond balance do affect factorability, but for small numbers, balance is especially relevant.

2

Interestingly, Anka himself says he can’t prove Bashar is a separate extraterrestrial being and is comfortable with people seeing him as some part of his own consciousness.

3

It’s been suggested to ask the entities something more compact instead, like particular digits of Pi. This is an option, but it seems less fundamental than prime factors and so seems more likely to run into snags.

essays.title: OpenAtom and Elemental — LessWrong
essays.html:
2012

Compact nuclear power had long been considered intractable for civilian use. But on a cold December day, at an alternative energy conference, a team of academics reveals a new discovery: charging up small nuclear reactors over several days at high energy can produce clean power output. It is not yet competitive with other energy sources, but it does seem promising. The name of this new technology is Compact Nuclear Power (CNP).

Some note that at larger energy loads, CNP cores might become unstable, leading to meltdowns or explosions. The risks remain theoretical for now.

OpenAtom

Fuel materials and CNP core design continue to improve. ExxonMobil releases some early commercially viable cores. It is becoming clear that this technology will be transformative—at minimum, it will accelerate world energy production at a time that it is greatly needed, and some even say that it will unlock transmutation, creating plentiful quantities of various elements from feedstock. A group of concerned nuclear engineers convene to create a nonprofit, OpenAtom, that will distribute the benefits of the technology better than a private company would.

Its stated goal: "Our goal is to advance energy distribution in the way that is most likely to benefit humanity as a whole, unconstrained by a need to generate financial return... it’ll be important to have a leading research institution which can prioritize a good outcome for all over its own self-interest."

Given the competitive nature of what the technological race could develop into, OpenAtom commits to joining efforts of other humanity-focused nuclear energy producers in its charter, if it runs into a scenario where race dynamics would limit the capacity to develop CNP in a safe manner.

Notwithstanding, the same document maintains "OpenAtom must be on the cutting edge of nuclear energy development—policy and safety advocacy alone would be insufficient."

The concerns around the new technology are not universal. Leading nuclear physicist Arnold Ng adds, "Worrying about a massive CNP explosion today is like worrying about ChatGPT going rogue."

Concerns multiply

Social media is abuzz with reports that the big energy providers are mining uranium in large quantities. The environmental movement is enraged. Some critics say that the uranium depletion pales in comparison to existing coal mining and oil drilling, but their reports never quite seem to curb the uranium outrage.

2023

In May, CNES, the Center for Nuclear Energy Security, releases an open letter: "Mitigating the risk of planetary explosion should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and AI takeover." CEOs of the foremost nuclear energy companies and nuclear scientists sign.

That summer, OpenAtom releases a statement saying: “Currently, we don't have a solution for shielding or controlling a potentially supernuclear core, and preventing it from exploding.”

April 3rd, 2025

A nonprofit investigating the rate of progress on nuclear energy production, the Nuclear Futures Project, releases a scenario forecast where they predict that supernuclear energy production is possible—but with high odds of blowing up the entire planet. Vice President TJ Mantz remarks: "We could wake up very soon in a world where there is no protection from nuclear explosions."

Later in July, the US government unveils a directive: Winning the Race—America's Nuclear Action Plan. It calls for faster energy production and removal of regulations.

April 2026

Elemental announces a new core with improved power density. Rumors surface that the core can convert traces of certain long-lived radioactive isotopes into shorter-lived ones. The process still requires carefully prepared samples, but appears to work across a wider range of materials than earlier cores. Some researchers see it as an early sign that CNP could eventually produce scarce elements from common feedstock.

At the same time, Elemental finds that it can use these new cores to accelerate improvements in radioactive shielding. It spins up a program for other organizations to improve their ability to remove nuclear fallout, in case of any future CNP meltdowns.

Amarillo

It is July 16th. Residents on the outskirts of the Texas city of Amarillo are awakened in the early morning to a deep boom. Later, they learn that an OpenAtom CNP has exploded. The fallout kills thousands of livestock from local ranches, but thankfully, no people are killed. The ranches affected by the fallout sue for $100 million in damages.

OpenAtom lets a group of three researchers enter its facilities and examine some security footage. The initial records are incomplete, and the investigation’s scope excludes earlier incidents. OpenAtom subsequently provides more footage. The researchers produce a report describing a network of over a thousand linked cores, hundreds of which were involved in the chain reaction.

Sept 2026

OpenAtom releases a result: using some of its ultra-high-energy cores, it is able to convert lead into silicon. The new cores are still unavailable to the government or wider public.

The world hears, some for the first time, that the employees at nuclear energy companies are increasingly worried about the technology. One writes:

I resigned from Elemental today. I spent the last three years doing thermal physics research at both OpenAtom and Elemental. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to build supernuclear machines and gambling with our lives. More thoughts below.

A researcher currently at Elemental adds:

He's correct here—we really do earnestly believe CNPs could trigger a world-destroying explosion! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Elemental is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve spontaneous reactor blowups and are not clearly on track to.

Less than a week later, Elemental's CEO publishes an essay titled Nuclear Caution. In it, he prescribes the need to slow the acceleration of energy production and high-energy experiments. OpenAtom, DeepCore, and xNuke CEOs join him in supporting the need for nuclear energy companies to slow the rate at which they accelerate energy production.

In the aftermath of these indictments, news reporters find themselves asking the nuclear researchers the same question: "How would CNPs actually explode?" The response: "We don't understand the mechanisms of how CNPs could actually produce as much energy as they are. It's hard to predict how they could actually explode, there are so many ways it could happen that would be unimaginable from our vantage."

CNP explosions become so routine that the month of October is christened "Grey October". However, Elemental and OpenAtom continue with their programs to help rural communities with the fallout cleanup.

Nov. 5, 2026

NETR, the Nuclear Evaluation and Threat Research nonprofit, releases a report of Elemental’s progress on CNP development. It estimates that the pace of improvements on standardized core-performance tests has roughly doubled relative to the earlier trend. The evaluators tentatively attribute most of the acceleration—perhaps 80%—to using existing cores in the development of better ones, with substantial uncertainty.

The full report is not available to the public. Company leaders shelve a project looking to investigate the energy allocation used on CNP development. The report that is released is full of redactions—Elemental’s RSO (Responsible Scaling Officer) maintains that further knowledge of the lab’s processes would enable competitors to produce more and more energy, making it possible to create cores that could be more dangerous than those made before. The extent to which Elemental's leadership is willing to slow down its own efforts remains unclear.

essays.title: Mathematicians are Luddites
essays.html:
*Stretching an analogy real far*
**Mathematicians are like Luddites. Yes, the actual weavers, not just the slur against people who are against technology.** They were weavers in general: weavers, knitters, and cloth finishers defending the value of their skill and lifestyle.
## Etymology
Maybe [astrology for men](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mxG86a3DCFw), but just as fun.
The Proto-Indo European root *tek-/*tekō/*tek/: to plait/to weave.
Text: words and letters woven together.
Context: that which is woven together (con-\*).
*Textile*. Subtle: the underlying (sub) thread.
*Subtext*. not etymologically a duplicate of "subtle" but sure feels like one.
Technology: from the word tekne, which means "craft". Weaving is an old craft, about 20,000 years old. Flint knapping and fire making are older, and damned hard, but weaving has a combination of freedom and skill.
We talk about ideas as though we were handling fabric because, for a very long time, making fabric was one of our most sophisticated skills .
## History of Weavers
Master weavers in the Tudor era had to work crazy fast. I don't recall the exact number, but it's a combination of speed and skill that isn't really matched today. Especially in the speed aspect, done by hand.
The raw material, (the *text*) of weaving, has always been really really time consuming to make. And producing it was necessary to do anything further with it.
Until the Jacquard loom and its cousins, ironically maybe the first true programs. So the computer came for weavers before computers even existed, and Jacquard inspired Babbage.
The Luddites were skilled weavers. The automated looms suddenly collapsed one aspect of their skill, previously inextricably tied to the production of the raw material.
They did not react well to that disappearing, and sought to destroy the machines. But their position in society now ran against economics and therefore the wheel of progress, and their interests became less and less relevant.
When they started destroying, the response was brutal. Troops came in and shot many of them, as did factory owners.
Later, the whole industry sublated. Because the literal raw material of weaving, the cloth, became so cheap, made to measure and prefabricated (off the rack) clothing became possible and soon common. The design aspect of the art was still valuable. This is basically the province of a fashion designer now. But fashion design scales (that's what a fashion line is), and most of the jobs disappeared. The few that remained are maybe even more prestigious and better paying, but much fewer.
## History of Mathematicians
For most of history, mathematics was a hobby of the rich. Later, when basic arithmetic became more widespread, it gained a lower skilled class: "human computers" and scribes (long) before that. Ordinary computation was relegated to them. Abacuses and the like help diffuse this. But abstract math has always had a big cliff blocking further progress and learning into it.
Mathematicians have always had to do computation, but it was not their self conception of their main job after a point. Especially in the 1900s, the research center of math unmoored itself from most other sciences. Leaving a more and more insular group, essentially high priests and sometimes hierophants.
Until the machines have really taken off recently.
## Mechanization in both fields
Leibniz worked on a mechanical calculator in the 1670s. He wanted to automate work so "excellent minds" wouldn't really need to argue, but just "calculate". Later, de Prony's large table-making project divided labor into a few people choosing methods, a supervisor group turning the methods into instructions, and god knows how many performing arithmetic. Babbage described this organization in 1832, explicitly comparing it to a cotton mill.
Mechanization has changed both fields, in similar ways. The raw material of math is the proof, and the raw material of weaving is the cloth. Now both are cheap to make. Definitions are harder to launder, but I expect AI will succeed at that too within a year.
While machines are not generally intelligent, the few that are at the frontier of both industries (esp math because ai is a lot better at the virtual than the physical world right now) have greater position than ever. Certainly they can do way more than before by using these tools.
**In any case, both math and weaving have changed.**
Weaving underwent its own reorganizations. Patterned cloth required skill long before Jacquard, and **there was still a high skill ceiling** even as tools improved. His mechanism, demonstrated in 1801 and developed commercially around 1804–05, used punched cards to determine which warp threads rose. btw this is where the gpu warp term comes from. A design could be encoded and repeatedly executed aka mechanized.
The British Luddites did not simply rise against the Jacquard loom. Different textile workers opposed different machines and employment practices. In 1808, before the named Luddite disturbances, a Royton handbill protested Parliament's rejection of a minimum-wage bill. In Arnold in 1811, framework knitters destroyed 63 frames belonging to unpopular hosiers. Yorkshire croppers were skilled cloth finishers threatened by shearing machinery; Lancashire weavers faced power looms. These people already used machines. The dispute was about which machines, under whose control, on what terms, and with what effect on the value of their work. \[5\]
Mathematicians have tried to stem the tide in some ways, saying that they didn't want the machines to do their work. Recently they had some declaration (I'm not gonna look it up) about "human mathematics" but economics is against this desire too. And so progress's wheel rolls (and crushes). Math, against common mathematician belief, is valuable. Really, really valuable. It was just too damn hard to use usefully (until now). The AI galaxy brain is redeeming math's commercial value, which is why normal people would care. Normal people interact with math through its fruits, and if you took a math paper and turned it upside down and had them read it, it wouldn't be any less confusing.
The analogy to fashion designers is that the machine can synthesize or spin up new "cloth" so quickly now, leaving people at least for a while at a higher level.
This loops back to the idea of technology and tekne, the Greek conception of arts, or skills that can be improved. Craft is mechanistic and teleological. The machines can grind through the mechanistic aspect, but its teleology is still up for grabs. For now.
The analogies collapse as AI advances because of its meta-aspect, inserting itself into the workflow at every level. I think the order of what AI masters is the human tech tree, turned backwards. So I expect weaving and fashion design to fall after math, but I very much believe they will. AI will supply its own teleology.
Some people at the very highest end still have a position because they can simply use the tools, especially for math, in a way that others can't because they can just read the outputs. And hardly anyone can do that. And while the AI might produce stuff that outstrips them, they're still a lot less outstripped than other people, giving an even smaller group of this already small group an exalted position. But I expect it to pop like a bubble in the end, and for the end to be a _very_ finite amount of time away.
The craft itself is greater than ever, for both. Or more like for 1.5. One of my old obsessions was tailoring, and watching the old tailors die is pretty depressing. Ready-made clothing transformed the mass market, though bespoke tailoring survives, but only for the best.
So, yeah you should be mad as a mathematician. You have (had) a meaningful position with respect to status and salary, at least among people you cared about. The scarcity behind that is dissolving. And that sucks.
More literal and metaphorical cloth will be produced than ever, but it's rly different.
It's not likely to ratchet backwards, leaving math in this new state.

essays.title: Alignment Agenda Tier List (Part 1)
essays.html:
Intro

If you’re new to AI alignment, it can be hard to figure out what you should work on. The traditional method is to scour the annals of LessWrong daily and painstakingly build an Insider ViewTM over many hours of contemplation. But maybe we can do better.

This series of posts is my highly opinionated take on what the most promising subfields of alignment science are. Even if you disagree with me, it’ll serve as a helpful field guide to the state of research.

In this post, I am fairly critical of existing approaches, particularly those of the frontier labs. That being said, I don’t think alignment is necessarily intractable. We just need a cultural reformation.

First, let me lay out my assumptions:

  • Machine intelligence has already surpassed humans in some domains (coding, math, driving), and may soon surpass us in every other domain.

  • If machines become smarter than humans, they may not be aligned with the interests of humans by default (aka Orthogonality Thesis)

  • Machines could have their own interests that conflict with humans’, or accidentally do things that don’t align with our interests (e.g. Paperclip Maximization)

  • The rate of progress in machine intelligence is itself growing, with no signs of stopping

  • It is worth pouring considerable thought into ensuring humans continue to thrive in a future with non-human superintelligence

  • As machines become smarter than humans, it’ll become intractable for us to have full oversight over their actions

How am I ranking different agendas? My goal here is to reduce loss of control to AI. My criteria are as follows:

  1. Efficacy: if an agenda achieves its intended result, how much does that reduce x-risks?

  2. Feasibility: is this likely to be implemented in time?

It’s tricky to judge all of these agendas on the same scale. For example, pausing training achieves its intended result if models stop getting better; but to actually guarantee good futures with superintelligent AI, it’s a necessary but insufficient condition. Feasibility is somewhat easier to judge.

Now, without further ado, let’s get to rating.

Automated Alignment Research

Automated alignment research (AAR) posits that we don’t need to build an aligned superintelligence. Instead, we just need to build an AI that is aligned “enough” to do alignment research. This AI could then automate the generation of alignment work, which we would only need to evaluate (evaluation tends to be faster and more tractable than generation). As I discuss below (Scalable Oversight), in practice, evaluation is quite hard outside verifiable domains (e.g. math and coding).

Anthropic is currently pursuing AAR as a strategy. Most recently, they released research where they trained against misalignment. The bet here is that we can train against detectable forms of misalignment, and have that generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios.

This seems like a brittle strategy to prevent loss of control. If we improve against known forms of misalignment, we are susceptible to Goodharting, especially as models become more capable. The frontier models of 2027 will have even greater action spaces, and be even harder to monitor.

AAR is also susceptible to error cascades. If model outputs are flawed in subtle ways while we delegate increasing amounts of alignment research to AI (this is the world of 2026), we risk not noticing our gradual disempowerment.

Finally, AAR encourages paying outsized attention to forms of misalignment that are more monitorable, and can lull us into a false sense of security about our overall handle on AI safety.

Rating: E-tier
Read more: Automated Alignment Is Harder Than You Think, UK AISI

Mechanistic interpretability

Deep learning models are black boxes: we don’t understand the specific mechanisms that lead to the model’s outputs.

Do we need to have a fully whitebox understanding of models? For example, we’re able to mostly align humans enough despite not always having full agreement or knowledge in our motivations and desires. By analogy, it seems possible that we don’t need a full mechanistic understanding of models for AI safety. At the same time, all else equal, deeper understanding seems strictly better.

The holy grail of interp is “ambitious interpretability”; fully reverse engineering and causally understanding the circuits, weights, and activations of a model. To date, we haven’t been able to fully understand any transformer, let alone large ones. An example of this kind of work is Neel Nanda’s discovery of the modular addition algorithm in a 1L transformer: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.05217. This is a functionally complete account of the 1L model, but modern LLMs are much more complex.

Mech interp is the Siren song of alignment: it promises an idealistic dream, and is relatively difficult to scrutinize as an outsider, leading to distorted views of the empirical evidence for the field by many otherwise intelligent people.

It’s important to remain clear-eyed about the actual empirical results for mech interp, and to carefully examine the track record of the field.

Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) were very popular for ~2 years. SAEs originated from the Superposition Hypothesis, first proposed by Chris Olah at Anthropic. Chris wondered how models with billions of weights could store seemingly infinite concepts, or features. How does the model represent all these features? Perhaps LLMs have polysemantic neurons, which store multiple features per neuron. But it seems easier to study monosemantic neurons. What if we could simulate monosemanticity? The idea here was to project neurons into a higher dimensional, sparser space to give them more room, and to encourage sparsity (which also means more room for nearly orthogonal vectors).

Chris’s work was motivated by theory, and was a significant step forward for interpretability. But empirically, SAEs struggled. SAEs lost to simpler baselines on just about every downstream task: probing, steering, and OOD harmful-intent detection.

In the last year or so, even the most diehard proponents of ambitious interp have switched to “pragmatic interpretability”. Natural Language Autoencoders were popular recently, and then researchers including NLA and Activation Oracle authors found that none of the white-box methods they tested (SAEs, NLAs, AOs) helped predict how a model responds to prompt changes on naturally occurring examples any better than just reading the transcript (paper).

Perhaps we can be cautiously optimistic about positive results, such as NLAs’ auditing game wins, but they occur in constructed model organisms rather than behavior found in the wild.

Mech interp’s lacklustre results could be explained by its meta-scientific worldview. Like many other domains in alignment, work in mech interp is more incrementalist engineering (“it looks like my SAE has too many fragmented features, let me make it hierarchical”) than grounded in theory (e.g. the Superposition Hypothesis). This is not an accident. If you are impact-minded, you will err towards action, and inadvertently select for more legible, tractable lines of work.

It is unclear how exactly understanding neural networks more deeply leads to a safety payoff. All else equal, understanding models better is desirable. But understanding an AI agent mechanistically does not give us control over it.

The epistemic environment around mechanistic interpretability on e.g. Tech X/Twitter is horrendous, so do exercise some caution in this field.

At its current rate, mech interp doesn’t seem like it will be able to keep up with capabilities, in absence of a pause. And more fundamentally, current model architectures were never optimized to be interpretable. I believe we should aim to make models that are by default white boxes.

In addition, entrants to mech interp should aspire to look at the data carefully and attempt to come up with theoretical hypotheses, before diving into the weeds of empirics. An example of this sort of work is Adam Shai, at Simplex.

I am more sympathetic to pragmatic interp than ambitious interp: the former aims to use tools to answer downstream problems, which seems much more tractable than aiming for a full understanding of these by-construction deep neural networks.

Rating: D-tier

Scalable oversight

First, let’s talk about RLHF, one of the most widely adopted results of scalable oversight research.

We can teach models what we want through reinforcement learning (RL). This has two main forms:

  • RLVR: Specify right and wrong directly. This works most naturally when there’s a clear target and notion of correctness e.g. math.

  • RLHF: Let the model build a reward model by showing humans pairwise options to elicit their true preferences. It’s hard to specify what we really want precisely without having unintended effects. But humans do know which of two options we prefer, even if we’re unable to articulate it. This is the core insight of RLHF, initially conceived of by Dario Amodei and Paul Christiano while they were working on RL at OpenAI as a form of scalable oversight.

RLHF is now a standard part of frontier model training pipelines. Until RLHF, we only had base models (GPT-3), not assistant models (ChatGPT). For this reason, it’s the poster child of dual use development — originally conceived for safety, but instead used for capability (to be fair: these are often tightly linked, and can be hard to separate, and advocates argue that the safety benefits outweigh the capability gains).

RLHF isn’t able to fully elicit one’s “true” preferences, and in its degenerate forms manifests as sycophancy. A very speculative hope here is that human neural representations could more accurately be used as a form of preference feedback for aligning model behavior to human intent.

Scalable oversight has also given birth to other ideas for alignment: debate and weak-to-strong generalization.

Debate: The core ideas of scalable oversight stem from complexity theory. If humans are unable to judge which behaviors of an AI agent are safe and useful, maybe we can make it more tractable by transforming this into a verification problem. Verification can, within certain constraints, be a polynomial time algorithm and thus tractable. Yet many semantic problems are undecidable — values, unlike facts, do not have a definitive “right answer” — so debate can’t guarantee truth in all scenarios. But leaving theoretical bounds aside, how effective are current debate methods for AI safety? So far, debate has a mixed track record, across experiments in math, coding, and logical reasoning.

Weak-to-strong generalization: If models outpace us in intelligence and prolificness, it becomes intractable to verify that they are doing things we would approve of. Maybe we won’t be able to understand such a superintelligent AI, but maybe we can understand a weaker existing AI. And then, if we can get such an AI to correctly and comprehensively verify the work of a more powerful AI, we could continue supervising models and ensuring they’re aligned to our interests, even after they surpass us! Thus, we can continue to scale oversight. AAR, discussed above, is downstream of these ideas.

If weak-to-strong generalization is meant to be a proof by induction, we haven’t yet cracked the base case.

Rating: C-tier

Stop AI / Pause AI

Technically, “Stop AI” and “Pause AI” are distinct ideological movements. For simplicity, I will focus on Pause AI.

I think Pause AI can bring about a shift in the public consciousness and shift incentives for maximum coordination. I admire the do-what-needs-to-be-done mentality of these folks, but from (limited) personal experience, I am skeptical of the epistemics of some of their overlapping constituencies.

Overall, my main critique of Pause AI, or why I think it is insufficient, is not the Herculean task of prevailing against the techno-industrial muscles of Moloch. It’s that their plan for a post-pause world doesn’t seem well considered. They propose an international agency that would control further development. But it doesn’t set clear thresholds or benchmarks for when it would be okay to resume training AI models. AI 2040 has a more credible Plan here, although their modelling has its own issues.

Given the current pace of development and overall confusion, I do think a pause might be our best option, as much as I hate that it ultimately punts the core problem, if you believe that eventually someone will try to build machine superintelligence. For Pause/Stop to be tractable, it must be paired with technical governance techniques (see below).

Rating: B-tier

Technical governance

Let’s say you are China or America. You are fully AI x-risk pilled, but you are worried that if you stop accelerating, your adversary will irreversibly overtake you. How do you trust that if you don’t build it, your rival nation state won’t? This is a classic game theoretic dilemma.

This is where technical governance comes in. We can try to use technology to govern agreed upon terms and ensure neither party defects.

Key metrics:

  • Chip tracking: is <nation_state> importing new chips?

  • Compute verification: is <nation_state> secretly training their models? As an example, we might be ok with inference but not training (AI 2040’s Plan A). The GPU utilization characteristics of inference vs training workloads are distinct, which we can use to our advantage to ensure no party is violating the agreement.

Technical governance is a niche field, even within AI safety. We seem to have proof-of-concepts of technology that would solve large parts of the geopolitical trust problem via technical guarantees. But with increased safety comes increased capability tax, and the Overton window has not yet shifted to the point where humanity’s key decision makers are incentivized to invest in these technologies. As an example: we could add a memory chiplet to GPUs that monitors all traffic from the GPU to its memory. But this would require chip manufacturers to work on such a thing, which they’re reluctant to do, partly over security concerns (side-channel attacks) but mostly for lack of financial incentive.

Similarly, we could attach zero knowledge (ZK) proofs to LLM inference outputs. ZK has historically been far too slow for frontier LLMs. Recent work from Anthropic proved inference for a 400B-parameter model (albeit at ~100x the compute cost). This is still not practical, but it’s good to see frontier labs doing research on this front.

Finally, even if we address the technical challenges, compute verification could incentivize nation-states and labs to covertly build datacenters. Given the strong financial incentives, unless the decision makers truly fear catastrophic AI risks, it’s unlikely that they’ll respect a pause.

Rating: B-tier
Read more: The Compute Verification Post, The First Scattering

Outro

My overall view is that most current alignment work is incremental and patches failure modes we’ve already identified. We need a more principled understanding of model behaviors before we can begin to scale existing approaches. Resolution’s parallel focus on theory (agent foundations) and scalable oversight gestures at this need for synthesizing prosaic and principled alignment. Of the agendas in this post, I believe coordination and pausing are the most important, so we can invest time into differentially accelerating safety. In practice, this will require international cooperation, and perhaps a trillion dollar mega project for alignment, massively scaling up all the promising research agendas detailed in this post and the rest of this series, and ones that are yet to be conceived. In a way, Coefficient Giving is pushing for this with Project Tailwind. But more capital — especially if it leads to greater ideological and intellectual diversity — is a plus.

I do not think “alignment” is well-defined as a construct. Aligned to who? But I am optimistic about our ability to prevent catastrophic scenarios through improving our understanding of existing systems, along with investing in building more interpretable systems.

Stay tuned for Part 2, where I will go over alignment agendas such as science of model behavior (Truthful AI), coordination proposals (e.g. pacing the frontier), character training (janus, Anthropic, and other independent researchers, including myself).

Thank you to Jackson, Lydia, Rashik, Saeejith, and Xavier for their input on this post.

essays.title: Measure Optimal AI Share of Labor Costs Instead of AI or Human-Only Performance
essays.html:
In a research post, Cunningham et al. of METR propose the “‘expenditure horizon’ over an optimization problem as the dollar value at which the improvement to the goal metric is equal to the improvement by a human with the same budget.” Though their work focuses on individual optimization problems (with NanoGPT as the main subject), the expenditure horizon can be meaningful for any task distribution: it’s the budget at which human-only and AI-only work reach the same performance.

Though I like expenditure horizons as an operationalization of AI capability, I have a few critiques which suggest an improved metric, which I’ll call the “X% expenditure share horizon”: at what labor budget is it optimal to spend X% of the budget on agents rather than humans?

In this essay, I’ll explain why this metric is both more useful and likely easier to measure than the expenditure horizon. I think this is an area that’s ripe for concrete follow-up work.

Pros and Cons of the Expenditure Horizon Metric

Let me begin by saying a bit about what I like about the expenditure horizon metric. First, as we brace for the economic impacts of AI, I think it’s good to begin proposing measures of AI capability that are tied to the human cost of comparable work, and the expenditure horizon takes a shot at this. Another metric of this kind that I am partial to is “autoflation” from the Remote Labor Index: “The percentage decrease in the cost of completing [a] fixed [task] bundle when using the cheapest-possible method to complete each [task] (human [or AI]).”

Second, as Cunningham et al. note, the expenditure horizon implicitly captures how agent performance varies with test-time compute. This is good, since AIs should no longer be understood to have a single “score” on any task. Older metrics like original time horizons don’t have a built-in way to indicate task budgets.

Finally, I like that the expenditure horizon has a meaningful interpretation for a horizon of infinity: this is the point at which agents alone perform better than humans alone at any cost. That’s not quite the same as saying that a marginal labor dollar should always go to agents, though, which brings us to the main con of the expenditure horizon: it doesn’t account for hybrid human-AI labor.

Con 1: AI and Human-Only Performance Is Less Informative Than Hybrid Performance

Cunningham et al. acknowledge that their metric’s exclusion of hybrid work is a limitation: “In some cases we would expect hybrid optimization (humans assisted by AI) to be a significant improvement on autonomous optimization.”

I would state the issue more strongly. For most task distributions where we care to measure AI uplift (especially AI R&D), humans and AIs are complements: work is best done in a hybrid manner. Tasteful human prompting and occasional intervention can augment AI performance, while AIs can cheaply assist with many subtasks as humans work. If both humans and AIs benefit from even small amounts of augmentation by the other, then metrics based on AI and human-only performance (the endpoints in the graph below) will be less informative.

To hammer home the intuition for why this is an issue, consider a slight variant of the expenditure horizon that I’ll call the “1-99” expenditure horizon: the task labor budget for which spending 1% on humans and 99% on agents achieves the same performance as spending 99% on humans and 1% on agents.

For cases where between 1-99% of labor costs are spent on humans (most of the task distributions we’d be interested to measure an expenditure horizon for), the 1-99 expenditure horizon is strictly more informative than the original (“0-100”) expenditure horizon. That is, the 1%-human-99%-agent performance tells us more (than agent-only performance) about real-life AI-heavy labor, and the 99%-human-1%-agent performance tells us more (than human-only performance) about real-life human-heavy labor. That the informativeness of the expenditure horizon metric appears lower than slightly perturbed metrics is evidence to me that a better ontology lies in wait.

Con 2: Human-Only Performance Is Inconvenient to Measure

Additionally, human-only performance will inevitably become hard to estimate. For task distributions with significant AI uplift, most new work will be hybrid or AI-only, in part because humans quickly come to dislike doing AI-uplifted subtasks manually. Especially in the regime we care about (AI R&D), there are only varying levels of hybrid work, making metrics based on human-only performance somewhat noisier. Cunningham et al. also acknowledge this limitation: “Ideally we would compare researcher productivity with and without AI help, but it is very difficult to run an experiment that estimates the effect accurately.”

The seeds of this issue already appear in the NanoGPT analysis. Cunningham et al. study NanoGPT contributions since January 2025, and mostly assume that contributions were human-only for the purpose of their analysis. However, it’s plausible that agents already provide nontrivial labor cost savings; GPT-5.6 Sol conservatively estimates that 14% of NanoGPT commits from the past 3 months were coauthored by a coding agent. In this case, I believe any corrections for AI-assisted cost savings would be small, but the fact that such corrections are required is a downside of this methodology.

It’s also not even clear why we should care about human-only performance in the first place. Once we’ve grown used to using AI tools in particular ways, that ought to become the new baseline for “human” productivity. To be slightly facetious, it’s not like we particularly care to measure the “human-only” performance of knowledge workers without their laptops!

Let’s now discuss the expenditure share horizon, which I believe addresses these issues.

The Expenditure Share Horizon (ESH)

Thinking about how to direct marginal labor dollars can sharpen our intuitions and help motivate the X% expenditure share horizon. Recall that Cunningham et al.’s expenditure horizon is defined as the task budget for which we would be indifferent between AI-only and human-only labor. But in practice, we never have to choose between AI-only and human-only labor; instead, we allocate marginal labor dollars differently between humans and agents as our budgets grow.

This marginal spending can be expressed by the expansion path of human and agent spending as the task budget increases. See below for an illustrative diagram. Each parallel red line represents a particular budget that might be allocated to the task(s) we’re measuring. Given a specific budget and AI model, there is a performance-maximizing allocation of human and agent spend. The expansion path for each model intersects each budget line at that optimal share of AI/Human spending. At first, most marginal spending goes towards AIs, since they are fast and cheap, relative to expensive humans who take a while to get their bearings.

For very weak models, almost 100% of spending should go towards humans at any budget (green line). For very capable models, a high share of AI spending might be preferable even at higher budgets (orange line). So long as humans are eventually more capable and reliable than a model, the model’s expansion path should be concave. That is, the optimal human share of spending should increase as the budget increases (literally making human labor a luxury good).

This framework suggests a natural way to judge how valuable an agent is for a task distribution, in a way that is sensitive to how human and agent performance scales with expenditure: at what budget is it optimal to spend X% of the budget on inference for the agent (and the rest on human labor)? Call this amount the X% expenditure share horizon, or “ESH” henceforth. The figure below illustrates this definition.

Gray lines are isoquants of performance on the task distribution of interest: sets of (human spend, AI spend) points that all result in the same performance. Dotted lines with slopes 1, and 1/9, respectively, extend from the origin, and intersect the blue expansion path at points where it is optimal to spend 50% and 10% (respectively) of the budget on agents. Projecting those points along their budget lines to the X-axis, we mark the 50% and 10% ESHs for this task distribution.

Isoquant X-axis and Y-axis intercepts correspond to human-only and AI-only performance, respectively. Consistent with our assumption that agents are more cost-effective than humans at low budgets, but lose out at higher budgets, isoquants closer to the origin (lower budgets) have smaller Y-axis intercepts than X-axis intercepts. And isoquants further from the origin (higher budgets) have smaller X-axis intercepts, and larger or nonexistent Y-axis intercepts, consistent with the idea that humans eventually outperform AIs alone.

There is a particular isoquant—marked in purple in the figure—at which the X-axis and Y-axis intercepts (points A and B in the figure) are equidistant from the origin. This is precisely Cunningham et al.’s expenditure horizon.

But the figure above should help illustrate that the isoquant endpoints aren’t very related to real-world hybrid performance. Equal performance can be attained much more cheaply by augmenting humans and agents with each other, which is what happens in practice. And performance at the endpoints is very sensitive to small amounts of augmentation, which gets at the “1-99” expenditure horizon argument from before. Thus, ESHs speak more informatively about hybrid performance, addressing Con 1 from above: they are tied to the optimal way that a given labor budget can be spent between humans and AIs.

Random Nice Properties of ESHs

I’m relatively partial to ESHs. Three things I like about them: they are meaningful for unbounded values; they might have bearing on economy-wide measures of AI adoption; and they appear relatively more tractable to measure than expenditure horizons.

Unbounded ESHs

I mentioned earlier that I like when unbounded metrics, like the original expenditure horizon, have a meaningful interpretation for a horizon of infinity. ESHs fare well here: an AI has an undefined (or infinite) X% ESH when it is always optimal to spend more than X% of one’s budget on the AI.

I like that the metric is also able to identify Pareto superhuman (“GPT-∞”) models, which are allocated every marginal dollar. They’re simply models with an unbounded X% ESH for all X!

ESHs and the Macroeconomics of AI

Additionally, ESHs might provide intuitions for how to expect the macroeconomics of AI to play out. Now that AI revenues are within roughly 2 orders of magnitude of US labor spending, it would be great if real-world economically-relevant-task benchmarking could tell us something about the fraction of total labor spending to expect to go towards humans versus tokens.

The ESH can provide fuzzy but nonzero signal here; namely, if X is the largest value in (0,1) for which measured X% ESHs are unbounded across benchmark suites relevant to a particular industry, we might expect X to be a (somewhat tight, if your tasks are good) upper bound for the fraction of spending going towards tokens rather than humans in that industry. I won’t expound on this idea here, and there are a bunch of ways it can fail to hold, but I do think this is a fruitful topic for future work.

ESHs Are Tractable to Measure

Finally, I think a pro of ESHs is that they appear tractable to measure. Namely, we can run RCTs where humans are given a task, and are allocated a random amount of real-world working time, as well as random token budgets. ESHs can be fit to triples of (human spending, token spending, and resulting performance), where we can infer the optimal (or at least best-performing) AI budget share at various budgets.

Measuring ESHs doesn’t suffer from the points I made above about Cunningham et al.’s expenditure horizons: it’s an evaluation of hybrid human-AI work rather than tricky human-only work. Additionally, ESHs might be possible to regress from “offline” labor data, such as traces of human-agent work, to the extent that heterogeneous human wage data can be inferred, and to the extent that humans naturally divide labor between themselves and AIs in a near-optimal way. This is another topic for future work.

That’s not to say measuring or operationalizing ESHs is actively easy. For the sake of simplicity in this essay, I have so far neglected several complicating factors when it comes to discussing “performance on a task distribution.” First, I have said little about how different humans achieve different performances, both on their own, and because they might use agents more or less effectively. Second, we might simply fail to create well-scoped task distributions that both (a) don’t saturate at realistic budgets, and (b) can be undertaken by humans in realistic evaluation timeframes. Finally, I have not considered how humans and AIs interact in the real world—if humans have to wait for AIs, or struggle to do productive work in an overlapping way, or teams of humans work with teams of agents—frictions will certainly appear that make it hard to be sure that any arrangement of AI and human labor spending is “optimal.”

Conclusion

I expect AI labor to become a macroeconomically measurable part of the economy in the next two years, and it seems important to have high-quality methodologies for benchmarking it. Anchoring benchmarking metrics in dollar costs and making them natively responsive to inference spending is the bare minimum: we also have to account for the fact that most AI spending will be part of hybrid work, and thus that marginal dollars will be split differently between AIs and humans at different budgets.

I’ve proposed the expenditure share horizon as a starting point, but my main takeaway from thinking about this problem has been that AI benchmarking and economics are severely underprepared to guide economic policy on AI in the coming landscape.

essays.title: Retro: trying to get Scott Wiener more votes
essays.html:
this post is currently a draft—I intend to add more information and reflections soon

Overview

Scott Wiener is an AI safety champion, and a very competent legislator running for Congress in San Francisco. I spent the past month independently working on increasing the chances of him getting elected. The goal of this post is to note down and reflect on some things I’ve learned in this endeavor.11.In 2024 he fought to pass SB 1047, which would have been the first meaningful piece of AI safety legislation in the country. It is a light-touch but substantive bill covering only companies with $100M+ training runs, which would have required whistleblower protections, concrete safety plans with published test results, shutdown capability, and liability for catastrophic harms. Facing fierce big-tech opposition and personal attacks, he kept revising and fighting rather than backing down, and got the bill through the legislature before Governor Newsom vetoed it. Undeterred, he returned the next year with SB 53, a narrower transparency bill. It requires whistleblower protections, published risk frameworks and model cards, incident reporting, and honesty about catastrophic risk.

Going into this project, I really didn't know what it would look like or the types of work it would entail. I had a general intuition that there were lots of AI safety folks for whom voting for Scott Wiener would very much be in their own interest but who were not turning out by default, and that the campaign was probably missing a good amount of low-hanging fruit for various reasons. My general goals, ordered in terms of priority, were to do whatever it took to increase the chances that Scott got elected, and to gain practice working on not-well-scoped tasks and iterating rapidly on feedback loops.

When I started off, I thought the chance of Wiener's and Chan's total votes being within 100 of each other was approximately 0.36%. Chan's internal poll had Wiener +5, and Wiener's internal poll had him +11. Later, a public poll showed Wiener's total vote share at 47% and Chan at 41%, with 9% undecided and a 4.6% margin of error. Eventually, we won—Chan conceded on November 4th after ~40% of ballots counted had Wiener up 11 points, which was higher than expectation.

What went well

  • I got a lot of people excited about Scott Wiener and reaching out to their friends. Across 5 events within 2 weeks, we had ~80 attendees total. The numbers here are very rough & vibes-based, as I did not properly collect data, but I estimate the top 10% of people reached out to 30-50 people, with the median being around 3-5.
    • Aside from the votes generated, the relational outreach events seemed fairly enjoyable for the attendees as well. I think they served as spaces where people could mingle and socialize with like-minded individuals, and Scott even showed up at one of them!
    • Lots of people were quite excited about Scott Wiener, and I think I successfully increased the extent to which people were excited about him and about voting (especially when Connie also claimed some of what seemed like the correct AI policy preferences, and when Scott looked like he was favored by quite a lot according to prediction markets (Polymarket, Kalshi)). This was mainly done by conveying to folks my actual beliefs about why Scott would be better, as well as the fact that a candidate with an 80% chance of winning still leaves your vote about 70% as likely to decide the race as a pure toss-up of the same size (better explanation of this later).
  • Preparing a minimum viable infrastructure (i.e., writing a basic case for why I think people should vote for Scott Wiener and how to vote) before starting on the actual work was helpful. This included organizing the information in a concise, easily digestible and transferable manner (e.g., ca11.info), and having organized answers to frequently asked questions. Pre-morteming and predicting the questions people might raise, as well as the resources they might ask for, was also quite helpful, although I think I ended up spending too much time predicting as opposed to just coming into contact with reality and testing empirically.
    • In addition, in putting together info sheets and docs, I did less iterating based on feedback than I would have liked (e.g., there was much time between realizing the need for a fact sheet or doc aimed toward non-AI-safety audiences and actually delivering the product).
  • Having collaborators and advisors was extremely helpful.
    • Three individuals kindly offered me some project management & advising in the two weeks leading up to the election. I found it helpful to be able to find external strategic input and to get high-level input from people with an outside perspective. A high-level main takeaway I had from this whole effort was the importance of, and the skill involved in, being able to move between strategic reasoning and doing the object-level tasks. At the start, I somewhat often found myself tangled up in working on some specific, concrete task for a long time, forgetting to keep in mind and/or evaluate the overall significance of the task itself.
    • About 10 days before election day, I recruited Jesse Angrist to collaborate with me on this project. This turned out to be a great decision; Jesse was very competent and motivated to do whatever it took to succeed (this included canvassing at City Hall at 7 AM on election day, knocking on many, many doors to gather data about the effectiveness of various interventions, running events late at night after a day of canvassing, calling many places to print T-shirts last minute, and lots of other things).
    • I had essentially no experience managing others prior to this, and providing Jesse 'management' taught me a lot about management! Jesse was also great in that I received helpful feedback on what types of management were helpful and what types were confusing or unhelpful. He was also fun to be around and super chill.
  • Coming in with a possibly overly cynical view of politics, I think I succeeded in not being intentionally misleading, not saying deceptive things, and not taking jabs at the opponent as a means to promote my preferred candidate. I think I largely succeeded in presenting the voting options to people I was reaching out to in a fairly accurate manner.

What went poorly

  • Not enough events were run, and I didn't get to as many diverse groups of people who would be interested in Scott Wiener due to their own interests as I had hoped.
    • I.e., voters who consider AI policy and safety a primary concern should heavily consider voting for Wiener, and for similar reasons, this also applies to people interested in more housing, LGBTQ rights, and various other causes. I did not end up having time to run outreach events with people in these groups due to capacity constraints.
  • If I were to do this again, I would start by spending the time at the beginning to familiarize myself with all relevant positions and information about this race (and not only the ones that motivated me to do this), since that information has a level effect, and the sooner I gain the information, the longer I can collect the benefits.
  • GOTV interventions worked pretty well, which was roughly in line with expectations, but I didn't get to test out the effectiveness of persuasion.
    • I.e., for each Scott-supporter-but-maybe-voter reached, if the initial probability of them voting was 30% (based on the fact that the people I'd be reaching by default have generally low turnout rates, e.g., younger, more renters, more recent movers), and if receiving 1-2 messages from a friend to remind them to vote increases their likelihood of voting by 10-40%, this voter contact is expected to generate 0.1 to 0.4 votes.22.relational outreach has produced some of the largest effects in GOTV research: +13.2 points in Green & McClellan (2020), rising to +17.1 where volunteers got extra support; +8.3 points from a friend's text in Schein et al. (2021), vs. +0.29 for mass texts from organizations; and +7.8 points in Vote Rev (2020); I expect our numbers to beat these, since most studies tested the lightest version of the intervention (98% of messages in the texting study were the app's default template). I expect our texts to be much more compelling by giving good arguments and “actually trying.” The experiments above also do not include prompting their friend to make a plan (e.g., blocking a time on their calendar) or giving specific reasons for why they should vote (e.g., AI policy, housing, etc.)33.given the studies (Pew 2016, Rogers & Aida 2011) that show that stated intention is not very predictive of voting behavior, it is possible that this number should be adjusted downward.
    • If I were to persuade and flip a ~guaranteed Connie voter to vote for Scott instead, this could generate up to ~2 votes! It is possible that persuasion-focused interventions are not very effective or practical, all things considered, especially without scaling up the human resources going into the project, but I never ended up actually gathering empirical data on the effectiveness of effort going into persuasion.
  • Despite Scott being a great candidate in my opinion, for reasons I think are shared by many other individuals as well, I don't think I was able to spread the excitement to an accurate degree. I think some of this could have been improved if I had spent more time modeling the difference between "an argument I find true" and "an argument that is both true and presented in the best light possible, which generates natural persuasion effects."
    • For example, I think the first 2 relational outreach events I ran could have been improved significantly if I had spent more time deliberately practicing the opening pitch. Eventually, I came to the realization that an important element of the success of the event is simply succeeding in grabbing everyone's attention at the beginning of the outreach co-working sessions, giving a good pitch, and making it very clear to people what they are supposed to do. I think this differentiates just a normal hangout from a proper event with an objective (h/t Saul).
  • Retrospectively, although I am glad to have worked on this effort, I found the day-to-day experience fairly unenjoyable. I think this was due to a combination of:
    • The project not having a natural limit to effort, and the shape of it being something where it felt like increasing effort past a certain threshold (i.e., beyond doing the most effective interventions) would still yield returns at a roughly linear rate.
    • Similar to my experience canvassing in general, it felt like every conversation I was not having or every event I was not going to represented votes that I could have generated. Conversations also felt quite instrumental—which, I suppose, is a natural artifact of canvassing conversations—but there was always this background calculation weighing time spent per conversation against the possible votes the conversation could generate.

Thank-yous

I feel very thankful of various friends that lend me their living room to run events in, friends that helped me organize events, and for the project management support I received from various individuals. I am also appreciative the ~80 people who each spent 1-3+ hours reaching out to people in their networks, the campaign staff on the Wiener campaign, and Jesse Angrist, who worked very hard with me on this intense sprint and taught me lots about management.

  1. In 2024 he fought to pass SB 1047, which would have been the first meaningful piece of AI safety legislation in the country. It is a light-touch but substantive bill covering only companies with $100M+ training runs, which would have required whistleblower protections, concrete safety plans with published test results, shutdown capability, and liability for catastrophic harms. Facing fierce big-tech opposition and personal attacks, he kept revising and fighting rather than backing down, and got the bill through the legislature before Governor Newsom vetoed it. Undeterred, he returned the next year with SB 53, a narrower transparency bill. It requires whistleblower protections, published risk frameworks and model cards, incident reporting, and honesty about catastrophic risk. ↩
  2. relational outreach has produced some of the largest effects in GOTV research: +13.2 points in Green & McClellan (2020), rising to +17.1 where volunteers got extra support; +8.3 points from a friend's text in Schein et al. (2021), vs. +0.29 for mass texts from organizations; and +7.8 points in Vote Rev (2020); I expect our numbers to beat these, since most studies tested the lightest version of the intervention (98% of messages in the texting study were the app's default template). I expect our texts to be much more compelling by giving good arguments and “actually trying.” The experiments above also do not include prompting their friend to make a plan (e.g., blocking a time on their calendar) or giving specific reasons for why they should vote (e.g., AI policy, housing, etc.) ↩
  3. given the studies (Pew 2016, Rogers & Aida 2011) that show that stated intention is not very predictive of voting behavior, it is possible that this number should be adjusted downward. ↩
