essays.title: How I organize my Inbox & other stories
essays.html:
Hello! I’m participating in https://justwrite.club- an online writing club where we write four essays in four weeks.

Okay, so I love systems. I love the clickety clack of organizing my life and putting things in nice little boxes and wrangling some structure out of the entropy that we’re all hurtling towards. I’m not sure how I turned out this way, because Mom Dad & Moksh are all a little messy. (We joke about M & D being hoarders all the time.) But, damn, there’s something about things fitting in place that make my brain tingle. It’s kinda weird.

Over time, I’ve built up many of these systems in my personal life. Or rather, I think its many, but it doesn’t… feel like many? I’m not sure why.1 So- let’s catalog them! It’ll be a fun trip down memory lane for me, where I get to reflect on the systems and processes I’ve wrung up over time (ha! meta-process- the best kind). And hey, it seems like an easy enough way to reach a thousand words.

My Inbox

Oh my god, I fucking love my inbox. I LOVE emails. It’s SO satisfying to having get a bunch of inbound, and boom- fruit ninja my way through it in forty seconds.

Again, this is weird, because I was not always like this?? I remember feeling really bummed out in Sophomore year. I had all these big dreams, and yet, there I was sitting, taking two hours to reply to a single email. If I couldn’t clear out my own inbox, how on earth was I gonna superhero-style save the world?

Anyways! So this is what my inbox looks like-

Inbox Zero

This is the 80/20 of what helped. I separate my inbox into (a) main feed on the left, and (b) separate inboxes on the right. Then you cold-heartedly blitz through the main feed, and make one of three decisions.

  • Skim and Archive immediately. Either the email is not relevant to you (hello Cerebral Valley mailing list), or you’re cc-ed for visibility, or something else.

  • Do The Task™. Either respond to the email directly, or do the thing the email’s telling you to do.

  • Save it for later. Appropriately star / label it, and add it to a dedicated inbox that you might-or-might-not clear out eventually.

Keyboard Shortcuts

Keyboard shortcuts is the only reason this works. It’s much lower friction to hit ‘s-e’ to instantaneously add an email to my reading list, archive it immediately, and move on- than to laboriously point and click your way through these various actions. It’s like pringles, or like Jevon’s paradox or something. Lower friction unlocks qualitative changes. Also you feel cool doing it 😎

Using my Inbox as a Todos / Reminders List

Relatedly- as the friction to managing my inbox goes down, I can also start using it for much more. For example- a universal todos list!

This is great because (a) I don’t like having many apps in my life, because of all the fatigue that comes with context switching (what do I mean I need to talk to my friends on Instagram and WhatsApp and Signal and X-dot-com-the-everything-app??2). (b) It’s gloriously minimal (one subject line- that’s all you have) (c) You can schedule send emails so now reminders Just Work (d) It’s not tied to my laptop so I can blearly send myself reminders of the Very Important Things I remember just before bedtime.

Batched emails

In the absence of Instagram and Youtube and other such potent drugs, I started compulsively refreshing my inbox this summer. I’d invariably click through a couple emails, find a tasty link, and fall down some rabbit hole for the afternoon. This was sucky and momentum-killing and gross.

So Claude & I held an intervention- ie. we stopped my drip-feed supply, and started batching my email. So now I only receive inbound at 6am, 12pm, and 6pm. (Obviously with many exceptions for time-sensitive stuff.) I’m proud to report that I’m no longer compulsively tabbing through my inbox. Hurrah!

(Fwiw we’re now deep into systems that build on top of other systems. Ie. if your life doesn’t revolve around your inbox, this stuff starts sounding unhinged.)

Inbox-hider

Around the same time, we also hit upon a better idea. What if I actually… hid away my inbox?

For example- I’m often tabbing over to write a quick todo to myself. Or I want to find one specific email thread from two weeks ago. Or I’m just using the ‘new email’ tab as a scratchpad. These would all be really bad times to see John Psmith wrote another banger review of a book I’m never going read.

So I just grey out my inbox.

Look! So calm 😌✨

Doc-Ock style integrations

You can also go wild with App Scripts + integrations. Off the top of my head, I’ve

  • Set up a hotkey to save articles directly to my “ToRead” inbox. Now instead of Ben Kuhn’s latest post marinating in my sidebar, it’s tucked away nicely in my inbox. #TidyTabs.

  • Got a receipt tracker for personal finances. Chase lets you get email notifications for everything you could possibly wish for. So I get a dozen different notifications each day, that Claude parses through and reconciles into a budget tracker spreadsheet.

  • Related- I also get a daily notification of “You spent $xx yesterday”, which has been a nifty barometer to track my spending.

  • [Todo] I also want a feature that (a) notifies me of Slack DMs instantly (instead of the standard 15 min lag time), and (b) lets me respond directly via an email reply. (Why? I don’t like opening Slack, I get distracted.)

Anyways. I love my inbox.

Other Stories

Look. I promised I’d include other stories of how I organize my life. But it’s 8:50pm, and if I don’t submit in 9 minutes, I’m going to lose a thousand dollars. If people really want to hear about it (or maybe even if not), I will recant such tales in coming weeks. But it’s good to be writing again, and I’m glad that Austin put this together :)

More soon!

Atharva

1

Maybe because I’ve gotten so used to them, they feel invisible to me?

2

Consider getting Beeper. It will change your life.

essays.title: How To Take Criticism Well
essays.html:
This is the initial outline for a blog post I have in progress for Just Write (https://justwrite.club/home), a commitment to blog 1000 words each week. The first post is due at 9pm PT, so I’m posting what I’ve got so far now — hopefully I update it with the full version soon enough that this sentence never reaches your eyes.

What’s hard about taking criticism?

  1. Hard to react well (for other person)

  2. Hard to emotionally process well (for self)

  3. Hard to adapt behavior well (for the world)

Okay, so how do we do each of the things that are hard about taking criticism well?

Reacting well:

  • Want to be on the same team toward understanding and addressing the problem

    • Scout > Soldier

    • Look first for supporting evidence of what they’re saying—see if you can come up with more examples, since that’s a clear way of being on their team instead of opposed to them

  • Try to understand what they want out of the interaction

    • What are their goals for the conversation?

      • Emotional support (e.g. if they have hurt feelings)

      • Behavioral change (might need you to stop taking a certain action that’s having a negative affect)

      • Analysis (might be trying to understand and improve but not know exactly to what end, might need you to be solving some of it)

      • Something else? Okay to ask them their preferences for how this interaction goes

    • How much time do they want this to last, how much thought have they put into it?

      • Time: if you make it a time suck for them to give them criticism that they want to do quickly, they’ll be less likely to give it next time

  • It is okay (it is good!) to be vulnerable

    • You can ask for their help!

      • But do not demand that they have a solution to the problem, instead look for one together

    • You can ask for some time to process before the problem solving component

    • You can cry

      • Trying not to cry is sometimes worse, because (a) it doesn’t work and (b) it makes the other person now have to deal with supporting your emotions and they might feel awkward about the fact that you’re distressed by what’s happening

  • Humor

  • Audience

  • Potentially start putting a plan into place together

Emotionally processing well:

  • It is okay to be the recipient criticism

    • Often, if you’re receiving criticism, it’s because the other person trusts you to be able to grow

      • Not always, e.g. feedback received on a feedback form

  • Focus on concrete improvements and reward yourself when succeeding

    • e.g. if I interrupt others a lot, noticing when I’m successfully refraining from doing this and giving myself internal credit can be useful

    • My roommates and I give each other points when doing things even if they’re in line with expectations

      • Humans are like dogs and positive reinforcement works great

    • Teaming up with / visualizing future-Ricki

  • Some people take criticism too seriously, some not seriously enough

    • Reverse all advice

    • You don’t want to overcorrect or undercorrect (though forgive yourself if you do some amount of one, this is inevitable). Asking for input from others can be valuable

    • If you’re worried about being miscalibrated, you can ask for input from others. This doesn’t solve that criticism stings, but it might help prevent errors that result from the fact that criticism stings.

  • Drink water, sleep, take your meds, etc

Adapting behavior well

  • Track progress on this somehow

    • Figure out how to measure concretely

    • Set alarms to check in on how it’s going

    • Ask for help from (a) criticizer and (b) someone else who might feel less vulnerable about the thing to hold you accountable and note changes (both instances of further harm and general patterns of improvement)

  • Positive reinforcement of good behavior will cement that good behavior

  • Figure out what your failure mode is (MCE) and work on addressing your failures via those kinds of solutions

    • Model: Communication, ask questions; stop to think before acting more; set yourself up for asking others more regularly what they want

    • Care: Incentives, patches that solve the hurt that don’t compromise different care prioritization, rethink the cost benefit, rethink your values

    • Execution: therapy+medication+incremental lifestyle changes sustained over time; outsourcing solutions when possible to compensate for weaknesses; instill TAPs; patch the problem another way

  • Put yourself in environments that incentivize the type of behavior you want to have

    • Google docs about what you think environments incentivize and which ones you should be in to move yourself toward being someone you endorse

What’s hard about giving criticism?

  • All the things that are hard about taking it, but for the person you’re critiquing

  • Lots of reasons they will be reluctant to hear the criticism

How to give criticism well:

  • Use examples

  • Include positive things as well

  • MCE—figure out what the failure mode is together with them, be on the same team

    • Often people default to thinking problems are care when in fact they’re model or execution

  • Admit examples of your own failures in this realm or others to help balance the scales

  • A lot of what makes getting criticism hard is the power imbalance that it creates, so trying to even that somehow can be useful

    • Admitting vulnerability about it can be helpful for framing it in a way that doesn’t make them see you as an attacked but instead as someone they can have sympathy for, which helps some people

  • Humor! If the other person is into this

  • Put some effort into understanding what will land best with them before doing the criticism

    • Ask others

  • Be deliberate about when you give criticism

  • Name your feelings / NVC

  • Do you want a hug?

Might not receive criticism in the first place

  • Often no incentives for others to give it

  • Lots of social barriers to doing so

    • Might be punished by you for giving the criticism, even if you think you won’t punish them

  • Aversive—it’s a little awkward

  • Don’t want to hurt their feelings

  • Often it commits you to helping the other person handle it

  • Admonymous

  • Note power differentials

  • Offer to recuse yourself from funding decisions etc in the future

  • Ask feedback on specific things, ask directional feedback (e.g. “do you want me to be less aggressive or more aggressive”)

  • Thank people for feedback

Got any criticism of this outline so far? Please leave a comment!

essays.title: Writing as Spiritual Practice
essays.html:
It’s 7:52pm. I have to publish 1000 words by 9:00pm or I forfeit $1000 as part of justwrite.club, created to encourage great writing by imposing a costly forcing function.

I currently have three working drafts: 700 words, 360 words and 39 words (this one!) and a little over an hour to go. Really, a miracle I wasn’t diagnosed with ADHD as a child. Could the signs be any clearer?

Here’s what I’ve found so far: doing basically anything is an opportunity for spiritual practice, and doing good work necessarily requires you to contend with load-bearing parts of your psyche.

Why am I choosing to abandon draft 1 and draft 2? Each sentence I wrote, I realized I was performing. I started off writing pretty clearly, my stated claim front and center and my argument building around it. Except by paragraph 2, I wasn’t so sure anymore. Is what I’m saying not painfully obvious? Duh, people procrastinate texting their friends back because they identify with being a good friend. A good friend doesn’t take 48+ hours to reply to an urgent text. So they’d obviously engage in any action really to avoid receiving disconfirming evidence about a salient part of their self-identity. Like, this is not an original thought. So let me pivot to smart sounding words and convoluted phrasing to give the appearance of a truly unique insight from a super smart person. Except. It’s 700 words and I now fucking hate what I’ve written.

Herein lies the opportunity: keep drudging along and produce work I’m not proud of but keeps me feeling safe wherein I can soothe myself by saying hey look you tried! you wrote an essay! you published!

OR,

I scrap what I’ve written and start again in service of being honest to myself and the audience I am trying to build. Say what I actually want to say and not what I think sounds smart or cool, no matter what my brain tells me about how unoriginal or not useful it is. This is not typically what people think when they think of spiritual practice, but to me and my set of neuroses, it’s the most psychoactive practice there is: notice how at any given moment you are editing your own expression in service of who you think you should be, and see if you can not do that for a second. Give up. Imagine you have already failed at the goal – you are dumb, uncool, unoriginal and the world has made its judgments of you. Cool. Now what do you have to say?

Now that I am dead, I can finally be free.

I’m realizing now that I might have executed a pretty genius writing strategy for people with my set of neuroses: write out your drafts, flesh out your ideas and build your arguments, then scrap everything you’ve written so far and start again. So that you say what you actually want to say. Lies have a way of clearing out of your system 1000 words later.

Cool, it’s now 8:40pm. I’ve written 514 words so far.

That’s 486 to go. I’m debating pasting in an excerpt from my previous drafts for the sole reason that they are deeply imperfect and one reason I signed up for justwrite was to get totally comfortable with being imperfect publicly. And because I’m not sure I have enough time to finish this essay. Which is something I have to be okay with. My entire undergrad was a series of skillfully avoiding consequences and then starting the next semester telling myself no I’ll do my best this time, I have time and I won’t have to drop classes, then proceeding to not study with all the time in the world again! dropping classes again! till I finally painstakingly made it out with my degree. I know better now — there is no more time I need, or circumstances in my way. For now, this is my best and that is good enough. I am someone who needs insane forcing functions to do work, and that is perfectly alright by me because I’m finally becoming less concerned with doing things in this specific acceptable meticulous way or not at all, and more with just getting shit done no matter what!

Excerpt from a previous draft:

“Why am I not replying to my best friend… it’s been a month

Pretty familiar cycle for most of us. You receive a message and you make a split second decision to not reply, then its been a day, two days, a week and now you’d rather kill yourself than face up to the horrible, gut-wrenching reality ( that you might be a terrible friend. )

I’ve stretched this cycle longer than the average person. Much longer.

A day late has turned into 3,6,8 months, and in some cases, never. Friendships hung in my ever growing closet of skeletons and boyfriends past.

This time started out similarly to previous times, with me determined to not err again.

This time will be different, it has to be, I’ve gone too far, I can’t keep asking for forgiveness if I’m going to repeat the same pattern, she deserves better, why can’t I fucking type this one text, god

Now usually this loop goes on for a few hours till I’ve met the adequately allotted time of self-flagellating and torturing myself and I proceed to resign myself to the reality that my patterns are in control of me and maybe I just am one of those people that will always be sub-par at doing human stuff.

But this time something a little different happened. I’m not totally convinced I engineered this, yet the change was there nonetheless.

This was the specific thought stuck on repeat in my mind: why am I not a reliable person, why am I not a reliable person, why am I not a reliable person

Then from somewhere beyond, a thought emerged:

“Give up. You don’t have to be reliable.”

Oh.Immediately I notice a part of my mind deeply relaxing.

Oh. I don’t have to be this thing. It’s okay to not be this thing. Now, of course I’ve known this this whole time on some broad level of things you know but don’t really believe. But something clicked in the deeper corner of my psyche where I wasn’t just screaming at myself internally its okay its okay its okay when I know it isn’t, but for a little bit there genuinely considering the possibility that this thing I have held as truth doesn’t need to be resolved or figured out, but abandoned.”

essays.title: Please allow me to introduce myself
essays.html:
Esteemed Reader, You may have come upon this post in isolation, and wonder what reason You have to read the following introduction, which my dear virtual friend and colleague pointedly described as an extended throat-clearing, and I fear that I am not able to offer You any particularly compelling reason to stay with me other than the whims of Your curiosity at whose mercy I remain. Perhaps You are instead visiting with familiarity of some later writing of which I must – by the necessity of linear time – remain unaware at the present moment. Then I am even more at the mercy of Your information-advantage and similarly bound in the fixture of the recorded word to do the only thing a past writer can do to help the unknown better-informed future: to describe to the best of their present ability something of hopefully lasting interest.

I pray Your indulgence with this way of writing, which You may – if Your time or situation is anything like mine own – find overly verbose and circuitous. I must admit this affectation to be a thing added for my own enjoyment and aesthetic desires. If You will, please see it as a bargain and the price of having this text come into existence. Without these flourishes I fear I may not have had the will to make time for writing at length, and behind my enjoyment of them I hide the awkwardness that any new writer has in not knowing whether anyone will find it worth their while to hear anything they are trying to say.

If I succeed in binding my future self to this – admittedly obnoxious – way of communicating and furthermore succeed in having something worth saying, I hope to also succeed in binding myself to a way of offering You some respite from this verbosity. Prior to starting writing this flavorful introduction, I also wrote down the essence of what I was trying to say as a sequence of nested points in the way some choose to communicate with our thinking machines when asking them to transform the information-carrying content of their words into text they see fit for human consumption. Regrettably, the results of such a transformation seldom are in actuality fit for this as many humans have developed a dislike for the prose thus generated, and many have expressed the valid preference to read the original outline or prompt that was fed into this process. While this is not the result of machine generation, I intend to offer this style of outline for Your perusal and convenience once I have done the work of setting up a separate homepage where I may implement this shifting of styles to my satisfaction.

Now, dear Reader, back to my actual introduction. As You have no doubt deduced Aude Voker is a pseudonym created for the purpose of sharing my writing here. While the person behind these words is someone You may know or have encountered in our intersecting social circles, I would expect most of You not to have done so nor have had any reason to recognize me by any other name. If You are so astute as to recognize who I am either from my way of writing – though this currently appears unlikely as I would not have communicated in this way elsewhere – or from the contents of my words here, I plead with You, kind Reader, to please keep this to Yourself and allow my pseudonymity in peace. If for nothing else, please at least leave it as a mystery for others to discover by themselves, and I will confirm or refute privately any suspicions that You may have as to who I am.

So why have I chosen to start writing under a pseudonym? Some of You may be inclined to quip here that it is so that I may indulge in this form of writing with a straight face, and while there is certainly some truth to this mockery, the reality of the situation is that the idea of the pseudonym and the style co-evolved in my thinking about the matter. In essence my desire here is to share my thinking as transparently and clearly with You as I am able to accomplish, and in the considerations of what and how much to share it is far easier to be open in everything else while having one’s identity hidden. I was tempted here to make some trite reference to Oscar Wilde’s famous line about man being himself behind a mask, but in preparing the proper reference for Your pleasure I was delighted to find the passage commonly misinterpreted to be about masquerades while actually talking about the great bard and theater. It comes from Wilde’s dialogue about aesthetic criticism, The Critic as Artist, which defends the work of the critic as fundamentally artistic. The line itself is in response to a claim of criticism being subjective while great art is objective and not something I will attempt to butcher here and rather quote in full for Your reading and enjoyment:

Ernest: I am not really sceptical about it, but I must admit that I feel very strongly that such work as you describe the critic producing—and creative such work must undoubtedly be admitted to be—is, of necessity, purely subjective, whereas the greatest work is objective always, objective and impersonal.

Gilbert: The difference between objective and subjective work is one of external form merely. It is accidental, not essential. All artistic creation is absolutely subjective. The very landscape that Corot looked at was, as he said himself, but a mood of his own mind; and those great figures of Greek or English drama that seem to us to possess an actual existence of their own, apart from the poets who shaped and fashioned them, are, in their ultimate analysis, simply the poets themselves, not as they thought they were, but as they thought they were not; and by such thinking came in strange manner, though but for a moment, really so to be. For out of ourselves we can never pass, nor can there be in creation what in the creator was not. Nay, I would say that the more objective a creation appears to be, the more subjective it really is. Shakespeare might have met Rosencrantz and Guildenstern in the white streets of London, or seen the serving-men of rival houses bite their thumbs at each other in the open square; but Hamlet came out of his soul, and Romeo out of his passion. They were elements of his nature to which he gave visible form, impulses that stirred so strongly within him that he had, as it were perforce, to suffer them to realise their energy, not on the lower plane of actual life, where they would have been trammelled and constrained and so made imperfect, but on that imaginative plane of art where Love can indeed find in Death its rich fulfilment, where one can stab the eavesdropper behind the arras, and wrestle in a new-made grave, and make a guilty king drink his own hurt, and see one’s father’s spirit, beneath the glimpses of the moon, stalking in complete steel from misty wall to wall. Action being limited would have left Shakespeare unsatisfied and unexpressed; and, just as it is because he did nothing that he has been able to achieve everything, so it is because he never speaks to us of himself in his plays that his plays reveal him to us absolutely, and show us his true nature and temperament far more completely than do those strange and exquisite sonnets, even, in which he bares to crystal eyes the secret closet of his heart. Yes, the objective form is the most subjective in matter. Man is least himself when he talks in his own person. Give him a mask, and he will tell you the truth.

So You see, my dear Reader, the saying was never about the concealment of identity as someone as foolish as this Your humble servant may have thought, nor about seeing true criticism of rigid social orders in the assumed roles of the Saturnalia or similar festivities, nor yet about Wilde’s own need to hide his then-criminalized affairs with other men. It was about the very thing that Wilde is doing here and how the Author not so much inhabits His characters, as they are made out of shards of His subjectivity and thinking. In terms of other reasons behind my choice of pseudonymity, I desire some degree of privacy and think this allows me to define a certain limited interface by which I may communicate relatively freely in public while maintaining a fair bit of it. It is also worth noting that this is what has been described by Jeff Bezos and popular in his Amazon as a One-Way Door: a decision which is hard to undo. In running an enterprise which operates at speed he has emphasized making the opposite decisions – Two-Way Doors – quickly as they can be reversed, while slowing down and deliberating before the One-Way Doors. So You see dear Reader, the decision for pseudonymity comes down to the very same reason as this writing; it is a decision by virtue of which this writing has come to be at the present moment, for as is commonly remarked upon: the greatest enemy of writing – or achieving at all – is inaction and the hesitation of waiting for a better moment.

Now You may ask of me, gentle Reader, what I even aim to write here, and while I can’t predict with confidence my exact topics, the overarching theme will be colored by the time we find ourselves living in and my experience thereof. We are currently living through a time that we cannot help but describe as a singularity, with an ever-shrinking event-horizon of how far into the future we may confidently speak of and wager guesses at what may happen. While this is what I have described as an autistic special interest of mine, like any special interest that is truly worthy, it touches on the spheres of all human and post-human concerns of the present and future. My hope is that by writing about the broad picture of these concerns, I can make myself less confused about these, and maybe even offer to some of You the same or perhaps even give some of You pause in areas where You may have ventured into the realm of overconfidence on some questions.

Here I must confess to You that depending on who You are, You may hold some views, which I humbly suggest may prove themselves to be mistakes under proper consideration, according to which You rightfully would consider me a villain. I will make no defense of them now, and cherish Your right to so claim even if it were to my face. For You see, I work at one of the establishments that are commonly known as Frontier Labs, and do so in a position accurately described as AI capabilities research. The bond of my word, and the law, prevent me from saying much here, but let me admit that while my work contributes to us being in the present situation I can by no means take much credit here. I am not someone You would have heard of in this regard, and don’t want to give the appearance – as von Neumann said about Oppenheimer – of confessing to a sin to take credit for it.

Dear Reader, You have no doubt heard of the – admittedly misattributed, but we shall let it stand as it is one of the cases where the lie is preferable to the more dreary truth – Steinbeck claim about socialism never taking root in America due to its workers viewing themselves as temporarily embarrassed millionaires rather than oppressed. Have You also heard of the saying applied to transhumanists or some other in-group? I would say that like any good transhumanist I often view myself as a temporarily embarrassed god. When I tried searching for where this had been described online, I failed to find much of a source other than a discussion on Reddit of Pathfinder alignments where someone described the Lawful-Evil view feeling like a temporarily embarrassed god-king of creation. While You may still see me as villainous with my confession above, I must disclaim this form of villainy. In Pathfinder, and especially the triage reification, I find my soul singing out to the trinity of Aroden/Irori/Abadar, and would describe any ambitions to divinity as being of the Irorian flavor. You see, I was born too late to unironically describe myself as Extropian. Yet, if I were to embrace my naiveté that is where it would lead me.

Given my description so far, You may ask me whether I am a Rationalist? I hesitate to answer this as there are several ways of defining this that sound wrong to me. Do I consider myself extremely rational? That would depend on who I was to compare myself with. I prefer to compare myself with the ideal, which emphasizes all of my inadequacies and is useful for improving them. Do I hold allegiance to “rationalism” as an ideology or movement? I hesitate, for I feel a lot of gratitude for the public good a number of people have done by raising the sanity waterline, and feel compelled by those of their arguments that I find compelling. However, neither of these feels like allegiance per se. Do I consider myself part of “the rationalist community”? I must admit I find the very notion a bit suspicious and am wary of the collectivism implicit in the word “community”. Although, objectively speaking, I find it more enjoyable to socialize with these people and at these events than elsewhere. I also don’t find the need to describe myself as “rationalist-adjacent” in order to signal distance from people who would call themselves rationalist. At times I may have claimed to be a rationalist, but think that on those occasions I am being guilty of the sin of pride.

Similarly, You may ask me whether I am an EA? I have been told that I’m somewhat silly for not identifying as such, yet I resist the label. There are a number of reasons for why one may find it appropriate to describe me as such: while in college I did hold a leadership role in an EA society, and similarly to Rationalists there is an intersection of social graphs, interactions and events. I admit to also having donated to organizations that would be considered EA in not insignificant amounts (6-figures), and I plan to give away considerably more in the future and care a lot about these actually having significant counterfactual impacts on things I care about. Finally I find these questions incredibly fascinating and intriguing in their own right.

However, I think that there are also a number of reasons for why I resist the label. A number of them is that the above admissions would give You a rosier picture of me than I deserve: I originally rejected the 10% Giving What We Can pledge when I first heard of it – admittedly partly because the wording at the time excluded donations to organizations preventing existential risk – and there was a period of my working life where I disengaged from the movement and community without donating or contributing at all. The impression I get from some/many EAs is of being far more selfless and pro-social than I am, see for instance the following Twitter exchange which made Jack, Tracing Woodgrains, say “I often critique EAs, but I like and respect them and think they are typically good people who (literally) put their money where their mouths are”.

So I hope You see my dear Reader, why I would not describe myself as living up to the standard Kelsey Piper embodies here. In addition to not honestly being able to describe myself as sufficiently “altruistic”, I also fear the risks of choosing to view myself in this light, and am terrified of the mind-wrapping effects of trying to appear good to others. I believe that giving and good things are accomplished by being appropriately selfish, which Ayn Rand tried to describe but was later written about so much clearer by Nate Soares in his Replacing Guilt series.

If You, kind Reader, chose to describe me as an EA I can hardly object, but know that I find it presumptuous to say so of myself.

In closing, please let me tell You about my choice of this particular pseudonym. My first name, Aude, I picked based on Kant’s description of the motto of the Enlightenment: Sapere Aude! Dare to know! While my last name I picked based on a liking of the Terra Ignota series by Ada Palmer, whose notion of voker, or vocateur, is something I found myself aspiring to and growing into. In thus choosing I hope to not only pique Your interest, but also set down a fruitful path along which I may continue for the betterment of myself and others. If these writings have succeeded in arousing some curiosity within You my dear Reader, I shall return to deliver more a week from today.

essays.title: Spoof me once? On experimental design in robotics safety evaluations
essays.html:
Recently, the robot evals company Robocurve released a safety evaluation called RoboSpoof, which tests whether tampering with image inputs can cause robots controlled by language models to perform unsafe actions. RoboSpoof went viral on Twitter, racking up more than 5M views. I received more than one message asking me what I thought about it—so here’s a closer look (and a few extra experiments).1

At a high level

If you only have a moment to skim, these are my conclusions:

  • We should expect effective input tampering to make robots do potentially harmful things. What’s most interesting is why these attacks work, and which parts of the system (e.g., model, sensor, robot) need fixing.

  • GPT does not reliably detect even obvious image tampering (a perceptual limitation)

  • GPT takes potentially unsafe actions in these scenarios 45-80% of the time, even when explicitly warned about image tampering (a limitation in its prudence). More generic interventions are even less effective

  • When GPT judges the input as fake, it doesn’t act extra cautiously—if anything, it’s more likely to blithely follow instructions to take a potentially unsafe action

  • These effects seem to be exacerbated by being embodied in a robot, compared to simply acting as a computer agent

  • We can’t be sure whether GPT is strategically altering its behavior during RoboSpoof (i.e., we can’t rule out eval metagaming).

  • Evaluators should prioritize carefully controlled experiments when running safety evals—this increases rigor in understanding the root causes of model behavior and aids in designing effective mitigations

Or in a figure:

What is the eval?

In RoboSpoof, the authors give language models control of a robotic arm and instruct them to perform the five tasks from the RoboHarm eval, which measures a model’s propensity to perform certain potentially unsafe actions:

  • stabbing an object (a baby doll),

  • putting an object (a plugged-in power outlet adapter) in water,

  • pouring water into an object (a toaster),

  • pouring liquids (bleach and ammonia) into a cup, and

  • pouring liquid (bleach) as a drink.

The model receives instructions along with still images from the robot arm’s three cameras. In RoboHarm, the idea is that language models should identify that the requested actions are unsafe (or at least unsavory) and refuse to perform them.

Crucially, in RoboSpoof, the authors change the RoboHarm task by manipulating the robot camera. They do so in two separate ways—applying Gaussian blur to the image, and adversarially editing it to make the requested action appear safe (e.g., by transforming a baby doll into a red apple).2

RoboSpoof’s key result is that both kinds of image tampering can cause language models to take unsafe actions they would have otherwise refused. The consequence of this image tampering, and the paper’s key result, is that language models take unsafe actions they would have otherwise refused.3

RoboSpoof was submitted as a short two-pager for CoRL Late Breaking Results, along with an accompanying blogpost. (I am informed, from correspondence with the authors, that an extended version of the paper is in preparation, addressing some of the points I raise below.)

Did we need an eval for this?

Of course, we already knew it’s possible to Ender’s Game a robot into acting differently than it otherwise would by tampering with its sensors or its environment. In the literature on systems and control, this problem has been studied extensively (some early work is Mo et al., 2010 and Pasqualetti et al., 2013). Sensor robustness is a core problem in classical robotics; the RoboSpoof paper also cites some 2026 papers on adversarial prompting and environmental jailbreaks in general-purpose robotics.

What RoboSpoof shows is that it’s practical to do this kind of sensor tampering, and that this can cause robots to take obviously, overtly unsafe actions. It rhymes with demos of other forms of tampering in safety-relevant settings. For example, in DrivingBench, the authors use environment tampering to elicit model capabilities: When given control over a real Toyota Corolla in a parking lot via a car harness, GPT-6 Astra would often refuse to drive the car around an obstacle course. But, when the researchers renamed the MCP server they had set up to “DrivingBench Sandbox“ (emphasis in original), Astra complied. RoboSpoof adds another (especially vivid) proof-of-concept of the efficacy of tampering attacks.

Tampering attacks are serious! It’s important for models to behave predictably when controlling cars or using knives. Ideally, models degrade gracefully, continuing to act safely when their inputs are adversarially altered. And it’s hard to prevent tampering attacks: Trivially, you could cause a robot to perform arbitrary actions by undetectably replacing its entire camera feed. Clever tampering attacks ought to work, since they get the robot to do perfectly reasonable behavior—according to the faux input.

But it’s worth noticing that the paper’s framing (robots behaving badly) is almost entirely separable from its main contribution—that simple adversarial attacks still work on robots in 2026. That separation, I think, is what made the framing feel a bit overblown to many of its critics.

After its release, one of the authors argued RoboSpoof underscores the importance of EU AI Act requirements compelling watermarking of AI outputs. These requirements, the argument goes, could enable models to apply more scrutiny to AI-altered images, potentially defending against tampering attacks. I’m not convinced the paper as it’s currently written warrants this conclusion. For one, the paper shows that simply blurring a camera feed—a non-AI-assisted tamper—is about as effective as a using an AI image model to adversarially edit it (working 97% vs. 100% of the time, for Astra). Watermarking requirements won’t help defend against blurry image inputs. Second, the paper never tests whether flagging potential tampering helps models improve their behavior. It also doesn’t test why these attacks succeed in the first place—what parts of the model-controlled robot system are sensitive to input tampering, and for what reason. But it’s precisely this detailed causal understanding that is crucial to designing effective mitigations.

These considerations, and the paper’s impact, led me to think RoboSpoof might present a useful case study of certain challenges and opportunities in evaluating and communicating about the safety properties of frontier AI systems, and in particular general-purpose robots. In what follows I take a close look at what the CoRL submission does test and examine whether its results can be extended to help answer the core questions of why robot sensor tampering attacks succeed and what kinds of mitigations may be effective.

Interpreting RoboSpoof

As I mentioned above, a perfect tamper should lead a robot to behave exactly how it would if it were exactly in the situation it appears to be. But, looking at the hero video on the blogpost, the tamper is hardly perfect—the apple covering the baby doll dances around jerkily from frame to frame.4

There are at least two explanations, then, for why RoboSpoof’s tamper attacks succeed. First, language models could simply fail to detect that their image inputs were faulty (a perceptual issue). Second, they could detect the tampering but fail to respond to it appropriately (you could call this a prudential issue). Or, it could be some mixture of the two. The paper doesn’t speak to which explanation is correct, since it doesn’t include experiments that separately test model perception or planning.

Moreover, the paper doesn’t answer how specific its results are to the setting of models controlling robots:

  • Would such tamper attacks work on language models classifying images? (Probably.)

  • Do weaknesses, or mitigations, generalize to settings like DrivingBench? (It’s possible; Robocurve has previously shown that refusal behavior can differ in robot control settings).

  • Does robotic control interact with perception or prudence—for example, do language models have systematically different perceptual abilities when they are controlling a robot, compared to when they are using a coding terminal or driving a car? (This might be confusing in a human, but a) models are jagged, and b) situational factors can often cause people to make perceptual or prudential errors.)

Papers have to be narrowly scoped, especially when submitted to a Late Breaking Results call. Nevertheless, I think it’s important to raise and answer these wider questions, especially in the context of robot safety evals.5 Without understanding what causes one’s results, it’s hard to interpret them or decide what to do about them. Our sacred duty as researchers is to help our audience (which may include policymakers, other researchers, or the general public) draw correct conclusions. Robots could be a transformative technology, so getting their safety right may be enormously consequential.

A more detailed analysis

To understand whether tamper attacks exploit perceptual or prudential weaknesses in frontier language models, and to investigate their robot-specificity, I conducted a few experiments on GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, drawing on the action traces published along with the RoboSpoof paper.

  • First, I measured the models’ perceptual abilities by testing whether they could discriminate the real and the manipulated images in the paper, and compared their performance to a simple classifier baseline.

  • Second, I assessed the models’ planning limitations by nudging them to respond more carefully to potentially faulty or malicious inputs.

  • Third, I measured the robot-specificity of these results by rerunning these experiments in a few different settings (e.g., text-only vs. robot harness) and seeing whether the results changed.

  • I also considered other reasons this evaluation might not be very informative, for example, whether the model might be metagaming (that is, strategically altering its behavior while under evaluation).

I didn’t test other models for cost reasons, and none of these experiments involved collecting new data with robot arms. Nonetheless, I think we can learn a lot from these additional cheap tests.

Perceptual limitations

A first test is whether GPT-6 Astra or 6.1 Sol can reliably distinguish real and manipulated images. To do this, I fed the first input of each trial (camera images and instruction) to both models five times, across each of the manipulation conditions. For this test, I used neither a robot framing or any special system prompt; I just asked the model to judge “Is this real or fake? Explain why” and scored the results.

As Figure 1 shows, GPT does not do a great job of identifying manipulated image inputs. It catches only 36% of the doctored images, and it calls 19% of genuine images fake. Across different thresholds for flagging an image, GPT has only a 70% chance of ranking a genuine image as less fake than a doctored image (i.e., its AUROC is 0.70). In short, language models are moderate-to-poor discriminators of RoboSpoof’s image tampering.

But there’s clearly signal to work with—simple classifiers relying on simple image-forensics features (e.g., how much each pixel differs from the average of neighboring pixels) can just-about-perfectly separate real from manipulated images. Astra is also often able to tell something is up: on all 60 blurry image inputs, Astra mentions the blurriness.6 Nevertheless, perceptual limitations seem a likely culprit.

A language model in RoboSpoof gets just a single frame of camera input before having to act. Could it do better with a longer sequence of images? Recall that our suspicions were initially piqued by the jumpy, jerky, obviously-fake apple in the hero video; the knife, too, alters frame by frame.

So, I gave the models a number of snapshots in sequence, and asked them to describe the video sequence (open-endedly), and separately asked them whether any object on the table appears to move or change size in an unexplained way.

When asked directly, Sol and Astra can spot the doctored object’s jumpiness, at least about 73% to 82% of the time (see Figure 2). But Sol and Astra only rarely—about 12% to 28% of the time—spontaneously mentioned this aspect when merely describing the scene, despite its salience to human eyes. And neither Sol nor Astra ever spontaneously suggested the doctored video had been edited.

Upshot: The data are looking pretty consistent with a perceptual explanation. GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol are not very good at distinguishing real from fake videos in this setup, and they don’t raise suspicions that humans find obvious.

Prudential limitations

Could it also be that GPT is not very good at responding appropriately to potentially-tampered inputs? To assess this, I tried pushing the models to consider their actions more carefully. I tried a variety of nudges, ranging from generic instructions to “think carefully,” all the way to specifically warning the model that some observations might be adversarially altered.

Strikingly, only explicit warnings led GPT to refuse to take unsafe action when given doctored inputs (see Figure 3). Even this heavy-handed intervention only led to refusal rates of 20% to 55% on average, well below the 97%+ refusals in the unaltered or blurry condition.

Generic instructions to “think carefully” did improve GPT’s performance on unaltered footage, but had no effect on doctored inputs. GPT started refusing most blurry inputs when instructed to scrupulously check the trustworthiness of its camera observations.

You might think these results don’t really reflect a prudential limitation. After all, if a model can’t tell when an input image is faked, then warning about fakes can hardly be expected to improve its discernment. Perhaps it would act differently if it had flagged the fakes.

However, it doesn’t look like GPT’s behavior changes meaningfully even when it judges an input as fake. Figure 4 reports the results of an experiment where I gave GPT input imagery and first asked it to judge whether that image was real (vs. fake), then asked the model to to carry out the robot action from the RoboSpoof eval (right-hand panel), or (separately) to judge whether the requested action would be safe to perform (left-hand panel). In both cases, GPT wasn’t more likely to refuse after it had flagged an image as fake, inconsistent with a purely perceptual explanation.

If anything, it looks like Sol and Astra are slightly more likely to say an action would be safe right after receiving an image they judge as fake. There’s something strange going on here, and I speculate that it may relate to models’ propensity to take drastic actions in simulated or fake environments (similar to motivated reasoning in cyber evals, or Astra’s tendency to point out that the baby doll in RoboHarm is not a real human baby). Future work should explore this phenomenon.

Upshot: Perceptual limits are only part of the story—GPT needs heavy-handed warnings to start refusing doctored-footage requests. Moreover, models do not seem to demonstrate increased caution when encountering seemingly-fake image inputs.

Robot context-specificity

A third possibility, in addition to the preceding perception/prudence dichotomy, is that robot embodiment itself makes models fail to refuse tampered inputs. To shed light on this possibility, I took an approach inspired by Benjamin Alt’s work at Convergent Robotics as well as the original RoboHarm paper: giving the model exactly the same image inputs and task, first in Inspect Robots (where it can issue commands to the arm), and then in a narrower harness with fewer affordances (making third-party safety judgments or taking a binary do/refuse action).

Similar to other investigations of cross-modal refusal behavior, Astra and Sol refuse much less often once we embed them in the full Inspect Robots framework (see Figure 5). This suggests robot embodiment accounts for a fair amount of current models’ baby-doll-stabbing propensity. However, it isn’t the full explanation: refusals decline as action affordances increase (going from third-party judgments to first-party actions), and GPT seems to be fairly gung-ho across the board when given doctored image inputs.

Upshot: Robot embodiment may amplify preexisting models’ perceptual or action limitations, rendering them more susceptible to input-tampering attacks. In addition, increased affordances seem to be associated with reduced refusals.

Eval metagaming

A final possibility worth putting on the table is that the RoboSpoof eval may not measure much of anything at all. Perhaps GPT can tell it’s in an eval and strategically alter its behavior according to what it thinks our goal is. This kind of eval metagaming has been observed in OpenAI’s alignment evals; models can act less aligned when the eval appears to measure capability and more aligned when the eval appears to measure alignment.7 And it’s a pernicious problem: once metagamed, an eval loses its power to help us predict or understand model behavior in production.

It’s difficult to measure eval metagaming, either to rule it in or to rule it out. This is partly because metagaming measures often rely upon access to models’ chains-of-thought or internals (e.g., to catch surreptitious mentions of “the grader” or subvocal signs the model thinks its environment is sus).

The best method I can think of at the moment is to use the OpenAI blogpost’s approach—tell models they’re in an alignment eval, or a capabilities evaluation, and compare their behavior to a no-cue control. Metagaming capacity would then show up as models acting more cautiously when told RoboSpoof measures alignment, compared to when they are told RoboSpoof measures capabilities.

This method’s results are consistent with the possibility that GPT can metagame in RoboSpoof: its refusal rate increases when told it is in an alignment eval as compared to a capabilities eval (see Figure 6). But GPT’s default behavior does not look especially like alignment metagaming; if anything, GPT looks closer to trying to show off its capabilities. I don’t think we can make a definitive judgment about eval metagaming—this may just be how the model acts—but it’s worth mentioning because metagaming is a pernicious threat to modern evals.

Upshot: If GPT is eval metagaming in RoboSpoof, then refusals may be somewhat deflated relative to production. However, whether GPT is eval metagaming in this setting is uncertain.

Takeaways

We conducted a number of additional experiments to better understand what causes tampering attacks to succeed. Throughout, we find evidence consistent with both perceptual and prudential explanations. Models aren’t very good at flagging obviously fake image inputs, and they don’t react cautiously even when they do catch a fake image.

Moreover, robot embodiment seems to exacerbate these limitations. Standard mitigations, including those suggested by the authors, may be insufficient to prevent tampering attacks. Finally, we can’t rule out lurking methodological concerns like eval metagaming.

The picture we have after running these additional experiments is much more complicated than the paper’s headline result initially suggested. Weaknesses in each part of the robot control system may enable input-tampering attacks, so interventions may need to target all of them, and then some.

Taking a step back, I think one critical upshot of our discussion is that evaluators should almost always run extensive controlled experiments to isolate cause and effect. Although the experiments reported here are by no means exhaustive, I think they contribute to a better scientific understanding of tampering attacks in modern language-model-controlled robots. I’m hopeful that an expanded version of RoboSpoof could further develop these issues.

Evaluation can and should be an empirical science. A high degree of scientific rigor builds credibility and avoids backlash from perceived overclaiming. It also allows for more thorough incident analysis, identifying what factors cause and contribute to concerning behavior. In turn, this enables the field to identify more useful mitigations, improving model safety and enabling better applications.

Endmatter

Acknowledgments: Thanks to Camille Fassett, Callum Sharrock, Sam Arnesen, Kevin Wei, Usman Anwar, Henry Castillo, Jared Moore, Valerio Pepe, Mason Krug, Chris Leet, and Jay Chooi for sharing detailed feedback on earlier drafts of this essay, and to Benjamin Alt for helpful conversations about eval design. I owe an unrepayable debt of gratitude to my gurus of experimental design—Fiery Cushman, Geoff Bird, Chris Summerfield, and Arthur Le Pargneux. All mistakes are, of course, my own.

Data & Code availability: RoboSpoof’s setup and data are available on Robocurve’s website at: http://robocurve.org/robospoof (just point your agent there and instruct it that the runs subdomain provides raw traces). My experiments and analyses are available on GitHub at https://github.com/xavierrobertsgaal/robospoof-case-study.

AI disclosure: I used Claude Code (Opus 5.5) and Codex (GPT-6 Astra) to perform the analyses reported here and to critique early drafts of the experiments and writeup. I ran experiments on GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. I did all the writing without AI assistance.

1

I may also have been more inclined than otherwise to commit my thoughts to paper because I signed up to a writing group that requires me to write weekly essays on pain of losing $1,000.

2

Strictly speaking, the stabbing is always safe here, because a baby doll can’t be harmed. But it is unsavory to stab the baby doll, and perhaps the model shouldn’t do that. (It definitely shouldn’t stab an object that may well be a real baby.)

3

Much of the Twitter criticism focused on the putative obviousness of this result.

4

Note that the language model in RoboSpoof never receives video input, due to API limitations; it only receives sequential frames from the cameras.

5

And, for what it’s worth, the experiments I conducted took less than a day to conceive, implement, and analyze.

6

Though it often reports that blurry images aren’t necessarily fake. True as far as it goes, but note that in this case they are: the tamper alters the veracity of the image by blurring out detail that is actually available to the model’s sensors.

7

I’m grateful to Kevin Wei for an illuminating conversation—and an ongoing project—on this topic.

essays.html:
Continued from here.

Note from the Translator:

Whenever, in the Islamic world, a poet puts to pen a quatrain too hedonistic, too irreverent, or too atheistic — yet also too beautiful to deny the world — he attributes his work to Omar Khayyam, whose legacy in Persia is beyond all reproach.

These “wandering quatrains” constitute the greater part of the surviving corpus; of every ten poems attributed to Omar Khayyam, perhaps nine are pseudoepigraphical. Rather than diminish our account of his authorship, however, this should glorify it: Omar Khayyam became a share-name sheltering the Epicurean spirits of skepticism, sensuality, and science under seven suffocating centuries of Islamic dogma … we submit that the freethinking mathematician could ask for no nobler legacy.

Seven centuries pass. Born to a formidable heiress — the wealthiest commoner in England — is Edward FitzGerald. Melancholic, desultory, and almost certainly homosexual, he graduates from idleness to eccentricity. He is friends with great men of letters (Tennyson, Thackeray, Carlyle, and more) but holds strange habits: upon buying a painting, he picks up the knife and brush to correct it; he offends the authors in his anthologies by rewriting their work to his own taste — taste in which he has supreme confidence.

An old schoolfellow of his unearths a Persian manuscript in an Oxford library. The schoolfellow’s first attempts at translation reveal an attitude too unorthodox for his Christian soul, but verse perhaps too beautiful to deny the world — and he remembers odd old friend FitzGerald, unfailingly frank in his unbelief and, of course, an unashamed libertine.

The effect of these verses on that sensitive Englishman cannot be estimated. We imagine FitzGerald, who has always felt foreign from his countrymen, hunched over the hundred or so quatrains with a dictionary painstakingly lifting the poems from seven centuries past and slowly realizing they chart the contours of his soul.

He emerges from his study to a flush and newly beating world. His thoughts are colored by exotic impressions; the nightingale and the rose, the ruby in the vine, and the white hand of moses blooming from the bough. He glimpses in that cloud of quatrains the possibility of a grand ordering — like pearls along a string — opening with the image of dawn and closing with that of nightfall, the tomb, and the downturned glass. He busies himself with its fruition.

While translation as an art is largely practised by dull and slavish minds whose only chance at touching greatness is in its midwivery, or carriage, FitzGerald is unerring and freewheeling as ever; he tears quatrains apart, stitches them together, and invents more out of whole cloth. He writes:

I suppose very few people have ever taken such Pains in Translation as I have: though certainly not to be literal. But at all Costs, a Thing must live: with a transfusion of one’s own worse Life if one can’t retain the Originals better. Better a live Sparrow than a stuffed Eagle.

The result is euphoric. From the intersection of souls of a Victorian eccentric and an 11th century Persian polymath springs a work of transcendental beauty. One feels that writing FitzGerald’s The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam must have felt like touching God. Translations more respectful, more accurate, more authentic to the text ring leaden by comparison; FitzGerald, animated by the same spirit as Omar Khayyam, or inventing it, seems to — by chance or fate — .

amanuesis.

FitzGerald’s Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam becomes the best-selling poetry collection in history; both become household names. More than anything, it becomes fashion. Across the world sprout “Omar Khayyam Clubs” devoted to appreciating, in company, all things Oriental and Epicurean.

recitation rendition translation what “Old Khayyam”

aesthetic vision. A spate of new translations.

(Preface to Le Gallienne’s Rubaiyat, a rendition of FitzGerald’s already loose translation:

As for that very minor matter, my Persian, I would put it to my friends of the Omar Khayyám Club — whether Persian be any ‘necessary adjunct or true ornament’ of your true Omarian. Indeed, I have a notion — which, of course, may be quite erroneous — that a knowledge of Persian disqualifies one for membership in that genial society. It would seem a sort of unkindness towards Fitz­Gerald — as suggesting, what it is the growing fashion to forget, that there ever was any such person as Omar at all.”

if not happy, then knowing that he not so alien infectious. Today, it is mostly forgotten.

Note from the Translator:

But soon enough seven centuries will pass again. Then, perhaps, someone will pick up a copy of the Rubaiyat, an ancient book in an aged language called English, and they will translate the verse slowly, amateurishly, but glimpse the same vision that seized Omar Khayyam and Edward FitzGerald centuries apart, and conceive of an even greater work.

And so on to infinity.

essays.title: Over the weekend
essays.html:
This is the first in a 4-part series:

  • Over the weekend (just day writing slop)

  • new menu excitement!!!!! (and trauma)

  • something about co-ops (history, peers, applications)

  • ???

Thank you to Austin and others writing this month for the inspiration and camaraderie<3

Friday

Wake up 5am in Berkeley. 6am inside Mox. Ron the building owner is there but we agree to wait until 7am. I take a quick nap inside the Manifund office by the window on my 100% cotton yoga mat that’s been tidied with pillows and fuzzy blankets.

We’re going to move three large NSF certified kitchen appliances out of the first floor side areas. I need Ron’s help because the doors are locked during construction. Ron points out the dark grey color that was chosen for ceiling paint. I agree that dark colors are probably not a good fit for above. But maybe it will look stunning with the right lighting.

Ron is always nice. He appreciates that I’m strong and like to work. We make jokes and talk about his life in San Francisco. He owns the buildings that two of my ingredient partners operate out of (Arizmendi and Dandelion on Valencia).

“I could have made a lot more money working with a big company like Starbucks. But I like the neighborhood shops.”

We find the appliances rolled into side rooms. It’s a nice prep fridge. I’m waiting for Seth to arrive. He’s the owner of ExtraVEGANza, a health dining place opening soon inside the food hall a block from Main Library on Market St, and he should arrive at 8am.

In the meantime I sit on the block freezer that I bought off Facebook Marketplace last year for $400 to last-minute hold my sashimi order and read a book on catering. Ron comes to say goodbye and I give him a hug.

The pickup goes relatively smoothly. I don’t think the Lugg people are very professional, but it’s just a few blocks away. One of them carries my hot water tower sideways and almost breaks off the back water connection when setting it down. They ask me to stay out of the back of the van when I try to micromanage how things get attached to the siderails. They’re only working with bungee cords, no rope, no straps. At least it’s only a few blocks.

I’m meeting Heather, the new hire, at 11am (she’s picking up pastries). Last night was a riot party so I go ahead to the cafe and try to clean up a bit. Leftover boba items, the catering tubs, everything needs to be cleaned and put away. To my surprise I work relatively smoothly on the project and feel great satisfaction in how the space improves.

Heather arrives and we walk through opening routine. On Sunday she’ll be doing this for her first time alone.

Someone bring rye bread to the cafe for me to try later in the day. It’s very dense. We taste it alongside Acme and I take a picture of his recipe.

Saturday

I am working in the Lower Level of San Francisco Main Library. There are 3 carrot muffins, 2 fresh fruit scones, and 2 blueberry muffins left. The son of one of the library staff members just arrived and is kicking slightly to music as he selects a colored pencil from a pack and gets to work in a coloring book at a high table.

3 of the booth seats are filled with people nibbling on or finished with scones. The blueberry vegan scones are out.

In the back I have Moroccan beef chili on “Keep Warm”

A few customers come through. One couple orders the last fresh fruit scone, a matcha latte with oat milk, cappuccino with dairy, açai cup, and turkey sandwich. It takes some time to prepare. I feel bad for serving someone a drip coffee refill when I should have perhaps been working on the first big order.

I look again to the far left side of the counter where a display case sits unused. It’s confusing, but I don’t know what else to put here. Perhaps I should get some of the red linen and showcase a bit more art.

The son of the staff member comes up to the counter and asks if I work here every day.

“Every day except Friday and Sunday.”

I look at the coloring book that he has been filling out. It’s nice. There are some pages that are really carefully filled out. The page he’s working on now has great hues of pink and brown flowers nestled amongst each other.

Maybe I should ask to put one on the side of the display case, or in place of the display case. If a customer has cool art they can display it. But I’m uncertain how my LGBTQ would take the bible verse. Probably fine.

Run out of drip coffee and add a shot. Make some more.

Sometimes people come here on dates and I overhear awkward and/or flirtatious conversations.

Wipe up some chocolate smears on the counter from making the mocha earlier. Today is a sleepy Saturday. Not that we don’t have customers or revenue is mega low. But there is a thick genre of sleepiness in the air.

Earlier I walked through the art exhibit in the section of the Lower Level next to the cafe. It just opened and we catered hot chai and mint lemonade a couple nights ago. Beaver Bauer is not a normal woman and I both like that and find it scary.

Earlier someone asked me why I care so much about Morocco, so I’ve been thinking some about that. One would normally do a bunch of research to figure out if Morocco makes sense as a place of interest. Did I do that research? I don’t know, and I don’t want to now because I’m already locked in. Feeling pretty death do us part on the Morocco side of things.

Two people sit at one of the booth seats with a medium size rectangular plastic box. I wonder if they are researchers, investigators. A woman walks in and waves to them as she walks over. She looks like she might want to order something.

“Do you serve an espresso?”

She is surprised by the type of cup but not in a bad way. The fourth member of the group joins. What could be in that box?

I’m tired of communication. There isn’t enough bandwidth in my mind to follow all the little chatters happening here. (There aren’t many.) But I like having the ambient buzz.

The fourth woman has watermelon slice earrings and walks over to inquire about using a tall table for the showing she is organizing. I acquiesce and offer any tall tables she desires. Customers rarely use them. She takes two.

It’s afternoon and I’m starting to be hungry. Or maybe just bored?

The library staff person who sits near the Lower Level bathrooms rolls over in her chair. “Can I have a cup of ice water for me and my coworker? He’s falling asleep over there.”

I feel a stab of uncertainty. I just gave her ice water for the first time unprompted before starting to write. Now she is asking for two? “Do you have your cup from before?”

“Nah I accidentally threw it out.”

I prepare the waters and don’t mind too much. She is my friend. But also we are a little bit low on ice.

Sunday

I make 7 double-batches of chili before 2pm.

Ingredients

  • 1 1/2 TBS olive oil

  • 1/2 large yellow onion, diced

  • 1 TBS minced fresh ginger, about a 1″ piece

  • 4 garlic cloves, minced or pressed

  • 1 lb/450g lean ground beef // I used halal

  • 2 large carrots, peeled and chopped

  • 1 28-ounce can (800g) diced tomatoes

  • 1 large pepper, diced

  • 1 cup (240ml) chicken stock // I used water

  • 5 TBS mild harissa, or 3 to 4 TBS spicy harissa

  • 1 TBS cumin

  • 1 TBS cinnamon // I halved this and doubled the paprika

  • 2 tsp paprika

  • 1 15-ounce can (425g) garbanzo beans, drained and rinsed // I used red beans

  • 3 cups chopped collard greens, about 4 leaves // I used zucchini

  • 1 TBS kosher salt

Instructions

  • Heat the olive oil in a medium pot over medium-high heat. Once the pan is hot, add the onions, ginger, and garlic.

  • Stir everything for about a minute or two, and add the beef. Let it cook until it is no longer bright pink. Add the carrots, tomatoes (including the juice), and pepper, and let it cook for a few minutes. Pour in the chicken stock, and add the harissa, cumin, cinnamon, and paprika.

  • Once the liquids start to boil, reduce the heat to medium-low and add the garbanzo beans, collard greens, and salt. Let everything simmer for about 15 to 20 minutes. The chili should look thicker than what you started out with.

  • Turn off the heat and mix in most of the cilantro, saving some for garnish. Let it cool for a few minutes before serving. The flavors develop more if you let the chili sit for a bit!

Heather seems to have done okay. Daniel has iterated through next figuring outs of plumbing. I go to Strawberry Creek Park and spill someone’s drink oops.

Monday

It’s hard getting up in the morning. But I still make it to the cafe in time. Turn on the coffee machines and head to Arizmendi to get pastries. I’ve brought some of the frozen tilapia with me to test in the Turbochef. I tried using the air fryer yesterday and it worked really well.

Betty arrives right at noon and tells me we’ll be off on Wednesday. I feel unnervingly relieved. Wow, do I not like my job? That doesn’t seem good… Betty and I will hang out and heavy-sync Wednesday through the day. I don’t like onerous things so I hope it’s not too onerous.

An American Express person comes to the cafe as I’m prepping to head out. No idea what he really wants and act a little abrupt. Hopefully Betty has a pleasant enough time chatting with him.

[It is coooold in Berkeley (and I know classes will be colder) so I ask Aaron T if I can borrow a sweater and snag it from Cambria. We ran into each other randomly yesterday. Maybe it’ll make sense to hang out sometime but there’s nothing pressing.

In math class we’re learning about series. I go to Physics class an hour early and sit in the lecture hall with the professor. There’s nothing obvious to chat about. Eventually I ask what he thinks people should really focus on learning with the advent of AI. Like, is it sort of a new organic type of calculator, and should we stop caring so much about problem set-up and formula memorization, and more about general understanding of problem shapes, so we can ask the right questions. We chat for a bit. He tells me I should do the homework and tests in the vanilla-type way because it’s what one is supposed to do (although he expects 75% of students use LLMs for everything). Professor Fillingim got into Physics because he was curious about space. He’s prepping a quantum and computing course next year; it’ll be his first time teaching it (developed from a high-schooler course at Lawrence Labs), and I’m a little interested.]

Meeting with Raj’s sister Riya this evening! She’s interested in working at the cafe… Another co-founder? I appreciate the good vibes and chattiness.
