essays.title: Polarizing ideas, the Antichrist, AI safety · Sefika Ozturk
essays.html:
P.S.: Intended to be heavily edited soon - still synthesizing my thoughts on this.

Peter Thiel is a very polarizing figure. When he was giving lectures in Rome, there was an article published about him, titled "Should we burn Peter Thiel?"

I was at Peter Thiel's Antichrist Lectures last month, and quickly saw that even just engaging with his ideas, let alone agreeing or supporting them, was very polarizing in a lot of the social circles I'm in.

Still, I got very nerdsniped by Thiel. Primarily, his epistemology and the way he deals with truth - for example, he hedges his bets by believing in multiple things at once, takes many contradicting actions knowingly, and that is very interesting to me.

This is also someone whose famous interview question is "What important truth do very few people agree with you on?" His whole worldview is built on the idea that the consensus is usually wrong. Someone who distrusts consensus that much has a good reason not to commit to any single truth either.

I also understand the arguments against him. Palantir is building mass surveillance technologies while Thiel preaches that a totalitarian world government will lead to the arrival of Antichrist. A mass surveillance system directly aids a totalitarian regime!

My friend who went to work for Palantir and I had a lot of discussions about whether Palantir is evil. He believes Palantir is morally neutral since if Palantir didn't do what they do, someone else would do it. I don't think this is a valid reason to justify a morally neutral stance, but I also have a difficult time believing in Palantir outright being an "evil" organization.

What makes an organization evil, versus an individual?

Reinhold Niebuhr wrote a book on this, Moral Man and Immoral Society. His argument was that groups are capable of things the individuals inside them would never do alone, because no single person feels responsible for the whole. Hannah Arendt called bureaucracy "the rule of Nobody," and she wrote that "the sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil." Deep stuff. I think this is causing a lot of problems, and I wonder how people can feel more responsibility for their individual actions.

To go back to an earlier point, what's the limit of colliding what a person does and what they think? How much can a person be compartmentalized? Can you admire a dictator's art?

Orwell said "One ought to be able to hold in one's head simultaneously the two facts that Dalí is a good draughtsman and a disgusting human being." I feel I can appreciate Dalí's art while recognizing his personal failures. But I do think this is risky. This may result in us being too forgiving to people who have genuinely hurt others a lot. But can we still listen to their ideas? Should we? And I guess this is especially different if they're running an extremely consequential company, as opposed to painting.

Can you hold two beliefs at once and hedge your bets? Or is this just stupid?

F. Scott Fitzgerald thought, "The test of a first-rate intelligence is the ability to hold two opposed ideas in mind at the same time and still retain the ability to function." Keats called it negative capability, being "capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason." Sort of relatedly, Robert Aumann proved that two rational people with the same priors can't agree to disagree, and I feel this is supposed to help me understand the situation better, but I can't fully say it does. Hume says "Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions." Perhaps Hume here is really clocking what's beneath my fascination with Thiel's ideology - I do think part of it is beyond his reasoning and how much sense his intellectual framework makes (like I said, there are a lot of contradictions), in that, I am also fascinated on an emotional level because I want to be more like him in some ways, and this is especially difficult to discuss with people because I can't justify it unless I accept that my justification will be emotionally primed.

And what about action - are we delaying actions by trying to understand the exact moral quality of them? Is it morally better or obligatory to be taking as many good actions as possible, rather than criticize people that we think are taking morally bad actions? Is the very act of taking actions more moral than not taking action? Thiel would say being able to competently take consequential actions is better than not taking an action, even if the action might not necessarily be the most morally good.

Max Weber has a philosophy that I can use as a framework here; he contrasts an ethic of conviction with an ethic of responsibility. The Bhagavad Gita also says "Action is better than inaction." (but act without attachment to the fruits of your action).

All of this brings me to safety in some convoluted way. I have recently been thinking more about safety, and I found myself being stuck and not taking actions for a long time. I started to think that perhaps just taking any action is better than taking no action. This is also quite risky, as AIS right now is almost like us trying to figure out how to make flying safe, while the plane is already in the air.

There's a saying that the rules of aviation were written in blood. I certainly don't want the rules of AI to be written in blood either. The plane keeps flying whether I touch the controls or not, and it becomes really easy to not touch the controls because I think I might cause things to go worse if I do.

Perhaps that's what Thiel's hedging is really for. It lets you act when you're uncertain. And so, I'm also personally starting to think, "which action is morally right?" isn't something to figure it out completely before starting to do stuff in the real world.

Recently I have been a lot more primed towards action, and things have been much better! I feel I am making a lot more progress than I was making for a long time. And I feel I owe that at least partly to Thiel, which is where this essay sort of comes from.
essays.excerpt: On Peter Thiel, hedging between beliefs, whether organizations can be evil, and why acting beats waiting in AI safety.

essays.title: Lightcone Commons: what I funded and why
essays.html:
I am an evaluator for Lightcone Commons (LC). LC is a platform for applicants to submit projects, for evaluators to rank them and for funders to choose the funding orders of several evaluators. It is not a foundation, in that it doesn’t have money that it spends how it chooses. And I do not have a permanent position working for Lightcone Commons. I get paid 2% of any money that a funder chooses to direct via my funding order. This pays for my time and also for any research that I pay others to do.

That said, what were my general and specific funding preferences?

Lightcone also has a beautiful page for looking through public information here.

General preferences:

  • I like AI policy that creates the ability to slow down AI if necessary, but doesn’t automatically push for immediate pauses. I like policy orgs which people I know in US politics respect. My current understanding is that it’s organisations that work with the administration, are respected by Republicans or that the AI companies listen to. Bipartisan organisations, I am told, are considered Dem. It’s not worth talking to random Senators, it should be those who tend to push/change legislation that gets passed. This is true even with a Dem majority. Policy will still need Trump’s non-veto and Republican votes.

  • I flag conflicts of interest but still recommend those orgs if they’re good. I don’t recommend myself or my company. Beyond that, I fund the work I think is best.

  • I’m less confident of AI safety work than the median evaluator. This is both because I tend to think AI safety work sometimes subsidises AI research and because I don’t know what good AI safety work looks like. I funded a few pieces of AI safety work that other evaluators said was valuable to them (notably Anima).

  • I like things that have incentive alignment, but might not get VC funding initially. Some version of Pangram that is trying to get on its feet. In practice there wasn’t much like this.

  • I rate epistemics/competent-small-operator projects more highly than the median evaluator. I want things which make trust and the information environment better and not worse. Overall, I wanted few organisations that I thought might damage trust, and some that would build it.

A quick caveat. When I talk about “what I recommended”, I am going to talk about dollars that moved according to my recommendations. About $5m was funded according to my recommendations (for which I was paid $100k). However because other people also recommended those things (and because some things were vetoed by funders) the final $ that moved according to my preferences was $11.2m down my list. So when I say ‘my dollars’ I mean that the dollars of recommendation that are allocated via me, which might be much smaller than the total amount a given organisation received.

What I recommended in the part that was funded, by type1.

  • By dollars (roughly): Policy 53%, epistemics 26%, Advocacy 17%, AI safety work 4%

  • In terms of conflicts of interest, about 30- 40% (~$2M of $5.2M) of my dollars went to people I am close with or have some clear conflict of interest. I flagged these to funders

Some organisations (mainly relating to policy) wished to remain private, so I have removed them. Specific rationales for redacted entries:

• As above I generally think AI is very important and reducing risk without necessarily leading to an immediate pause is a high priority. That’s true of several of the private entries, that seemed common sense risk reduction and were trusted by politics people I trust. If you are a wealthy person who can give to Republicans I have more recommendations.

• Then there are some lobbying orgs that seemed very good value for money that lobbied on a range of topics, run by people I trust.

Otherwise this is my funding order:

Again, not all this is ‘my’ ‘money’ since often these were partially filled up by others who agreed with my recommendations.

Rationales:

  • Sparrow infrastructure ( $1.24M in my order) - I like Lighthaven and for an (unaffiliated) attempt at ‘Lighthaven East’ core funding seems cheap. I talked to some political people and they seemed to think that having a space to bring AI safety people and political people together was a good idea. Rationality meetups ( $700k) - I like Skylar a lot and respect his judgement and ability to manage people. Rationality has been valuable in my life and if, I suspect, this whole AI thing goes on for a while longer than people expect I would like more people who come into contact with notions of having ideas that can be proven wrong, trying to actually get to the right answer, holding things lightly etc.

  • AI Impacts ( $700k) - I think Katja was deeply prescient in getting AI surveys going in the mid-2010s. And I, and I think many other people find her work illuminating and her a useful person to discuss AI with. Yes, she’s my ex, which I flagged, but if you look through the kinds of people she has worked alongside, I think she has been an underrated partner in a significant part of AI discourse over the last decade.

  • Manifold Markets ($100k) - I often use Manifold while working to sense check various forecasts and I like to support infrastructure. Unclear how that will continue going forward, with AI forecasting, but let’s see. I recommended this donation, but that everything over $150k go as an investment.

  • Technology Strategy Roleplay ($300k) - I tend to think that roleplay is a good way to get people into the mindset of making decisions. I wish politicians roleplayed a lot more to get a sense of some obviously bad decisions to avoid. This team is well respected.

  • 80,000 Hours, the video team specifically ( $1.16M) - I think that Chana and her team manage to talk honestly about AI risk, trying to acknowledge the caveats. On the Sam Altman video they took a subject I had looked into quite deeply and told me new things while not getting anything wrong I’d heard from elsewhere. I want more output from them.

  • Anima Labs ( $300k) - People I trust said that it helped them make sense of AI while not seeming like work that was subsidising the AI companies.

  • AI Wow ($50k) - I found Peter pretty inspirational when I saw his workflows. I would like more people speeding up orgs in the AI safety space and $50k seems like fine to get a person started (though in future I’d like him to be paid by organisations).

  • Sentinel research ($250k) - I like nuno’s horizon scanning work and often use it in my own. I would like to see more from him.

  • MIT AI Research RCT ($100k) - it seemed sensical. I cannot remember the full details.

  • Swift Centre ( $150k) - Sometimes there are people who want forecasts who are unable to pay for them. I would like the swift centre (who I work for very part time) to be able to offer these.

I want to note briefly how frank I am being here. Please disagree with me and I hope in future rounds I will feel my rationales are more robust, but this was the work and I did it. I am not going to pretend I always had better reasons than I say here (though sometimes I did, and can’t say) and sometimes I will just have more to say. If you think something was ludicrous or reasoning bad, please say so.

I think that’s the meat of the discussion, but here are some other comments:

How I differ from the other evaluators

  • Eyeballing, my funding was the second-most uncorrelated with the main picks.

  • There were a lot of big consensus picks I didn’t go for. If political, it was because they seemed to be talking to the wrong politicians (not those who would likely get votes through). If advocacy because I couldn’t trust them to make things better not worse, though I worry I was too cautious there. I am interested in finding good-not-bad advocacy orgs this time.

I was surprised that $5m was routed by me and have been told that it was probably because my list looked so different to others. I wasn’t sure how much money I was going to get from this, nor is this my full-time job. I think I would have spent more time on it if I had realised $5m was going to be allocated through me. I think had I done so perhaps I would have had even more go via me.

It is a bit strange to be someone who can so dramatically affect the lives of ones friends but also feels strongly motivated to ‘say’ true things. I expect this to only get stranger in future rounds. I enjoy people thinking I am worth arguing with and convincing, though it’s hard having to rate projects lowly that one knows.

Please apply!

If I can give one piece of advice, please apply if you have an effective project. I want good projects to recommend at the top of my order.

I intend to write another article about what a good project and application looks like, but in short, I am interested in projects that focus on:

  • Liability

  • Advocacy orgs I can trust

  • Effective lobbying in anywhere

  • Improve epistemics generally (watch this space)

  • Things that will improve governance in countries/states

And a good application looks like:

  • Why should I care

  • What is a simple description of why you should get a marginal dollar

  • Who knows of your project and respects it

But I’ll write these more carefully in another blog. Apply!

https://www.lightconecommons.com/apply

Also I am leading an epistemics fund, sponsored by Ought. You can read more about that here and I’d appreciate retweets when I write about it tomorrow morning:

https://epistemic.fund/

1

essays.title: Live disagreements with people around me
essays.html:
I’m pretty interested in conveying the costs of letting AI development proceed unchecked to the general public. In relation to this, I feel like I run into a lot of disagreements with people around me.

Misc very quickly written points on which my own impression has seemed very different from others in recent months:

1. It’s way, way, way more important that we stop dangerous AI soon than that we ensure that we don’t stop AI too much

I have the sense the sophisticated and worldly position here is to be very concerned about ‘over-regulation’ and about not doing exactly the right regulations. But it’s an obvious pragmatic fact that the stakes of overregulation are minuscule compared to the stakes of underregulating here. And the stakes of mis-regulation are very often going to be unintended slowing, which is in the same bucket.

2. If we stopped AI development, the risk of not starting up again for an extremely long time is low

This one just feels kind of crazy to me, like I may be missing something. In combination with the above point, it feels like if I met someone who was on fire, and they didn’t want me to put out the fire, in case they couldn’t figure out how to get warm again, ever. Like, forever is a long time, and if this thing is so great, you’re probably not going to forget about it! It’s like you think the current instantiation of yourself (or society) is so much more agentic than your future selves, that it’s worth huge costs to keep power in the current version’s hands.

3. Getting the public involved is not very dangerous

Some people seem to think of the public as like a kind of wild and crazy god one could awaken, with very high variance results. I think this doesn’t give them nearly enough credit. While I disagree with the public on quite a lot of points, I think disagreements are a lot more salient than agreements. We might disagree a lot on exactly how the FDA proceeds or who gets in how much trouble for doing what with which drugs. But we agree that broadly medical interventions and drugs are dangerous for people, and on wanting more safety around things that kill people, and I bet a lot of the details I don’t notice are better than nothing. And in a specific case where the default is insanely dangerous, bringing more people with power into the room, who are liable to stop things that are dangerous, and couldn’t really at this point make it much worse, seems pretty safe.

4. Public comms is not that rife with downside risks

There is a general sense that it is riskier to donate to groups hoping to talk to the public, because they can have large scale effects and make everyone look bad. So people donate their money to ‘safe bets’ such as e.g. technical safety. I think this is generally very miscalibrated. Talking to the public incompetently isn’t as far as I can tell much more likely to have reputational risks than doing other stuff incompetently, because everyone is in public. I don’t see many examples of this happening at a scale larger than the positive effects.

5. Pausing advanced AI soon greatly increases our chances of surviving

For one thing, I’d say the world’s degree of not giving a shit about safety in this case of advanced AI right now is extremely unique among issues, and if we wait for long enough for people to reckon with what’s happening at all, it is very unlikely to proceed in such wildly reckless way later on.

Also, I just expect us to make a lot of progress in understanding current AI models and organizing ourselves to not do crazy things if we have another decade to work out the kinks.

6. We don’t need a plan before we pause

People seem to think we do. I don’t know what’s up with that.

7. Raising the alarm is very important at the moment

I feel like people around me mostly agree that raising the alarm is good, but I’m surprised by the frequency of ambivalence about it. Partly this is to do with earlier points and related things, such as ‘what if people become too scared about AI and something bad happens’.

8. Working on marginally improving safety of models at the AI companies is not remotely competitive with raising the alarm at the moment

From my current vantage, it seems like people building AI do not mostly expect if AI left our control soon for it to be solidly aligned with a high probability. And they don’t seem to think we are close to that. So for a high chance of success, we really need to avoid that happening and we can make a lot of progress on that on the margin. Whereas if we know we are far from safety right now, adding marginal safety in a scenario where we are about to lose control seems pretty hopeless.

9. Doing advocacy doesn’t seem to have adverse effects on people doing it

I’ve heard a couple of times that people who do advocacy seem to go crazy. I don’t know of anything that seems like solid evidence of this, and weak or circumstantial evidence seems to only involve a handful of people.

And one where I feel like I haven’t heard so much disagreement lately:

10. It matters what the public think / political will is growable

I’ve been interested in talking to the public for a long time, and people have often disagreed with me. My sense is that they have often thought it seemed pointless. Because the public doesn’t have power. But I think the public does have power, and not just because they can ultimately vote. People care what other people think, including elites, and experts and people with power. Nobody is coming to their views in a vacuum. This matters.

essays.title: What did I do wrong?
essays.html:
Here is a pattern of male behaviour:

  • Bob goes up to Alice. She is friendly

  • They talk a little

  • Bob make some kind of attempted escalation (eg asking if she wants to talk at length)

  • Alice refuses

  • Bob says “please can you tell me what I did wrong”

Something has gone wrong here.

This is behaviour I have engaged in. I’ve seen men do it, particularly more autistic, rationalist, and ask-culture men. And I think it’s not working for us.

The story from Bob’s perspective:

  • Bob is a chill, straightforward guy. He likes and respects women and wants to flirt with or maybe date them. He understands that sometimes women get creeped out, and he doesn’t want to do that. He goes up to this woman, who he maybe knows a little, and he talks a little.

  • The woman, Alice, seems receptive and friendly, and so he decides that he might be onto something here. Perhaps she likes him.

  • He attempts to escalate, perhaps by asking for a longer conversation, asking for a date, or, in certain settings, asking if they can sit down together or touching her arm.

  • The woman, Alice, demurs.

  • Bob is confused. Is Alice upset? Has he done something wrong? Is there behaviour that he can correct in the future?

  • Now, he and Alice are at the same party or in the same community, or perhaps they’ve just met common members of the human species. He knows from his interactions with other men that it’s a reasonable thing to ask someone why it didn’t work and so he does:

  • “Oh, why did that not work?”

  • Alice refuses to answer, perhaps even looking slightly upset.

  • Whatever has happened, Bob thinks he has made an acceptable social move. Why is Alice being upset? Maybe she’s one of these sensitive women he’s heard about.

  • He flaps his mouth a little. Perhaps he asks again.

  • Alice refuses more firmly this time. Or expresses discomfort. Perhaps she leaves.

  • Bob leaves confused and a little concerned that Alice might say that he’s a creep.

As a coda to this story, Bob might just fear this happens. Rather than being able to escalate with Alice, he instead becomes nervous, self-deprecating, or hostile in expectation of this outcome.

This isn’t always male behaviour. I’ve seen more autistic/rationalist women do this too. What seems to them a completely fair way to ask for more information is not taken as such by a less autistic, more normy, less ask-culture woman.

The story from Alice’s perspective:

  • Most of the events Alice goes to are 80%, male. She doesn’t mind this. She likes men, but at times, they can get a little bit exhausting.

  • So Bob wanders over, and he’s friendly enough. Alice is polite. They don’t necessarily have loads of chemistry, but that’s okay.

  • Alice feels it coming seconds in advance. Bob has decided to shoot his shot, which, again, is fine depending on whether he’s the first or the fifth man to do that this evening.

  • She politely says no.

  • Now Bob begins to push for more information.

  • Internally, she rolls her eyes. It’s not that this is an unfair request, but she doesn’t know Bob. It’s actually quite difficult to get this kind of thing right, for it not to be cruel, for it to be actionable. Men often ask this as if it’s trivial, but what is she gonna say. Perhaps she didn’t find him attractive, perhaps she’s very busy, perhaps his entire body screams some message and he clearly isn’t aware because if her were he’d stop screaming it. To answer every guy would be tiring or socially risky both. He doesn’t have the social credit with her to justify that amount of effort, especially if he’s the third guy this evening.

  • But Bob doesn’t stop there. Now he’s spluttering or apologising or asking more questions.

  • This confirms the worst of her fears. He’s already transgressed the social boundary, and now he’s continuing to go forward.

  • She leaves, perhaps curtly, with a bad taste in her mouth. And maybe he’ll bring this up next time.

Again, as a coda, perhaps she just fears this response so she doesn’t respond negatively, perhaps she ends up in a tiresome text conversation or is generally wary of talking to men like Bob or going to events like this.

What are the differences between these stories.

The stories share the basic elements, and hopefully one can see how they are the same set of events to both participants.

But first of all, Bob doesn’t seem aware of how many men may go up to talk to Alice like this. He’s not really tracking whether this kind of interaction is one that she likes or dislikes.

He sees her friendliness as a connection between them, but given what we know, it isn’t clear how she should behave. If she is standoffish, people might think she’s a bitch. This amount of friendliness might, in fact, be a moderate “no signal.” She could probably be much more friendly: she could smile, laugh, and touch his arm. There are all sorts of things she could do. Would he notice if she isn’t? Would I?

It’s not unreasonable for him to try some kind of small escalation, but in his world, it’s quite cheap for her to say no. In hers, particularly if she’s doing it much more often than he is, it might be cheap in this instance but expensive overall. Therefore, she may have less energy to spend on an individual “no”.

He then compares his request for more information to how his male friends would respond in a situation where such a thing is very acceptable. If I upset a friend, it’s reasonable to ask, “Why did that upset you?” But to a woman at a party, I don’t really know her. One doesn’t have the same relationship with her as one has with one’s male friends, or even maybe one’s female friends, right?

Now, at the crux of the whole piece, both of them see different behaviours as socially unacceptable. He sees it as socially unacceptable that she doesn’t give him the time of day to explain how things went, and she sees it as socially unacceptable that he doesn’t take her no with grace.

And so we can get into this sad situation where both are hurt and less likely to expect this conversation to go well in the future. And perhaps Alice stops attending events like this.

How much computation am I asking of her.

has this concept of Ladybrain, the part of a woman that works out if she wants sex (as opposed to Horneebrain, the part that’s horny). But neither brain likes doing unnecessary thinking. Take a moment, does it get you in the mood to feel put upon? To feel bothered? Does it make you feel like someone is a good, safe partner?

In this story, Bob likes and wants good things for Alice, but it’s possible that she doesn’t experience it like that. And if he fails to track that, that is a negative sign in itself.

With my male friends I have a lot in the bank. The common inheritance of mankind allows us men to nod in the street and have an argument about anything. But with a random woman, especially at a male heavy event, my balance is lower. And so I may have to build rapport or if I make a move and it’s rejected, there may not be enough left to ask a questions about why.

Or am I not thinking?

In my case, I often just don’t want to know. I enter these conversations already flinching. I fear rejection and so I don’t want to see it in her eyes or in her stance. And I think that anxiety makes it hard to be a good conversational partner.

Recently a woman told me that she didn’t have time for the questions I was asking her. And in some way, it was just.. okay. I thanked her and didn’t say more. She was clearly overtaxed already. I think three years ago that could have destroyed me. And with that I was able to empathise with her. She was stressed. You hate to see it.

I’ve seen it in other men where they just radiate this slightly harassed sense that women are against them. They have a chip on their shoulder as large as an iceberg. And sometimes they are simultaneously working to improve or asking women what the issue is. But they are stuck in the wrong frame. What can a woman say at that point. This might be you. And if so I recommend asking your friends, being generally vulnerable and saying “I expect to be defensive about this”. Cos if it’s a big issue you probably don’t want to see it.

I think Slutcon was good for this, because it actually gave a space to ask such questions. To say “okay, but why didn’t that work”. But sometimes I meet a man and I know exactly what his problem is. And I have no idea how to tell him.

Take a breath, ask later

I think if I am free of fear, at the moment of rejection I can often take a breath and reorient. What is the right thing for this moment? And sometimes she might invite more and if she doesn’t, often I’ll leave it.

Ultimately, why do I have to know right now? Why does it have to be resolved in this conversation? If things didn’t work out, we can chat in future and I can learn why she isn’t interested, without pressing her here and now. Cynically, the reason to ask immediately is because I don’t intend to talk to her again and I want to get everything now.

I tend to think that the typical woman reads my motives better than I do. And looking back sometimes I probably have been showing a throwaway interest. And perhaps that has been visible.

Concrete suggestions

Some thoughts on this:

  • Consider how often she is hit on in a given evening. The more male the event the more times it will be

  • Consider that giving good feedback is hard and requires context. You just might not have it.

  • What is your actual level of connection? I think it’s one thing if she’s touching your arm, but another if she is smiling. She might just be being polite. Again it depends a lot on how often she deals with an interaction like this one.

  • Is a “no” actually okay? Can I smile and leave. Or am I terrified and is that scrunching everything else up. Do I so deeply not want to hear a no that I am not looking for the signs.

  • Am I able to bear watching her face and thinking about how she feels? If no, why not?

  • This applies non-romantically too. Sometimes I don’t want to see how a person feels, I want to get in and get out. Or I have the sense of wanting connection without actually doing what’s necessary for it.

I think this blog is a little judgier of men than I’d like (I’m doing Just Write so I wrote it quickly) so I am not saying it’s always the man’s responsibility, but this is a frame that’s been helpful for me. I would like people to get on better. And often “What did I do wrong” is not the best thing to ask directly after a “No”.
